# PREFACE

The following work is part of that project which the learned <term>Dr. Lardner</term> <note>original: "Dr. LARDNER"; Nathaniel Lardner (1684–1768) was an influential English theologian and author of "The Credibility of the Gospel History," a foundational work in the study of early Christian evidence.</note> had planned in order to give a full and comprehensive view of the *Credibility of the Gospel History*. The world has long possessed the majority of those treatises which were intended to complete it: including *The Testimonies to the Occasional Facts Mentioned in the New Testament*; *The Testimonies of Christian Writers to the Books of the New Testament*; and also *The Testimonies of Jews and Heathens to the Books and Principal Facts*. The remaining part, as the doctor himself informs us (a), was intended to contain *The Testimonies of Christian Writers to the Principal Facts of the New Testament* and also *The History of the <term>Heretics</term> of the Two First Centuries* <note>In the context of early church history, "heretics" refers to groups like the Gnostics or Marcionites whose beliefs diverged from what became the orthodox Christian canon.</note>.

This history is now presented to the public. It was primarily written by the doctor himself and remained with him for several (b) years. Some parts of it were completely prepared for the press, having received his final corrections.

***

(a) See Preface to *The Credibility, etc.* Part 2, Vol. 12, p. 5, 6.
(b) Ibid. p. 7. <note>original: "Ibid."; abbreviation of the Latin "ibidem," meaning "in the same place," referring to the previously cited book.</note>

# PREFACE.

The following work is part of the project which the learned Dr. Lardner had planned to provide a full and comprehensive view of the credibility of the Gospel history. For a long time, the public has possessed most of those treatises intended to complete it, including: *The Testimonies to the Occasional Facts Mentioned in the New Testament*; *The Testimonies of Christian Writers to the Books of the New Testament*; and also *The Testimonies of Jews and Heathens to the Books and Principal Facts.* As the doctor himself informs us (a), the remaining part was intended to contain *The Testimonies of Christian Writers to the Principal Facts of the New Testament* and also *The History of the Heretics of the First Two Centuries.*

<margin>(a) See the Preface to *The Credibility of the Gospel History*, Part 2, Volume 12, pages 5–6.</margin>

This history is now presented to the public. It was primarily written by the doctor himself and remained among his papers for several years (b). Some parts of it were completely prepared for publication, having received his final corrections.

<margin>(b) In the same place <note>original: "Ibid."</note>, page 7.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the editor's explanation of how he completed Dr. Nathaniel Lardner's unfinished manuscript on the history of early Christian heretics. # PREFACE.

In other parts, only a few hints were written (c), which I have endeavored to follow with faithfulness and precision. I have carefully studied and prioritized those passages from ancient authors that appeared—based on scattered observations or loose papers—the worthy author intended to include, using them to draft what was necessary to complete each article.

The additions in some of the chapters of the second book are very significant. Under the articles on Basilides <note>A Gnostic teacher in Alexandria in the early 2nd century</note> and Marcion <note>A prominent 2nd-century Christian leader whose teachings were later rejected as heretical; he proposed a sharp distinction between the God of the Old Testament and the God of the New</note>, these additions make up more than half the text. The chapter on Leucius <note>Supposed author of several apocryphal "Acts" of the Apostles</note> is almost entirely new, as Dr. Lardner had written only two pages. The chapter on the Elcesaites <note>A Jewish-Christian baptist sect that originated in the early 2nd century</note> is also new from the end of the third section onward.

I have published nothing concerning any heretic except where the learned writer had either drafted a portion or left some hints or references. At first, I intended to begin the second book with the history of Simon Magus and to add a short chapter concerning Menander, his student and successor. However, after reading several authors with that goal in mind, I found I still lacked many sources that I could not easily obtain. Without studying those, it seemed improper to publish anything on such an obscure and complex subject. Furthermore, upon further consideration, it seemed most advisable to give to the public—

<margin>(c) This was the case with a great part of the 8th and 9th sections of Book 1, with the whole 10th section, and with all the sections in that book after the 11th.</margin>

<page-num>v</page-num>

-> # PREFACE. <-

...to publish this work of Dr. Lardner’s on its own. For although there are many substantial additions of my own in it, they are all founded either on hints or references in the Doctor’s papers, or on passages from those very authors whom he himself so frequently quotes in this and other parts of his *Credibility* <note>original: "Credibility"; referring to Lardner's massive multi-volume work, *The Credibility of the Gospel History*</note>.

In 1769, Mr. Joseph Jennings—the nephew and executor of Dr. Lardner—entrusted me with the papers related to the present history. He asked me to review them and to request the assistance of my late, respected, and learned friend, the Reverend Samuel Merivale, to prepare them for publication <note>original: "the press"</note>. Mr. Merivale declined to take on any role beyond carefully examining the articles once they were organized and ready for the press. Accordingly, as soon as each article was finished, the manuscript was delivered to him, and I am pleased to say it met with his approval. All the chapters, except for the two regarding **Basilides** <note>A Gnostic teacher in Alexandria in the early 2nd century</note> and **Leucius** <note>The reputed author of several apocryphal "Acts" of the Apostles</note>, were completed before his death.

I am aware <note>original: "sensible"</note> of many imperfections in this publication which would have been avoided had the esteemed author lived to complete it himself. It is, however, hoped that even in its present form, it deserves the attention of the public.

As for the additions, I must ask the world to judge them with fairness <note>original: "candour"</note>. For I am very aware that they are
far

# HISTORY OF HERETICS, etc.

## BOOK THE FIRST.

### *General Observations concerning Heretics.*

#### SECTION I.

#### *The Meaning of the Word Heresy.*

<margin>Section I.</margin>
HERESY, in Greek, signifies (*a*) election or choice, and is used (*b*) for any opinion which a person chooses as best or most probable.

Heresy and heretic are often used by ancient writers as words of neutral <note>original: "indifferent"</note> meaning. And (*c*) the various ways of philosophizing were called sects or heresies. (*d*)

---

<columns>2</columns>

(*a*) "Furthermore, *heresy* in Greek is named from election [choice]: because, clearly, everyone chooses for themselves that discipline which they think to be better." <note>original Latin: "Αἵρεσις autem græcè ab electione dicitur: quod scilicet eam sibi unusquisque eligat disciplinam, quam putat esse meliorem."</note> *Jerome on Galatians, chapter 5, volume 4, part 1, page 302.* Compare Suicer under the word *Heresy*, and Le Clerc, *Ecclesiastical History*, Year 83, numbers 2 and 3.

(*b*) "Heresy is that which follows some reasoning according to appearances, or which seems to follow it." <note>original Greek: "Αἵρεσις η λογῳ τινι κατα το φαινομενον ακολουθσα, η δοκεσα ακολουθειν."</note> *Suidas. See also Diogenes Laertius, book 1, preface, sections 19, 20.*

(*c*) "And Hippobotus says... there are nine heresies and schools of the philosophers." <note>original Greek: "Ιπποβοτος δε .. εννεα φησιν αιρεσεις ειναι των φιλοσοφων και αγωγας."</note> *Suidas and Diogenes Laertius, in the same place.*

<column-break/>

"A certain Celsus completed the opinions of all the philosophers who founded various sects... in six large volumes." <note>original Latin: "Opiniones omnium philosophorum, qui sectas varias condiderunt . . . sex non parvis voluminibus quidam Celsus absolvit."</note> *Augustine, On Heresies, in the Preface.*

(*d*) "But Cato, being a perfect Stoic, both holds those views and is in that heresy [sect], etc." <note>original Latin: "Cato autem perfectus Stoicus, et ea sentit, et in ea est hæresi. &c."</note> *Cicero, Paradoxes of the Stoics, Introduction, Ed. Verbrugge, part 10, volume 15, page 3820.*

<summary>This page defines the word "heresy" based on its Greek etymology, meaning "choice" or "election," and explains that in antiquity, it was a neutral term used to describe various schools of philosophical thought.</summary>
<keywords>Heresy, Etymology, Greek philosophy, Sects, Jerome, Suidas, Diogenes Laertius, Augustine, Cicero</keywords>

--- Page 26 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of the term "heresy," providing specific biblical and historical examples of its usage. It transitions from a general definition to showing how the word was used neutrally to describe Jewish sects before it acquired a more negative meaning in later Christian writings.</meta>

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE WORD HERESY

<margin>Section I.</margin> Examples of the neutral <note>original: "innocent"</note> meaning of the word *heresy* occur in the New Testament. For instance, in Acts 5:17: *Then the High Priest rose up, and all those who were with him (which (d) is the sect of the Sadducees).* Also in chapter 15:5: *Then (e) there rose up certain members of the sect of the Pharisees who believed.* And in 26:5: *According to (f) the strictest sect of our religion, I lived as a Pharisee.*

The historian Josephus, in a similar way, speaks of the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes, calling them (g) sects or heresies without any sense of criticism. They were simply (h) the various schools of philosophy among the Jews. (i)

In several places in the New Testament Epistles, such as 1 Corinthians 11:19, Galatians 5:20, 2 Peter 2:1, and Titus 3:10, the words *heresy* and *heretic* are used in a negative sense. I also believe the word carries a sense of reproach in Acts 24:5, where *Tertullus* the orator, pleading before the governor *Felix*, says of Paul: *We have found this man to be a pestilent fellow... and (k) a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.* The meaning also does not appear entirely neutral in Acts 28:22: *As (l) concerning this sect, we know that it is everywhere spoken against.* Nor in chapter 24:14: *But this I confess to you, that (m) after the Way, which they call heresy, so I worship the God of my fathers, believing...*

---

<columns>2</columns>

(d) "The existing sect of the Sadducees." <note>original Greek: "Η ουσα αιρεσις των σαδδουκαιων."</note>
(e) "Certain of those from the sect of the Pharisees." <note>original Greek: "Τινες των απο της αιρεσεως των Φαρισαιων."</note>
(f) "According to the strictest sect of our religion." <note>original Greek: "Κατα την ακριβεστατην αιρεσιν της ημετερας θρησκειας."</note>
(g) "I began to conduct my life as a citizen following the sect of the Pharisees, which is very similar to the school called Stoic among the Greeks." *Josephus, Life, number 2.* <note>original Greek: "Ηρξαμην τε πολιτευεσθαι τη Φαρισαιων αιρεσει κατακολουθων, η παραπλησιος εστι τη παρ ελλησι σωικη λεγομενη."</note>
"...a family very distinguished in the sect of the Pharisees." *Ibid, number 38.* <note>original Greek: ". . γενος δε σφοδρα λαμπρω της των φαρισαιων αιρεσεως."</note>
"At this time there were three sects of the Jews... of which one was called Pharisees, another Sadducees, and the third Essenes." *Antiquities of the Jews, book 13, chapter 5, number 9.* <note>original Greek: "Κατα δε τον χρονον τουτον τρεις αιρεσεις των ιουδαιων ησαν . . ων η μεν Φαρισαιων ελεγετο, η δε σαδδουκαιων, η τριτη δε εσσηνων."</note>

<column-break/>

(h) "For there are three forms of philosophy pursued among the Jews: the first are called Pharisees, the second Sadducees, and the third, which is thought to practice a special holiness, are called Essenes." *The Jewish War, book 2, chapter 8, number 2.* <note>original Greek: "Τρια γαρ παρα ιουδαιοις ειδη φιλοσοφειται, και τη μεν αιρετισαι Φαρισαιοι, τη δε σαδδουκαιοι, τριτον δε, ο δη και δοκει σεμνοτητα ασκειν, εσσηνοι καλουνται."</note>
"There were three philosophies among the Jews." *Antiquities, book 18, chapter 1, number 2.* <note>original Greek: "Ιουδαιοις φιλοσοφιαι τρεις ησαν."</note>
(i) More can be seen regarding the Jewish sects at large in this work: Part I, Book I, chapter 4.
(k) "...and a leader of the sect of the Nazarenes." <note>original Greek: ". . πρωτοστατην τε της των ναζωραιων αιρεσεως."</note>
(l) "For concerning this sect, etc." <note>original Greek: "Περι μεν γαρ της αιρεσεως ταυτης, κ.λ."</note>
(m) "...according to the Way, which they call a sect." <note>original Greek: ". . κατα την οδον, ην λεγουσιν αιρεσιν."</note>

<summary>This page discusses the dual usage of the word "heresy" in the New Testament and historical texts, noting how it originally referred neutrally to a "sect" or "school of thought" (like the Pharisees) before taking on a derogatory meaning.</summary>
<keywords>heresy, sect, Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, Josephus, New Testament, Nazarenes, linguistics, etymology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of how the word "heresy" (meaning a sect or chosen way) was applied to the early Christian movement. It transitions from Paul's defense in the Book of Acts to the stricter, negative definitions of heresy formulated by early church fathers like Tertullian.</meta>

# HERETICS AND HERESY. SECTION I.

*...believing all things which are written in the Law and the (n) Prophets.* In this passage, the Apostle honestly admits before *Felix* that he was a Christian, or belonged to that "Way" which most of the Jewish people called heresy, or a sect—specifically, a new sect or heresy. At the same time, he suggests (though without being overly worried about avoiding the label) that the system and principles he professed and taught were so consistent with the Law and the Prophets that there was hardly any sufficient reason to call it heresy, or to consider its followers a new and distinct sect.

Among Christians, these words are very frequently used in a negative sense. The reason for this seems to lie in what Tertullian says regarding the original meaning of the word heresy—namely, *a chosen opinion and doctrine*: (o) that there should be no heresies among Christians, and that (p) a heretic loses the status of a Christian. This is because (p*) there is nothing left for them to invent <note>original: "invention"; here meaning the act of creating or choosing one's own religious doctrines rather than following tradition</note>. They ought all to adhere to the doctrine taught by, and received from, Christ and his Apostles.

---

<margin>
(n) The reader, if they wish, may see what was previously said about this text in the first part of this work: *Book 1, chapter 8, section 7, page 423 of the 3rd edition, or page 407 of the 1st edition.*
</margin>

<margin>
(o) "But in almost every letter, while stressing that we should flee from corrupted doctrines, he [Paul] condemns heresies, which produce these corrupted doctrines. Heresies are named from a Greek word meaning 'choice,' which someone uses either to establish or to adopt them. We, however, are not permitted to introduce anything based on our own will, nor to choose what someone else has introduced of their own will. We have the Lord’s Apostles as our authorities, who did not choose anything of their own will to introduce, but faithfully assigned the teaching received from Christ to the nations." <note>original: "Sed et in omni penè epistola de adulterinis doctrinis fugiendis inculcans, hæreses taxat, quarum opera sunt adulteræ doctrinæ: hæreses dictæ ac Græca voce ex interpretatione electionis, quâ quis sive ad instituendas, sive ad suscipiendas eas utitur. Nobis vero nihil ex nostro arbitrio inducere licet, sed nec eligere quod aliquis de arbitrio suo induxerit. Apostolos Domini habemus auctores, qui nec ipsi quicquam ex suo arbitrio, quod inducerent, elegerunt; sed acceptam a Christo disciplinam fideliter nationibus adsignaverunt. De Præscr. Hær. cap. 6. p. 232. B. p. 202. Ed. Fran."</note>

Therefore, he argues that (q) Marcion is clearly proven to be a heretic because he chose a faith different from what he had previously received in the catholic <note>original: "catholic"; here referring to the "universal" or mainstream church before the later denominational splits</note> church. And (r) Adam, he says, might even be called a heretic because he made a choice that went against the divine command.

Regarding the boldness of those men who introduced new opinions, he humorously remarks that (s) "invention" is a heretical privilege, and that (t) heretics, much like poets and painters, feel they have a certain license allowed to them.

It is also common for mainstream Christian writers to criticize those called heretics for taking names based on a specific man or leader. (u) Justin Martyr specifically does this. # HERETICS AND HERESY.

used as equivalent to an opinion, and particularly a wrong opinion or false doctrine; yet, that is not the most ancient sense of the word, but rather a *sect* or *party*. And indeed, it must be understood in this way in several passages cited at the beginning of this article.

I may just add that Chrysostom, Theodoret, and others, whose words are cited by Suicer <note>Johann Caspar Suicer (1619–1684), a Swiss theologian known for his dictionary of Greek ecclesiastical terms.</note> (z), do not understand "heresies" in 1 Corinthians 11:19 to mean wrong opinions, but rather contentions and divisions.

### SECTION II. *It is difficult to define what Heresy is, or who is a Heretic.*

<margin>SECTION II.</margin>
But though so much has been said to settle the meaning of the word, it is not easy to show by an exact definition what heresy is, or who counts as a heretic. This much is acknowledged by Augustine, who says that (a) every heresy is an error, but not every error is a heresy. In another place he says: It (b) seems to him that heresy occurs when a man, for the sake of

<column-break/>

<note>original (y): "...recta doctrina abhorrentes, et hæretici vocati, qui eas tuebantur: quamvis peculiarem nullam fectam, quæ feorfim a ceteris Chriftianis ageret, condere adgrederentur. Quo tamen fenfu in Apoftolorum fcriptis non occurrunt."</note>
Those shrinking from right doctrine were called heretics, as were those who maintained such views; although they did not attempt to found any peculiar sect that acted separately from other Christians. In this sense, however, the word does not occur in the writings of the Apostles. <note>Jean Le Clerc, *Ecclesiastical History*, Year 83, n. iii.</note>

<note>original (z): "Diximus vocem αἱρέσεως hac tertia fignificatione fumi, 1 Cor. xi. 19. Hic tamen diffimulandum non eft, veteres non intelligere doctrinam orthodoxiæ contrariam, fed contentiones, &c."</note>
We have said that the word *haireseos* <note>Greek for heresy/choice</note> is taken in this third meaning in 1 Corinthians 11:19. Here, however, it must be admitted that the ancient writers do not understand it as doctrine contrary to orthodoxy, but as contentions and divisions. <note>Suicer, Vol. *haeresis*, p. 119, 120.</note>

<note>original (a): "Non enim omnis error hærefis eft: quamvis omnis hærefis, quæ in vitio ponitur, nifi errore aliquo hærefis effe non poffit. Quid ergo faciat hæreticum, regulari quadam definitione comprehendi, ficut ego exiftimo, aut omnino non poteft, aut difficillime poteft."</note>
For not every error is a heresy; although every heresy, which is considered a fault, cannot be a heresy unless there is some error. Therefore, what makes a heretic can, in my opinion, either not be defined by a standard rule at all, or only with great difficulty. As will be explained in the course of this work. <note>Augustine, *On Heresies*, preface, volume 8.</note>

<note>original (b): "Nunc vero, cum inter hæc duo plurimum interfit: quandoquidem hæreticus eft, ut mea fert opinio, qui alicujus temporalis commodi, et maxime gloriæ principatufque fui gratia, falfas ac novas opiniones vel gignit, vel fequitur."</note>
But now, since there is a great difference between these two: for a heretic is, in my opinion, one who—for the sake of some temporary advantage, and especially for his own glory and status—either creates or follows false and new opinions. But the person who believes such men is someone misled by a certain appearance of truth and piety. <note>Augustine, *On the Usefulness of Believing*, chapter 1.</note>

# OBSERVATIONS ON

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Sect. 8.</margin> These slanders <note>original: "calumnies"</note> seem to have begun with Christianity itself. There is evidence that they appeared very early. Tacitus, speaking of the Christians in the time of Nero, says they (*d*) were generally hated for their wickedness; that is, they had a bad reputation among the common people. And, as Mr. Turner observes (*e*), Melito of Sardis (*f*)—an apologist for the Christian religion around the year 170—traces the origins of these lying accusations back to the reigns of Nero and Domitian. I will quote a long passage by Mr. Turner on this subject at the bottom of the page (*g*). Certainly, these accusations existed and were widespread before Justin became a Christian. For he assures us (*h*) that during his time as a pagan, he thought it impossible for Christians to face death with such steadfastness and resolve as they did if they were actually cannibals <note>original: "men-eaters"</note> and addicted to lewdness.

Repressaque in præsens exitiabilis superstitio rursus erumpebat." Tacitus, *Annals*, Book 15, Chapter 44.</note>

(*e*) *Ibid, page 4.*

(*g*) I cannot agree that the lewd behavior of Carpocrates, Epiphanes, and their followers gave the first occasion for accusing the Christians of promiscuous and incestuous lust. For it is generally agreed that Carpocrates began his heresy in Hadrian's <note>original: "Adrian's"</note> reign, about the same time that Justin became a convert to Christianity, 130 AD. If Carpocrates had been the first to cause these insults to be cast at Christians, how could Justin be ignorant of it, since he lived at the same time? That *Apology* <note>A formal defense of the Christian faith written to the Roman Emperor.</note> was written, as some believe, in the year 145, or about 140 at the earliest. The Valentinians <note>Followers of Valentinus, a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who developed a complex system of divine "aeons."</note>, Carpocratians, and other heretics existed before that time. Justin had already written against all heretics in general; yet he freely admits he did not know them to be guilty of the crimes so frequently discussed at that time.

V. The most ancient Christian Apologists <note>Early Christian writers who defended the faith against legal and philosophical attacks.</note> generally attribute the slanders <note>original: "calumnies"</note> then cast upon Christians to other causes, and not to the wickedness of any among them called heretics. Justin Martyr, as was previously observed ($q$), says that their accusers themselves scarcely believed the charges brought against them. He also notes ($r$) that where these charges had been believed to some degree, it arose from the wickedness of the heathens themselves, which made them prone to believe such things of others as they practiced themselves. Tatian ($s$) and Theophilus of Antioch ($t$) speak of these slanders without suggesting that heretics provided the occasion for them. Athenagoras plainly says ($u$) that the general wickedness of the heathen people was the ground for charging Christians with such base practices.

# Section 8. OBSERVATIONS ON HERETICS.

VI. It appears from <term>Tertullian</term> (f) that in his time, it was not known that any among the <term>Christians</term> were guilty of the crimes attributed to them by their adversaries. The only basis for these charges, according to him, was common rumor and uncertain reports (g), without any proof. If such things had been done by anyone assuming the name of Christians, and it was known they had done them, his defense would have been different. He would have argued that although there were indeed instances of such abominable practices among <term>heretics</term>, there was no such instance among genuine <term>Christians</term>. 

Since, therefore, he absolutely denies the charge without making any such distinction, it is plain he knew of no heretics who were guilty of such abominations. <term>Theophilus of Antioch</term> likewise says (h) that these reproaches had no support other than common rumor. Nor was it known to the <term>Martyrs of Jesus</term> (i) that such things were ever practiced.

<margin>Original Latin and Greek source notes:</margin>

<note>original Latin: "ejusmodi, ea non dubitamus falsa esse. Heraldus ad Minutium..." — "of such a kind, we do not doubt those things are false." Desiderius Heraldus in his notes on Minucius Felix, chapter 9, page 86. Leiden, 1672.</note>

<margin>(f)</margin> We are called the most wicked of men regarding the ritual of infanticide <note>original: "Sacramento infanticidii"; a reference to the slander that Christians murdered and ate infants during the Eucharist</note> and the food derived from it, and for incest following our banquets. It is said that dogs—the overturners of lights and the pimps of darkness—bring on the shamelessness of impious lusts. We are always called such, yet you do not care to root out the truth of what we have been called for so long. <term>Apology, chapter 7, page 8</term>. 

It is well, however, that time reveals all things, even according to your own proverbs and sayings, by the arrangement of nature which has ordered it so that nothing remains hidden for long, not even what rumor does not conceal. Justly, therefore, rumor alone has so long been the witness of the crimes of Christians. You bring forward this witness against us, which, because it once boasted and has strengthened into an opinion over such a long time, has until now been unable to prove it. <term>Ibid. page 9, Beginning</term>.

<column-break/>

<margin>(g)</margin> Therefore they believe things about us that are not proven, and they do not want them to be investigated lest they be proven not to be true. <term>Ibid. chapter 2, page 4. B</term>. 

What other trouble does a Christian suffer except that of his own sect? Which no one has proven to be incestuous or cruel for so long a time. <term>To Scapula, chapter 4, page 87, End</term>.

VII. Another argument against the truth of these accounts is that they are simply unbelievable. When <term>Justin Martyr</term> <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD) was an early Christian apologist who wrote to the Roman Emperor to defend Christian morality.</note> asked Trypho the Jew whether (*k*) he believed the common reports concerning the Christians, Trypho readily answered that they were incredible, for human nature was not capable of such things. This is also shown at length by (*l*) <term>Minucius Felix</term> <note>A Roman lawyer and Christian apologist whose dialogue, the *Octavius*, defends Christianity against pagan slurs.</note> and (*m*) <term>Tertullian</term>. They sometimes appealed to the pagan public, asking if they themselves were capable of doing the same things they charged against the Christians, under those same circumstances. At other times, they ridiculed the gullibility of those who believed such things of others when they themselves were unable to do the like. In this last argument, Tertullian appears to triumph beyond all control.

---

<columns>2</columns>

(*k*) <note>original Greek: Τουτο δε εστιν ο λεγω, μη και υμεις πεπιστευκατε περι ημων οτι δη εσθιομεν ανθρωπους, και μετα την ειλαπινην αποσβεννυντες τους λυχνους, αθεσμοις μιξεσιν εγκυλιομεθα . . . . Περι ων δε οι πολλοι λεγουσιν, (εφη ο Τρυφων) ου πιστευσαι αξιον· πορρω γαρ κεχωρηκε της ανθρωπινης φυσεως. — "And this is what I mean: do you also believe regarding us that we eat humans, and that after our banquet, having extinguished the lamps, we wallow in lawless lusts? ... Regarding those things which the masses say, Trypho replied: they are not worthy of belief, for they are far removed from human nature." *Dialogue with Trypho*, page 227, section B.</note>

(*l*) <note>original Latin: Illum jam velim convenire, qui initiari nos dicit, aut credit de cæde infantis et sanguine. Nemo hoc potest credere, nisi qui possit audere. — "I would now like to meet the man who says or believes that we are initiated by the slaughter and blood of an infant. No one can believe this, except one who is capable of daring to do it." *Minucius Felix*, Chapter 30, pages 288–289.</note>

Look, we offer eternal life as the reward for these crimes. They promise it. Do you believe it for the moment? For I ask this: even if you believed it, would you consider it worth reaching such a life with such a conscience? Come, sink the blade into the infant, who is no one's enemy, guilty of nothing, everyone's son. Or if that is someone else's job, you just stand by the dying human... catch the fresh blood; soak your bread in it, eat freely. Meanwhile, as you recline at the table, count the places where your mother and sister are. Note them carefully so that when the 'canine' darkness falls [when the dogs knock over the lamps] you do not make a mistake... Having been initiated and sealed by such things, you live forever. You who believe such things of a man are also capable of doing them. You are a man yourself, just like a Christian. If you cannot do it, you should not believe it. For a Christian is a human being, just like you." *Tertullian's Apology*, Chapter 8.</note>

<summary>This page argues that the horrific accusations against early Christians—such as cannibalism and incest—were rejected by contemporary writers like Trypho the Jew and Tertullian as being physically and psychologically impossible for human beings to commit. These authors challenged their accusers to consider if they themselves would be capable of such acts, concluding that if the accusers could not do them, they should not believe others did either.</summary>

<page-num>34</page-num>

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>SECTION 8.</margin>control. With a peculiar energy of expression, he challenges any one of the pagans to come into Christian assemblies and try whether he could perform such an action himself, or even bear to be present while it was carried out by others. He enters minutely into the particular parts of the atrocious charge and proves, by a direct appeal to the human heart, that no creature constituted as we are can possibly be guilty of such abominations. On the subject of infanticide <term>infanticide</term> <note>The crime of killing an infant.</note>, he shows (*n*) the utter incredibility of a charge that is directly inconsistent with some of the distinguishing beliefs of the Christians of those days. For instance, they would not make use of blood mixed with any food at their feasts; they even abstained from animals that were strangled or that died of natural causes, lest they should be contaminated.

The same arguments will serve for the heretics, for they are charged by later writers with the (*o*) same things that were before (*p*) attributed to the early Christians (*q*).

<column-break/>

<margin>(*n*) <note>original: "Erubescant error vester Christianis, qui ne animalium quidem sanguinem in epulis esculentis habemus, qui propterea quoque suffocatis et morticinis abstinemus, ne quo modo sanguine contaminemur, vel intra viscera sepulto . . . . . Porro quale est, ut quos sanguinem pecoris horrere confiditis, humano inhiare credatis. Ib. C. ix."</note> Your error should blush before the Christians, who do not even include the blood of animals in our edible feasts. For this reason, we also abstain from things strangled or that died of themselves, so that we might not be contaminated by blood in any way, even when it is hidden within the internal organs. . . . Furthermore, how can it be that you believe those whom you know to shudder at the blood of cattle would pant for human blood? *Tertullian, Apology, Chapter 9.*</margin>

<margin>(*o*) <note>original: "Εαν δε εγκυμονηση η γυνη, . . . . κατασπαντες το εμβρυον εν ολμω τινι κοπτουσιν υπερω, και ανακαμιξαντες μελι και πεπερι και αλλα τινα αρωματα, και μυρα προς το μη ναυτιαν αυτους . . . μεταλαμβανουσιν εκαστος τω δακτυλω απο του κατακοπεντος παιδιου, και ουτως την ανθρωποβοριαν απεργασαμενοι ευχονται λοιπον τω Θεω . . . και δηθεν τουτο το τελειον πασχα ηγηνται. I give the English of this in Mr. Turner's words. "The Gnostics," says <term>Epiphanius</term> <note>A 4th-century bishop known for his "Panarion," a massive work attacking various heresies.</note>, "by some violent method or other, used to draw a child out of its mother's womb and beat it to pieces in a mortar; and lest this odd sort of food should be nauseous to a squeamish stomach, they mixed it with honey and pepper and other spices. When this was done, they all tasted of it. And this they called a 'perfect Passover.' Upon this monstrous and incredible story I observe, etc. etc." *Calumnies upon the Primitive Christians, p. 54, 55.*

Similar things were also said of the <term>Montanists</term> <note>An early Christian movement (2nd century) that emphasized prophecy and rigorous fasting; they were often viewed as heretical by the mainstream church.</note>, as we shall see hereafter.

<summary>This page argues that the horrific accusations of cannibalism and infanticide leveled against early Christians and heretics were logically impossible given their strict dietary laws against consuming any blood. It highlights how these same "monstrous" slanders were recycled by later writers to attack groups like the Gnostics and Montanists.</summary>

### SECTION IX. The ancient Heretics believed in the unity of God.

<margin>SECTION 9.</margin>The ancient heretics believed in only one God. This is stated by several learned and judicious modern scholars who have made a diligent search into the opinions of these men, and are far from sparing them or showing them favor. Massuet <note>René Massuet (1666–1716), a Benedictine scholar known for his edition of the works of Irenaeus.</note> in particular observes that (u) Irenaeus <note>Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD) was a Bishop and early Christian theologian who wrote "Against Heresies" to refute Gnosticism.</note> in his long and detailed arguments

<margin>
(u) Valentinus was so far from denying the unity of God that, according to Irenaeus’s testimony, he openly professed it. For Irenaeus says in Book 1, Chapter 22, Section 1: *“Almost all the heresies that exist say indeed that there is one God, but they change him through their opinions.”* <note>original: "ſere quotquot ſunt hæreses deum quidem unum dicunt, ſed per ſententiam immutant."</note> He does not say they multiply him, but that they change him... by establishing someone other than the supreme Father of all to be the creator of the world... And Irenaeus explains this very point in Book 4, Chapter 33, Section 3: *“He will judge all those who follow Valentinus, because they confess with their tongues one God the Father, and that all things come from him; but they say that he who made all things is the result of a falling away or a flaw.”* <note>original: "lingua quidem conſitentur unum Deum Patrem... ipſum autem qui fecerit omnia defectionis ſive labis fructum eſse dicit"</note>
</margin>

<margin>
Therefore, Valentinus openly professed one God. And it is certainly unlikely that either the earlier Gnostics... or Valentinus, and all those who had embraced the Christian religion (having rejected the superstition of the Gentiles and confessed to having at least some faith in the gospel), would want to revive from the grave the profane and detestable polytheism <term>polytheism</term> <note>The worship of or belief in multiple deities.</note> that all Christians hated, or would want to profess an immense number of divine persons. Nor would Irenaeus have allowed such a great wickedness to go unpunished, he who was set on exposing all the outrages of men and the monsters of error...

They supposed the creator of the world—that is, of this visible material world (*x*)—not to be God, but an angel. They may sometimes call him God. "Your three <term>principles</term> <note>original: "archai" (Greek); refers to the fundamental sources or origins of the universe</note>," (*z*) says the orthodox disputant, "are they equal in power?" "Far be it," says the Marcionite, "they are not equal." "Which then is the most excellent?" replies the orthodox. "It is the principle of good that is the most powerful," answers the Marcionite. "The others are subject to him," says the orthodox. The heretic acknowledges they are so. The orthodox still argues: "If so, do the inferior principles not act according to the will of the more excellent one?" The Marcionite answers, "When they do evil, they do not act according to his will. Nevertheless, he is infinitely more powerful than they. So when Christ came, he vanquished the devil and abolished the religion of the Creator." It is therefore very wrong to accuse the Marcionites <note>Followers of Marcion, a 2nd-century teacher who distinguished between the God of the Old Testament (the Creator) and the God of the New Testament (the Father)</note> of holding two or three supreme Gods. All that can be reasonably said is that they did not think the title of "God" to be an incommunicable title <note>i.e., a name belonging exclusively to one being</note>, nor that it expressed the nature and perfections of the Supreme Being. For this reason, they did not scruple to give it to the Creator. As for the devil, in calling him a "God," they said they only followed the style of scripture, where (*a*) he is called "the God of this world." For they knew very well that (*b*) he was no more than an angel, as Tertullian expressly says.

Dr. Cudworth <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), a prominent English philosopher and theologian</note> seems to have viewed this matter in a light somewhat similar to the previous representation. For having endeavored to prove that the heathen philosophers did not believe all their gods to be so many *uncreated, self-existent deities*, he proceeds in the following manner: *(m)* "The next significant appearance of a multitude of *self-existent deities* seems to be in the Valentinian *thirty gods* and *Æons* <note>In Gnostic theology, Æons are divine beings or emanations that represent various attributes of God</note>, which have been taken by some for such; but it is certain that these were all of them, except for one, 'generated' [created]; they being derived by that imaginative inventor of them from one self-originated deity called *Bythus* <note>meaning "Depth" or "Profundity"</note>. ### SECTION 10. *They made great use of the Scriptures.*

<margin>SECTION 10.</margin>
The ancient heretics held the Scriptures in high regard. It will likely fall to me later to show which parts of the sacred writings each of them used. For now, I only observe in general that they endeavored to support their specific opinions (p) by appealing to these inspired books. To me it seems very certain that (q) everyone who builds their faith upon revelation must rely on either Scripture or tradition—that is, either written or oral tradition—assuming they live after the first announcement of the revelation they claim to accept. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> therefore rightly (r) blames those who relied too much on their own reasoning when deciding matters of pure revelation.

Irenaeus <note>Bishop of Lugdunum (modern Lyon) in the 2nd century, known for his major work *Against Heresies*</note> includes the following passage in his major work against heresies: "Such (s) is the certain truth of our Gospels that the—"

From where else could they speak regarding matters of faith, if not from the literature of faith? <note>original: 'Sed ipsi et de scripturis agunt et de scripturis suadent. Aliunde scilicet loqui possent de rebus fidei, nisi ex literis fidei.'</note>

Ch. 39. p. 246. p. 212. Fr.*

<meta>This page continues the argument from Irenaeus that even early heretical groups acknowledged the authority of the four Gospels by attempting to use them to justify their own beliefs.</meta>

SEC. 10. ...heretics <note>original: "hereticks"</note> themselves bear testimony to them, as every one of them tries to prove their specific doctrines from those very books.

But the Ebionites <note>A Jewish Christian sect that emphasized following Jewish law and viewed Jesus as a human prophet</note> can be refuted using the Gospel of Matthew, which is the only one they accept. Marcion <note>A 2nd-century teacher who rejected the God of the Old Testament and the Jewish roots of Christianity</note> uses only the Gospel of Luke, and even that in a censored <note>original: "mutilated"</note> form. Nevertheless, based on the parts he keeps, it can be shown that he speaks sacrilegiously against the one true God. Those who separate Jesus from Christ—claiming that Christ remained incapable of suffering <note>original: "impassible"</note> while Jesus suffered—prefer the Gospel of Mark. However, if they were to read it with a sincere love for the truth, they could be convinced of their error by that very text. The Valentinians <note>Followers of the Gnostic teacher Valentinus, known for complex mythologies about the divine realm</note> accept the Gospel of John in its entirety to support their theories about pairs of <term>aeons</term> <note>In Gnostic thought, these were divine beings or emanations that came from the ultimate God</note>; yet they can be refuted by that same Gospel, as I have shown in the first book of this work. Therefore, since people with such different opinions agree with us in using these writings as evidence, our proof for the authority of these Gospels is certain and beyond doubt.

<margin>
...cutting down the Gospel according to Luke; based on the parts which are still preserved by him, he is shown to be a blasphemer against the only existing God. Those, however, who separate Jesus from Christ, and say that Christ remained incapable of suffering while Jesus suffered—preferring the Gospel according to Mark—can be corrected if they read it with a love of truth. But those who follow Valentinus, making the fullest use of that which is according to John, will be exposed by it as saying nothing correctly regarding their pairings, just as we have shown in the first book. Since, therefore, those who contradict us provide testimony for us and use these [Gospels], our demonstration regarding them is firm and true. *Irenaeus, Book 3, Chapter 11, Section 7.* <note>original Latin: "cundum Lucam circumcidens... firma et vera est nostra de illis ostensio."</note>
</margin>

Many other passages could be cited from various writers to show that the ancient heretics tried to support their views with the words of the Scriptures—whether from the Old Testament, the New Testament, or both. Even those who rejected the Old Testament insisted on the authority of the New.

He observes that they endeavored to impose upon people by alleging texts of Scripture for their particular tenets, though they quoted them (*u*) in a very unfair and mutilated manner. They appealed to them because they were the only writings whose authority was universally allowed. Even those of them who would not believe the giver of the Law and the inspirer of the prophets to be the supreme Lord of the universe, or the father of Jesus Christ, still acknowledged the divine authority of some parts of the New Testament and received its declarations as authentic and decisive. # OBSERVATIONS ON

<margin>Section 10.</margin> the Scriptures of the New Testament. Epiphanius has provided an extensive and detailed account of the way in which Marcion <note>Marcion of Sinope (c. 85–160 AD) was a prominent early Christian heretic who rejected the Old Testament and edited the New Testament to fit his own dualistic theology.</note> mutilated the Scriptures. Yet, Epiphanius says (*a*), Marcion's heresies can be disproved even from what he chose to keep of the Gospel and the Epistles. Indeed, of all the heretics, Marcion seems to have taken the greatest liberty in altering and cutting down the writings of the New Testament. Nonetheless, after a lengthy argument against him, Tertullian clearly shows (*b*) that the principal and most important doctrines of the Gospel remained just as certain as before, even in Marcion's mutilated copy. The same writer says elsewhere (*c*) that it was the usual custom of heretics to insist upon one or two specific texts without regarding the general meaning <note>original: "tenour"</note> of the Scriptures. Augustine often blames heretics (*d*) for perverting Scripture to support their errors. He explains that their fault lay in this: not that they rejected or despised the Scriptures, but that they misunderstood them and applied incorrect interpretations to them (*e*).

He says all heretics attempt to defend their false opinions (*f*) by using the authority of the divine Scriptures. Nevertheless, the

(*b*) <note>original Latin: Misereor tui Marcion... "I feel sorry for you, Marcion; you have worked in vain. For the Christ Jesus in your Gospel belongs to me." (Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book 4, chapter 43).</note>

(*c*) <note>original Latin: His tribus capitulis... (*d*) <note>original Latin: Omnes enim hæretici... "For all heretics who accept their authority seem to follow the Scriptures themselves, while they are actually following their own errors. Thus, they are heretics not because they despise the Scriptures, but because they do not understand them." (Augustine, *Letter 120*).

# HERETICS AND HERESY.

<margin>SEC. 10.</margin>
The Scriptures ought not to be considered the occasion of these errors. Augustine also speaks of some (*g*), who, though they rejected the Old Testament, attempted to prove their opinions from the Gospels and Epistles.

In like manner, St. Jerome says (*h*) that if heretics reject the Old Testament, they may be refuted from the New, which they do accept. The same author sometimes complains (*i*) that heretics strive to support their doctrines by quoting passages of Scripture that have no connection to one another. He says (*k*) that neither heretics, nor the less-educated among the faithful, understand the Scripture in a manner becoming its majesty. The same learned ancient father adds (*l*) that heretics corrupt the truth of the Gospel by wrong interpretations. He calls them "miserable wine merchants" <note>original: "wine coopers." Jerome uses the Latin word *caupones*, which refers to innkeepers or wine sellers notorious for diluting wine with water to increase profits.</note> who turn wine into water. In his commentary upon Jeremiah 13:23, he says that (*m*) the heretics who hold the view of "different natures" <note>This refers to the Gnostic belief that humans are born with different fixed natures (spiritual, psychic, or material), rather than having free will.</note> use this testimony against the church.

(Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book 1, Chapter 4).</note>

He informs us that (*o*) it was their custom to argue from every part of Scripture: from the Old and New Testaments, from the prophets, the apostles, and the evangelists. 

Tertullian speaks to much the same effect, saying that (*p*) heretics try to support their mistaken ideas through incorrect interpretations of Scripture. He further adds (*q*) that they could be refuted by Scripture alone if they would abide by its rulings and focus on it exclusively. 

Ambrosiaster’s <note>Ambrosiaster is the name given to the unknown author of a series of commentaries on the epistles of St. Paul, once thought to be by Ambrose.</note> (*r*) definition or description of heretics is that (*s*) they are people who try to support their opinions through Scripture, imposing their own meaning onto the divine word and attempting to defend their errors with the authority of the sacred writings. Vincent of Lérins <note>original: "Vincentius Lirinensis"</note> testifies to the same thing. ### SECTION XI. *Some of them also used Apocryphal Books.*

<margin>SECTION 11.</margin>HEGESIPPUS, as we are informed by Eusebius, speaking (*y*) of the books called Apocryphal <note>Apocryphal books are those of doubtful authenticity or those not accepted as part of the official biblical canon.</note>, says that some of them were forged by certain heretics in his own time. Irenæus affirms that (*z*) they quoted a countless multitude of apocryphal and spurious books which they had forged themselves.

Amphilochius is said (*a*) to have published a book concerning the spurious writings forged by heretics, though it is not mentioned by Jerome (*b*) in his biographical account of Amphilochius.

We cannot, therefore, clear the heretics of this charge. It seems to be supported by sufficient evidence in the testimony of the writers just quoted. I have already had occasion to mention several compositions of this kind. One is the Gospel of Peter, censured by (*c*) Serapion and forged by one of the Docetæ <note>The Docetæ were early Christians who believed that Jesus’s physical body and sufferings were only appearances or illusions, rather than physical reality.</note>. I have noted elsewhere (*d*) several pieces attributed to Leucius, who held the same opinion. The reader may also wish to consult the relevant chapter in Eusebius. Perhaps none of the sects were entirely free from this fault. There were some books that may be called apocryphal, composed by the Uni- <note>The text ends mid-word, likely continuing as "Unitarians" or "Universalists" on the next page.</note>

<header>HERETICS AND HERESY. SEC. II.</header>
<sig>H</sig>

Unitarians or Ebionites, that is, such as maintained one principle <note>The "one principle" refers to the belief in the absolute unity of God, as opposed to the dualism of other sects.</note>: others by those who held two principles, and were Docetæ <note>The Docetæ believed Jesus’s physical body was an illusion.</note>.

With regard to this, however, several things may be observed:

I. Most of these apocryphal pieces—whether gospels, or acts, or circuits and travels, or revelations—went under the names of apostles (*e*), or apostolical men. In general, they bear testimony to the transcendent excellence of Jesus and his doctrine, and the truth of the main things concerning him.

II. It does not clearly appear what degree of credit was given to these writings, or that they were equally respected by any with the genuine and undisputed books of the New Testament. For these genuine books, as we have already seen and may see further hereafter, heretics had a great esteem and endeavored to prove their doctrines by them.

III. The Catholics <note>In this context, "Catholics" refers to the mainstream or orthodox Christian church of the time, rather than the modern Roman Catholic Church specifically.</note> themselves are not free from this charge. There were several books forged by them and ascribed to persons who were not their real authors. Among these may be reckoned the *Acts of Paul and Thecla*, the *Sibylline Poems*, the books ascribed to Hydaspes, Hermes Trismegistus, and various others. This much has been admitted by several learned writers, particularly (*f*) Isaac Casaubon. Mr. Mosheim (*g*), many years since,

Jerome, Preface to Matthew.</note>

### SECTION XII. *They respected the Apostles and apostolic traditions.*

<margin>Section 12.</margin>
This is partly evident from the two previous points: their use of the New Testament scriptures and their creation of forged books (if they indeed forged any) in the names of the Apostles or apostolic men. It has been frequently noted by modern scholars that Basilides <note>Basilides was an early Christian gnostic teacher in Alexandria, active around 117–138 AD.</note> claimed to have received his specific views from Glaucias, a companion of Peter; and Valentinus <note>Valentinus was the most successful early gnostic theologian, who founded a school in Rome.</note> claimed to have heard them from Theodas, a disciple of Paul (*k*).

Tertullian, writing against the heretics, assures us (*l*) that they could not deny—and even admitted—that the Apostles knew all the doctrines of the Gospel and agreed with one another in what they taught. The most they dared to assert in support of their specific views was that the Apostles did not reveal the whole truth to everyone. But this will appear more clearly in the history of the various individual heretics. I shall mention only two or three general points here to prove that the Apostles and apostolic traditions were respected by them.

Ptolemaeus, a follower of Valentinus, in a letter to Flora, having observed (*m*) that the ceremonial and typical laws of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Hebrew Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy).</note> were annulled by the appearance of the Truth, adds,

Potter edition. p. 764. D. Paris edition.*

(*l*) <note>original: "Sed, ut diximus, eadem dementia est; cum confitentur quidem nihil apostolos ignorasse... quaedam secreto, et paucis demandasse."</note> But, as we said, it is the same madness; since they indeed confess that the Apostles were ignorant of nothing, nor did they preach things different among themselves; however, they claim that the Apostles did not wish to reveal all things to everyone: for they committed some things openly and to all, and some things secretly and to a few. *Tertullian, De Praescriptione Haereticorum, chapter xxv. p. 240. # OBSERVATIONS ON

<margin>Sec. 13.</margin>
Some are said to have borrowed from one, some from another school of philosophy. According to <term>Tertullian</term> <note>original: "Tertullian"; an influential early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD)</note>, <term>Hermogenes</term> (*t*) and <term>Marcion</term> (*u*) borrowed from the **Stoics**, and <term>Valentinus</term> <note>original: "Valentin"</note> from the **Platonists**. The tenets of all the different schools of philosophers (*w*) were understood by these writers to be inconsistent with a belief in the resurrection of the body.

In some of their peculiar tenets, he supposed them to be influenced by the principles of **Zeno** and **Heraclitus** (*x*), and in others by those of **Epicurus** and **Plato**.

<term>Origen</term> (*y*), who often mentions <term>Basilides</term>, Valentinus, and Marcion together, charges all three with scorning <note>original: "contemning"</note> the Christian religion by introducing philosophical schemes.

---

<note>original: "Quid ergo Athenis et Hierosolymis?..."</note> What then does Athens have to do with Jerusalem? What does the Academy have to do with the Church? . . . Let those see to it who have produced a Stoic, Platonic, and dialectic Christianity. For us, there is no need for curiosity after Jesus Christ, nor for further inquiry after the Gospel. *De Praescriptione Haereticorum, chapters 7, 8.*

(*t*) <note>original: "A christianis enim conversus ad philosophos..."</note> For having turned from Christians to philosophers—from the church to the Academy and the Portico—he [Hermogenes] took from the Stoics the idea of placing matter alongside the Lord; matter which was itself always there, neither born nor made, having no beginning at all and no end, out of which the Lord afterward made all things. *Adversus Hermogenem, chapter 1.*

(*u*) <note>original: "Ubi tunc Marcion Ponticus Nauclerus..."</note> Where then was Marcion of Pontus, the ship-master, a student of Stoicism? Where then was Valentinus, a follower of Platonism? *De Praescriptione Haereticorum, chapter 30.*

(*w*) <note>original: "At cum monet cavendum a subtiloquentia..."</note> But when he warns us to beware of clever speech, philosophy, and empty deception, it would be a long task and a separate work to show that all heresies are condemned by this sentence, because they all consist of the power of clever speech and the rules of philosophy. But let Marcion acknowledge the principal boundary of his faith from the school of Epicurus, introducing a dull 

<column-break/>

Lord <note>Marcion proposed a "higher" god who was passive and indifferent to judgment, unlike the Creator God</note>, so that he might say he should not be feared; and placing matter alongside God the Creator from the porch of the Stoics; denying the resurrection of the flesh, about which no philosophy agrees. Our truth is so far removed from such inventions that it both fears to provoke the anger of God, and trusts that He brought all things forth from nothing, and promises that He will restore the same flesh, and is not ashamed that Christ was born from a virgin's womb—while the philosophers, heretics, and the heathens themselves laugh at such things. *Adversus Marcionem, Book 5, chapter 19.*

(*x*) <note>original: "Ipsæ denique hæreses a philosophia subornantur..."</note> Finally, heresies themselves are equipped by philosophy. From there come the <term>aeons</term> <note>original: "æones"; in Gnosticism, these were various emanations or divine beings that make up the spiritual world</note> and some unknown forms, and the trinity of man in Valentinus: he had been a Platonist. From there comes Marcion’s "better God" characterized by tranquility: he had come from the Stoics. And the idea that the soul is said to perish is observed from the Epicureans. And the fact that the restoration of the flesh is denied is taken from the common school of all philosophers. And where matter is made equal with God, that is the discipline of Zeno; and where something is alleged about a fiery God, Heraclitus intervenes. *De Praescriptione Haereticorum, chapter 7.*

# HERETICS AND HERESY

<columns>2</columns>

<term>Epiphanius</term> <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD) was a bishop known for his fierce defense of orthodoxy and his massive work cataloging eighty different heresies.</note> says that (z) all <term>heresies</term> <note>original: "heresies"; from the Greek 'hairesis', meaning a choice or a school of thought, used here to mean beliefs that contradict established church doctrine.</note> in general had arisen out of heathen fables. However, it has been disputed among modern scholars which specific philosophy the heretics borrowed from the most. The origin of the <term>Valentinian Aeons</term> <note>original: "Valentinian OEons"; in Gnosticism, Aeons are the various emanations or "powers" that come from the supreme God. Valentinus was a famous 2nd-century teacher who developed this complex system.</note> in particular has been the subject of significant debate and has led to diligent inquiries by learned men.

Some have supposed that these notions were derived from the Jewish <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>original: "Cabbala"; an ancient tradition of Jewish mysticism.</note>. This idea, however, <term>Massuet</term> <note>René Massuet (1666–1716), a Benedictine monk and scholar who edited the works of Irenaeus.</note> strongly opposes (a). He asserts that <term>Valentinus</term> (b) and his followers borrowed instead from the <term>Gentile</term> <note>original: "Gentile"; meaning non-Jewish, specifically the pagan Greek and Roman poets and philosophers.</note> poets and philosophers.

### SECTION XIV. *This Variety of Opinion is no Just Objection against the Truth of the Christian Religion.*

<margin>SEC. 14.</margin>
No good argument can be drawn from the number of different opinions among Christians to invalidate the truth of their common religion. Yet <term>Celsus</term> <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of Christianity who criticized it for being fractured into many sects.</note> made this an objection, to which <term>Origen</term> <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), one of the most prolific and influential early Christian theologians.</note> has (c) given a good reply.

<column-break/>

[These men], like those who brought the "golden tongues" out of Jericho, have tried to introduce the misguided sects of the philosophers into our churches and thereby pollute the entire church of the Lord. <note>original: "isti linguas aureas de Jericho..."; a reference to the theft of forbidden spoils from Jericho (Joshua 7), used as a metaphor for bringing "forbidden" pagan ideas into the church.</note> *From the Homilies on Joshua, Homily 7, p. 414.*

(z) <note>original: "Εκ γαρ ελληνικων μυθων πασαι αι αιρεσεις συναξασαι εαυταις την πλανην κατεβαλον."</note> "For all heresies, having gathered error for themselves, have been founded upon Greek myths." *Heresies, book 26, number 16, p. 98.*

<margin>Sec. 14.</margin> He <note>Referring to Origen (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar and theologian who wrote a famous defense of Christianity against the critic Celsus.</note> observes, “There never was anything important in itself, or promising great advantages to those who pursued it, but that different opinions were formed about it. This is the case with **medicine** <note>original: "Phyſick"; in this context, it refers to the science and practice of healing.</note>, which is useful and even necessary to mankind. But whether it is considered as a science or a practice, there are many different opinions concerning it. 

The same is the case with philosophy, which proposes to lead us to truth and to teach us to live well. Yet even here, people differ very widely from one another. The same is the case with Judaism, out of which has sprung a great variety of **sects** <note>original: "ſects"; groups with differing religious interpretations.</note>. 

It is no wonder, therefore, that Christianity—a matter of such infinite importance—could excite the curiosity of many and cause different men to form different opinions concerning some of its doctrines and discoveries. But just as one would not be considered a prudent person who totally rejected the use of medicine when sickness made it necessary because there were some differences in opinion about the theory of the disease; nor a wise person who renounced all philosophy because philosophers disagreed among themselves; so it would not be a sign of good sense to reject the writings of Moses and the Prophets, or to renounce Christianity because of some differences in opinion among their adherents.”

We may perceive from many ancient **orthodox** <note>original: "catholic"; used here in its original sense of the "universal" or mainstream church before the later denominational splits.</note> writers that they themselves saw this difficulty, but they answered it very reasonably in the following manner: That these **divisions** <note>original: "diviſions"; referring to the various competing groups within early Christianity.</note>

(*i*) "Indeed, if we apply those bronze shovels—that is, the voices of heretics—to the altar of God where the divine fire is, and where the true preaching of God is, the truth itself will shine better by comparison with falsehoods. # HERETICS AND HERESY.
## SEC. 14.

Clement of Alexandria had long before met with this objection, taken from the variety of opinions among Christians, and urged by both Jews and Gentiles as a sufficient reason against embracing the gospel. The sum of what he says, which the reader will find at length in the note (n) below, is to this purpose: "That among the Jews there were several <term>sects</term> <note>Distinct groups within a religion, often with differing interpretations of its laws or traditions.</note>. And among the Greeks, the followers of their most admired philosophers were split into a variety of opinions. That our Lord himself had foretold that tares should grow up among the wheat, and that corruptions will always creep into the best things. Among physicians also, there are various prescriptions and opinions, and different methods of cure; yet no sick person would on this account decline the use of medicine <note>original: "physic"</note>, when his health could be thereby restored." He therefore concludes by asserting, "That it was very weak and absurd to urge such objections as these against embracing those truths which tend to correct and purify the bad dispositions of the soul."

# OBSERVATIONS ON
## SECTION 14.

<margin>Section 14.</margin> Two observations seem to naturally arise from the matters discussed in this section. The first is: Heresies, far from being truly harmful to the cause of Christianity, actually proved to be of great service to it. This is because the alterations made by Marcion <note>A 2nd-century teacher who rejected the Old Testament and edited the New Testament to fit his own dualistic theology.</note>, Apelles <note>A student of Marcion who modified his teacher's ideas, emphasizing a single primary principle of good.</note>, and others to their copies of the scriptures—done to suit their own various opinions—must have put the <term>catholic Christians</term> <note>original: "catholic Christians"; here referring to the "universal" or mainstream church of the time rather than the specific Roman Catholic denomination.</note> on their guard early on. It motivated them to preserve their own copies with the greatest care, keeping them genuine and complete. They did this to expose the falsehood of the ideas their opponents had embraced and to reveal the underhanded methods those opponents used—such as corrupting and cutting up the sacred writings—to better hide their errors and their inconsistency with the true teachings of <term>divine revelation</term> <note>The concept of truth communicated by God to humanity, specifically through the Bible.</note>. Because they represented this practice as shameful in their opponents and constantly criticized it as vile in their writings against heretics, they were sure to avoid such behavior themselves with the utmost caution.

Second, the many heretics we hear of today, along with the number and variety of divisions that existed among early Christians, serve as evidence that the religion of Jesus had made great progress in the world. In addition to the more standard and <term>orthodox</term> <note>Those who hold to the established, accepted doctrines of the church.</note> followers, there were various others who managed to form their own societies and cause trouble for the main body of Christians. This suggests that, taken all together, the total number of Christians must have been very large. At the same time, this diversity of opinion, far from undermining the truth of the Christian religion, actually confirms it. It should be noted that all these groups—though they sincerely hated one another due to their mutual opposition and differed on many minor details—still agreed on the core points of the faith. This is very clear from several previous sections.

<summary>The author argues that early heresies benefited Christianity by forcing the mainstream church to preserve scripture accurately and by proving, through their sheer number, the widespread reach of the religion.</summary>
<keywords>Heresy, Marcion, Apelles, Scripture preservation, Church History, Christian expansion, Orthodoxy, Catholic Christians</keywords>

# HERETICS AND HERESY.

### SECTION XV. *Curiosity and an inquisitiveness of mind were dispositions frequently indulged by Heretics.*

<margin>Section 15.</margin> Heretics were, in general, men of a curious and inquisitive turn of mind who greatly indulged this disposition. This led them to speculate upon many points of doctrine concerning which the scriptures had afforded little or no light. However, according to the philosophy then in fashion—with which their minds were but too deeply <term>tinctured</term> <note>original: "tinctured"; meaning their thinking was deeply colored or influenced by these external philosophical ideas.</note> (o)—these were esteemed matters of importance and points that would lead them to many curious and sublime speculations. By giving way to these, they imbibed a set of notions which were dignified with the name of "wisdom" and which they regarded as true. Unhappily, they set about engrafting these onto the religion of Jesus, to which they were by no means suitable. When the scriptures were in some cases plainly inconsistent with these notions, they insisted on making the scriptures yield to their philosophical opinions (p). Thus the simplicity of truth was banished, and endless divisions arose. Although in many cases their curiosity and inquisitiveness were carried to an improper extent, they nevertheless set out with just views in order to have

Ea est enim materia sapientiæ secularis, temeraria interpres divinæ naturæ et dispositionis. Ipsæ denique hæreses a philosophia subornantur. ### SECT. XVIII. *The seeds of these Heresies were sown in the days of the Apostles.*

<margin>Sec. 18.</margin> Several of the ancient fathers (f) understand the apostle Paul as referring to some appearances of this kind when he exhorts (g) the primitive Christians to avoid philosophy, and questions about endless genealogies, and the contradictions of "science" falsely so called <note>The Greek word used here is *gnosis*, which means "knowledge." The author is suggesting that Paul was warning against the early stages of Gnosticism.</note>.

<columns>2</columns>

(f) "Hence come those fables and endless genealogies, and fruitless questions, and talk that spreads like a cancer; the apostle restrains us from these, expressly testifying that philosophy ought to be avoided when writing to the Colossians." <note>original: "Hinc illæ fabulæ et genealogiæ interminabiles..." Tertullian, *On the Prescription of Heretics*, Chapter 7.</note>

"I add to this the recognition of those very doctrines that existed in the time of the apostles, as pointed out by those same apostles. Paul, in the first epistle to the Corinthians, notes those who deny or doubt the resurrection. This opinion is peculiar to the Sadducees; a part of it is used by Marcion, Apelles, and Valentinus. Writing to the Galatians, he lashes out against the observers and defenders of circumcision and the law; this is the heresy of Ebion. Instructing Timothy, he also rebukes those who forbid marriage; this is how Marcion and his follower Apelles teach. And when he names 'endless genealogies,' Valentinus is recognized. John, indeed, in the Apocalypse is commanded to punish those who eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality. There are also now others, the Nicolaitans; it is called the Cainite heresy." <note>original: "Adhibeo super hæc ipſarum doctrinarum recognitionem..." Tertullian, *On the Prescription of Heretics*, Chapter 33.</note>

"Some, being led away from the truth, introduce false discourses and vain genealogies, which provide questions rather than the building up of God, which is in faith." <note>original: "Επι την αληθειαν παραπεμπομενοι τινες..." Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book 1, Preface.</note>

"Will anyone hesitate to pronounce the same: that these are the fables and endless genealogies which the spirit of the apostle foresaw and condemned while these heretical seeds were even then budding?" <note>original: "Dubitabitne idem pronuntiare..." Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, Chapter 3.</note>

which were then springing up, and which would increase; and that he afterwards wrote his epistles in order to guard them against these corruptions and to confirm them in the faith.

This opinion—that the foundation of these heresies was laid in the times of the apostles and sprang up immediately after—is a probable opinion in itself and is embraced by several learned modern scholars, particularly by Vitringa (*i*) and by the late Reverend Mr. Brekel of Liverpool (*k*).

<columns>2</columns>

(*i*) For so, when Paul in the first epistle to Timothy, chapter 6:20, warns against the "contradictions of knowledge falsely so-called" <note>original: *αντιθεσει της ψευδωνυμυ γνωσεως* (antithesei tēs pseudōnymou gnōseōs)</note>, referring to the opposing parallels of science falsely so named, and against fables and "endless genealogies" <note>original: *γενεαλογιαις απερανταις* (genealogiais aperantais)</note> or infinite successions (1 Timothy 1:4), there is no other way this can be more suitably applied than to those most subtle disputes concerning the divinity and its various emanations <note>In Gnosticism, "emanations" refers to the various levels of being or "Aeons" flowing from the supreme God.</note>. These were the topics that occupied the Jews and others devoted to Platonic and Pythagorean philosophy, and in which they placed the greatest part of their secret and higher knowledge. This is also how Irenaeus and Tertullian seem to have understood Paul’s meaning, and in my view, they understood it correctly. *See Tertullian, On the Prescription of Heretics, Chapter 33, p. 244. A. and Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 1, in the preface. Vitringa’s Observations on Titus 3:9, Vol. 2, p. 161.*

(*k*) In his answer to Mr. Deacon, against the pretended purity of the first three centuries, he observes that if this point were thoroughly examined, it would appear that the Christian church preserved her virgin purity no longer than the apostolic age—at least if we may give credit to Hegesippus. *See Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, Book 3, Chapter 32.*

<column-break/>

Another ancient writer, Papias <note>original: "Paphias"</note> by name, speaks of some persons in his time who taught other precepts than those that were delivered by the Lord and proceeded from the truth itself. *Eusebius, as above, Chapter 39, p. 111. A.* To mention the corruptions and innovations in religion during the first four centuries is completely unnecessary, as it is so well known that even before the reign of Constantine, there emerged a kind of pagan <note>original: "heathenish"</note> Christianity which mixed itself with the true Christian religion. *Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History, Book 1, Chapter 22. Brekel’s Manuscript.*

## HISTORY of HERETICS:

### SECTION 1.

...schemes. Saturninus, like Menander, held that there is one Father, unknown to all, who created angels, archangels, principalities, and powers <note>In Gnostic theology, these refer to various ranks of celestial beings.</note>. He said that the world and everything in it were made by seven specific angels. Man, too, was created by them. He taught that the Savior was unborn, incorporeal (having no physical body), and was a man in appearance only <note>The belief that Christ's human form was an illusion is known as Docetism.</note>. He says that the God of the Jews was one of those seven angels. And because all the principalities opposed his Father, Christ came to overthrow the God of the Jews and to bring salvation to those who believe in him—specifically those who possess a "spark of life" within them. This person was the first to teach that there are two kinds of men created by the angels: some good and others bad. And because demons assisted the worst of men, the Savior came to condemn bad men and demons, and to save the good.

<margin>Since demons assist the most wicked, the Savior came for the destruction of evil men and demons, and the salvation of the good. They say that marrying and procreating is from Satan. Many who follow him also abstain from animal meat, deceiving many through this kind of feigned self-restraint. <note>original Latin: "quoniam dæmones pessimos adjuvant, venisse salvatorem ad dissolutionem malorum hominum, et dæmoniorum, salutem autem bonorum. Nubere autem et generare, a Satana dicunt esse. Multi autem qui sunt ex eo et ab animalibus abstinent, per fictam hujusmodi continentiam seducentes multos."</note></margin>

He says that marriage and procreation are the work of Satan. Many of his followers also abstain from eating animal meat, deceiving many people through this feigned temperance <note>original: "temperance," here meaning self-restraint or asceticism</note>.

<margin>They claim that certain prophecies were spoken by those angels who fashioned the world, and others by Satan—whom he presents as an angel who is an adversary to the world-makers, and especially to the God of the Jews. <note>original Latin: "Prophetias autem quasdam quidem ab iis angelis, qui mundum fabricaverunt, dictas, quasdam autem a Satana: quem et ipsum angelum adversarium mundi fabricatoribus ostendit, maxime autem Judæorum Deo."</note> *Irenaeus, Book 1, Chapter 24 (alternatively 22), section 1, etc., pages 100, 101.*</margin>

They insist that some prophecies originated from the angels who made the world, while others came from Satan, whom they also consider to be an adversary of the world's creators, especially the God of the Jews.

-># SATURNINUS<-

## SECTION II. *He was an obscure person and likely had only a few followers.*

<margin>SECTION 2.</margin>

I have thought it not amiss to transcribe this article by Irenaeus <note>Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD) was a Greek bishop known for his writings against heresy.</note>, hoping that we may make some good use of it in the chapter on Basilides. I do not intend to expand on the history of Saturninus because he was a very obscure person, and his opinions were so similar to those of Basilides.

Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738) was a French Protestant theologian who wrote a famous history of Manichaeism.</note> observes that (b) Clement of Alexandria makes no mention at all of Menander and Saturninus. For this reason, he concludes that they made very little impact on the world and had but few followers.

Saturninus, however—called *Saturnilus* by some—is mentioned by most writers on heresies. Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius (c. 310–403 AD) was the Bishop of Salamis and a staunch opponent of heresy.</note> adds very little to what Irenaeus wrote. At the beginning of his article, he uses an expression denoting (c) his obscurity <note>original Greek: Μετα τουτον σατορνιλ☉ τις ανεση (Meta touton Saturnilos tis anestē) — "After him, a certain Saturnilus arose."</note>. Theodoret (d) seems to simply transcribe Irenaeus. Furthermore, the accounts of (e) Philaster and (f) Augustine are so similar to the others that I shall only refer to them. It is proper to mention in this place the order of the earliest heretics as listed by different authors. In Irenaeus (g), they stand as follows: Simon, Menander, Saturninus, Basilides, Carpocrates. In Epiphanius, the order is: Simon, Menander, Saturnilus, Basilides, the Nicolaitans, the Gnostics, and the Carpocratians; this order is also followed by Augustine. Theodoret’s list is the same as Irenaeus’. In Philaster, it is: Simon, Menander, Saturninus, Basilides, and the Nicolaitans.
