He supposes him to have flourished about 123 AD. Cave (*n*) <note>William Cave (1637–1713) was an influential English church historian.</note> places him about 112 AD, or soon after. Grabe (*o*) <note>John Ernest Grabe (1666–1711) was a German Anglican theologian known for his work on early Christian texts.</note> says Basilides began to spread his notions in the time of Trajan, but chiefly under Hadrian, and probably did not die before the beginning of the reign of Antoninus the Pious. Theodoret says that Menander was the teacher of Saturninus and Basilides, and that (*r*) both lived during the time of Hadrian.

# HISTORY OF HERETICS

SECTION 2. Chapter (_ff_) proceeds: "But Basilides, in order to appear as if he had discovered a more sublime and more probable scheme, went much farther. He taught that from the self-existent father was born Nus <note>original: *Nun*; meaning Mind or Understanding</note>; from Nus was born Logos <note>the Word</note>; from Logos came Phronesis <note>Prudence or Providence</note>; from Phronesis came Sophia <note>Wisdom</note> and Dunamis <note>Power</note>."

<note>The following text is translated from the Latin of Irenæus, *Against Heresies*.</note>

Basilides, however, so that he might seem to have discovered something deeper and more plausible, immensely extended the scope of his doctrine. He showed that Nus (Mind) was born first from the Unborn Father; from him was born Logos (Word); then from Logos, Phronesis (Prudence); from Phronesis, Sophia (Wisdom) and Dunamis (Power). From Dunamis and Sophia, he taught that Virtues, Principalities, and Angels were born, whom he calls the "first" group, and by them the first heaven was made. 

Afterward, through a series of derivations from these, others were made, who created another heaven similar to the first. They say a third heaven was formed, and from those descending downward, a fourth; and in this manner, one after another, successive levels of Principalities and Angels were created, totaling 365 heavens. For this reason, the year has as many days as there are heavens.

The angels who occupy the lowest heaven—the one visible to us—established everything that is in the world. They divided the earth and its nations among themselves. Their leader is the one thought to be the God of the Jews. Because he wished to subject the other nations to his own people (the Jews), all the other princes resisted and worked against him.

The Unborn and Unnamed Father, seeing their destruction <note>referring to the souls of men caught in the conflict between these angelic rulers</note>, sent his first-born, Nus (who is called Christ), to liberate those who believe in him from the power of those who built the world. He appeared on earth as a man to these nations and performed miracles. 

Therefore, he did not actually suffer. Rather, a certain Simon of Cyrene was forced <note>original: *angariarum*; pressed into service</note> to carry his cross for him. It was this Simon who, through ignorance and error, was transformed to look like Jesus and was crucified. Jesus himself took the form of Simon and stood by, laughing at them. Because he was an incorporeal power and the Mind (Nus) of the Unborn Father, he transformed himself however he pleased, and thus ascended to the one who had sent him.

Therefore, those who know these things are liberated from the principalities who built the world. One ought not to confess the one who was crucified, but rather the one who came in human form and was *thought* to be crucified—who was called Jesus and was sent by the Father so that, through this divine arrangement, he might dissolve the works of the world-builders.

Basilides also taught that salvation belongs only to the soul, for the body is corruptible by nature. He claimed that prophecies came from the princes who built the world, and the Law specifically from their leader, who led the people out of the land of Egypt. He taught his followers to despise things sacrificed to idols <note>original: *idolothyta*</note> and to consider them of no importance, using them without any hesitation. They also practiced other activities and every kind of lust with indifference. They utilize magic and incantations. They also map out the local positions of the 365 heavens, just as astronomers do. They adopted the theories of mathematicians and incorporated them into their own doctrine. Their leader is Abraxas, and for this reason, his name contains the number 365. 

*Irenæus, Book 1, Chapter 24 [alternatively Chapter 22, 23], pages 101, 102.*

The same learned writer <note>This refers to Isaac de Beausobre, mentioned on the previous page</note> further argues in this manner: Clement of Alexandria was well acquainted with Basilidian theology. He also takes notice of the opinion of some philosophers who spoke of seven heavens below the sphere of the fixed stars. How could he fail to mention such an unusual opinion as that of 365 heavens if it were held by the Basilidians? This is especially unlikely since he takes every opportunity to refute them, because this heresy had many followers in Alexandria at that time.

<header>Section 5.</header>

## BASILIDES.

...matter, in order to give it form and beauty. They judged it unworthy of God to create perishing and mortal beings. Most importantly, they could not tolerate the idea that God was the author of the many evils found in this world. They argued that if God had made this world, it would have been perfect. However, since it contains many imperfections, they believed it could not be the work of a God who is infinitely perfect and infinitely good.

Therefore, they chose to attribute the creation of this world to angels. According to this view, these angels saw that matter, which was eternal, was being tossed about in a chaotic and disorderly way, and they decided to bring order to it. Using the world of spirits to which they belonged as a model, they intended to create a physical version of it using matter. God, who was aware of their plan, did not step in to prevent it. Our world was thus created by angels with the silent <note>original: "tacit"</note> consent of the Supreme Being. Their view on the formation of the world was the opposite of the opinion held by orthodox or Catholic Christians.

<margin>(e) History of Manichaeism, Vol. 2, p. 2, No. 1.</margin>

For as <term>Beausobre</term> <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738) was a prominent French Protestant theologian and ecclesiastical historian</note> observes, <gloss>(e)</gloss> the orthodox Christians always tried to establish the unity of the creative principle; however, the philosophers who claimed to be Christians stubbornly held the opposite error. Their goal was to defend divine Providence and to present physical matter <note>original: "the material principle"</note> as the source of all evil. Their intention was praiseworthy, but their reasoning was flawed. The systems they created did not solve these difficulties but only masked <note>original: "palliate"</note> them. Furthermore, in their very first principles, they directly contradicted the divine authority of <term>Moses</term> and the prophets, which ultimately undermined the divine authority of <term>Jesus Christ</term>. Yet, they denied that this was the case and continued to hold a high level of respect for the Son of God. Wherefore...

SECTION 5. Therefore, it is unjust to attribute to them impious sentiments which they never held, but which they disavowed in their whole conduct.

By some, Basilides is said to have attributed the formation of this world to the inferior *angels*. However, I think that is not clear. For if he did, he differed in this from Saturninus, who, according to *Irenaeus*, seems to have taught that the world was made by seven angels. Saturninus does not represent these angels as being of an inferior rank, but rather of the first order—as next to the Aeons <term>Aeons</term> <note>In Gnostic theology, Aeons are the various emanations or "levels" of divinity that bridge the gap between the supreme God and the material world.</note>, or the first emanations from the eternal and inexpressible <note>original: "ineffable"</note> Father. 

Moreover, in the writings of *Clement* of Alexandria—who did not write based on hearsay reports, but who has provided us with the very words of Basilides himself—Basilides is spoken of as maintaining honorable thoughts of the angel creator, or the chief of the angels who made the world. For he said that (f) the creator formed the world for the honor of the invisible God, whose image and prophet he was. He also stated that the creator (g) was worthy to be praised and was a very great God.

When a distribution of things was later made, the chief of the creator-angels took the people of the Jews as his particular share. This doctrine was generally accepted by many ancient writers and is partly based on *Deuteronomy* 32:8. According to the version of the *Seventy* <term>the Seventy</term> <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, that passage states: "When the Most High divided the nations and separated the sons of *Adam*, he set the boundaries of the people according to the number of the angels of God." They also attempted to support this opinion using *Daniel* 10:13, 21 and 12:1.

### SECTION 6. *His Opinion concerning the Person of Christ.*

<margin>SECTION 6.</margin>
We proceed to the account that Irenaeus gives of their doctrine concerning the person of Christ. The eternal Father, seeing the ruin of the world, sent his first-begotten, *Nus* <term>Nus</term> <note>Nus (Greek: Νοῦς) translates to "Mind" or "Intellect." In Gnostic systems, it represents the first emanation from the supreme God.</note>, or Understanding, for the salvation of those who believe in him, and to deliver them from the power of the angel creators. He appeared as a man and performed many miracles; but he was not crucified, as the Jews, having made a mistake, crucified Simon of Cyrene <note>original: "Simon the Cyrenian"</note> in his place.

Here it is appropriate to observe what Basilides said in honor of Jesus. He supposed him to be the first-begotten of the Father, and to have come into this lower world for the salvation of men, with an express order and commission from the Father. He likewise supposed Jesus to have performed many miracles here.

But he did not think Jesus was a real man, but only appeared to be one. Many ancient (b) writers say this, to the extent that it is difficult to deny or contest it. And yet, perhaps we may soon see something that might make us hesitate about this conclusion. For, as Beausobre says, (i) undoubtedly Basilides did not believe in the incarnation or the hypostatic union <term>hypostatic union</term> <note>The traditional Christian doctrine that Jesus Christ is one person with two distinct natures: fully divine and fully human.</note> of the Son of God with flesh. But even so, he never denied that Jesus was a real person in whom the Understanding (the Son of God) displayed his power, whom he filled with his gifts and illuminations, and invested with extraordinary influence.

<margin>(b) ...at first [they erred] concerning his flesh itself: either contending it had no reality, according to Marcion and Basilides; or [contending it was] of a specific quality, according to the heresies of Valentinus and Apelles. *Tertullian on the Resurrection of the Flesh, chapter 2, page 379, D; page 314, 29.* <note>original Latin: "...in ipsa prius carne ejus extraverunt: aut nullius veritatis contendentes eam secundum Marcionem et Basilidem: aut propriae qualitatis, secundum hereses Valentini, et Apelles."</note></margin>

<margin>And he [Basilides] also taught concerning Christ, to those who thought he had appeared, that he was like a phantom in appearance, that he was not a man, and had not taken on flesh. *Epiphanius, Heresies 24, number 3.* <note>original Greek: "Και αυτός περί Χριστού, οις δοκεί πεφηνέναι, ομοίως διδάξαι· εικάζειν δε φησιν αυτοίς φαντασίαν είναι του φαίνεσθαι, μη είναι δε άνθρωπον, μηδέ σάρκα ειληφέναι."</note> (i) *Ibid. page 25, number 6.*</margin>

### SECTION VII. *On the Story of Simon of Cyrene, and whether he believed that Christ suffered.*

<margin>SECTION 7.</margin>
Regarding the story of Jesus taking the form of Simon of Cyrene <note>original: "Simon the Cyrenian"</note> and transforming Simon into his own likeness, it is so absurd a story that I must admit it seems incredible to me. It must certainly be a misrepresentation based on some mistake—possibly based on the logical conclusions drawn by others from his opinions, which were conclusions he himself did not accept.

Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738), a French Protestant theologian known for his history of Manichaeism.</note> also states plainly (*k*) that the ridiculous comedy of Simon being transformed into Jesus and crucified in his place is a fable that Irenaeus <note>Irenaeus was a 2nd-century bishop who wrote "Against Heresies," a primary source for early Gnostic beliefs, though often criticized for bias.</note> found from an unknown source. And, as the same insightful writer observes, Massuet (*l*) noticed that this account is contradicted by Clement of Alexandria; however, Massuet chose to correct Clement using Irenaeus, rather than Irenaeus using Clement. But, says Beausobre (*m*), I cannot be of that mind. The testimony of Clement appears to me vastly more valuable than that of Irenaeus, because he knew the Basilidians, had read their books, and quotes them. His testimony is especially preferable on this occasion, as it is not so much Clement speaking as Basilides himself.

The argument is this: Basilides acknowledged that the attributes of goodness, holiness, and righteousness belong to God. As a good being, he can never do evil to anyone. As holy, he cannot but hate sin, of which he is never the author. As righteous,

---

(*k*) *Ibid.* <note>original: "Ib." — abbreviation for 'ibidem', meaning 'in the same place.'</note>

(*l*) Clement of Alexandria does not seem to have paid enough attention to that distinction when he wrote in the fourth book of the *Stromata* that Basilides had dared to say the Lord was a man endowed with the power of sinning. This seems false if it refers to the true Christ, whom he [Basilides] indeed confessed to be a man; however, it might be acceptable if it is understood as referring to the counterfeit Christ—namely Simon of Cyrene—who was nailed to the cross under the appearance and form of Christ. <note>original: "Ad eam distinctionem . . . haud satis attendisse videtur Clemens Alex. dum scripsit. lib. iv. Iren. p. lxi. n. 117.</note>

(*m*) *History of Manichaeism* <note>original: "Hist. de Manich."</note> Vol. 2, p. 25, note 6.

<page-num>83</page-num>

<margin>(n) But Basilides’s theory, having found a pretext, says that the soul, having sinned in another life, undergoes punishment here: the elect soul through the honor of martyrdom, and others by being purified through their own punishment. (*Ibid.* 506. D. 507.) He says it is an evil to have the desire to sin... for everything is rather [to be called evil] than that evil should be something inherent [to God's creation]. Then further down, concerning the Lord, he speaks of him as a man. If, however, setting aside all these arguments, you come to challenge me with specific examples, saying, "This person did not sin, yet they suffered," I would say: "If you permit me, they did sin." <note>original Greek: "Αλλά τον Βασιλίδη η υποθεσις... ου ημαρτεν"</note></margin>
himself, he may and will correct sinners. But for the same reason, he will never permit the innocent to be punished. The orthodox acknowledged the same divine attributes, but they did not approve of the conclusions which Basilides drew from them. They believed God to be righteous, and yet they supposed that he might permit innocent beings to suffer. As proof of this, they cited the example of the martyrs, who were delivered up to the most grievous pains to exercise their virtue and confirm the gospel. Basilides answered <margin>(n)</margin> that martyrs are not perfectly innocent, because no man is without fault. If any suffer, God is punishing in them either evil desires or actual sins—though these may be secret and unknown to others—or sins which the soul had been guilty of in some other body <note>Basilides believed in the pre-existence of souls and reincarnation, suggesting that present suffering could be punishment for sins committed in a past life.</note>. God, who knows all things, even the most secret, never punishes anyone who has not deserved it. The favor shown to martyrs lies in this: that their pains appear to have an honorable cause, though they are indeed the punishment for their sins, committed either in this life or in a pre-existent state.

<margin>(o) In this way, even if you speak of a sinless man, and I see him suffering, although he has done no evil... <note>original Greek: "Ουτωσιν δη και τον αναμαρτητον..."</note></margin>

This argument put him in great distress, for it was difficult for him to escape the logic without sounding blasphemous. ### SECTION 8. *Beausobre’s View of the Sentiments of Basilides concerning Christ.*

<margin>Section 8.</margin>
After this argument, Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre, a prominent historian of early Christian sects.</note> sums up *(r)* the sentiment and doctrine of Basilides concerning the Saviour:

1. According to him, Jesus was a real, true man since he suffered. However, whether he believed Jesus to be born of a virgin does not appear.

2. The Divine Understanding, *Nous* <note>original: "Nus" (Greek: νους), meaning mind, intellect, or reason.</note>, which is the same as the Son of God, descended into this man and made use of him as an instrument to give to mankind the knowledge of the true God and the means of salvation. By him, he published his doctrine and performed great miracles in confirmation of it.

3. We cannot say the exact manner in which he conceived of the union of the divine intelligence with the human nature of Jesus; but he did not think him to partake of any of the infirmities of human nature, or to be so united as to suffer.

4. Since Jesus was only a man—though a most excellent man in whom the first-begotten of the Father chose to dwell—it may be said without blasphemy, not that he ever sinned, but that it is not impossible that he might have. It is better to make this supposition than to allow Providence <note>God's divine guidance and justice.</note> to be the cause of any evil, as it would be if a perfectly innocent person suffered.

5. If Jesus committed any fault (which Basilides did not affirm), it must have been before the Christ or the Spirit descended upon him at his baptism.

6. The ministry of the Saviour being finished, Jesus was taken and crucified,

HISTORY OF HERETICS:

<margin>Section 10.</margin> Irenaeus is thought to refer to the followers of Basilides *(y)* when he speaks of certain heretics who held a similar opinion. It may be supposed that Irenaeus intends the same group when he says they have no hesitation about eating food offered to idols. Origen also informs us *(z)* that they at least diminished the honor usually given to martyrdom. The author of the additions to Tertullian’s *(a)* *Prescriptions* plainly states that they denied the necessity of it, as do Philaster *(b)* and Epiphanius *(c)*; all of these authors likely copied their information from one another.

However, I do not think we should conclude from this that there were no martyrs among the Basilidians, or that they believed they were exempt from suffering for the sake of the truth. We can see from Basilides' ideas mentioned previously that it might reasonably be said he diminished the honor given to martyrs. Some critics might even conclude that he denied martyrdom was a duty, or that confessing Jesus in times of danger was required of us. But this is a conclusion drawn for him by others based on some of his opinions, rather than something he himself admitted. For it appears from several passages previously quoted from Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Christian theologian who quoted Basilides extensively.</note> that Basilides esteemed martyrdom as an honorable suffering, even though he believed certain sins were accounted for through that suffering.

### SECTION XI.
#### *He believed that only the soul would be saved.*

Irenaeus also assures us *(d)* that Basilides taught that only the soul would be saved, while the body is by its nature corruptible and incapable of immortality. In this instance, we may undoubtedly rely upon Irenaeus's account. Generally, all those who held the doctrine of two principles <note>The dualist belief that the universe is governed by two opposing forces, typically a good spiritual force and an evil material force.</note> and maintained a negative opinion of matter—viewing it as evil in itself and the cause of all suffering in this sublunary <note>Earthly; literally "under the moon."</note> world—denied the resurrection of the flesh or the body *(e)*.

This was also likely one reason why some claimed that Basilides discouraged martyrdom and denied that believers were required to confess the name of Jesus in times of danger. To deny that the body which suffered would have any share in future rewards <note>original: "recompenſes"</note> was seen as discouraging martyrdom, as it removed a major incentive for men to submit to death for the sake of Christ.

Other ancient writers, such as Philaster *(g)* and Epiphanius *(h)*, make similar claims.

<meta>This page continues the defense of Basilides against charges of moral laxity. The author argues that Basilides’ theological framework and his reliance on the teachings of Jesus regarding internal purity prove he could not have viewed all actions as "indifferent" or morally neutral.</meta>

# HISTORY OF HERETICS:

<margin>SECTION 12.</margin> Regarding this last claim by Irenaeus, which subsequent writers merely copied, it is proper to observe:

1. That making no distinction between things, or saying that all actions are "indifferent" <note>In this context, "indifferent" refers to the belief that actions have no moral value and do not affect one's spiritual standing.</note>, is absolutely inconsistent with the views of Basilides concerning the Deity, as expressed in the passage cited previously. He argued that no evil should be attributed to Providence <note>God's divine guidance and care for the world.</note>; his strong reluctance to accept what seemed to be the consequences of his doctrine regarding martyrs further confirms this. Certainly, such a person could not regard all actions as equal, or fail to distinguish between virtue and vice, righteousness and unrighteousness. On the contrary, he believed that the former must be strictly followed and the latter must be detested. Furthermore, in the section concerning Saturninus—from whom Basilides likely did not differ on this point—Irenaeus explicitly says that it was *his* opinion that the Savior came for the condemnation of bad men and demons, and for the salvation of good men. He also notes that many of Saturninus's followers practiced great temperance <note>Self-control, particularly regarding physical desires.</note>. Therefore, there are indeed good and bad actions by which people are defined; God approves of those who do the one and dislikes those who do the other.

2. There are still surviving passages from Basilides preserved in the works of Clement of Alexandria which show that he held correct sentiments concerning these matters, condemning evil thoughts and intentions as much as outward actions. In the passage I am referring to <margin>(i) For the man who desires to commit adultery is an adulterer, even if he does not succeed in the act; and he who desires to commit murder is a murderer, even if he is unable to kill. <note>original Greek: Δη γαρ ο μοιχευσαι θελων μοιχος εστι... κ. λ.</note> *Miscellanies*, Book 4, p. 506. C.</margin>, he seems to have in mind our Lord’s words in Matthew 5:21–28, and his doctrine is the same. In another place, Clement records <margin>(k) The followers of Basilides say that when the apostles asked if it is better not to marry, they say the Lord replied... those who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the eternal kingdom, they say, [did so] because of the [difficulties] that result from marriage. <note>original Greek: Οι δε απο βασιλειδυ, πυθομενων φασι... κ. λ.</note> *Miscellanies*, Book 3, p. 426. A. B.</margin> the commentary of Basilides and his followers upon Matthew 19:10–15 to be to this [effect]—

<margin>Section 12.</margin> ...this purpose. "Some," they say, "have a natural aversion to women. Those who have this constitution do well not to marry. These," they say, "are such as are eunuchs from their birth. Others are so out of necessity, such as those who perform in the theater <note>Likely referring to athletes or performers who practiced celibacy to maintain physical strength or focus.</note>, who for the sake of glory practice continence <note>Self-restraint, specifically celibacy or abstaining from sexual relations.</note>. Some have been mutilated by an accident and are also eunuchs by necessity, not by choice. Finally, there are some who make themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven; these, though they have a desire for marriage, decline it, fearing the encumbrances <note>original: "incumbrances"; the burdens, distractions, or legal difficulties of a particular state of life.</note> of that state."

Whereupon Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738), a French Protestant theologian known for his extensive history of Manichaeism and early Christian sects.</note> observes <margin>(l) *History of Manichaeism, Vol. 2, p. 43.* <note>original: "Hist. Manich. T. ii. p. 43."</note></margin>: Here we see the true sentiments of Basilides upon the subject of continence, about which men thought differently at that time. Some made it a necessary virtue and condemned marriage as a "work of the flesh." Others exalted continence as the most sublime virtue, though they did not condemn marriage as evil and sinful. Others considered it not as a virtue in itself, but as a state of life which had its usefulness and convenience—especially in times of persecution—because it delivered a Christian from the cares and concerns inseparable from the married state. This last seems to have been the sentiment of Basilides. He did not esteem continence as a virtue in itself. If there were two honest and faithful men, he did not give preference to the one who remained single over the other who lived in lawful marriage. He was willing for everyone to follow the condition to which they were called by nature. He despised an affected and hypocritical continence. He set no value upon forced virginity, or upon those who made a show <note>original: "ostentation"</note> of it so that they might be preferred over others. But he approved of that continence which was pure, free, and chosen for the kingdom

## SECTION 13.
### A Probable Account of the Basis for this Charge.

It may be asked here: if this is so, how did it happen that Irenaeus <note>Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD) was a Greek bishop known for his role in guiding and expanding Christian communities and for his book *Against Heresies*, which attacked Gnosticism.</note> and others charge Basilides and his followers with immoral doctrines and practices?

I answer that this may have resulted from several causes. People are too susceptible to forming wrong impressions and harboring prejudice against those who hold different views and whom they believe to be in error. Furthermore, if some followers of a doctrine are truly bad, critics are often ready to infer that all are like that, or that they are acting according to their core principles. 

Besides, some of the ancient heretics held principles that were liable to be abused, and their adversaries might possibly have concluded that they actually *were* abused by those who maintained them. The Basilidians <margin>(e) See Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, page 375, parts C and D, Paris edition; page 448, Potter edition. See also many quotations to the same purpose under the chapter on Marcion.</margin> and some others <margin>(p) "Yes," he says, "one should not fear God, but love him... for fear is a downfall of the soul." <note>original Greek: Ναι, Φησιν, ου χρὴ θεον φοβεῖσθαι, αλλα αγαπαν. ... Αλλ' ο φοβος εκπτωσις εστι ψυχης.</note> Simon, cited in the *Clementine Homilies*, 17, number 11, page 735.</margin> held a notion that God was not to be feared, but loved only. Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note> indeed represents it as a common opinion among heretics <margin>(q) "They deny that God is to be feared. Therefore, all things are free and unrestricted for them." <note>original Latin: Negant Deum timendum. Itaque libera funt illis omnia et foluta.</note> *On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 43, page 248B, page 213. 43.</margin> that God was not to be feared; from this, he infers that they were given up to all kinds of licentiousness <note>original: "licentiousness of manners"—habitual disregard for moral restraints, particularly regarding sexual conduct.</note>.

I therefore entirely agree with Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738), a French Protestant theologian who wrote extensively on the history of Manichaeism and Gnosticism.</note>, who <margin>(r) "It is very likely that this is what caused impure and profane manners to be attributed to the Basilidians and other Gnostics. What should one think of people who profess not to fear God?" <note>original French: Il est bien vraisemblable, que c'est la ce qui fit attribuer aux Bafilidiens, et aux autres Gnoftiques, de moeurs impures et profanes. Que doit on penfer de gens, qui font profeffion de ne point craindre Dieu.</note> *History of Manichaeism*, Vol. 2, page 32, note 7.</margin> thinks it highly probable that this led many to attribute immoral behavior to the Basilidians and other Gnostics. ...together with certain fumes and bindings <note>original: ligatures</note>. **Irenæus** (a) himself says that the Jews even *now use* this invocation—the name of God—to drive away demons. **Origen** (b) likewise informs us that the names of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, when joined to the name of God, have such power that they are used not only by the Jews in their prayers to God and in casting out demons, but also by all other exorcists. And in another place he asserts (c) that many use this expression, "the God of Abraham," to cast out demons without even knowing who Abraham was. 

If, therefore, **Justin Martyr**, **Irenæus**, and **Origen** believed the use of certain names to be so powerful in expelling demons, it is not at all improbable that the **Basilidians**—who undoubtedly were filled with the same notions of demonology that had overrun the whole world—should use the name of Jesus to deliver those whom they supposed to be possessed from the power of demons; or that they should regard baptism and faith as sufficient protection against their influence. But they ought not to be accused of magic on this account. Superstitious and faulty they undoubtedly were, but not more so than many of the Catholics <note>referring to the "orthodox" or mainstream church</note>. The magicians, says **Clement of Alexandria** (d), boast that they have demons as ministers of their impiety, and as it were enrolled in the number of their domestic servants; and they claim to force them to become their servants by their incantations.

### SECTION XV. Of the meaning of Caulacau, and his Definition of Faith and Hope.

<margin>Section 15.</margin>
The Basilidians use the word *Caulacau*, (e) and apply it to a person: Theodoret says (f) it refers to the Savior of the world. It is taken from Isaiah 28:10 (g) where we have—

***

(e) "Just as the name of the world is that in which they say the Savior descended and ascended, which is Caulacau. Therefore, he who learns these things, and knows all the angels and their causes, will himself become invisible and incomprehensible to all the angels and powers, just as Caulacau himself was." <note>original Latin: "Quemadmodum et mundus nomen esse, in quo dicunt descendisse et ascendisse salvatorem, esse Caulacau. Igitur qui hæc didicerit, et angelos omnes cognoverit, et causas eorum, invisibilem et incomprehensibilem eum angelis et potestatibus universis fieri, quemadmodum et Caulacau fuisse." From Irenaeus, Book 1, Chapter 23, pages 98, 99, edited by Grabe.</note> **Beausobre** would amend this passage—which **Grabe** says is corrupted—by changing "world" <note>original Latin: "mundus"</note> into "of the world" <note>original Latin: "mundi"</note>, and leaving out the first "to be" <note>original Latin: "esse"</note>. But he admits this will not agree with the following sentence, where *Caulacau* is attributed to a person and is not the name of the world. This matches what **Theodoret** says. I think a sense may be made out by reading in connection with the preceding context, as follows: "And next they endeavor to explain the names, elements, angels, and virtues of these 365 feigned heavens, as also the name of this world (that is, the name assigned it in their system of astronomy), into which the Savior descended and then ascended from it again, who himself was called Caulacau." The meaning then will be: they endeavor to explain the names, elements, angels, and virtues of these 365 feigned heavens, as also the name of this world into which the Savior descended and from which he ascended again, who was himself called *Caulacau*. He who knows all these angels and can explain their origin and causes will himself become invisible and incomprehensible to all these angels and powers, just as *Caulacau*, or the Savior himself, was.

(f) "And they call the Savior and Lord 'Caulacau'." <note>original Greek: "Τον δε σωτηρα και Κυριον Καυλακαυαν ονομαζουσι." From Theodoret, *Haereticarum Fabularum Compendium*, Book 1, Chapter 4, page 195. D.</note>

(g) The words in the original are "Line upon line, line upon line" <note>original Hebrew: "קו לקו קו לקו" (Kav lakav, kav lakav)</note>. If we consider this as derived from the Hebrew word *qawah* <note>original Hebrew: "קוה"</note>, meaning "to stretch out," it may metaphorically refer to the stretching of the mind toward an object, and therefore may signify hope or expectation. This is how the **Seventy** <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> understood it. And as the **Basilidians** were most prevalent in Egypt, they undoubtedly used this translation, and would therefore naturally understand the words in the sense given there. If understood in that sense and applied as a name to our Savior, it seems to imply what is asserted above.

### SECTION XVII. *On the Number, Expense, and Pagan Origin of those Gems called Abraxas.*

<margin>Section 17.</margin>They are, I say, very numerous. The collections that have been made of these things are very large, and many more may exist that are not yet discovered, while others are undoubtedly totally lost. Their high value <note>original: "costliness"</note> is evident in both their quantity and the materials used. They are indeed too significant to have been the production and possession of all the Christians of the first three centuries, even if every one of them had taken delight in such things. That they are pagan and Egyptian is obvious at first sight. And truly, Montfaucon <note>Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741), a French Benedictine monk and scholar who founded the discipline of palaeography</note> was right to place his illustrations of Abraxas immediately after his Egyptian deities. I put in the margin (1) some passages from him, acknowledging all these three particulars: their numbers, costliness, and pagan 

<columns>2</columns>
(1) I. Who would have thought that this monstrous religion would be adopted by men professing the Christian religion, and be mixed with its sacred mysteries? Who would have ever believed that the foolish and monstrous opinion of the most superstitious of all nations concerning the gods would be joined with the secret and most holy mysteries of the true religion? Yet that is what the Gnostics, Basilidians, and Valentinians did in the second century of the church. Irenaeus, Epiphanius, Jerome, and other fathers gave only a sample of this kind of heretical impiety; but the monuments left by those heretics which have survived to our age teach us many things which, lacking those clues, would have been buried in eternal oblivion. <note>original Latin: "Quis putaret portentofam illam religionem a viris chriſtianam religionem profitentibus adoptandam... <margin>(m) From that workshop, it seems, came that huge number of small stones seen in many European museums, a supply of which is being newly unearthed every day. SECTION 19. If the Basilidians made use of the word Abraxas, as it appears from Irenaeus (z) they did, it is very probable they applied it to the secrets <term>arcana: deep mysteries or specialized knowledge</term> of their philosophy, rather than to their theology. Jerome assures us (a) that it is the same as *Mithras*. Now, *Mithras* is the deity whom the Persians worship, representing the Sun. This immediately explains why Abraxas is said to be the chief of the 365 heavens, or the angels who reside in them and rule over the 365 days of the year. For the Sun, being the fountain of light and the immediate cause of day, may with great propriety be said to preside over all the days of the year. In the language of symbols <term>hieroglyphical: here meaning symbolic or metaphorical language, rather than Egyptian script</term>, he may also be said to contain within himself the parts of which the year is composed.

# BASILIDES.

<margin>SECTION 19.</margin>
...posed to rule over it. The word **Abraxas** is made up of those letters of the Greek alphabet which, in counting (b), have the numerical value of 365. It is therefore a technical term, very much in the spirit of Cabalistic <note>original: "cabbalistic"; referring to Jewish mystical traditions involving the secret meanings of numbers and letters</note> or Oriental philosophy. This, combined with that preference for hieroglyphics for which the Egyptians were famous, explains the symbolic figures that appear on several of those gems and stones called "Abraxas stones" by Montfaucon (c). There is, however, not enough evidence to prove that all his classifications are entitled to that name, because on very many of them, that word is not found. And there is even less proof that they belonged to the Basilidians.

1 + 2 + 100 + 1 + 60 + 1 + 200 = 365.
Mithras <note>original: Μειθρας</note> has the same numerical value. *See Spanheim, Ecclesiastical History of the Second Century on the Basilidians.*

(c) Outside the series of common forms used on coins and marbles, we place those used in amulets, commonly called *talismans*. Amulets of this kind, carved on gems and stones of various shapes and sizes, are also called Abraxas. They are seen in large numbers in various museums, and specifically not a few in ours, filled with monstrous figures, charms, and unusual characters... Indeed, these Basilidians, named after their founder Basilides, thought there were many powers <note>original: *virtutes*</note> and angels. The first and most important of these—and, as Epiphanius says, the highest power and origin of the angels—they called Abraxas. This is because these letters, when taken numerically, make 365: the number of days in which the sun completes its course... they counted the same number of powers... With these 365 powers

This is why they depict this power—Abrasax (often written as Abraxas)—with rays and other solar symbols on small stones and gems... Furthermore, they represent the sun through all these things. For the rooster <note>original: *Gallus Gallinaceus*</note>, as the herald of the sun, is a solar symbol. The whip is the tool for driving the solar horses; hence, on many such Abraxas gems, a four-horse chariot <term>quadriga: a chariot drawn by four horses abreast</term> is shown, driven by a youth with rays—specifically, the sun... In some places, Mithras (sometimes Mithrax) is also inscribed near the lion figure; this was the name by which the pagans <note>original: *gentiles*</note> called the sun. This worship spread from the Persians to the Romans and Greeks. <note>original Latin: *Extra seriem vulgarium... ad Romanos et Græcos emanaverat.*</note> *Montfaucon, Greek Paleography, Book 2, chapter 8, pages 177, 178.*

HISTORY of HERETICS:

### SECTION 20. The Gems called *Abraxaei* were used by the Heathens as Charms.

Everyone knows that in the system of ancient mythology, Apollo and the Sun were considered the same. Apollo was also the god (d) of healing. Because of this, and in the true spirit of hieroglyphics <note>symbolic picture-writing</note> and mythology, these gems were undoubtedly used by the heathens—and probably by some superstitious Christians who, having been only recently converted, still kept a taste for their former absurdities—as amulets or charms to drive away fevers <note>original: "agues"</note> and other diseases. It is not unlikely that such items were found among the orthodox Christians as well as among the Basilidians. In fact, the scholar Montfaucon acknowledges and proves this (e) by quoting Chrysostom <note>an influential 4th-century Church Father</note>, noting that long after the Basilidian heresy was extinct, the Christians at Antioch used to tie brass coins of Alexander the Great around their feet and heads to ward off or cure diseases. It is not surprising, then, that in Egypt—a country overrun with superstition—some of the new converts to Christianity weakly joined with the heathens in using charms and amulets.

<note>(d) "Medicine is my invention; I am called the helper throughout the world, and the power of herbs is subject to us" <note>original: "Inventum medicina meum est; opiferque per orbem Dicor: et herbarum subjecta potentia nobis"</note> — Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book 1, lines 521–522. [Montfaucon] says of those who use incantations and bindings, and who tie brass coins of Alexander the Great to their heads and feet: "Is this our hope? Shall we, after the cross and death of the Savior, place our hope in a king of a profane religion?" — *Montfaucon’s Antiquity Explained, p. 373.*</note>
<note>(e) That superstitious custom of wearing coins of Alexander the Great, as if they had some power to help, was common among the Christians of Antioch. Against this truly damnable custom, Chrysostom, in his second catechism to the people of Antioch, writes: "What should be said of those..." As we have seen above in the inscriptions on many small stones, they were intended to cure diseases. Delusions of this kind have been used in almost every century of Christianity. — *Ibid. 377, 378.*</note>

### SECTION 21. *The Christians accused of worshipping Serapis.*

<margin>Section 21.</margin> THIS appears to be based on fact, according to a letter from the Emperor Hadrian preserved by Vopiscus <note>original: "Adrian... Vopiscus"</note> <note>Flavius Vopiscus was one of the six traditional writers of the *Augustan History*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note> (f). At that time, it seems a common rumor had spread through Egypt that the Christians worshipped Serapis <note>Serapis was a Graeco-Egyptian god associated with healing and the afterlife.</note>. The letter (g) goes so far as to say that the Jews, the Samaritans, and the Christians—and even the chief leader of the synagogue, the Christian presbyters and bishops, and the Patriarch himself—worshipped Serapis as well as Christ. Had this accusation been confined to only a portion of the Christians or Jews, or had any specific group of heretics been mentioned, one might have thought it possible. But the charge is so general that it can never be true. We must therefore look for something in the customs of those times that would account for the rise of such a slander <note>original: "calumny"</note>. I believe the use of amulets—which likely prevailed among some Christians in Egypt, just as we know it later did in Antioch—explains it. The Emperor makes no mention of the Basilidians, but charges the Christians at large with the crime. It may therefore be attributed to the mainstream Christians <note>original: "catholics"</note> just as much as to them. The truth of the matter seems to be this: the Emperor knew very little about the Christians,

<margin>(f) *History of the Augustan Writers [Historiae Augustae Scriptores]*, Vol. 2, p. 719, etc. Leiden edition, 1671.</margin>

<margin>(g) In Egypt, a rumor and false accusation arose that the Christians worship Serapis. Wherefore Hadrian, in his letter found in Vopiscus, says: "Egypt, which you used to praise to me, my dearest Servianus, I have found to be entirely fickle, unstable, and flying at every breath of rumor. Those who worship Serapis are Christians; and those who call themselves bishops of Christ are devoted to Serapis. There is no ruler of a Jewish synagogue there, no Samaritan, no Christian presbyter, who is not also an astrologer <note>original: "Mathematicus"</note>, a soothsayer <note>original: "Aruspex"</note>, or a physical trainer <note>original: "Alyptes"</note>. Even the Patriarch himself, when he comes to Egypt, is forced by some to worship Serapis, and by others to worship Christ." *Montfaucon, Greek Palaeography, p. 178.*</margin>

### SECTION XXII. *An Examination of Montfaucon’s Figures.*

<margin>SECTION 22.</margin> By an examination of specific details, as given by Montfaucon <note>Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741) was a French monk and scholar who published a massive illustrated work on ancient antiquities.</note> himself, I shall clearly prove that these gems are of pagan origin. Many of the figures and inscriptions on them are extremely <note>original: "to the last degree"</note> obscene and idolatrous, and consequently could not be the production of any Christian sect whatever. They must be pagan, and for the most part Egyptian. "It appears to me," says Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738) was a prominent historian of early Christian sects.</note> (*b*), "altogether incredible that a sect which made profession of Christianity should have adopted the monsters worshipped by the Egyptians; or that a man who boasted of deriving his doctrine from Matthias <note>Matthias was the apostle chosen to replace Judas Iscariot.</note> and from an interpreter of Saint Peter, and who received the Gospels and the Epistles of Saint Paul, should make images of the Deity at a time when Christians had the most intense <note>original: "excessive"</note> aversion to all sorts of images, even the most innocent."

(*o*) I believe, therefore, that *Abraxas* or *Abrasax* is composed of two Greek words. Therefore, Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> did not consider it proof that these incantations belonged to Christians simply because the Hebrew names of the true God were mixed with others. On the contrary, he asserts (*u*) that they did not belong to any Christian sect, but rather to those who were outsiders to our common salvation—people who would never give the title of Savior, God, Master, or Son of God to Jesus. 

One of the gems of this fifth class, which has *Iao* on its front (*x*), is inscribed on the back with these words: “Grant me favor and victory because I have uttered your hidden and ineffable name.” This is based on a superstitious belief held among some Jews that whoever could correctly pronounce the name "Jehovah" <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter biblical name of the God of Israel.</note> had great favor with God and could even perform miracles. Therefore, this is more likely the work of a magician than an amulet belonging to any Christian sect. Montfaucon <note>Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741), a French scholar who studied ancient antiquities.</note> mentions (*y*) two items in this category that both bear the name Alexander. These are undoubtedly of pagan origin and were probably intended for the same purpose as those mentioned earlier, which the people of Antioch used to ward off diseases.

<margin>(u) "This does not belong to the Christian teachings, but to those who are strangers to salvation and who refuse to address Jesus as Savior, God, Teacher, or Son of God." <note>original Greek: *ω ὡ χριστιανων λογοσ, αλλα τουτη αλλοτρίων σωτηριας, και ιδαιωσ απηγορευμενων Ιησου, ἤ Σωτηροσ, ἤ Θεου, ἤ διδασκαλου, ἤ υιου Θεου.*</note> *Against Celsus*, book 6, p. 296, Cambridge edition; *Collected Works*, Vol. 1, p. 654, Benedictine edition.</margin>

### SECTION XXIV. *The origin of the superstitious custom of using Abrafadabra as a charm.*

<margin>SECTION 24.</margin>
It is not improbable that from this word *Abraxas* came the superstitious custom of writing the word *Abrafadabra* <note>modern: Abracadabra; the author notes the 'S' or 'C' variation later.</note> (*b*) upon a slip of paper in order to cure a semi-tertian fever <note>original: "semitertian ague," a form of malaria characterized by a fever that recurs every two days.</note>. The most ancient writer who speaks of this is Quintus Serenus Sammonicus (*c*), the tutor to the younger Emperor Gordian. He certainly did not profess Christianity, and from this, there is a strong probability that it was a pagan charm. Notwith- <note>catchword: Notwithstanding</note>

---

<margin>(*a*) It is established that these fictions of Basilides migrated from Egypt to Rome. For in these Basilidian gems, we sometimes see figures of Roman gods on one side, and those Abraxas names on the other; and in some, we see symbols of Latin and Egyptian gods mixed together. To this, Prudentius certainly seems to allude:

<margin>(*b*) One usually writes *Abraçada-bra*, but it should be written *Abrafadabra*. The 'C' in Greek inscriptions is an 'S' <note>The Greek letter sigma (Σ) was often written in a lunate form (C), which looks like a Latin 'C' but sounds like 'S'.</note>, as everyone knows. *Beausobre, History of Manichaeism, page 56, note.*</margin>

<margin>(*c*) More deadly is that which is commonly called *hemitritaeon* <note>a semi-tertian fever</note> in Greek; this our ancestors could not, I think, nor did they wish to, say in our own language. You write on paper what is called *Abrafadabra*, and repeat it more often below, but subtract the top letter, and let the individual elements be missing more and more from the shapes—which you will always take away, while keeping the rest—until the letters are reduced into a narrow cone. Remember to bind these to the neck with linen thread, etc.

## SECTION XXV. *Beaufobre's Observations on Chifflet, and Arguments against these Gems being Christian.*

<margin>SECTION 25.</margin>

He argues against these gems being the invention of the Basilidians for several reasons.

<margin>First, from the improbability of the thing.</margin>
First, it is simply incredible in itself that a follower of the religion of Jesus, and a philosopher, would create images of the Deity at a time when Christians had an unconquerable dislike for such figures—and especially that he would make such monstrous and indecent ones.

Secondly, he further argues from the silence of the Church Fathers who wrote against and refuted the Basilidians. Irenaeus does not say a single word about such customs. Should it be said that Irenaeus wrote in the West and therefore might not have been well acquainted with their customs in the East, Beaufobre observes that Clement, <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Church Father who lived in Egypt, where the Basilidians originated.</note>

->BASILIDES.<-

Clement of Alexandria, who lived in Alexandria—the very center of the Basilidian heresy—would certainly have noticed and criticized them for such impurity and gross idolatry if it had been common among them. Besides, as most of these antiquities are precious **stones**, they were not used merely as amulets, but as **seals** or **rings**. Clement, therefore, would have had reason to speak of such things in his *The Tutor* (*Pædagogue*) <note>original title: *Pædagogue*; a 2nd-century work by Clement of Alexandria providing a guide for Christian life and ethics.</note>. In that work, he mentions (f) and speaks out against unnecessary ornaments, particularly pearls and precious **stones**. The figures attributed to the Basilidians are engraved on these kinds of **stones**. As he never speaks out against these specific designs, or accuses the Basilidians of using them, it is most certain that they were not accustomed to having them.

To this may be added that in his treatise on the best manner of living (g), where he lays down rules concerning the rings which Christians may wear consistently with their profession, he strictly forbids their having on the **stones** or **seals** any representation of idol deities; because they are objects on which a Christian cannot even look without sin. He earnestly warns them against every representation that was contrary to decency and modesty. Could he then omit cautioning the faithful at Alexandria against the use of those abominable figures which are now attributed to the Basilidians? This is especially unlikely as he does not hesitate, on every fair occasion, to attack the followers of this sect. These figures have every characteristic of the things which he absolutely forbids: they are **idolatrous**, they are **immodest**, and they are **obscene to the last degree**.

### S E C T. XXVI. *Further Observations on Chifflet.*

<margin>Section 26.</margin> Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738), a French Protestant theologian known for his history of Manichaeism.</note>, after a detailed examination of many of the figures in Chifflet's <note>Jean-Jacques Chifflet (1588–1660), a scholar who published works on Gnostic gems.</note> work, observes that they actually disprove, rather than confirm, the system proposed by that writer. ### SECTION 28. *Conclusions Drawn from the Foregoing Observations.*

<margin>Section 28.</margin>Upon a review, therefore, of the whole of this long discourse concerning the Abraxas of the Basilidians and the figures which have been attributed to them, I cannot help concluding—very much in the words of Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738), a French Protestant theologian and influential historian of Gnosticism and Manichaeism.</note>—the following: 
1. That *Abraxas* was not the god of the Basilidians. 
2. That this name signifies nothing but the sun, which was never worshipped by them. 
3. That the figures found in both Chifflet <note>Jean-Jacques Chifflet (1588–1660), a physician and antiquary who wrote on "Abraxas" stones.</note> and Montfaucon <note>Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741), a Benedictine monk and pioneering scholar of ancient artifacts.</note> are for the most part Egyptian. 
4. That there is no kind of proof that any of them belonged to the Basilidians. 
5. That those which have *Iao*, *Sabaoth* <term>Hebrew names for God: Yahweh and "of Hosts," often used in ancient magical charms.</term>, etc., upon them were the works of magicians who never made any profession of Christianity. 
6. That some of these figures derived their origin from the Simonians and Ophites <term>Early Gnostic sects; the Simonians followed Simon Magus, and the Ophites were known for their veneration of the serpent.</term>, who were not Christians either in belief or profession.

# HISTORY OF HERETICS:

Sect. 29. opinions on many points. Marcion <margin>(r)</margin> received only the Gospel of St. Luke. Basilides certainly received the Gospel of St. Matthew; for there are several references to it in his explanations of doctrines or practices, which are given to us by Clement of Alexandria, <margin>(s)</margin> and there is no proof that he rejected the other three. Neither Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clement, Origen, nor Theodoret accuse him of this, or of rejecting any of Saint Paul’s epistles. On the contrary, there is positive evidence from the same Clement that Isidore, his son, <margin>(t)</margin> received the First Epistle to the Corinthians. And there is from Origen a clear proof to the contrary of what Jerome lays to his charge when he ranks Basilides with Marcion as a corrupter of the Gospel. For the former writer [Origen], in his answer to Celsus—who accused the Christians in general of corrupting the Scriptures—says <margin>(u)</margin> that he knew of no Christians who had altered the text of the Gospel, except the followers of Valentinus and Marcion, and perhaps those of Lucan. <note>Lucan, or Lucanus, was a follower of Marcion.</note> This confirms the explanation given later of that passage from Origen where mention is made of the "Gospel of Basilides": that Origen means nothing more by that expression than his commentaries upon the Gospel. Ambrose and Jerome copied this idea from Origen.

That Basilides paid great respect to the Gospel is evident from his writing *Commentaries* <margin>(x)</margin> upon it, which he divided into twenty-four books. Two fragments of these may be seen in Grabe, <margin>(y)</margin> one taken from the thirteenth and the other from the twenty-third book of these Commentaries. <note>John Ernest Grabe (1666–1711) was a scholar who published a collection of early Christian writings called the *Spicilegium*.</note>

Sect. 29.

## BASILIDES.

He also certainly accepted the epistle to the Romans, as appears from Origen’s Commentary upon the fifth chapter. There, Origen quotes the words of chapter 7, verse 9: *when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died.* Upon this he observes (z) that Basilides, without attending to the sense and connection of the passage, endeavored to deduce from the first part of the verse—namely, *I was alive without the law once*—his absurd and nonsensical notion of a Pythagorean metempsychosis <term>the belief in the transmigration of souls, or reincarnation</term>. Therefore, he must have allowed the authority of this epistle. 

Furthermore, as he is not accused of rejecting any other books of the New Testament—except by St. Jerome, and even then only in a cursory <note>original: "curſory"; brief or superficial</note> manner where his name is joined with that of Marcion—there is reason to believe that he accepted the whole New Testament as authentic. However, he perverted the meaning of many passages and drew very absurd and foolish conclusions from many others.

## SECT. XXX. Of the Gospel of Basilides.

<margin>SECT. 30.</margin>

<gloss>T</gloss>HERE is mention made in Origen’s Commentary (a) on Luke of a "Gospel of Basilides." Ambrose has spoken (b) of the same, as has Jerome (c) also. The two latter undoubtedly copied this information from Origen. The most probable opinion is that the twenty-four books of Commentaries, which Agrippa Castor speaks of, (d) were the very same work referred to as the "Gospel of Basilides."

(z) "I, says Paul, have died, for sin began to be reckoned to me." But Basilides, not noticing that these things ought to be understood as referring to the natural law, dragged the apostolic words toward absurd and impious fables into Pythagorean dogma: that is, he tries to establish from this saying of the apostle that souls are poured across into various other bodies <note>original: "Ego inquit (Paulus) mortuus ſum, coepit enim mihi jam reputari peccatum. Volume 2, p. 530. Basel, 1571.* See also Grabe, *Spicilegium*, Vol. 2, p. 43.

### SECT. XXXI. *Of the Prophets Barcabbas and Barcoph.*

<margin>SECT. 31.</margin> As for the prophecies of the prophets Barcabbas and Barcoph, or Parchor (h), these were undoubtedly some Eastern books that Basilides encountered during his journey into the East and brought back with him to Alexandria. They were not forgeries of his own creation, as Eusebius <note>A prominent 4th-century historian of the early Christian Church</note> would have us believe.

->BASILIDES<-

### SECTION 33. *These Things Prove the Authenticity and Wide Spread of the Scriptures of the New Testament.*

<margin>Section 33.</margin>
From this entire section, it appears that the writings of the New Testament were spread abroad among Christians at an early date, and that commentaries and expositions were very soon written on different parts of them, particularly on the Gospels. This tended to make knowledge of them more widespread and to keep them uncorrupted; because by this method, those who might try to falsify them in any way would be detected sooner and more easily.

### CHAPTER III.
Of Carpocrates and his Followers.

## SECTION I. Some Account of Carpocrates and Epiphanes from Clement of Alexandria and other ancient Authors.

SECTION I. We come now to the Carpocratians. I will examine their history and time, their general principles, their moral principles and conduct, and finally, their testimony regarding the Scriptures.

Clement of Alexandria <note>A prominent Christian theologian and teacher in Egypt during the late 2nd century.</note> speaks of them in these exact words: "The *(a)* followers of Carpocrates and Epiphanes believe that women should be held in common; a view which has brought much discredit to the Christian name." He informs us that Epiphanes—whose works are still in existence—was the son of Carpocrates, who was an Alexandrian. His mother’s name was Alexandria, and she was born on the island of Cephalonia <note>original: Cephalene</note>. Epiphanes lived to be only seventeen years old; after his death, he was honored as a god at Same <note>original: Sama</note> on the aforementioned island. There, they built a stone temple to him featuring altars, a grove, and a museum. Every new moon, on the day Epiphanes was consecrated, the people of Cephalonia gather and celebrate his birthday with hymns, drink offerings <note>original: libations</note>, sacrifices, and feasts. He was *(b)* instructed by his father in the full circle of sciences, particularly in Platonic philosophy.

# HISTORY OF HERETICS:

## SECTION I.
Regarding the Samaritan heresies <note>Early Christian writers often traced the roots of all heresies back to Simon Magus, a Samaritan mentioned in the Book of Acts.</note>, all these followed: the (g) Menandrians, the Marcionites, the Carpocratians, the Valentinians, the Basilidians, and the Saturnilians. It is now common for learned (i) modern scholars to consider him a Valentinian. Whether this is correct or not, I cannot pause to investigate.

### SECTION III. The *Additions* to Tertullian's *Book of Prescriptions* do not differ much (x) from the authors already quoted.

<margin>(x) "Carpocrates also started this sect. He says there is one primary power in the higher realms. Unam esse dicit virtutem in superioribus principalem: ex hac prolatos angelos, atque virtutes: quos distantes longe a superioribus virtutibus mundum istum in inferioribus partibus condidisse.* From *De Praescriptione Haereticorum*, chapter 48, p. 252.</note></margin>

### SECTION IV. On their Opinion regarding the Person of Jesus Christ.

Irenaeus immediately goes on to state what they thought of the person of Jesus: that (y) he was born of Joseph and was like other men, except that his soul was more firm <note>original: *firma*; in this context, it suggests a soul that is strong, stable, or intellectually resolute.</note> and pure, and that he remembered what he had seen while with the eternal Father <note>original: *ingenito Deo*; literally "the unbegotten God." This reflects the Gnostic idea that the soul pre-existed in a higher realm before birth.</note>. He says that Jesus was educated among the Jews and obtained power to surmount his sufferings, after which he ascended to the Father. He also taught that those souls who believed in him should do the same; that is, the ascent applies only to their souls.

<margin>(y) "Jesus was born of Joseph; and since he was like other men, he differed from them only in that his soul was firm and pure, and remembered what it had seen during its journey with the unbegotten God. Because of this, power was sent to him from the Father so that he might escape the world-makers <note>term: "world-makers" (Latin: *mundi fabricatores*). In Gnostic thought, these were the inferior angels or the Demiurge who created the physical world.</note> and ascend to him; and those who embrace similar beliefs would do the same. They say that the soul of Jesus, being raised in the Jewish tradition, despised their customs, and for this reason received the powers by which he abolished the suffering and passions that afflicted mankind." <note>original: *Jesum autem e Joseph natum, et cum similis reliquis hominibus fuerit, distante a reliquis secundum id, quod anima ejus firma et munda cum esset, commemorata fuerit quæ visa essent sibi in ea circumlatione, quæ fuisset ingenito Deo...* Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, p. 203.</note></margin>

Epiphanius says (z) their opinion concerning Christ was that he was born of Joseph and Mary, but excelled other men in temperance, and the holiness and virtue of his life. He also speaks of their belief that the mind of Christ possessed a wonderful strength or firmness, and that he remembered what he saw in his pre-existent state, and similar ideas. Theodoret...

<margin>(z) "He says regarding our Lord that he was born of Joseph, just as all men are from the seed of a man and a woman... but that he excelled in his life, in temperance, virtue, and righteousness. Because, he says, he had a soul more exalted than other men, etc." <note>original Greek: *Invenit de τ8 κεφ8 ημων απο ιωσηφ λεγει, γεγονεναι, καθώς και παντες ανθρωποι εν σπερματος ανδρος και γυναικος... βι8 δε διεννηχέναι, σωφροσύνη τε και αρετη και ειςα δια καιοσύνης. Επειδη δε, φησιν, τω παροι εχε υψωτην παρά τας αλλας ανθρωπ8ς, και λι.* Epiphanius, *Panarion* 27.11, p. 102.</note></margin>

From which he concludes— <note>original: *Christum non ex Virgine Maria natum, sed ex semine Joseph, hominem tantummodo genitum: sane præ ceteris justitiæ cultu, vitæ integritate meliorem: hunc apud Judæos passum: solam animam ipsius in cœlo receptam, eo quod et firmior et robustior ceteris fuerit. # HISTORY OF HERETICS:

<margin>Section 5.</margin> Some of them thought they might excel Jesus. Others, who did not go so far, still supposed they might excel Peter, Andrew, Paul, and the other apostles. Theodoret, in a similar way, says that *(f)* if any man had a purer soul than that of Jesus, he might excel the Son himself. Tertullian *(g)* also speaks of this notion of theirs; though, perhaps, after all, it is only a consequence drawn by critics from their opinion concerning Christ—specifically, the belief that he was a mere man. At least, there may be reason to suspect that their viewpoint is not being presented in the best light <note>original: "not expressed to advantage"</note>. At the most, it seems not to be a positive assertion, but a hypothetical case: supposing a man were to have a very pure soul, and that he despised this world and its possessions, and remained steadily virtuous in very trying circumstances, he might equal, and in some respects excel, Christ and his apostles. That this was only said for the sake of argument is evident from the fact that they thought Jesus greatly excelled all men in capacity, firmness of mind, and holiness of life—though others may resemble him, as all good Christians will allow.

| (f) "If anyone should have a purer soul," he says, "he will even surpass the dignity of the Son." <note>original: Ει δε και καθαρωτεραν τις σχοιη ψυχην, υπερβησεται, φησι, και τε υιου την αξιαν. p. 196. B.</note> | (g) "But Carpocrates also claims so much for himself from those above, that his disciples already both equal and, when they wish, prefer their own souls to Christ, let alone the apostles; which they have conceived from a sublime virtue, a despiser of the world’s powerful principalities." <note>original: *Sed et Carpocrates tantundem sibi de superioribus vindicat, ut discipuli ejus animas suas jam et Christo, nedum apostolis, et peraequent, et cum volunt, praeferant: quas perinde de sublimi virtute conceperint, despectrice mundi potentium principatuum. De Anim. c. 23. p. 325. B. p. 275. 5.*</note> |

...Homer, Pythagoras, and other philosophers, and that they honor them with incense and worship. However, it is notable that both in his (n) summary and his larger work, he (o) says that they possessed or honored these images and pictures only in private. Perhaps, therefore, this story is not true—or at least not entirely. If they possessed pictures of the philosophers as well as of Jesus, it is likely they paid him superior respect. As for the claims regarding incense and other superstitious rites, these may be complete fiction.

### SECT. VIII. *A general View of what they believed.*

<margin>SECT. 8.</margin>
From all this, we now perceive that the Carpocratians believed in one God, eternal and incomprehensible, who created angels and powers of various orders. This lower and visible world was created by some of these powers <note>Gnostic groups often believed that the physical world was created by lesser spiritual beings (demiurges) rather than the supreme God.</note>. They maintained that Jesus was the son of Joseph and Mary, and that he possessed a most pure soul of great capacity and understanding. This soul retained the memory of things he had seen while with the Father, which (p) he then revealed to humanity here on earth. They believed he performed miracles and excelled in holiness and all virtue. He lived among the Jews and suffered death, after which his soul ascended to heaven and returned to God. We see as well that they believed in the pre-existence of human souls and expected only the salvation of the soul, rather than the resurrection of the body.

### SECT. IX. *They are accused of asserting there is no Difference in the Nature of Things.*

<margin>Sect. 9.</margin>

<header>HISTORY OF HERETICS:</header>

### SECTION 11. The utter improbability of these accusations shown from a variety of considerations.

Now after all this, what can be said? The Carpocratians are in so much discredit that it must be risky to say anything tending to soften the criticisms <note>original: "censures"</note> that have been passed upon them. 

Nevertheless, I believe there are people in the world with enough fairness <note>original: "candour"</note> to be willing to hear what may be argued on their behalf.

1. I assume, then, that what was previously said—showing that heretics were not the cause of the slanders <note>original: "calumnies"</note> cast upon the early Christians—must reduce the conviction that the charges against the Carpocratians are definitely true.

2. I have not observed any stain <note>original: "blot"</note> on the personal characters of Carpocrates or Epiphanes. Carpocrates was a very learned man who had a wife and one son. He educated the boy himself, and he proved to be a remarkable person in terms of learning.

3. While we are told that they claimed there was no difference in things (that is, no moral distinction between actions), there are considerations which may satisfy us that this is not a true account. Such a claim is inconsistent with their opinion concerning Christ, who, as they said, excelled in virtue and holiness of life, and possessed a much better and stronger mind than any other man. Some of them even said that if any man were to have a purer soul and to despise the world more than Christ did, he might even surpass him. This shows that they placed a high value upon virtue. Moreover, according to Irenaeus, they said Christ had taught that nothing is necessary for salvation but faith and love (or charity). These, therefore, were necessary. Consequently, they did not say that all things were indifferent or alike—neither good nor evil.

In their view of *faith and love*, they seem to have included every branch of moral righteousness. When they added that Christ said all other things were indifferent, they likely meant specifically the ceremonial laws <note>original: "positive rites"</note> of the law of *Moses*. These laws were neither good nor evil in themselves before the divine appointment; Christ did not speak of their ending <note>original: "abrogation"</note> as clearly and *publicly* as he did about other necessary things, which is why the early Christians formed very different opinions about them.

4. Clement and others say that Carpocrates and Epiphanes taught the "community of women" <note>The practice of sharing wives among a group.</note>. As proof, he quotes a passage from Epiphanes. Shortly afterward, Clement observes that some think Plato taught the same doctrine. But those who hold that opinion, he says, are mistaken. He only says that (c) women are available <note>original: "common"</note> before marriage, so that men may choose from among them and seek whichever one they please in marriage <note>original Greek: "It seems to me that someone misunderstood Plato's Republic, claiming that women are common for those who are about to marry, just as the theater is common to the spectators." (Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, Book 3, p. 430. D.)</note>. If this meaning can be applied to Plato's words, why might a similar explanation not clear Epiphanes? That some passages from the ancient heretics were unclear and liable to be misunderstood may appear from a passage by Isidore, cited by Epiphanius (d). According to Epiphanius's interpretation, this passage contains a disgusting <note>original: "execrable"</note> lack of moral principle, teaching men to commit sexual immorality <note>original: "lewdness"</note> and then claim they have suffered no harm <note>original: "received no damage"</note> from it. ### SECTION XII. *What Scriptures they received.*

The evidence regarding their testimony to the scriptures will be brief. Epiphanius, in his summary, says they (i) rejected the Old Testament. Perhaps they did. But I do not know that to be certain. Possibly, however, the fact was only that they did not respect the instructions of Moses and the Prophets as much as <note>original: "equally with"</note> those of Christ and his Apostles.

Tillemont says they (k) received the Gospel of Saint Matthew and refers to Epiphanius, who says that (l) Cerinthus and Carpocrates endeavored to prove from the beginning of that gospel that Jesus was born of Joseph and Mary. Irenaeus says they (m) endeavored to pervert those words of our Lord which are in Matthew 5:25–26 and Luke 12:58. But I suspect <note>original: "apprehend"</note> that they received not only that gospel, but the other gospels likewise, and all the other books of the New Testament, as they were received by other Christians in their time. For Irenaeus says they gloried in Christ as their master. They believed that he came from God, or that having taught the will of God on earth and died, he ascended to heaven. They appear, from passages previously quoted, to have respected Peter and Paul and all the Apostles of Jesus. It is likely, therefore, that they received their writings. It is manifest from Irenaeus’s...

## CHAP. IV.
### OF CERINTHUS.
#### SECT. I. *Ancient Authors who speak of Cerinthus.*

<margin>Sect. I.</margin>As the dates of Cerinthus's life are uncertain, I shall immediately transcribe the passages of various <note>original: "divers"</note> authors concerning him, beginning with Irenaeus, for the sake of his antiquity.

<margin>(a) And a certain Cerinthus in Asia taught that the world was not made by the primary God, but by a certain power very separate and distant from that principal authority which is over the universe, and ignorant of the God who is over all. He suggested that Jesus was not born of a virgin (for this seemed impossible to him); that he was the son of Joseph and Mary, in the same way as all other men, but was more powerful in justice, prudence, and wisdom than other men. And that after his baptism, the Christ descended into him from that principal authority which is over all in the form of a dove, and then he announced the unknown Father and performed miracles. At the end, however, the Christ flew away again from Jesus, and Jesus suffered and rose again; but the Christ remained incapable of suffering <note>original: "impassible"</note>, being spiritual. Irenaeus, Book 1, chapter 26 (otherwise 25), page 105. Greek edition: page 102. <note>original Latin: "Et Cerinthus autem quidam in Asia, non a primo deo factum esse mundum docuit..."</note></margin>And (a) <term>Cerinthus</term> in <term>Asia</term> taught that the world was not made by the supreme God, but by a certain power, separate from him, much below him, and ignorant of him. Once again, that learned and pious ancient writer says that (*i*) John, the disciple of the Lord, wrote his Gospel to refute the doctrine recently taught by Cerinthus, and much earlier by those called Nicolaitans (a branch of the Gnostics <note>original: "who are a branch of that which is falsely called knowledge [Gnosis]"</note>), and to show that there is one God who made all things by his word. He intended to show that it is not as they say—that there is one being who is the Creator and another who is the Father of our Lord; and that there is one who is the Son of the Creator, and another, the Christ, who descended from above upon the Son of the Creator, remained incapable of suffering <term>impassible: unable to feel pain or change; a technical theological term</term>, and finally returned to his *pleroma* or fullness. St. Jerome (*k*) says something to a similar effect concerning the reason for St. John writing his Gospel.

Let us now consider Epiphanius’s account. His summary is to this purpose: the (*l*) Cerinthians, also called Merinthians, are Jews (or of Jewish descent) who pride themselves on circumcision. They claim that the world was created by angels, and that Jesus became the Christ through his growth in virtue.

In his larger work, he says that (*m*) like the Carpocratians, they say Jesus was the biological son of Joseph and Mary, and that the world was made by angels. Indeed, they differ little or nothing from them, except that they (*n*) are in favor of observing Jewish rites, at least in part. They say that the law and the prophets proceeded—
