# CERINTHUS

<margin>Section 1.</margin>

Once more, that learned and pious ancient [Irenaeus] says that (i) John, the disciple of the Lord, wrote his Gospel to refute the doctrine recently taught by Cerinthus—and much earlier by those called Nicolaitans <note>The Nicolaitans were an early Christian sect mentioned in the Book of Revelation, often associated with Gnosticism</note>, a branch of the Gnostics <note>Gnostics: a group of early religious movements that emphasized secret knowledge (gnosis) and often distinguished between a supreme God and a lesser creator of the physical world</note>. He sought to show that there is one God who made all things by his word, and not, as they claim, that the Creator is one being and the Father of our Lord another. They also claim that the Son of the Creator is one person, while "the Christ" is another—a being from the higher realms who descended upon the Son of the Creator, remained incapable of suffering <term>impassible: a theological term meaning unable to feel pain, change, or emotion</term>, and at length returned to his *pleroma* <term>pleroma: a Greek word meaning "fullness," referring to the totality of divine powers in Gnostic theology</term>. St. Jerome (k) says something similar concerning the reason for St. John writing his Gospel.

Let us now consider Epiphanius’s account. His summary is to this effect: the (l) Cerinthians (also called Merinthians) are Jews, or of Jewish descent, who pride themselves on circumcision. They claim that the world was created by angels and that Jesus became "the Christ" through his growth in virtue.

In his larger work, he says that (m) like the Carpocratians <note>The Carpocratians were a 2nd-century Gnostic sect who believed in the transmigration of souls and that Jesus was the biological son of Joseph</note>, they claim Jesus was born of Joseph and Mary and that the world was created by angels. Indeed, they differ little or nothing from them, except that they (n) favor observing Jewish rites, at least in part. They say that the law and the prophets proceeded

# HISTORY of HERETICS:

**SECTION 1.** In this way, Cerinthus became the author of another heresy or sect. Having spent a long time in Egypt studying philosophy, he eventually traveled to Asia and gathered disciples whom he named after himself (the Cerinthians). He taught that there is one (d) God over all. However, he claimed that this God did not create the world; instead, it was created by other powers that were separate from Him and ignorant of His existence. 

He maintained, as was common among Jewish thought at the time, that Jesus was the biological son of Joseph and Mary. However, he believed Jesus surpassed all other men in wisdom, self-control <note>original: "temperance"</note>, righteousness, and every virtue. He taught that "the Christ" <note>interpreted by Cerinthus as a divine spirit or power</note> descended upon Jesus from above in the form of a dove. After this, Jesus preached about the previously unknown God and performed the miracles recorded in the Gospels. Cerinthus further claimed that at the time of his suffering <note>original: "passion"</note>, the Christ departed from him, so that only the human Jesus suffered. 

He fabricated several "revelations" that he claimed to have seen himself, adding various warnings and threats. He taught that the Lord’s kingdom would be terrestrial (on earth), where Christ would reign. He envisioned a thousand-year period in Jerusalem characterized by eating, drinking, marriage, sacrifices, and festivals. 

He believed the Lord’s kingdom would last for that duration. Many writers opposed him, including the authors mentioned previously, as well as Caius and Dionysius, the Bishop of Alexandria. There is also a famous story that the Apostle John (the author of the Gospel), once went to a bathhouse and saw Cerinthus there. John supposedly said, "Let us flee from here, lest the bathhouse collapse because Cerinthus is inside, and we perish along with him."

<margin>(d) He taught that there is one God over all. He said that Jesus was born naturally of a man and a woman, Joseph and Mary, similar to the Jews, but excelled in self-control, justice, and other virtues. He claimed the Christ descended on him in the form of a dove, and then he preached the unknown God and performed miracles. At the time of his suffering, the Christ departed, while Jesus endured the suffering. He fabricated certain revelations as if he had seen them himself and included various threats, saying the Lord's kingdom would be on earth. <note>original Greek: ένα μεν είναι τον των ολων θεος... H. T. l. 2. c. 2. p. 219. This refers to Theodoret's *Haereticarum Fabularum Compendium* (Compendium of Heretical Fables).</note></margin>

It also recounts the famous anecdote of the Apostle John fleeing a bathhouse to avoid him.</summary>

### SECTION 2. Observations Regarding the Time of Cerinthus.

I now proceed to make some remarks. Other authors have spoken <term>sect. 2.</term> of <term>Cerinthus</term>. However, I hope to include their accounts within the following observations.

One thing is very noticeable: these three learned writers vary significantly. <term>Epiphanius</term> and <term>Theodoret</term> say various things about <term>Cerinthus</term> which <term>Irenaeus</term>, the most ancient source, does not mention. So that I may not omit any important detail, I shall consider the time and history of <term>Cerinthus</term>, then his beliefs <note>original: "sentiments"</note>, next his conduct <note>original: "manners"</note>, and lastly the scriptures he accepted.

<term>Baronius</term> <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607) was an Italian cardinal and ecclesiastical historian</note> discusses <term>Cerinthus</term> across several years of the first century, not long after our Savior's ascension. <term>Le Clerc</term> places him at the year 80, and <term>Basnage</term> at the year 101, in their respective church histories. By some, he is considered a heretic of the first century, and by others of the (e) second century. It is noteworthy that <term>Epiphanius</term> places the <term>Cerinthians</term> after the <term>Carpocratians</term>. Furthermore, <term>Irenaeus</term> suggests that the doctrine of the <term>Cerinthians</term> had been taught long before by the <term>Nicolaitans</term>. <term>Theodoret</term>, in a passage not yet cited, says it (f) was reported that <term>Cerinthus</term> sowed the seeds of his principles while the excellent evangelist <term>John</term> was still living. This implies that <term>Cerinthus</term> did not emerge in the early days of the apostles, but only a short time before the death of St. <term>John</term>.

<note>(e) "I am not now disputing Cerinthus's age, which at least in terms of the spreading of his error seems more recent than John, as will be shown below... Indeed, we have little doubt that Cerinthus only appeared in the second century, and certainly not before [the emperors] Hadrian or Antoninus Pius." (original Latin: *Non disputo nunc de Cerinthi aetate, quae saltem quoad erroris propalationem Joanne recentior videtur...*) Lampe, *Prolegomena*, p. 69, 182, 184, 186.</note>

<note>(f) "And they say that Cerinthus, while the most excellent and famous author of the divine Gospel [John] was still surviving, sowed the weeds of his own heresy." ### SECTION III. *Observations tending to illustrate his History.*

<margin>Section 3.</margin> As for his history, there is scarcely any one thing in which the three previously mentioned writers of histories on heresy agree, except for this: that he was from Asia, or that he lived there primarily. Epiphanius speaks much of the opposition made by Cerinthus to the apostles regarding the requirement of circumcision. However, the other two writers say nothing of this. Furthermore, the truth of this claim is disputed by some learned modern scholars, particularly (k) Basnage and (l) Lampe. They argue that there was no need for any specific leader in that affair, as it stemmed from the prevailing sentiments of the Jewish people, especially the Pharisees,

They might speak of Jesus as a man only, even if they believed him to be born of a virgin. Epiphanius, in his article on the Alogians <note>A group that rejected the Gospel of John and the concept of the "Logos" or Word.</note>, having observed Matthew's account of our Lord being born of a virgin and that he was descended from David and Abraham, says: "hence (s) Cerinthus and Ebion argue that Jesus was a mere man, as do also Merinthus, and Cleobius (or Cleobulus), and Claudius, and Demas and Hermogenes." But what reason has Epiphanius to ascribe to all these—particularly to Demas and Hermogenes—the same opinion that he sometimes ascribes to Cerinthus: that Jesus was born as other men are? However, if they received the genealogy in Matthew, as he says they did, (t) they might argue that Jesus was truly a man, but they must have acknowledged that he was born of a virgin.

### HISTORY OF HERETICS:

<margin>Section 4.</margin> They accepted that the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> descended upon Jesus at his baptism. This is consistent with our Gospels. However, they likely did not view the Holy Spirit as a person, but as a power, as Epiphanius describes it. Regarding the claim that the Holy Spirit, or "the Christ," was incapable of suffering <term>impassible: Incapable of suffering or feeling pain.</term> and left Jesus to suffer alone, their actual opinion may simply have been that the divine nature in Jesus—the power that came down upon him at baptism and by which he performed miracles—did not suffer.

Irenaeus and Epiphanius, in the passages cited earlier, stated explicitly that Jesus rose again after he had suffered; Theodoret does not deny this. Nevertheless, in another passage, he says they (u) believed that Christ—or rather Jesus, who suffered and was crucified—had not yet risen, but would rise again during the general resurrection of the dead. Philaster and Augustine (x) say the same. I cannot tell what they meant by this, but I consider the earlier account to be correct: that they said Jesus had already risen. Regardless, we have further proof here that these people believed in the resurrection of the dead. In this belief, they also differed from those called Gnostics <note>Gnostics generally rejected the idea of a physical resurrection of the body, focusing instead on the liberation of the soul.</note>.

He was zealous for circumcision and the rites of the Mosaic law, as Epiphanius states repeatedly, though Irenaeus and Theodoret do not mention this. It is somewhat strange that he would be so zealous for the law if he also taught that the world was created by angels and that the God of the Jews (who delivered the law) was not the supreme God, but only an angel. According to Jerome, Cerinthus's primary error was (y) his attempt to combine the law with the gospel.

Translation: "...having suffered and been crucified, [he] has not yet risen, but is destined to rise when the general resurrection of the dead takes place." Heretical Fables, Book 2, Chapter 3.</note>
(x) <note>See page 150, notes (p) and (q).</note>

<header>Section 4.</header>

# CERINTHUS.

Once more, Cerinthus is supposed to have been a Millenarian <term>Millenarian: A person who believes that Christ will reign in person on earth for a thousand years (the Millennium) before the final judgment.</term>. So says Theodoret, though neither Irenaeus nor Epiphanius make any mention of it. What Theodoret says must have been taken from the works of Caius and Dionysius, or the extracts from them in Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, of which we gave a large account (*x*) formerly. This is also mentioned (*a*) by Augustine. However, Philaster and the author of the appendix to Tertullian are silent on this head, and Le Clerc (*b*) seems scarcely convinced that this error is rightly attributed to him.

Unde etiam Chiliastæ sunt appellati. H. 8."</note></margin>

<margin>(b) Caius, who flourished toward the end of the second or beginning of the third century, reported in a dialogue (quoted by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 3, chapter 28) that Cerinthus—who through revelations written as if by a great apostle forged portents as if shown to him by angels—introduced this doctrine. In it, he affirms that after the resurrection, the kingdom of Christ will be on earth, and that the flesh, returning to Jerusalem, will again be enslaved to desires and pleasures. Indeed, he said that this enemy of the divine scriptures, wishing to deceive, claimed that a period of a thousand years would be spent in marriage feasts. <margin>(c) The morals of Cerinthus were no more holy than his doctrine, according to Dionysius of Alexandria. For this was his opinion: that the kingdom of Christ would be earthly. And those things for which he himself burned with desire—being subject to the pleasures of the body and addicted to the flesh—he dreamed the kingdom of God would consist of: in the satisfying of the lust of the belly and those parts below the belly; that is, in food, drink, and marriages. And so that he might veil such pleasures with a more honorable name, he claimed they would occur in festivals, sacrifices, and the slaughtering of victims. <note>original: "Non erant Cerinthi mores... in festis, et sacrificiis, et hostiarum mactionibus. Besnage Annales. An. 101. XI."</note></margin>

### SECTION VI. What Scriptures were received.
Cerinthus accepted the scriptures of the Old Testament. Of this, I believe, there can be no doubt, as it is not denied by anyone. It is clearly assumed by those writers who speak of his zeal for the specific requirements of the Law of Moses.

<header>CERINTHUS. SECTION 6.</header>

There is also reason to question the truth of this claim, based on what <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD) was a bishop and a staunch opponent of heresy; his works are a primary, though sometimes biased, source for early church history.</note> Epiphanius himself says elsewhere. For (r) he informs us there was a tradition that when some of them had died without baptism, others were baptized on their behalf, for fear that when they were raised at the general resurrection in the future, they might be punished for that failure. It was supposed that St. Paul refers to this practice in 1 Corinthians 15:29. <note>The verse asks, "Otherwise, what will they do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why then are they baptized for the dead?" This remains one of the most debated passages in the New Testament.</note> But he says there is another and better interpretation of that text. He afterwards (s) argues against them using the Book of Isaiah and the Gospels of St. Luke and St. John, which seems to imply that they respected these parts of Scripture as well as the Gospel of Matthew, some of St. Paul's writings, and the Revelation of St. John. Upon the whole, then, it appears highly probable that Cerinthus flourished in the late first or very early second century. And it is certain that the Old Testament and several of the books of the New Testament were received by him.

#### *Of Prodicus and his Followers.*

### SECTION I. *Of the Account of him from Clement of Alexandria.*

<margin>Section 1.</margin>Prodicus is missing from the works of Irenaeus, the additions to Tertullian's *Prescriptions*, Eusebius, and Philaster. From this, as well as from some other passages in Clement, we see that there was a sect or heresy named after Prodicus.

They say they are by nature the children of the supreme deity. But they dishonor their high birth and freedom. For they live

(*d*) What Theodoret further says will be considered when we come to speak of the Adamians <note>The Adamians or Adamites were a sect that reportedly practiced religious nudity, claiming to have returned to Adam’s state of innocence.</note>. What I have noted here was observed long ago by Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a French philosopher and author of the "Historical and Critical Dictionary."</note>, whose words under the entry "Prodicus" are these: "I ought to add, that with regard to another circumstance, Theodoret

He makes him say of Prodicus what is properly and directly said of some others, and cannot be applied to him except in general, and by means of several indirect arguments." In another place, he (§) joins Prodicus with Carpocrates, the Cainites <note>The Cainites were a Gnostic sect that allegedly revered Cain as the first victim of the Demiurge (the creator god of the Old Testament).</note>, and some others, and says, "They taught that souls were sent into this world to practice all manner of sensuality and iniquity, and by such pursuits, to pay homage to the angels who had created the world." It is very apparent then, that the authority of Theodoret is not additional to that of Clement; for what he says concerning Prodicus, he takes from him, and does not even quote him fairly.

## SECTION III. 
### *Observations on the Account given to us by Clement of Alexandria <note>original: "Clemens Alexandrinus"</note>, which make it probable they were not such licentious people <note>original: "Livers"</note> as they are said to have been there.*

<margin>SECTION 3.</margin>
1. It is hard to believe that men could be quite as bad as is suggested there, who boasted of serving God and who claimed to excel the Gentiles <note>In this context, non-Christians or pagans.</note> and people of the world. It does not seem likely to me that men could be totally abandoned to every excess if Clement thought it worthwhile to argue with them so mildly, yet forcefully, as he does using the words of St. Paul, St. John, and likewise our Lord (which I have omitted in the previously cited passage). He seems to have been of the opinion that these men would be influenced by this argument, which is more than could be hoped for from men who were openly or determinedly wicked and immoral <note>original: "profligate"</note>.

2. It is somewhat probable that Clement did not know for certain that they allowed themselves to practice those things which are generally agreed to be evil. For he only says they did them in private and tried to hide that knowledge from the world.

3. The situation seems to me to be this: These men held certain principles and used certain expressions that could be misinterpreted—or which Clement thought might be misinterpreted—and understood as supporting the practice of wickedness. However, they likely did not see that consequence, nor did they intend for such deductions or conclusions to be drawn from their doctrine. Even if there were nothing more to be alleged <note>original: "alledged"</note> in favor of this than what has already been said, this observation might still be considered to have some degree of probability.

## SECT. IV.
### *They are accused of believing the uselessness of Prayer.*

I proceed to another passage. Clement is discussing prayer. Some, he says, <note>original Greek: "Ει δε τινες και ωρας τακτας απονεμουσι ευχης..." — "But if some assign fixed hours for prayer, such as the third, sixth, and ninth... yet the Gnostic prays throughout his whole life." *Stromata* book 7, page 722.</note> have appointed times of prayer—the third, sixth, and ninth hours of the day, for instance. But a Gnostic <note>A term used by Clement to describe the "true" Christian who possesses deep spiritual knowledge.</note> prays throughout his whole life. Here, he says, <note>original Greek: "Ενταυθα γνομενος, υπωπιαθη, την περι τω μη δει ευχεσθαι..." — "Arriving at this point, I am reminded of those who say one must not pray... specifically this [sect] of [Prodicus]."</note> I am reminded of others with a different opinion, particularly the sect of Prodicus, who say we do not need to pray at all. This, then, is another opinion attributed to these people: that prayer is needless. 

Clement immediately adds that they should not boast of this impious opinion as if it were a new invention of their own; it was the opinion of the Cyrenaic philosophers <note>A Greek school of philosophy that emphasized pleasure as the supreme good and often held skeptical views on traditional religion.</note> before them. Tillemont <note>original French: "Ce qu'ils avoient tiré des philosophes Cyrenaiſciens." — "Which they had taken from the Cyrenaic philosophers." From Tillemont’s *Memoires Ecclesiastiques*, Volume 2, regarding the Carpocratians.</note> says they learned it from the Cyrenaic philosophers, but that does not appear to be Clement's meaning. 

It does not, I think, clearly appear what their specific error was. Clement proceeds to argue the point, but he does not argue as if he thought them to be wicked or abandoned men. Their opinion, whatever it was, seems to have been deduced from certain notions of the divine goodness and from a misapplication of some texts of Scripture. They likely believed that good men did not need to ask, but might hope for all necessary things without particular petitions or express requests for them. Therefore Clement argues...

<margin>SECTION 4.</margin> He argues in this manner: (1) It is universally agreed that God fully knows who is worthy of receiving good things and who is not. ### SECTION VI. They are accused of denying the necessity of suffering for religion.

**T**ertullian says that (*m*) Prodicus was against men exposing themselves to danger in the profession of religion <note>original: "profession of religion"; this refers to the public declaration or practice of one's faith, especially during times of Roman persecution.</note>. ### SECTION VII. Of the time and general character of Prodicus and his followers.

<margin>Section 7.</margin>
**H**aving examined all these passages, we may perhaps form a conjecture about the time and general character of this sect, the followers of Prodicus, even though we do not have very exact accounts of their specific principles. They are not mentioned by any original writers except <term>Clement</term> <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150 – c. 215 AD).</note> and Tertullian. As for <term>Theodoret</term> <note>A 5th-century bishop and historian who wrote about various Christian sects.</note>, he relies solely on Clement for his information and is inaccurate in that article. Prodicus and his followers are generally supposed to be successors of the <term>Carpocratians</term> <note>A 2nd-century Gnostic sect known for their radical views on social norms and religious law.</note>.

### CHAPTER VI.

#### *Of the Adamians or Adamites.*

### SECTION I. *The Accounts of these People from Epiphanius and Austin.*

<margin>SECTION I.</margin>
According to Epiphanius’s summary (*a*), the Adamians meet together, men and women, as naked as they were born. In this state, they perform readings, prayers, and other acts of religious worship. I have transcribed a portion of Augustine's <note>original: "Austin's"; a common historical shortening of Augustine.</note> article in the margin (*c*), as he follows the same summary.

When they arrive at the door, both men and women remove their clothes and enter the meeting place naked. Their leaders and teachers do the same, and they sit together without distinction of gender. In this naked state, they perform their readings and other religious rites. Among them are those who profess celibacy and virginity, and...

### SECTION II. *Arguments suggesting that such heretics never actually existed.*

### SECTION 2.
These are the Adamites. I believe the following considerations will demonstrate that such a group never truly existed.

1. They are not mentioned by any ancient writer before Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop known for his "Panarion," a catalog of 80 heresies.</note>, as far as I can recall—not by Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Eusebius, Philaster, or any others.

2. Epiphanius had no certain knowledge or reliable account of them, as he explicitly admits multiple times. He had (*g*) heard reports about them from many people, but he had never been personally acquainted with any of them. Nor had he found any written record of them. Furthermore, he (*h*) did not know whether such people still existed at that time, or whether the description that had been provided to him

Is this not enough to satisfy us that there never were any Adamites? ### SECTION III. *An Objection regarding the Practice of the Gnostics, and Answers.*

<margin>SECTION 3.</margin>
It may be objected here that, in another place, Epiphanius says the ($i$) Gnostics prayed naked; therefore, there must have been people who could be called Adamites.

To which I answer:

1. That the Gnostics and the Adamites are not the same sect or people. According to Epiphanius, the Gnostics were an immoral <note>original: "vicious"</note> people and practiced lewdness in their assemblies. But he does not make any such charge against those whom he calls Adamians. These, as he represents them, endeavored to imitate Adam and Eve not only in their nakedness but also in the innocence of their original state in Paradise.

Another point which fully shows that the Gnostics and Adamians are quite different is that Epiphanius had never encountered any written accounts of the latter, nor had he known any of them personally.

2. What Epiphanius says of the Gnostics is not true. To use the words of Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738) was a French Protestant theologian known for his history of Manichaeism.</note>, Clement (k) of Alexandria was well acquainted with the Gnostics, especially those of Egypt. This behavior does not match the boldness <note>original: "impudence"</note> of men who supposedly practiced total nakedness during divine service.

#### *Of Marcus and his Followers, called Marcosians.*

### SECTION I. *Of his Time, his Country, and the Sect from which he sprang.*

# MARCUS

<margin>Section 1.</margin>Many learned modern scholars are of the opinion that (k) Marcus belonged to the Valentinian school, merely making some alterations to the systems of Valentinus, and Ptolemy and Colorbasus, his immediate predecessors and masters. They seem to have good reason for this view from (l) Irenaeus himself and (m) from Tertullian. Nor should Jerome <note>original: "Jerom"</note> be considered to disagree, even though he calls Marcus (n) a "Basilidian Gnostic." Nevertheless, (o) Rhenferd and (p) Beausobre say the Marcosians were Jews, or Judaizing Christians. (q) Grabe likewise admits that they were of Jewish descent.

It may be argued that Marcus was an Asiatic, because Irenaeus speaks of his having seduced the wife of a catholic <note>In this historical context, "catholic" refers to the "universal" or orthodox church, rather than the specific modern Roman Catholic denomination.</note> deacon in that part of the world (r).

We might be inclined to conclude from Irenaeus's manner of writing that Marcus himself had come into Gaul and made many converts there. This is also how Jerome (s) understood him.

### SECTION II. *He is accused of being a Magician.*

<margin>Section 2.</margin> I now intend to take notice of what Irenaeus relates. But because his account is long and obscure in several parts, it must be abbreviated.

Marcus, he says, deceived many people <note>original: "not a few persons"</note> of both sexes, improving upon the schemes of the aforementioned Ptolemy <note>original: "Ptolomee"</note> and Colorbasus, and pretending to make great discoveries above all others. He was exceedingly <note>original: "exceeding"</note> skillful in all magical arts. By these means, he had great success, persuading men to listen to him as if he were the most knowledgeable of all (*x*).

Not only Irenaeus, but Tertullian (*y*) and Theodoret (*z*) also call Marcus a magician. However, several of the writers on heresies whom I generally quote say nothing specifically of that matter—such as Philaster, Augustine <note>original: "Augustin"</note>, and the author of the additions to Tertullian.

<header>MARCUS.</header>

<margin>Section 2.</margin> Irenaeus gives several instances of the magical arts of Marcus; one may be supposed to have a relation to the Eucharist. Consecrating (*a*) a cup with wine and using a long invocation, he makes the wine appear red or purple, to persuade his followers that the "Grace" from above causes her blood to distill into it. He also places cups into the hands of women, so that they may consecrate them and perform the same action. He also gives them a smaller cup, while he holds another of a larger size in his own hands. When they empty their cup into his, even though his is larger, it is filled and even overflows. However, I conclude that such things as these, if they were really done, are not proofs of magic. They are only sleight-of-hand tricks <note>original: "slight-of-hand tricks"</note> by which inattentive spectators, especially those who are willing to be deceived, may be misled.

### SECTION IV. *Some Observations upon these Accusations.*

<margin>SECTION 4.</margin> Regarding all of this, I beg leave to say that these claims might not be true. 

*First*, such accusations are regularly reported as a matter of course concerning almost all heretics, whether there are good reasons for them or not. 

*Secondly*, Irenaeus, it seems, was not fully acquainted with these people. This may appear more clearly later on. 

*Thirdly*, nothing is said of these things by Tertullian (or the author of the additions to his work), nor by Theodoret or Philaster. However, Epiphanius undoubtedly includes the same reports, as he transcribes the work of Irenaeus. 

*Fourthly*, Irenaeus has inserted into his work a character description of Marcus in eight verses, written, as he says, by a solemn and pious person of his time (*e*). In these verses, Marcus is called an idolater, an astrologer, and a magician, and his impious or erroneous notions are criticized; yet, nothing is said of his or his disciples' debaucheries <note>original: "debaucheries" — sexual immorality or excessive indulgence in sensory pleasures. This was a standard "stock accusation" used against groups deemed heretical.</note>. Such behavior should not, and could not, have been omitted by the poet if such things had been common among these people and generally known to the world.

### SECTION V. *The Marcosians are said to have regarded the letters of the alphabet as mysterious.*

<margin>SECTION 5</margin>
These people are said to have placed a great deal of mystery in the letters of the alphabet and thought that they were very useful for finding out the truth. Many instances and a long account of this may be seen in Irenaeus, who must be consulted by those who desire to know the specific details. However, I shall place in the margin what Theodoret *(f)* says regarding this matter, as well as the entire article *(g)* from the additions to Tertullian's book, *Prescriptions against Heretics*. I shall give only one instance: they said that *(h)* Jesus had in him all numbers and, therefore, is said to be Alpha and Omega <note>Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing the beginning and the end. The Marcosians used "gematria," a system where letters also represent numbers, to find hidden meanings in names and titles.</note>.

### SECTION VI. *They are falsely accused of holding two principles and being Docetists.*

<margin>SECTION 6.</margin>
Here I would observe that by the author just mentioned, and *(i)* some others, they are spoken of as holding "two principles" <note>original: "two principles" — the dualistic belief that there are two equal and opposing primary forces or gods, such as Good and Evil, or Spirit and Matter.</note>, and as if they were Docetists <note>original: "Docetes" — early Christians who believed that Jesus Christ's body was not real flesh and blood, but only an appearance or a ghost-like "shadow" that did not truly suffer on the cross.</note>, and denied—

*(g)* "There were some after these, namely Marcus and Colarbasus, who composed a new heresy from the Greek alphabet. For this reason, they say, Christ said: 'I am Alpha and Omega.' Finally, they claim Jesus Christ descended—that is, a dove came into Jesus which, in its Greek name *peristera* <note>original: "περιστερα"</note>, is pronounced and has the numerical value of 801. These people run through Omega, Psi, Chi, Phi, Upsilon, Tau... all the way to Alpha and Beta, and they calculate groups of eight and ten... They imagine another god besides the Creator. ### SECTION VII. *They continued in the practice of Baptism and the Eucharist.*

<margin>Section 7.</margin> We saw previously some reason to believe they observed the Eucharist <note>The Eucharist, also known as Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper, is the Christian rite commemorating the Last Supper.</note>. That they also practiced baptism is apparent from Irenaeus *(k)* and Theodoret *(l)*. If we were able to accurately determine their specific form of baptism, I believe it would likely have been very consistent with the instructions recorded at the end of the Gospel of Matthew <note>Matthew 28:19: "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."</note>.

### SECTION VIII. *Regarding their opinion of Jesus Christ.*

<margin>Section 8.</margin> Their opinion concerning Jesus Christ is described at length by Irenaeus, to whom I refer the reader *(m)*. His account is hardly intelligible; at best, it is too long and too obscure to be included here. However, they seem to have held a concept of the great dignity and excellence of his—

---

<margin>"A certain Marcus also founded a heresy, denying the resurrection of the flesh and asserting that Christ suffered not truly, but in appearance only. ### SECT. IX. *Of their Rites of Redemption, and the Meaning of them as given by Rhenford.*

<margin>Sect. 9.</margin>They had some rites of redemption, which Irenaeus (*u*) speaks of as very strange and absurd. He even seems to ridicule them. However, it is probable that Irenaeus did not thoroughly understand them.

Rhenford says that (*x*) by the word "redemption," these people meant a form of confession or a form of prayer. Grabe also admits that he is (*y*) convinced by what Rhenford has written regarding this obscure subject.

Irenaeus speaks as if they had several of these rites. But it seems they were chiefly two: one at baptism, when the (*z*) minister gave an exhortation or proposed a form of confession to the person being initiated <note>original: "initiated"; the process of being formally admitted into a religious group, here through baptism</note> or baptized. Then the person being baptized made a confession of faith, and the bystanders or spectators wished peace or happiness to all on whom that name rested. The other was performed (*a*) when someone was near death, or during a dangerous sickness. The confessions and prayers were in the Hebrew or Syriac language, which was frequently used by them, as Theodoret (*b*) says. And Irenaeus, not understanding that language, nor any one—

---

<margin>(*u*) Chapter 21. [otherwise 18.] *p.* 93, 98.</margin>
<margin>(*x*) So that by "redemption," which they explain in this or that way, nothing can be understood but a formula by which they profess their faith regarding redemption or the redeemer. <note>original Latin: "Adeo ut per redemptionem, quam hoc illove modo edisserunt, nihil nisi formula intelligi possit, qua fidem suam de redemtione, vel redemtore, profiteantur."</note> *De Redem. Marcos. &c. p.* 34. *n.* 207.</margin>
<margin>(*y*) That by the "redemption" mentioned here and a little later, a certain formula of prayer is to be understood, is shown not only by the context of Irenaeus himself, but is also clearly confirmed by the nature of Jewish ritual, which I shall provide as explained from the discussion of the learned Jacob Rhenford. <note>original Latin: "Per redemtionem, quam hic et paulo post memorat, certam orationis formulam intelligendam esse, non modo ipse Irenæi contextus ostendit, sed et Judaici ritus ratio plane confirmat..."</note> *Grab. ad Iren. cap.* 13. *al.* ix. *p.* 61.</margin>

### SECTION X. *They believed the facts recorded in the Gospels.*

<margin>SECTION 10.</margin> If we are to trust Irenaeus’s account of these people, they believed the facts recorded in the Gospels and accepted most or all of the scriptures of the Old and New Testaments.

Some of the facts observable in Irenaeus’s account are these: that Jesus was born of a virgin, as previously mentioned; that (*h*) John the Baptist preached the baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins; and that (*i*) Jesus was baptized, at which time a dove appeared. They also believed that he revealed the Father, or taught the will of God, as mentioned before; and that he went (*k*) up onto the mountain with three of his disciples, where he was gloriously transfigured and Moses and Elijah <note>original: "Elias"</note> appeared. Furthermore, they held that (*l*) he was nailed to the cross at the sixth hour of the day <note>By ancient Jewish timekeeping, the sixth hour was noon.</note>. We should also (*m*) mention the story of the person who came to Christ, saying, "Good master, what good thing shall I do to inherit eternal life?"; (*n*) the request of the sons of Zebedee for the primary places in his kingdom; and the fact (*o*) that the apostles of Christ were twelve in number.

### SECTION XI. *They accepted the Scriptures of both the Old and New Testaments.*

<margin>SECTION 11.</margin>
It is exceedingly obvious that the Marcosians accepted the scriptures of the Old and New Testaments. As the first book of Irenaeus is now divided, there are two chapters which show which (*p*) texts or passages from Moses <note>The Pentateuch, or first five books of the Bible</note> and the Prophets they cited <note>original: "alledged"</note> in favor of their hypothesis or scheme. There is also a third chapter (*q*) giving an account of their forged apocryphal scriptures, and which texts of the Gospel or New Testament they misinterpreted <note>original: "abused"</note>. In the preface to the second book, Irenaeus, while reviewing the first book and its contents, observes particularly that (*r*) he had taken notice of the scriptures they used.

### SECTION XII. *A detailed list of the Books of the New Testament used by them.*

<margin>SECTION 12.</margin>
I shall show in some detail the texts and books of the New Testament used by them.
Since they believed Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary, it is likely they accepted the first chapters of St. Matthew and St. Luke, as well as other parts of these Gospels.
They argued from (*s*) Matthew 18:10, (*t*) Matthew 11:28, and other passages that do not need to be mentioned here; and also from (*u*) Luke 2:49,

### CHAP. VIII.

### *Of* HERACLEON.

#### SECT. I. *Ancient Writers who speak of him, and of the Time when he lived.*

<margin>Section I.</margin>Heracleon’s home country is unknown. Irenaeus mentions him *(a)* and Ptolemy in his arguments against the Valentinians <note>A Gnostic sect founded by Valentinus in the 2nd century</note>. Clement of Alexandria speaks of him as one *(b)* of the most prominent followers of Valentinus's school. Origen says he was considered a disciple *(c)* of Valentinus. Yet the period in which he lived is not easily determined. Grabe is convinced that he *(d)* was a contemporary of Valentinus. Basnage discusses him *(e)* around the year 125, and Cave places *(f)* him at the year 126. Massuet admits that he is not able *(g)* to determine his dates exactly. In the writings of Epiphanius, the order given is Valentinus, Secundus, Ptolemy, Marcus, Colobarsus, and then Heracleon. And he suggests *(h)* that Heracleon borrowed from the Marcosians, or agreed with them on several points. In Philaster *(i)*, the order is Valentinus, Ptolemy, Secundus, Heracleon, Marcus, and Colobarsus. In Theodore<insert>t</insert> <note>The catchword "odoret" at the bottom of the page indicates the text continues with "Theodoret"</note>...

## SECTION IV. Containing Remarks on the preceding Passages, particularly concerning which Parts of the Scriptures he accepted.

<margin>SECTION 4.</margin> I now make some remarks. 1. By Levi, Heracleon means (u) Lebbaeus, who is also called Judas and Thaddeus. <note>Lebbaeus, Judas, and Thaddeus are various names attributed to the same apostle in early Christian traditions.</note>

2. According to Heracleon, several of the apostles did not suffer martyrdom. He specifically mentions Matthew, Philip, Thomas, and Levi. And possibly he had John in mind as well, though he does not mention him by name. Grabe says: This (x) passage from Heracleon deserves particular notice, as he says of all these apostles that they did not die as martyrs. To whom—even though he was a heretic—greater regard ought to be given because of his early age than to the legendary accounts of modern writers who claim that all the apostles suffered violent deaths. Beausobre approves of this observation by Grabe and says (y) the testimony of this writer is worthy of credit in a matter of this nature, since it is no part of his heresy, and considering his learning and the fact that he lived near the time of the apostles. Nor does Clement of Alexandria contradict him.

3. The author of *Praedestinatus* <note>An anonymous 5th-century work cataloging various Christian heresies.</note> attributes this doctrine to Heracleon: that (z) a baptized person, whether righteous or not,

(x) <note>original Latin: "Apprime vero notandum testimonium Heracleonis, asserentis ex sanctis apostolis Matthaeum, Philippum, Thomam, et Levi sive Lebbaeum, Jacobi fratrem, citra martyrium mortem obiisse. ### Of C E R D O N.

#### S E C T. I. *Of his Time.*

<margin>Sect. 1.</margin>Irenaeus says twice that *(a)* Cerdon came to Rome in the time of Hyginus, the ninth bishop of Rome after the apostles. <margin>SECT. 2.</margin> Epiphanius's summary states that (b) Cerdon learned his doctrine from Heracleon, though he added some of his own ideas. He traveled from Syria to Rome and spread his beliefs during the time of Hyginus <note>Hyginus was the Bishop of Rome around 138–142 AD.</note>. He held two opposing principles and claimed that Christ was not born <note>This refers to the doctrine of Docetism, which argued that Jesus only appeared to have a physical body.</note>. He denied the resurrection of the dead and rejected the Old Testament. In his more detailed entry, Epiphanius writes that (i) Cerdon followed Heracleon and arrived in Rome from Syria during the time of Hyginus, the ninth bishop after the apostles. Like many other heretics <note>meaning those whose views diverged from the established Church</note>, he believed in two principles and two Gods: one was good and unknown, the Father of Jesus; the other was the Creator, who was evil and known, and who spoke through the Law, appeared to the prophets, and was frequently seen. He also taught that Jesus was not born of Mary and that he possessed flesh only in appearance. He denied the resurrection of the body and rejected the Old Testament. He stated that Christ descended from the unknown Father to overthrow the power and rule of the Creator of the world, as many other heretics do. After staying a short time in Rome, he passed his venom <note>original: "venom"—the author’s critical term for Cerdon's teachings</note> to Marcion, who succeeded him.

Theodoret's account of Cerdon is as follows: he (k) lived during the time of the first Antonine <note>Emperor Antoninus Pius, reigned 138–161 AD.</note>. He taught that there is one God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was unknown to the prophets, and another God, the Creator <note>original: "Maker"</note> of the universe and the giver of the Mosaic Law. He described the latter as "just" and the former as "good." For (l) the Creator orders in the Law "that an eye should be given for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth," but the good God in the Gospels (m) commands <note>original Greek: Ο δε αγαθος εν τοις ευαγγελιοις κελευει (Ho de agathos en tois euaggeliois keleuei).</note>...

...commands that *to him who strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also*; and that to him who would take away your coat, you should give your cloak also. Theodoret notes that Cerdon failed to observe that in the Law it is commanded (*n*) *that if a man meets his enemy's ox going astray, he should bring it back; and not fail to help his beast when it is lying under its burden*. Furthermore, that Christ (who, according to Cerdon, is alone good) threatens (*o*) *hellfire to him who calls his brother a fool*; and, showing himself to be just, said: (*p*) *with the same measure you use, it shall be measured to you again*.

Cerdon, like Marcion—though this is not often mentioned—was a great admirer of virginity <note>In this context, a commitment to celibacy as a higher spiritual state</note>, and

<margin>Section 3.</margin> Cerdon recommended it <note>Referring to virginity or celibacy from the previous page</note> to his followers, as we learn from Theodoret (*f*).

Irenaeus says (*t*) that when Cerdon was at Rome, he several times renounced his errors and was received back into the community. But at length, for returning to them again or for teaching them in a clandestine <note>secret or hidden</note> manner, he was finally excluded from the church. That passage, as well as others from Irenaeus, is transcribed by Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History* (*u*). And Valesius <note>Henri Valois (1603–1676), a French classical scholar</note>, in his notes upon that passage of Eusebius, argues that Cerdon was not ejected but separated himself from the church.

Tertullian, in his (*x*) *Prescriptions against Heretics*, tells a similar story of Marcion. But it is generally supposed by learned men that Tertullian was mistaken. Rigaltius (*y*) <note>Nicolas Rigault (1577–1654), a French scholar</note> has made this observation, and Beausobre (*z*) <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738), a French Protestant theologian known for his history of Manichaeism</note> is clearly of the opinion that Tertullian confounded <note>confused</note> Marcion with Cerdon. Tillemont is also of the same sentiments (*a*).

(*f*) Cerdon and Marcion, indeed, established laws regarding virginity... and so forth. <note>original Greek: Κερδων μεν ουν, και μαρκιων, την παρθενιαν ενομοθετησαν. . . κ. λ. *Theod. H. F. l. v. c. 24. inf.*</note>

(*t*) Cerdon... coming to the church and making a confession, continued in this way: sometimes teaching in secret, then again making a confession, and at other times being convicted for the things he taught wrongly, and withdrawing from the company of the brothers. <note>original Greek: Κερδων δε . . . εις την εκκλησιαν ελθων, και εξομολογουμενος, ουτως διετέλεσε, ποτε μεν λαθροδιδασκαλων, ποτε δε παλιν εξομολογουμενος, ποτε δε ελεγχομενος εφ’ οις εδιδασκε κακως, και αφισταμενος της των αδελφων συνοδιας. *Iren. l. 3. c. 4. n. 3.*</note>

(*u*) But finally Cerdon was convicted because, after so many repeated confessions, he secretly spread the pestilential poison of his error and removed himself entirely from the Church. For Irenaeus does not say that Cerdon was cast out of the church, but that he separated himself entirely from the Church. ## SECTION IV. *Which Scriptures he accepted.*

<margin>Section 4.</margin>
The authors cited previously inform us that Cerdon rejected or despised the Old Testament. Since they say nothing about him rejecting any of the books of the New Testament, we ought to conclude that he accepted them just as other Christians did.

Indeed, the author of the additions to Tertullian’s book, *Prescriptions against Heretics*, says that <margin>(b) To these is added a certain Cerdon... This man repudiates the prophecies and the law... He receives only the Gospel of Luke, and yet not even that in its entirety. Of the Apostle Paul, he accepts neither all the epistles nor the whole of them. He rejects the Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse as if they were false. <note>original Latin: Accedit his Cerdon quidam... Hic prophetias et legem repudiat... Solum Evangelium Lucæ, nec tamen totum recipit. Apostoli Pauli neque omnes, neque totas epistolas sumit. Acta Apostolorum et Apocalypfin quasi falsa rejicit. Præscr. c. 51. p. 253. al. 217.</note></margin> (*b*) Cerdon accepted only the Gospel of St. Luke, and even that was not complete; he also claims that Cerdon did not accept all of St. Paul's epistles, nor the entirety of those that he did accept. Furthermore, he says Cerdon rejected the Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>. But since Irenaeus and other ancient authors are totally silent about this, it may be considered untrue. This was actually the viewpoint of Marcion <note>Cerdon's famous pupil, who significantly expanded these ideas</note>. It is likely one of those matters in which Marcion is said to have gone beyond everyone who came before him.

### S E C T. I. *A general account of him from Irenaeus.*

<margin>Section 1.</margin>
As we have now reached Marcion, it may be best to provide a full passage from Irenaeus as a summary account, which we will comment upon later.

Marcion (*a*) of Pontus, the successor of Cerdon, expanded his doctrine with even greater audacity <note>original: "ampliavit doctrinam impudorate," meaning he shamelessly grew the scope of the heresy</note>. He blasphemed the one who is declared to be God by the Law and the Prophets, saying that he appears to be the author of evil, a lover of war, inconstant, and self-contradictory. However, Marcion claims that Jesus came from the Father, who is superior to the God who made the world. He came into Judea in the time of Pontius Pilate, the governor under Tiberius Caesar. He appeared to those in Judea in human form,

(*a*) <note>The following is a translation of the original Latin text from Irenaeus's *Against Heresies*.</note>
"But Marcion of Pontus, succeeding him [Cerdon], expanded the doctrine, shamelessly blaspheming him who is announced as God by the Law and the Prophets. He called him the creator of evils, one who desires war, inconstant in his judgments, and self-contradictory. He claimed that Jesus, coming from that Father who is above the God who built the world, came into Judea in the times of Pontius Pilate the Governor, who was the procurator for Tiberius Caesar. He appeared in the form of a man to those who were in Judea, abolishing the Prophets and the Law, and all the works of that God who made the world, whom he also calls the Ruler of the World <note>original: Cosmocratorem</note>. Furthermore, he mutilated the Gospel according to Luke, removing everything written about the birth of the Lord, and taking away many parts of the Lord’s teaching in which the Lord is recorded as clearly acknowledging the creator of this universe as his father—thus handing down to his followers not a Gospel, but a fragment of a Gospel. In a similar way, he also cut away the epistles of the Apostle Paul, removing whatever the Apostle clearly said about that God who made the world—specifically that He is the father of our Lord Jesus Christ—as well as those passages where the Apostle, quoting the Prophets, taught by foretelling the coming of the Lord.

He also taught that only the souls of those who had learned his doctrine would receive salvation."

This is according to Irenæus <note>Irenæus (c. 130–202 AD) was a bishop and theologian known for his writings against heresy</note>. This passage from such an early writer will be very useful to us, though I do not need to follow his exact order in everything.

### SECTION II. *Regarding the Time in which he lived.*

<margin>SECTION 2.</margin> It is not easy to determine Marcion’s dates exactly. William Cave <note>A 17th-century English church historian</note> suggests that (b) he came to Rome in the year 127 and, around the year 130, became a follower of Cerdon and an open heretic. John Mill, who also follows John Pearson regarding the early dates of Pope Hyginus, is of much the same opinion. Antoine Pagi (d) dates the spreading of Marcion’s heresy to the year 144. However, he believes that this heresy—as is common in other cases—may be said to have had several beginnings, depending on different calculations. 

According to Pagi, Marcion came to Rome soon after the death of Hyginus, which he says cannot be dated later than the year 141. But Marcion had already broached his opinions in Syria, and probably had begun to do so during the reign of Hadrian, or at least at the beginning of the reign of Antoninus Pius. Upon coming to Rome immediately after the death of Hyginus, when the episcopal see <note>The office or jurisdiction of a bishop</note> was vacant, the church elders <note>original: "Presbyters"</note> did not receive him. He then returned to Asia and spread his principles with greater zeal and openness around the year 144, which is where Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage</note> places Marcion’s activity.

(d) *Critique on Baronius, 144. number 3.* <note>original: "Crit. in Baron. 144. n. 3."</note>

# MARCION. SECTION 2.

<margin>Marcion.</margin> Petavius <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a Jesuit scholar and theologian</note> was very much of the same opinion, and I have placed his *(e)* words at some length in the margin.

Let us now observe some particulars from the ancient writers. Irenæus <note>A 2nd-century bishop of Lugdunum (Lyon) known for his work "Against Heresies"</note>, who, as we have seen, says that Cerdon was in Rome during the time of Hyginus and makes Marcion his disciple or immediate successor, also says in another place that *(f)* Marcion was most active under Anicetus <note>Bishop of Rome from approx. 155 to 166 AD</note>, who was the tenth in the succession of the bishops of Rome.

Clement of Alexandria *(g)* speaks of Basilides, Valentinus <note>original: "Valentin"</note>, and Marcion as all living during the reign of Hadrian <note>original: "Adrian"</note> and the first, or elder, Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, reigned 138–161 AD</note>, at roughly the same time, though Marcion lived somewhat after the other two.

Tertullian speaks of Marcion as *(h)* the first who had taught that there was a different God, one superior to the Creator. He often mentions the time in which Marcion lived, but never with exact precision, as if he lacked certain information about it. He once

And I do not know if two periods of his life should be distinguished, as happens in most heresies: so that he first broke out under Hadrian, but later under Antoninus he earned a famous name for himself by propagating his errors far and wide... The death of Hyginus is placed in the 18th year of Antoninus, before which time it is necessary that Marcion had spread his heresy; since Justin, who offered his Apology to Antoninus, and indeed at the beginning of his reign, mentions Marcion. HISTORY OF HERETICS:

SECTION 2. Tertullian once speaks (i) of Marcion and Valentinus <note>original: "Valentin"</note> together, as both flourishing in the time of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, Roman Emperor 138–161 AD</note> and during the episcopate of Eleutherius <note>Pope/Bishop of Rome c. 175–189 AD</note>. In another place, he speaks of Marcion as certainly being a heretic of Antoninus's time, (k) but he was not concerned <note>original: "solicitous"</note> to know exactly in what year his heresy arose.

Celsus <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity</note>, who might have written about the year 150, mentioned the Marcionites, as we learn from Origen (l).

But perhaps the works of Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist and philosopher, c. 100–165 AD</note> may lead us nearer to the time of Marcion than anything else. He wrote against Marcion. That work is mentioned by (m) Irenaeus, as well as by (n) Eusebius. It is reckoned (o) to be different from his work against all heresies, mentioned by himself in his (p) first apology—in which (q) he twice speaks of Marcion as still living. That apology was written in the time of the elder Antoninus, in the year 140, or not long after. Consequently, it is reasonable to think that Marcion had appeared by 130, or very soon after. For Marcion had many followers when Justin wrote that apology. And when he says that Marcion was still living, it is implied that he had been a prominent figure for some time.

### SECTION III. *The History of Marcion as given by Epiphanius.*

<margin>SECTION 3.</margin>
The common account of Marcion, taken from Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD) was a bishop known for his "Panarion," a massive work attacking various heresies</note>, is to this effect: He was born at Sinope, in Pontus <note>An ancient region on the southern coast of the Black Sea, in modern-day Turkey</note>, where his father was a Bishop. For some time, as Epiphanius says, Marcion lived a retired life in strict celibacy <note>original: "continence"</note>. But after developing an affection for a young woman and being guilty of sexual immorality <note>original: "uncleanness"</note> with her, he was excommunicated by his father. His father would never readmit him afterward, even though Marcion earnestly pleaded with him and made professions of sincere repentance. Being troubled by the reproaches and shame he met with in his own country, he went abroad and arrived in Rome soon after the death of Hyginus <note>Bishop of Rome from approx. 138 to 142 AD</note>. Here, he attempted to be received into communion and, moreover, aimed to be made a Bishop. But being disappointed in both those attempts—the Presbyters <note>church elders</note> of that city rejecting him—he was exasperated. Whereupon he joined himself to Cerdon <note>A Gnostic teacher in Rome who influenced Marcion's theology</note>, who a little while before had begun to spread his own peculiar opinions in the city of Rome.

That Marcion was a native of Pontus is accepted by everyone. This was stated by Irenaeus at the beginning of the long passage previously transcribed from him, and likewise by many other ancient authors. He is called a sailor or mariner by Rhodon in the works of Eusebius, and very often by Tertullian. But for what reason—

### SECTION IV. *The Story of his deceiving a young Woman held doubtful by many.*

<margin>Section 4.</margin> The story told by Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD) was a bishop known for his "Panarion," a massive work attacking various heresies</note>, of Marcion’s deceiving a young woman, is also in the Appendix to Tertullian’s *Prescriptions* <note>original: "De Praescriptione Haereticorum," a work by Tertullian outlining legalistic arguments against heretics</note>. (*x*) But it may be called into question. I see that (*y*) the learned and excellent Ittigius <note>Thomas Ittig (1643–1710), a Lutheran theologian and church historian</note> doubted the truth of it.

I think there are in Epiphanius’s account some particulars that give the whole story an appearance of improbability. For why should Marcion’s father refuse to receive him into communion upon confession and repentance—which seem to have been sincere—if indeed he had fallen in such a way as is said? And his future conduct appears to have been free from reproach. Moreover, his attempt to be received at Rome, and even to obtain

### SECTION V. *Several Observations tending to show its implausibility.*

<margin>Section 5.</margin>
Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738) was a French Protestant theologian known for his "History of Manichaeism," which critically examined early Christian heresies</note> ($z$) has a long argument upon this point, taken from the silence of ancient writers and consisting of many particulars. I shall abridge it:

1. Irenaeus <note>Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202 AD) was a primary opponent of Gnosticism and a major early Christian theologian</note> appears to have been totally unacquainted with this affair. But is it possible that he, who had been at Rome, should be ignorant of it if it were true? Or, if he had known it, could he have avoided mentioning it? Moreover, he writes against a heretic who condemned marriage as a state not sufficiently pure. How could he forget to say that this same person had been guilty of fornication, if he knew it?

2. Tertullian wrote five books against Marcion. He did not neglect any occasion to denounce <note>original: "decry"</note> his opponent. Nevertheless, he says nothing of this scandalous incident <note>original: "adventure"</note>.

This would have been so much to his purpose that it cannot be imagined Jerome would have omitted it if he had known anything of it, since he does not even omit conjectures and the slightest reports that tend to blacken the reputation of a heretic.

### SECTION 5.
...the devil put a cowl <note>A monk's hooded garment, used here as a symbol of religious deception.</note> upon him, so that he might deceive the children of light. And afterwards: Marcion imitated the serpent and recommended fasting. How does it happen that Ephrem does not here unmask the man and show his hypocrisy; namely, that at his very first start he had shamefully fallen and violated that virtue <note>The virtue of chastity.</note> which was the glory of his sect, and by which many people were deceived?

->*Some Reason to Suspect it was the*<-
->*Invention of Epiphanius.*<-

### SECTION 6.
BUT what then shall we say regarding Epiphanius? <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403 AD), a bishop known for his fierce "Panarion" against all heresies.</note> One does not know well what to say. But if he had any authority <note>original: "authority," meaning a source or historical evidence.</note> for his claim, it must have been weak. We may be inclined to suspect it was an invention of his own. Philaster and he seem to have drawn from the same source. They both say (g) that Marcion was from Sinope, and that he proposed to explain to the elders of Rome our Lord's parable concerning old wineskins and old garments. I do not remember reading these particulars in any authors more ancient than these two, who lived at roughly the same time; this leads me to conjecture that they copied one and the same original source. Nevertheless, the story of Marcion's "fall" <note>The specific accusation of sexual misconduct.</note> is not in Philaster. This shows that Philaster never knew it, and that it was not in the author whom he used. This may lead people who are a little suspicious to distrust Epiphanius, and believe he is the author of the story himself.

<margin>(g) Marcion... by birth a Pontic, from the city of Sinope, arrived at the city of Rome, and while living there sowed his wicked heresy; and by questioning the elders of the holy Catholic Church, he offered them the deadly error of his own thinking, saying this: "What is it that is written in the Gospel, as the Lord said: 'No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on old wineskins...'? And again: 'There is no good tree that bears bad fruit, nor a bad tree that bears good fruit,' etc." <note>original: "Marcion, . . . genere Ponticus, de civitate Sinope, urbem Romam devenit..."</note> *Philaster, Heresy 45, pages 94-95. Compare with Epiphanius, Heresy 42, number 2, page 303.*</margin>

## SECTION VII. He began to propagate his errors in his own country, for which he was expelled by his father.

<margin>Section 7.</margin>
Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738), a French Protestant historian known for his critical history of Manichaeism and early Christian sects.</note> therefore concludes from all these proofs that the scandalous adventure of Marcion is at most only a false report which Epiphanius had encountered. He argues that the crime of this heresiarch <note>The founder or leader of a heretical sect.</note>, for which his father expelled him from the church, was actually the errors which he had begun to publish in his own country. 

Beausobre is not the only person who thinks that Marcion had published his notions in his own country, even though many of the ancient writers consider him a disciple of Cerdon <note>A Gnostic teacher in Rome who influenced Marcion's dualistic views.</note>, with whom he first became acquainted in Rome.

## SECTION VIII. His way of life was very unsettled.

<margin>Section 8.</margin>
Marcion came to Rome soon after the death of Hyginus <note>Bishop of Rome, traditionally dated c. 138–142 AD.</note>, while that see <note>The office or jurisdiction of a bishop; here referring to the papacy.</note> was vacant. Not meeting with much encouragement there, he went again into Asia in a short time. However, he must have returned to Rome if it was there that Polycarp saw him. Marcion’s unsettled and wandering course of life is reflected upon by Tertullian and Saint Ephrem.

(b) <note>original: "Tradit S. Epiphanius, Marcionem, e patrio solo expulsum, Romam profugisse, atque subinde alia ex aliis loca mutasse. Quapropter eumdem Caino comparat S. Ephræm. ...ditorem ejuraverat, mundum sibi ubique infessum habuit fremens. Quamobrem a Tertulliano Hamaxobio instabilior dictus est. Lib. 1. cap. 1. Alleman. B. O. T. I. p. 119."</note> Saint Epiphanius relates that Marcion, having been expelled from his native soil, fled to Rome and thereafter moved from one place to another. For this reason, Saint Ephrem compares him to Cain. Because he had renounced his Creator, he found the world everywhere hostile to him as he groaned. Therefore, he was described by Tertullian as being "more unstable than a wagon-dweller" <note>original: "Hamaxobio," referring to nomadic Scythians who lived in wagons; a metaphor for a person with no fixed home.</note>. Book 1, chapter 1. Assemani <note>original: "Alleman." likely referring to Joseph Simonius Assemani, author of the *Bibliotheca Orientalis* (B. O.).</note>, *Bibliotheca Orientalis*, Tome 1, page 119.

Ephrem <note>Saint Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373 AD), a prominent Christian theologian and hymnwriter.</note> also notes this. Marcion was once an orthodox Christian <note>original: "catholic"</note>, as Tertullian often states, (i) and from that fact, Tertullian argues that Marcion’s opinions were a novelty rather than original Christian teaching.

### SECTION IX. He had a great Number of Followers.

<margin>Section 9.</margin> Marcion had many followers. Epiphanius <note>Bishop of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), author of the "Panarion," a work cataloging and refuting various heresies.</note> says that (k) he deceived multitudes of people, and that his sect <note>original: "heresy"</note> still existed in his own time in Rome, Italy, Egypt, Palestine, Arabia, and Syria, as well as in Cyprus, Thebes, Persia, and other places.

Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100–165 AD).</note> suggests that (l) Marcion had influenced many people of all social ranks in various locations.

Tertullian, having mentioned Apelles, Valentinus, and Marcion, speaks (m) as if there were a greater number of followers belonging to these leaders than to any other dissident groups.

Theodoret <note>Bishop of Cyrrhus (c. 393–457 AD), a theologian and church historian.</note> converted (n) about a thousand Marcionites in his own district <note>original: "diocese"</note>. In his preface to the second book of his *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, he says (o) that only a few followers of Valentinus, Marcion, and Mani <note>The founder of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that competed with Christianity.</note> remained scattered in various cities of Syria. He considers this a failure on the part of the church leaders of that time, who he believed were not vigilant enough to uproot the small remains of these movements.

"Just as you yourself admit in a certain letter; and your own people do not deny it, and our people prove it." <note>original Latin: "Sicut et ipse confiteris in quadam epistola: et tui non negant, et nostri probant."</note> *Ibid. chapter 2, page 359, A.*

# MARCION.

<margin>Section 9.</margin>
Tertullian speaks (p) of the deserters of Marcion—that is, those who still followed him in various <note>original: "divers"</note> points but differed from their master in others.

Rhodon, whom we mentioned previously (q) as flourishing around the year 190, says (r) that in his time, the Marcionites were divided into several parties. He identifies the leaders of these groups as Apelles, Potitus, Basilicus, and Syneros.

The great number of books published against Marcion in the second century and afterward shows the prevalence of his doctrine. In listing the works of various authors as I have proceeded, the reader has undoubtedly observed this. In the table at the end of the second volume of my previous work, there are (s) references to various <note>original: "divers"</note> writings of this kind.

Irenaeus (t) (whose words are also cited by (u) Eusebius) says that Polycarp, when he came to Rome during the time of Anicetus <note>Anicetus was Bishop of Rome from c. 155 to 166 AD.</note>, converted many followers of Valentinus and Marcion. This is also noted by Jerome (x) in his entry on Polycarp. This seems to show that although Marcion met with no encouragement from the presbyters <note>Presbyters: elders or leaders within the early Christian church.</note> of Rome, as Epiphanius says, he nevertheless gained converts there among other people.

His followers are supposed to have held him in great veneration. However, when they were blamed for calling themselves "Marcionites" after their leader, they answered that others called themselves "Catholics," (y) though that name was not given to

### SECTION 10. *On His Opinions and the Number of Principles Which He Held.*

<margin>Section 10.</margin> This may suffice for Marcion’s time and history. We proceed now to his opinions.

Theodoret says that (a) Marcion held four <term>principles</term> <note>original: "archai"; fundamental, self-existing sources or origins of the universe.</note>, or "unbegotten substances," as he expresses it. These were: first, the good and unknown God, whom he also calls the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; second, the Creator, whom he called "just" and sometimes "evil"; and besides these, Matter, and the evil one who governs it. However, if the Marcionites ever called the Devil "God," I suppose it was only figuratively and in conformity to Scripture, where he is sometimes called "the god of this world" and is said to rule in "the children of disobedience."

Some attribute the doctrine of three principles to Marcion and his followers, such as (b) Epiphanius and (c) Cyril of Jerusalem. But Augustine says that (d) Marcion held two principles;

Theodoret says that (a) Marcion held four <term>principles</term><note>In this context, "principles" refers to eternal, uncreated sources or substances that exist from the beginning.</note>, or "unbegotten substances," as he phrases it. However, if the Marcionites ever called the Devil "God," I assume it was only figuratively and in accordance with the scriptures, where he is sometimes called "the god of this world" and is said to rule over "the children of disobedience."

### SECT. XI. *His concept of the Creator, the world formed by him, and the God superior to him.*

<margin>Sect. 11.</margin> At the beginning of the long passage quoted earlier, Irenaeus says that Marcion blasphemed the Creator and claimed that Jesus came from the Father, who is superior to the God who made the world. In another place, he says that (*l*) the Marcionites have two Gods who are very different from each other, one being much better than the other. In another passage, he notes that (*m*) they divide the deity into two: one good and the other severe <note>original Latin: judicialem (judgmental or focused on law)</note>.

In the same way, Justin Martyr says that (*n*) Marcion taught people to believe in another God, superior to the Creator, who was the supreme God the Father. According to them, he was (*o*) invisible, inaccessible, and perfectly good.

# MARCION. SECT. II.

According to Marcion and his followers, the Creator—the God of the Jews—made this lower and visible world (*p*). The supreme God, the Father, also had a world of his making, but it was superior to this one: immaterial and invisible. Justin Martyr says that, according to Marcion, the supreme Deity had made greater and better things than the Creator of this visible world (*q*). Tertullian writes to the same effect, and I have placed his words at the bottom of the page (*r*). Jerome says the same (*s*).

Some ancient writers claim that the Marcionites believed in two Gods: one good and the other evil. However, elsewhere they describe them as calling one "good" and the other a "judge" or "severe" <note>The Marcionites distinguished between the 'Good God' of the New Testament and the 'Just God' or 'Severe Judge' of the Old Testament, rather than a strictly 'evil' deity.</note>. This must be their true meaning.

For this reason, it may be helpful to examine passages from several ancient authors regarding this matter.

Jerome states that Marcion taught that Jesus was the son of the good God—that is, he was not the son of the same God spoken of in the prophets (*t*),

(*p*) "Do you certainly confess God as the Creator? Certainly, you say, etc." <note>original Latin: *Certe Deum confiteris Creatorem? (*q*) "He has made them acknowledge someone else as being greater, who made things greater than this [world]." <note>original Greek: *Αλλον δε τινα, ως οντα μειζονα, τα μειζονα παρα τουτον ομολογειν πεποιηκεναι.*</note> *page 70 B.*

(*r*) "When you say that he also has his own condition, his own world, and his own heaven. Now there is a question about place, relating both to that higher world and to its God himself. For behold, if he also has his world below him, above the Creator, he certainly made it in a place." <note>original Latin: *Quum dixeris esse et illi conditionem suam, et suum mundum, et suum coelum...*</note> *Against Marcion, book 1, chapter 15, page 440 B, C.* "Therefore, since another world does not appear, just as its God does not, the consequence is that they divide the two types of things—visible and invisible—between two authorial Gods, and thus they claim the invisible things for their God." <note>original Latin: *Non comparente igitur mundo alio...*</note> *Ibid, chapter 16, page 441 B.*

### SECTION 14. *The Marcionites were wrong to divide the Deity.*

<margin>SECTION 14.</margin>
In dividing the Deity <note>By "dividing the Deity," the author refers to Marcion's dualism—the belief in two separate gods: one who was "just" (the Creator of the Old Testament) and one who was "good" (the Father of Christ).</note>, Marcion and his followers were undoubtedly wrong. However, they seem to have adopted this opinion out of respect for God’s attributes. They believed that if a good God had made the world, there would be neither sin nor misery; instead, everyone would be both holy and happy. Their reasoning on this point is provided to us by Tertullian <note>original: *(b)*</note>, along with some other arguments <note>original: *(i)*</note>.

---

<columns>2</columns>

<note>original: *(b)*</note> If God is good, and has foreknowledge of the future, and is able to prevent evil, why did he allow man—circumvented by the devil—to fall from obedience to the law into death? For if he were both good, so that he would not want such a thing to happen; and foreknowing, so that he was not ignorant it would happen; and powerful, so that he was able to prevent it; then what could not happen under these three conditions of divine majesty would by no means have occurred. <note>original: *Against Marcion, Book 21 [likely Book 2], chapter 5, page 456. C.*</note>

Struggling with the question of evil—"where does evil come from?" <note>original: *unde malum?*</note>—and with his senses dulled by the very scale of his curiosity, Marcion found the Creator declaring, "I am he who creates evils" <note>This refers to a literal reading of Isaiah 45:7 in the Latin Vulgate, where "evil" often meant "calamity" or "disaster" rather than moral wickedness.</note>. Thus, finding in Christ what seemed to be a different arrangement—one of sole and pure benevolence, distinct from the Creator—he easily argued for a new and foreign divinity revealed in his Christ. With a little leaven from that point, he corrupted the whole mass of faith with heretical bitterness. The blind thought they saw two Gods more easily because they had not seen one fully. Therefore, the one God whom he was compelled to acknowledge, he destroyed by defaming him regarding evil; the other God, whom he tried to invent, he constructed by preferring him. <note>original: *Ibid. Book 1. chapter 2. page 431. B. C.*</note>

<column-break/>

<note>original: *(i)*</note> A great argument for another God is the permission of foods against the law, as if we ourselves do not also confess that the burdens of the law have been dismissed; but they were dismissed by the one who imposed them, and who promised a renewal. <note>original: *Ibid. Book 5. chapter 7. page 589. D.*</note>

Long ago we maintained the double power of the Creator, both as judge and as good—the letter killing through the law, the spirit giving life through the gospel. These things cannot make two Gods, for although they are different, they have come to be reckoned in one. If, therefore, the Apostle [Paul] defended the greater glory of the New Testament which remains in glory over the Old, which was to be abolished, this also suits my faith, which places the gospel before the law—and see if it does not suit mine even more. <note>original: *Ibid. Book 5. chapter 11. page 591. A. B.*</note>

Are we ignorant that Marcion and other heretics—who tear apart the Old Testament in contempt for the Creator, that is, the just God—worship and adore another sort of "good God" whom they have fashioned from their own hearts? <note>original: *Jerome, on Ezekiel, chapter 9, page 751.*</note>

They blaspheme, mock, and despise the God of the Old Testament. <note>original: *Ibid. end of section.*</note>
