<margin>SECTION 14.</margin> ...which they brought from the Law, and other parts of the Old Testament, to prove that the being from whom it originated was different from the supreme or good God.

The Marcionites <note>original: *(k)*</note> in the dialogue attributed to Origen <note>This refers to the *Dialogus de recta in Deum fide*, once thought to be by Origen but now usually attributed to Adamantius.</note> frequently use the same sort of reasoning, taken from certain actions of inspired men and from certain commands under the Law, which they considered opposite to the conduct and commands of Christ and his apostles under the Gospel.

With respect to the argument they drew from the goodness of God to prove that he could not be the Creator of this world, it only pushed the difficulty back one step further. As Beauſobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738) was a French Protestant theologian known for his history of Manichaeism.</note> therefore justly observes <note>original: *(l)*</note>, the system of these men was liable to as great objections as that of the Catholics <note>The "Catholics" here refers to the orthodox, mainstream church of the time.</note>. For the same perfections which made it seem unlikely that the supreme being would make such a world as ours would also have obliged him to prevent <note>original: *(m)*</note> the Creator from making it; or would have led him to direct the Creator in his works of creation, overseeing him so as to prevent the bad effects that his operations might have otherwise produced.

### SECT. XV. *They were believers in a future Judgment, and in the Necessity of Human Actions.*

<margin>SECTION 15.</margin>
Although in some instances—according to several passages already quoted from Tertullian and others—they seem to criticize justice, calling it "severity," <note>original: (n)</note> and representing it as incompatible with the character of goodness in God; and for that reason imagining for themselves another God, <note>original: (o)</note> different from the Creator, a God of pure goodness; yet they <note>original: (p)</note> admitted that there would be a future judgment. But then the Creator <note>original: (q)</note> was to be the judge,

<column-break/>

<margin>(*n*) How great is your perversity toward both orders of the Creator? You designate him as a judge, and yet you reproach the severity of a judge—which is appropriate to the merits of the cases—as if it were cruelty. You demand the Best God, yet you disparage his gentleness—which is appropriate to his goodness according to the capacity of human mediocrity—as if it were insignificance. Neither the great nor the small pleases you, neither the judge nor the friend. <note>original: *Tertullian, Adv. Mar. Lib. 2. cap. 27. p. 475. A. B.*</note></margin>

<margin>(*o*) You who have dreamed of another God who is only good because you cannot endure a judge: although we have shown him also to be a judge. Or if he is not a judge, he is certainly a perverse and useless founder of a discipline that is not to be enforced—that is, not to be judged. Do you not reject God as judge when you prove God is not a judge?—Furthermore, when you are forced to pronounce injustice regarding the worst things, you are driven by the same logic to judge justice regarding the best things. Therefore, as much as injustice is an evil, so much is justice a good. <note>original: *Ibid. Lib. 2. c. 11. p. 462. D. 3. A.*</note></margin>

<margin>(*p*) See how you hear. He threatened those who would not hear. If something is given by the God of Marcion, it will also be taken away by him. <note>original: *Ibid. Lib. 4. cap. 19. p. 531. D.*</note>

Therefore, you now fear sin; and by fearing, you have proven that he who prohibits sin is to be feared. <note>original: *Ibid. Lib. 1. cap. 27.*</note>

ADAMANTIUS: Is God a just judge, or not? MARCIONITE: God is a just judge. AD: Whom does he judge? MAR: He judges the devil and his angels, and those people who seek refuge with him. <note>original: *Dial. Con. Mar. sec. 3. p. 81. Bas. 1674.*</note></margin>

<margin>(*q*) By whatever name he threatens removal, it will not be from that God who does not know how to threaten because he does not know how to be angry. <note>original: *Ibid. Lib. 4. c. 19. p. 531. D.*</note>

It is much more foolish when, having been asked what will happen to every sinner of their God, they respond that he is cast away, as if from his sight. Is this not also a matter of judgment? For he is judged as one to be cast away, and certainly by a judgment of condemnation. And what will it be to be cast away except to lose what he was going to obtain if he were not cast away—that is, salvation?—But what is the end for that castaway? They say he will be overtaken by the Creator’s fire. <note>original: *Ibid. Lib. 10, 27, 28.*</note>

That the Creator and Maker and visible God of the Jews exists, and that he is a judge. <note>original: *Epiphanius, Haer. 42. p. 304. A.*</note></margin>

At the very least, they denied the resurrection <note>original: ($z$)</note> of the same physical body. <margin>Section 17.</margin>
...passage in Clement of Alexandria <note>original: Clemens Alexandrinus</note>, (d) which implies that this was not the opinion of the Marcionites. For he informs us there that although the Marcionites had taken their ideas about the evil of biological birth <term>Generation</term><note>The process of procreation or being born into the physical world.</note> from some philosophers he had mentioned earlier, they still differed from them in some specific ways regarding this point. For these philosophers asserted that matter was not evil in itself, but only when considered as the prison of the soul. They claimed the soul was divine in its nature and was thrust into this world as a place of punishment; they believed that souls embodied under these circumstances required purification. Clement expressly says this was not a sentiment embraced by the followers of Marcion. Instead, it was the opinion of those who held that souls were thrust into bodies, tied to them, and poured from one to another, as if from one vessel to another. Therefore, in this passage, Clement asserts that the Marcionites did not believe in the transmigration of souls. And Epiphanius—who knew they borrowed some of their ideas about matter from philosophers who believed in the transmigration of souls—might have too hastily concluded that they agreed with those philosophers on that point as well.

### SECTION XVIII. *Some Account of their Notion that Christ delivered the Wicked and left the Good.*

<margin>SECTION 18.</margin>
In the passage cited earlier (*e*), to which I now only refer without transcribing it again in full, Irenæus says that Marcion taught that when Christ descended to Hades <term>hell</term><note>original: "hell"; here referring to the common Greek concept of the underworld or the place of the dead.</note>, he delivered many people considered wicked, but left there the Patriarchs and many other good men of the Old Testament.

Epiphanius (*f*) also states that, according to Marcion, the Lord descended to Hades and saved Cain, Korah <note>original: "Corah"</note>, Dathan, Abiram, Esau, and all the nations who did not worship the God of the Jews. However, he left there Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, and Solomon. Theodoret (*g*) writes to the same effect: that Cain, the people of Sodom, and other wicked people came to the Lord Jesus in Hades, obtained salvation, and were taken by him into his kingdom. Conversely, Abel, Enoch, Noah, the Patriarchs, and the Prophets were not delivered because they would not come to him. Tertullian also makes a clear reference to (*h*) this matter.

Regarding this, Isaac de Beausobre (*i*) has made several observations which most readers will readily accept as a probable explanation for Marcion’s specific notion.

1. It was, he says, a very general opinion that Jesus Christ went to Hades and preached there, and brought from there all <meta>catchword: that</meta>

# HISTORY OF HERETICS:

<margin>Section 18.</margin> ...who believed in him. The ancients held the opinion that eternal life cannot be obtained except through faith in Jesus Christ. Because they believed God is too merciful to let people perish simply for not having heard the gospel, they supposed that the Lord also preached to the dead, so that they might have the same opportunity as the living.

2. In the language of Marcion, and the Church Fathers as well, "hell" <term>Hades</term><note>In this context, "hell" refers to Hades, the general realm of the dead, rather than exclusively a place of punishment.</note> does not necessarily mean the place of the damned. Within that space is Tartarus (the place of torment) and Paradise, or the "bosom of Abraham" (a place of rest and refreshment). In that part of Hades, Jesus found the righteous men of the Old Testament. They were not suffering, but were in a place of comfort and pleasure. For, as Marcion says in the writings of Tertullian, "your Christ <note>Referring to the Christ of the Jews/the Creator</note> promises the Jews rest in Hades after this life, even in the bosom of Abraham." <margin>(k) "Furthermore, your Christ promises the Jews their former status through the restoration of the land, and after the course of life, refreshment in the underworld in the bosom of Abraham." <note>original: "Ceterum vester Christus pristinum statum Judæis pollicetur, ex restitutione terræ, et post decursum vitæ apud inferos in sinu Abrahæ refrigerium." Adv. M. L. 3. c. 24. p. 499. A.</note></margin>

3. Christ preached the gospel to those righteous men; but because they had never heard of the invisible or supreme Deity (who, as Marcion claimed, was unknown before the coming of Christ), they suspected that the Creator <note>In Marcion's system, the "Creator" or Demiurge was a lesser god who gave the Old Testament law, separate from the Supreme God of Love revealed by Jesus.</note> intended to tempt them. This suspicion prevented them from believing in Christ. Marcion likely derived this thought from those passages in the Old Testament where God warns the Israelites not to listen to prophets who preach about "another God," even if they perform signs and wonders. In such cases, the Law taught that Jehovah, whom they served, was only testing them to prove their loyalty.

The Creator [punished] Korah, Dathan, and Abiram <note>Korah, Dathan, and Abiram were biblical figures who led a rebellion against Moses and were subsequently swallowed by the earth as divine punishment.</note>, as well as the people of Sodom and Gomorrah, and other wicked men; and Christ made an offer of mercy to those miserable souls, who had been suffering for many ages the punishment for their crimes. They embraced his offer and repented, and he took them with him into his kingdom. All of this is supported in no small way by what Irenaeus says. There is still more on this subject in the works of Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738) was a prominent French Protestant theologian who wrote extensively on the history of Manichaeism and other early Christian sects.</note>, whom I suggest the inquisitive reader consult.

### S E C T. XIX. *Marcion's Opinion about the Person of Christ: That He Was Not a Real Man.*

<margin>Section 19.</margin>
Marcion was so far from believing that our Savior was born of a virgin, that he did not allow (*l*) that he was born at all. He thought the Son of God took on the outward form of a man (*m*) and appeared (*n*) as a man; and (*o*) without being born, or gradually growing up to the full stature of a man, he showed himself at once in Galilee as a fully grown man. It is thought that his version of the Gospel of St. Luke began with these words: (*p*) "In the fifteenth year of Tiberius <note>Tiberius Caesar, the second Roman Emperor (reigned 14–37 AD).</note>, God descended into Capernaum, a city of Galilee." At least Tertullian seems to suggest this. And Epiphanius...

---

<columns>2</columns>

(*l*) "But nature," he says, "does not allow a virgin to give birth." <note>original: "Sed et virginem inquit parere, natura non patitur." Against Marcion, Book 3, chapter 13, p. 487. D.</note>

(*m*) "Since for that reason he did not take on a real body... He who had no body could not be anointed at all; and he who could not be anointed could in no way be called 'Christ' [the Anointed One]." <note>original: "Cum propterea nec corporis susceperit veritatem.—Qui corpus non habuit, ungui omnino non potuit: qui ungui omnino non potuit Christus vocari nullo modo potuit." Ibid. chapter 15, p. 490. B.</note>

(*n*) "For in this way Marcion preferred to believe he was a phantom, denying the reality of a complete physical body in him." <note>original: "Sic enim et Marcion phantasma eum maluit credere, totius corporis in illo dedignatus veritatem." On the Soul, chapter 17, p. 319. D.</note>

<column-break/>

(*o*) "Such a process [of birth and growth]," you say, "was not necessary, because he would immediately prove himself to be the Son, the messenger, and the Christ of God through the evidence of his miracles." <note>original: "Non fuit inquis ordo ejusmodi necessarius, quia statim se et filium, et missum, et Dei Christum rebus ipsis esset probaturus per documenta virtutum." Against Marcion, Book 3, chapter 3, p. 478. A.</note>

(*p*) "In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, he proposes that God descended into the Galilean city of Capernaum." <note>original: "Anno decimo quinto principatus Tiberiani proponit Deum descendisse in Civitatem Galileæ Caphernaum." Ibid. Book 4, chapter 7, p. 506. D.</note>

<margin>Section 19.</margin> Epiphanius (*q*) says nearly the same thing. It is evident from many (*r*) passages in ancient authors—but particularly from Tertullian—that it was the doctrine of the Marcionites that Christ first appeared in the fifteenth year of Tiberius's reign <note>Tiberius Caesar (reigned 14–37 AD). The fifteenth year of his reign is roughly 29 AD.</note>. They also supposed (*s*) that at the first moment of his appearance in this world, he was completely prepared to enter his great work, and that he immediately took on the role of a Savior.

Similarly, Irenaeus, in the passage quoted from him at the beginning of this article, says (*t*) that Marcion taught that Jesus came into Judea in the time of Pontius Pilate and appeared to the Jews in the form of a man.

Tertullian informs (*u*) us that, according to the doctrine of the Marcionites, Christ had the appearance of a human body though not the reality of one. He appeared to have flesh, though he really did not. They thought they had a solid foundation (*x*) on which to base this opinion because angels had appeared in the Old Testament in bodily shapes.

...shapes, and had conversed with men, and yet were not really men. They also endeavored to prove the same points from Philippians 2:6–8 (*y*) because they observe that the Apostle says: being in the form of God, he emptied himself and took the form of a servant—the *appearance*, not the *reality*. Likewise, being in the *likeness* of man meant he was not *truly* man; and again, being found in the *figure* of a man meant he was not in the *substance*—that is, not in the *flesh*.

That Marcion denied Christ’s birth <note>original: "nativity"</note> (*z*) is evident from many passages by Tertullian, several of which I have placed in the notes (*a*). Some of my readers will be pleased to see them collected together.

Book 5, chapter 20, p. 614. D.*

Ibid. (*a*) <note>original Latin: "Marcion ut carnem Christi negaret negavit etiam nativitatem: aut ut nativitatem negaret, negavit et carnem. — Plane nativitas a Gabriele annuntiatur. — Odit moras qui subito Christum de cœlis deferebat. Aufer inquit molestos semper Cæsaris census, et diversoria angusta, et sordidos pannos, et dura præsepia. — Servent potius pecora pastores, et Magi ne fatigentur de longinquo. — Sed nec circumcidetur infans, nec ad templum deferatur: nec in manus tradatur Simeoni. — Taceat et anus illa. — His opinor consiliis tot originalia instrumenta Christi delere, Marcion ausus es, ne caro ejus probaretur. B. C. D.*

"He himself," they say, "testifies that he was not born by saying, 'Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?'" See Luke 8:19, 22. *Against Marcion, Book 4, chapter 19.*

<note>original Latin: "Desiderantes rationem qua non putaveris natum esse Christum necesse est quatenus hoc putas arbitrio tuo licuisse, ut aut impossibilem, aut inconvenientem Deo existimaveris nativitatem. De Carne Christi. c. 3. p. 359. A. B."</note> Desiring the reason why you did not think Christ was born, it is necessary—since you think this was permitted to your own judgment—that you either considered birth impossible for God, or unsuitable for Him. *On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 3, p. 359. A. B.*

To be circumcised or to be fastened [to a cross]? To be brought up or to be buried? To be placed in a manger or to be hidden in a tomb? — Or did you not cut away the sufferings from Christ for this reason: that as a phantom <note>original: "phantasma"</note>, he was free from the feeling of them? — We have said before that he could have equally undergone the empty mockeries of an imaginary birth and infancy. *On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 5, p. 364. B. C.*

### SECTION XX. *Tertullian's Arguments against this Notion.*

<margin>SECTION 20.</margin>
As Christ, according to this account, had the appearance of a body but not the reality, Tertullian (*b*) often charges Marcion with making Christ deceitful. He alleges that he could not be Christ <term>Christ: from the Greek *Christos*, meaning "the Anointed One."</term> if he had no body to be anointed. He asserts, therefore, (*c*) that he must have taken the name of Christ only because it was a popular title and character, without which the Jews would not have been inclined to receive him.

This deceitfulness of Jesus—according to the doctrine which Marcion held—is something Tertullian endeavors to prove in many different ways and in a great variety of passages, which are too long and too numerous to be included here. Only two of (*d*) them are provided below.

However, some of the followers of Marcion (*e*) believed Christ had real flesh, though they would not admit that

---

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>(b) <note>original Latin: "Si et mentitum alicubi dicis creatorem, longe majus mendacium est in tuo Christo cujus corpus non fuit verum. Ad. Mar. L. 2. c. 28. p. 475. D."</note> If you say the Creator lied at any point, there is a far greater lie in your "Christ," whose body was not real. *Against Marcion, Book 2, chapter 28, p. 475. D.*</margin>

<margin>(c) <note>original Latin: "Si enim Christus unctus est, ungui utique corporis passio est. Qui corpus non habuit ungui omnino non potuit. Christus vocari nullo modo potuit. Sed quomodo inquit irreperet Judæorum fidem nisi per solemne apud eos et familiæ nomen. Adv. Mar. Lib. 3. c. 15, 16. p. 490. B. C."</note> For if Christ was anointed, being anointed is certainly a physical experience of the body. He who had no body could not be anointed at all. He could in no way be called "Christ." "But," he says, "how would he gain the faith of the Jews except through a name that was familiar and sacred to them?" *Against Marcion, Book 3, chapters 15, 16, p. 490. B. C.*</margin>

<margin>(d) <note>original Latin: "Quid dimidias mendacio Christum, totus veritas fuit. Maluit crede nasci, quam ex aliqua fe parte mentiri, et quidem in semetipsum. Ut carnem gestaret sine ossibus duram, sine musculis solidam, sine sanguine cruentam, sine tunica vestitam, sine fame esurientem, fine dentibus edentem, fine lingua loquentem, ut phantasma auribus fuit sermo ejus per imaginem vocis. De Carne Christi. c. 5. p. 362. A. B."</note> Why do you divide Christ with a lie? He was entirely truth. Believe me, he preferred to be born rather than to lie in any part of himself, and especially concerning himself. To suggest he carried flesh without the hardness of bones, solid without muscles, bloody without blood, clothed without a garment, hungry without hunger, eating without teeth, or speaking without a tongue—this would mean his speech was a phantom to the ears, through an image of a voice. *On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 5, p. 362. A. B.*</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>original Latin: "Ecce fallit et decipit et circumvenit omnium oculos, omnium sensus, omnium accessus et contactus. Ergo jam Christum non de cœlo deferre debueras, &c. Ibid. c. 5. p. 362. C."</note> Look, he cheats and deceives and bypasses the eyes of all, the senses of all, the access and contact of all. Therefore, you should not have brought Christ down from heaven, etc. *Ibid., chapter 5, p. 362. C.*

<margin>(e) <note>original Latin: "Sed quidam discentes Pontici illius, supra magistrum sapere compulsi, concedunt Christo carnis veritatem,—dum omnino non natam—Pervenimus igitur ex Marcione ad Apellem qui—solidum Christi corpus sed fine nativitate suscepit—prædicans ut Angelus quidem illius Philumenes. De Carne Christi, c. 6. p. 362. C. D."</note> But certain students of that man from Pontus <note>Marcion was from Pontus, on the Black Sea</note>, compelled to be wiser than their teacher, grant the reality of Christ's flesh—while maintaining he was not born at all. We come, therefore, from Marcion to Apelles, who accepted a solid body for Christ but without birth, preaching as an Angel of that Philumene <note>Philumene was a prophetess associated with Apelles</note>. *On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 6, p. 362. C. D.*</margin>

### S E C T I O N XXI. *Marcion believed there were to be two Christs.*

<margin>Section 21.</margin>
Marcion acknowledged Jesus to be Christ, but not *(f)* the Christ foretold by the Jewish prophets. He could not deny that a Christ or Messiah was spoken of in those scriptures, but he said that a *(g)* person different from our Lord Jesus Christ was meant by them. He allowed, as Tertullian expresses it, *(h)* that the prophets of the Creator had promised a Savior to the Jewish nation who should deliver them out of the hands of their enemies and restore them to freedom. But he pretended that this deliverer was not the Son of God, and that the <term>Oracles: divine communications or prophecies</term> of the Old Testament did not apply to Jesus Christ. So that this man, as Tertullian observes, *(i)* who was so opposed to Judaism, did himself follow Jewish views in...

---

<column-break/>

*(f)* <note>original Latin: "Quum igitur hæretica dementia eum Christum venisse præsumeret, qui nunquam fuerat annuntiatus; sequebatur ut eum Christum nondum venisse contenderet, qui semper fuerat prædicatus: atque ita coacta est cum Judaico errore sociari et ab eo argumentationem sibi struere, quasi Judæi certi et ipsi alium fuisse qui venit non modo respuerint eum ut extraneum, verum et interfecerint eum ut adversarium." — Since, therefore, heretical madness presumed that a Christ had come who had never been announced, it followed that it should contend that the Christ who had always been predicted had not yet come; and so it was forced to join in the Jewish error and build an argument for itself, as if the Jews were certain that another was the one who came—not only rejecting him as a stranger but even killing him as an enemy. *Against Marcion, Book 3, chapter 6, p. 480. B.C.*</note>

*(g)* <note>original Latin: "Sic nec illam injectionem tuam potes sistere ad differentiam duorum Christorum: quasi Judaicus quidem Christus populo soli ex dispersione redigendo destinetur a Creatore: vester vero omni humano generi liberando collatus sit a Deo optimo." — Thus you cannot maintain that objection of yours regarding the difference between the two Christs: as if the Jewish Christ is destined by the Creator only for the gathering of the people from their dispersion, while your Christ was granted by the supreme God for the liberation of the entire human race. *Against Marcion, Book 3, chapter 21, p. 496. A.*</note>

<note>original Latin: "Certe si nondum venit Christus Creatoris, propter quem hæc passuri prædicantur.— Redde statum Judææ quem Christus Creatoris inveniat et alium contende venisse." — Surely if the Creator's Christ—for whom it is predicted these things must be suffered—has not yet come... Restore the state of Judea which the Creator's Christ may find, and then argue that another has come. *Against Marcion, Book 3, chapter 23, p. 498. D.*</note>

*(h)* <note>original Latin: "His quum accedunt et sui Christi: alter qui apparuit sub Tiberio, alter qui a Creatore promittitur." — To these are added even their own Christs: one who appeared under the reign of Tiberius, the other who is promised by the Creator. *Against Marcion, Book 1, chapter 15, p. 441. A.*</note>

*(i)* <note>original Latin: "Nunc quia cum Judæis negas venisse Christum eorum; recognosce et exitum ipsorum quem post Christum relaturi prædicantur ob impietatem, qua eum et despexerunt et interemerunt." — Now because you deny with the Jews that their Christ has come, acknowledge also their end which it was predicted they would suffer after Christ because of the impiety with which they both despised and killed him. *Against Marcion, Book 3, chapter 20, p. 497. D.*</note>

<summary>This page describes Marcion's radical doctrine of "two Christs": he believed the Jewish Messiah of the Old Testament was a separate, future political figure, while Jesus was a spiritual savior sent by a different, higher God. Tertullian argues that this view paradoxically aligns Marcion with the Jewish rejection of Jesus as the prophesied Messiah.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Marcion's belief that there were two distinct "Christs." The previous page ended by noting that Marcion, despite his opposition to Judaism, ironically adopted certain Jewish views regarding the coming of a Messiah.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Section 21.</margin>
...in the most shameful manner. Marcion, says that writer (*k*) <note>original: Tertullian</note>, is in favor of two Christs: one who appeared in the time of Tiberius <note>Tiberius Caesar, the Roman Emperor (reigned 14–37 AD) during whose rule Jesus was crucified</note> for the salvation of all nations; and another, the restorer of the Jewish state, who is still to come.

This doctrine of two Christs is also asserted by the Marcionite follower (*l*) in the dialogue attributed to Origen. In a work also said to be written by Athanasius (*m*), we are informed that Marcion supposed that just as Jesus came from the "good God," there was to be another Christ from the "just God." He believed this because each of these gods was to be the father of a Christ unique to himself: the good God of one, and the just God of another. <note>Marcion famously distinguished between the "Just God" (the Creator or Demiurge described in the Old Testament) and the "Good God" (the supreme, merciful Father revealed by Jesus).</note>

### SECTION XXII. *He also allowed the truth of our Savior's miracles.*

<margin>Section 22.</margin>
Marcion accepted the truth of our Savior's miracles. He asserted that Jesus thereby showed himself to be the Son of God and to be sent from the Father. He believed these miracles were sufficient evidence of his divinity, even without the support of ancient prophecies. So says Tertullian. (*n*) That this was his opinion appears further from Tertullian's manner of arguing with him. For he—

---

<column-break/>

(*k*) <note>original Latin: "Constituit Marcion alium esse Christum qui Tiberianis temporibus a Deo quon- dam ignoto revelatus sit in salutem omnium gentium: alium qui a Deo Creatore in restitu- tionem Judaici status sit destinatus, quan- doque venturus."</note> Marcion established that there is one Christ who, in the times of Tiberius, was revealed by a God formerly unknown for the salvation of all nations; and another who is destined by God the Creator for the restoration of the Jewish state, who is to come at some future time. *Ibid. Book 4, chapter 6, p. 506. C.*

(*l*) <note>original Greek: "Δειϰνυται εν τω δια νομω ϰαι προφητων χριςον μηδεπω εληλυθεναι."</note> It is shown through the Law and the Prophets that Christ has not yet come. *Dialogue Against the Marcionites, section 1, p. 35.*
<note>original Greek: "Εναργεϛερα μοι εϛιν αποδειξις τω μη ειναι υιον τω διϰαιω τον χριςον: Ο γαρ τε νομω επω εληλυθει."</note> It is a clearer proof to me that Christ is not the son of the Just [God]: for the one promised by the Law has not yet come. *Ibid. p. 34.*

(*m*) <note>original Greek: "Αυτη Μαρϰιωνος η δυϛσεβεια, Θεον λεγοντος διϰαιον ιδιω χριϛω πατερα, ϰαι Θεον ετερον αγαθον ιδιω χριϛω πατερα."</note> This is Marcion's impiety: saying that the Just God is the father of his own Christ, and the other Good God is the father of his own Christ. *Against Sabellius, Vol. 2, p. 42. A. Bened.*

(*n*) <note>original Latin: "Non fuit inquis ordo necessarius, quia statim et filium et missum et Christum Dei rebus ipsis probabatur per documenta virtutum."</note> You say that the [prophetic] order was not necessary, because he was immediately proved to be both the Son and the messenger and the Christ of God by the facts themselves, through the evidence of his miraculous powers. *Against Marcion, Book 3, chapter 3, p. 478, A.*

He chooses to assert (*o*) that this proof is inconclusive because Jesus Christ assured his disciples that some would arise who would perform false miracles. We need not examine this reasoning. It shows that Marcion accepted the reality of Christ's miracles and thought them a sufficient foundation for believing in him. But Tertullian, by way of opposition and in the heat of controversy, rashly does what he can to weaken one very strong, if not the strongest, argument for the truth of the Christian religion.

### SECTION XXIII. *And of his Death.*

<margin>Section 23.</margin>
The Marcionite doctrine concerning our Savior was (*p*) that, out of his love for the human race and for their sakes, he descended into this world (*q*) and submitted to great humiliation. Although from Tertullian's arguments (*r*) and from their not acknowledging him to have had real flesh, it may be supposed they did not allow him to have truly suffered. However that may be, they believed he was betrayed by (*s*)

---

<columns>2</columns>

(*o*) "But I will deny that this evidence alone was suitable as testimony for him, which he himself later disqualified. Siquidem edicens multos venturos, qui signa facturos et virtutes magnas edituros—temerariam signorum et virtutum fidem ostendit, ut etiam apud Pseudo christos facillimam." *Ibid. p. 478.*</note>

(*p*) "You despise this respect for nature, Marcion—Certainly Christ loved man. For his sake he descended, for his sake he preached, for his sake he cast himself down in all humility even to death, and death on a cross; he certainly loved the one whom he redeemed at a great price." <note>original Latin: "Hanc venerationem naturae Marcion despuis—Certe Christus dilexit hominem.—Propter eum descendit, propter eum praedicavit, propter eum omni se humilitate dejecit usque ad mortem, et mortem crucis: amavit utique quem magno pretio redemit." *De Carne Christi (On the Flesh of Christ) chapter 4, p. 360. B.*</note>

(*q*) "For if God is indeed more sublime, he laid the height of his majesty so low in such humility that he was even subjected to death, and death on a cross; why should you not think that some humble traits were suitable for our God as well, which are yet more tolerable than Jewish insults, gallows, and tombs?" <note>original Latin: "Si enim Deus est quidem sublimior, tanta humilitate fastigium majestatis suae stravit, ut etiam morti subjiceretur, et morti crucis; cur non putetis nostro quoque Deo aliquas pusillitates congruisse, tolerabiliores tamen judaicis contumeliis et patibulis et sepulchris." *Adversus Marcionem (Against Marcion) Book 2, chapter 27, p. 475. ### SECTION XXIV. *And Resurrection.*

<margin>Section 24.</margin>They must also have believed in our Lord's resurrection. (*x*) For they included in their Gospel the account of him addressing the apostles after that event, (*y*) saying, "Why are you troubled? See my hands and my feet, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have." But they seem to have interpreted it (*z*) in this manner: "A spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I do *not* have."

---

<columns>2</columns>

(*t*) "My God ordered someone to be killed; yours willed himself to be killed; he is no less a murderer of himself than of the one by whom he wished to be killed." <note>original Latin: "Deus meus aliquem juſſit occidi: tuus ſemetipſum voluit interfici; non minus homicida in ſemetipſum, quam in eum a quo vellet occidi." *Ibid. Lib. 2. c. 28. p. 475. D.*</note>

(*u*) "The Creator, seeing the Good One dissolving his law, plotted against him, not knowing that the death of the Good One became the salvation of men." <note>original Greek: "Ο Δημιουργος ιδων τον αγαθον λυοντα αυτου τον νομον επεβουλευσεν αυτω, μη ειδως οτι ο θανατος τω αγαθω σωτηρια ανθρωπων εγενετο." *Dial. Con. Mar. ſec. 2. p. 53. fin.*</note>

(*x*) "Thus he was a phantom even after the resurrection when he offered his hands and feet for the disciples to inspect. He said, 'Look at me, for it is I,' because 'a spirit does not have bones, as you see me having.' How do you interpret this voice, Marcion, you who bring Jesus from a God who is only excellent, simple, and good? Behold, he cheats and deceives, etc." <note>original Latin: "Fuit itaque phantaſma etiam poſt reſurrectionem cum manus et pedes ſuos diſcipulis inſpiciendos offerret: aſpicite inquit quod ego ſum, quia ſpiritus oſſa non habet, ſicut me habentem videtis. Quomodo hanc vocem interpretaris Marcion, qui a Deo optimo et ſimplici et bono tantum, infers Jeſum? Ecce fallit et decipit, &c." *De Carne Chriſt. c. 5. p. 362. B.*</note>

(*y*) "And he said to them, 'Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having.'" <note>original Greek: "Και ειπεν αυτοις τι τεταραγμενοι εστε, και διατι διαλογισμοι αναβαινουσιν εν ταις καρδιας υμων; Ιδετε τας χειρας μου, και τους ποδας μου, οτι αυτος εγω ειμι. Ψηλαφησατε με και ιδετε· οτι πνευμα σαρκα και οστα ουκ εχει, καθως εμε θεωρειτε εχοντα." *Luc. 24. 38. 39.*</note>

<column-break/>

(*z*) "But concerning the reality of the body, what could be clearer? When they were hesitating whether it might be a phantom—indeed, believing it was a phantom—he said, 'Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts enter your hearts? See my hands and feet, for it is I myself; since a spirit does not have bones, as you see me having.' And Marcion, I believe, deliberately did not want to erase from his gospel those things that contradicted him... He therefore wants it to be spoken as if, 'a spirit does not have bones, as you see me having,' refers back to the spirit: 'as you see me having [the nature of a spirit],' that is, *not* having bones, just like a spirit." <note>original Latin: "De corporis autem veritate quid poteſt clarius? Quum hæſitantibus eis ne phantaſma eſſet, immo phantaſma credentibus: quid turbati eſtis inquit, et quid cogitationes ſubeunt in corda veſtra? Videte manus meas et pedes, quia ego ipſe ſum: quoniam ſpiritus oſſa non habet, ſicut me videtis habere. Et Marcion quædam contraria ſibi, illa credo induſtria eradere de evangelio ſuo noluit—. Vult itaque ſic dictum, quaſi, ſpiritus oſſa non habet ſicut me videtis habentem, ad ſpiritum referatur, ſicut me videtis habentem, id eſt non habentem oſſa ſicut et ſpiritus." *Adv. Mar. L. 4. c. 43. p. 374. D. 375. A.*</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Marcionites’ beliefs regarding Jesus. Specifically, it examines how they reconciled their denial of Christ’s physical body with their firm belief in his recorded miracles.</meta>

<page-num>235</page-num>
-> # M A R C I O N. SECT. 24. <-

That they firmly believed our Savior's miracles is evident from this, because Tertullian, in arguing with them **(a)**, shows that by denying that he had a body and actually suffering, they weakened the evidence of all his miracles <note>original: "works of power"</note>; for if our senses might be mistaken about the one, they might likewise be mistaken about the other. But as he knew they allowed the reality of these miracles, he used this reasoning to lead them to a belief in the other as well. Indeed, from very many of his arguments to prove the reality of Christ's body, it appears they admitted the reality of his miracles; for he argues **(b)** thus: "Without his having a real body, his miracles and all his actions were deceptive, and only in appearance; and his example is something we have no concern with." These conclusions were considered absurdities and falsehoods by them; therefore, they admitted the truth of the miracles.

In the dialogue referred to before **(c)**, the Marcionite expressly says that Christ had opened the eyes of many who were blind.

---

<margin>
**(a)** Christ would not be called a man without flesh—just as he would not be God without the Spirit of God, nor the Son of God without God the Father. Thus, the assessment of both substances displayed him as both man and God: on one hand fleshly, on the other spiritual; on one hand weak, on the other extremely powerful; on one hand dying, on the other living. This is the nature of the divine and human conditions: his miracles <note>original Latin: "virtutes"</note> proved the Spirit of God, and his sufferings <note>original Latin: "passiones"</note> proved the flesh of man. If miracles cannot exist without the Spirit, then likewise sufferings cannot exist without the flesh. If the flesh and its sufferings were a fiction, then the Spirit and its miracles were also false, etc. <note>original Latin: "Non diceretur homo Christus sine Carne.—Sicut nec Deus sine spiritu Dei nec Dei filius sine Deo patre. Ita utriusque substantiæ census hominem et Deum exhibuit... Si caro cum passionibus ficta, et spiritus ergo cum virtutibus falsus, &c."</note> *On the Flesh of Christ, ch. 5, p. 362. A. B.*

**(b)** Flesh that is not flesh, a man who is not a man: therefore Christ, who is God, is not God. Why did he not also carry a phantom of God? Shall I believe him regarding his inner substance when he has failed regarding his outer substance? Now, since the flesh of Christ is found to be a lie, it follows that everything done through the flesh of Christ was done deceitfully: his meetings, his touch, his eating together, and even his miracles. For if he freed someone from a defect by touching them, or was touched by someone, what was physically done cannot be believed to have truly happened without the reality of the body itself. A supposed appearance, a supposed act: an imaginary worker, imaginary works. <note>original Latin: "Caro nec Caro, Homo nec Homo: proinde Deus Christus nec Deus... Jam nunc quum mendacium deprehenditur Christus caro, sequitur ut et omnia quæ per carnem Christi gesta sunt, mendacio gesta sunt; congressus, contactus, convictus, ipsæ quoque virtutes... Putativus habitus, putativus actus: imaginarius operator, imaginariæ operæ."</note> *Against Marcion, Book 3, ch. 8, p. 483. C. D.*

**(c)** But our Lord, being good, opened the eyes of many who were blind. <note>original Greek: "Ο δε κυριος ημων αγαθος ων πολλων τυφλων ηνοιξεν οφθαλμους."</note> *Dialogue Against the Marcionites, sec. 1, p. 29. end.*
</margin>

### SECT. XXV. *And of the principal Facts related concerning him.*

<margin>Sect. 25.</margin>
From all these testimonies, and from the arguments alleged by Tertullian as represented here, as well as from others he introduces to prove the excellence (*d*) and worth of man and the certainty of his being a creature of the Supreme God, it appears that the Marcionites believed the entire history of our Savior's appearance in a human form and of his death on the cross. They also believed that he was crucified between two <term>malefactors</term> <note>original: "malefactors"; modern: criminals</note>. (*e*) However, the detail of his garments being divided by the soldiers was removed by Marcion from his gospel because it was foretold by the Psalmist in Psalm 22:18. They furthermore admitted the truth of the miraculous (*f*) earthquake and darkness at the time of his crucifixion. They acknowledged (*g*) his having twelve apostles and that one of them was a traitor.

---

<margin>(*d*) Finally, look at yourself; consider man both internally and externally. This work of our God will please you, which that "better" God of yours loved; for whose sake he took the trouble to descend from the third heaven into these most impoverished elements, and for whose cause he was even crucified in this small cell of the Creator. <note>original: "Postremo te tibi circumfer, intus et foris considera hominem. Placebit tibi vel hoc opus Dei nostri, quod tuus dominus ille Deus melior adamavit: propter quem in hæc pauperrima elementa de tertio cœlo descendere laboravit: cujus causa in hac cellula creatoris etiam crucifixus est."</note> *Adv. Mar. Lib. 1. c. 14. p. 439. D.*</margin>
<margin>(*e*) And indeed Barabbas, a most guilty man, is given life as if he were good. But Christ, the most just, is demanded for death as if he were a murderer. Moreover, two wicked men are fastened to the cross with him, so that he might be counted among the lawless. Marcion clearly removed the account of his clothing being divided by the soldiers (partly by lot) because he looked back at the prophecy of the Psalm. Therefore, you might as well take away the cross itself. <note>original: "Et Barrabas quidem nocentissimus, vita ut bonus donatur. Christus vero justissimus ut homicida morti expostulatur. Sed et duo scelesti configuntur illi, ut inter iniquos scilicet deputaretur. Vestitum plane ejus a militibus divisum, partim forte concessum, Marcion abstulit, respiciens Psalmi prophetiam. Aufer igitur et crucem ipsam."</note> *Adv. Mar. Lib. 4. c. 42. p. 573. A.*</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>(*f*) Behold, even the elements are shaken, for their Lord was suffering. Otherwise, if it were an adversary being harmed, the heavens would have bloomed with light, the sun would have insulted him more with its rays, and the day would have lingered longer, happily watching the Christ of Marcion hanging on the <term>patibulo</term> <note>original: "patibulo"; a Latin term for a cross or gibbet</note>. <note>original: "Ecce autem et elementa concutiuntur, Dominus enim patiebatur ipsorum. Ceterum adversario læso, cœlum luminibus floruisset, magis sol radiis insultasset, magis dies stetisset, libenter spectans pendentem in patibulo Christum Marcionis."</note> *Ib. Lib. 4. c. 42. p. 573. D.*</margin>
<margin>(*g*) "Woe," he says, "to him by whom the Son of Man is betrayed." Therefore, it is clear that "woe" is to be understood as a cry of curse and threat, attributed to one who is angry and offended—unless Judas was to commit such a great crime without punishment. Furthermore, if he knowingly allowed a man whom he had himself chosen for his company to fall into such a crime, etc. <note>original: "Væ ait per quem traditur filius hominis. Ergo jam væ constat imprecationis et comminationis inclamationem intelligendam, et irato et offenso deputandam, nisi si Judas impune erat tantum sceleris relaturus. Porro si sciens passus est hominem quem ipse comitatui suo asciverat in tantum scelus ruere, &c."</note> *Ibid. Lib. 4. c. 21. p. 571. D. See also Dialogue Against Marcion, section 1, p. 8: "first he sent twelve" [πρωτος απεστειλεν ιβ].*</margin>

The Marcionites also accepted the truth of the appearance of Moses and Elias <note>Elijah</note> on the mount of Transfiguration. They also acknowledged the reality of that voice from heaven which said, "This is my beloved son, hear him." (*b*)

### SECT. XXVI. *The behavior of the Marcionites was virtuous, and they had many Martyrs.*

<margin>SECT. 26.</margin>
With respect to the conduct <note>original: "manners"</note> of the Marcionites, they are not charged by their adversaries with being immoral <note>original: "vicious"</note>. In fact, in the very passage (*i*) where Tertullian upbraids them for their doctrine—which represents God as being purely good and not an object of fear—his own argument shows that they respected the will of God and were eager to obtain his favor as the greatest possible good.

The entire direction of his reasoning assumes that they did not participate in the immoral pursuits of the heathens. Like other Christians, they avoided the savage spectacles of the Circus <note>The Roman chariot racing arena, often associated with violence and pagan rituals</note> and the licentious <note>immoral or crude</note> plays of the Theater. They did not allow themselves to indulge in carnal <note>physical or sexual</note> desires, even though their adversaries claimed that their theological principles should logically lead them to indulge in such things.

---

<margin>(*b*) "For even in this you ought to have been especially ashamed: that you allow him to be seen with Moses and Elijah in the seclusion of the mountain, even though he had come as their destroyer. This is surely what that voice from heaven intended to be understood: 'This is my beloved son, hear him.' That is to say, do not hear Moses and Elijah anymore. Therefore, the voice alone was sufficient without the appearance of Moses and Elijah." <note>original: "Nam et hoc vel maxime erubescere debuisti, quod illum cum Moyfe et Elia in secessu montis conspici pateris, quorum destructor advenerat. Hoc scilicet intelligi voluit vox illa de cœlo; hic est filius meus dilectus, hunc audite. Id eft, non Moysem jam et Heliam. Ergo fufficiebat vox fola fine ostentatione Moyfi et Heliæ."</note> *Ibid. Book 4, chapter 22, page 556. D.*</margin>

<margin>(*i*) "Come then, you who do not fear God because he is good, why do you not boil over with every lust—which is, as far as I know, the greatest fruit of life for all those who do not fear God? Why do you not frequent the customary pleasures of the raging circus, the savage arena, and the lewd theater? Why do you not, in times of persecution, immediately save your soul by offering incense <note>A common test for Christians to prove they had renounced their faith by sacrificing to Roman gods</note> and denying your faith? 'Far be it from me,' you say. Therefore, you already fear sin, and by fearing it, you have proved that he who forbids sin is to be feared. It is another matter if you obey someone you do not fear." <note>original: "Age itaque qui Deum non times quafi bonum, quid non in omnem libidinem ebullis, summum quod fciam fructum vitæ omnibus qui Deum non timent? Quid non frequentas tam solennes voluptates circi furentis, et caveæ fævientis, et fcenæ lafcivientis? Quid non et in perfecutionibus statim oblata acerra animam negatione lucraris? Abfit, inquis, abfit. Ergo jam times delictum, et timendo probafti illum timeri qui prohibet delictum. Aliud eft fi quem non times obfervas."</note> *Against Marcion. Book 1, chapter 27, page 451. A.* See also what follows to the end of the chapter.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Marcionites' moral character, emphasizing their virtuous lives and their willingness to face martyrdom, while also introducing their strict asceticism regarding marriage.</meta>

<page-num>238</page-num>
<header>HISTORY OF HERETICS:</header>

<margin>Section 26.</margin>
In short, it is evident that these people were generally strictly virtuous; that they dreaded sin as the greatest evil; and had such a genuine regard for Christ as to undergo martyrdom rather than offer incense to idols. They seem, indeed, to have had a great number of martyrs. *Asterius Urbanus* (*k*), or some other ancient author who wrote against the Montanists <note>A prophetic Christian movement that began in the 2nd century</note> around AD 232, observed—in response to their boasts about the number of their martyrs—that the Marcionites and other heretics were also known to have had many martyrs. This passage is provided to us by the historian *Eusebius* without being contradicted, which makes it probable that this was indeed the case. *Clement of Alexandria* (*l*) also blames certain heretics who, based on his descriptions, appear to be Marcionites, for offering themselves up for martyrdom in a foolish and reckless manner.

### *They Disdained Marriage and Highly Praised Virginity.*

<margin>Section 27.</margin>
<margin>(k) "For some of the other heresies also have a great many martyrs—and first of all, those from the heresy of Marcion who are called martyrs claim to have a great many martyrs for Christ." <note>original Greek: Και γας των αλλων αιρεσεων τινες πληρες οσης εχασι μαρτυρας—και πρωτοι γε οι απο της Μαρκιωνος αιρεσιας μαρτυρησαι καλυμένοι, πληρες οσης εχασι Χρισυ μαρτυρας λεγύσιν.</note> *Cited in Eusebius, Book 5, ch. 16, p. 182 D.*</margin>
<margin>(l) "We also say this to those who have set themselves to be saved; for there are some, not of our own, who share only in the name, who hand themselves over [to death], being hated by the one who confiscates property... while others are fanatics." <note>original Greek: Λεγομεν δε και ημεις της επιτηδευσαντες το σωζεσθαι, εισι γαρ τινες εκ ημετερων μονα τα ομοιοματος κοινωνοι, οι δη αυτοι παραδιδοντες εαυτους... (likely referring to reckless self-sacrifice).</note> *Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, Book 4, p. 481 C.*</margin>
<margin>(m) "Next follows the matter of marriage, which Marcion, being more rigid than the Apostle [Paul], forbids. For although the Apostle, even if he prefers the good of self-restraint, nevertheless permits marriage to be contracted and used. He advises that it be maintained rather than dissolved. Marcion, however, takes away marriage entirely, etc." <note>original Latin: Sequitur de nuptiis... quas Marcion constantior Apostolo prohibet... ...author of all the sin and misery that exists in the world. His followers (k) moreover argued that the Law and the Gospel could not come from the same being, because there are, in their opinion, several things contained in the former that are inconsistent with many things in the latter. They said the Creator is represented as ignorant or imperfect in knowledge, such as when he called out to Adam (l) and asked where he was. They claimed he is fickle (m) because he gives contradictory commands; and he is inconsistent because he is said to have repented (n)—regretting that he made Saul king and also that he created mankind (o). Because of the wickedness that so generally prevailed, he destroyed almost everyone except for Noah and his family. According to the Marcionites, such punishment manifested a change of mind, and consequently an imperfection in the divine intellect, as well as a deficiency in goodness.

(t) They brought so many objections against the Law and the Prophets that they sounded more like the arguments of pagans <note>original: "heathens"</note> than of people who embraced Christianity, no matter how unorthodox <note>original: "heretical"</note> their views were.

Against these objections, and many others too numerous to mention, Tertullian defends the Old Testament with very strong arguments. This can be seen at length in his second book against Marcion, where he shows (u) that the moral laws are excellent and certainly come from God, as recorded by Moses. Moses lived before the famous pagan law-givers like Lycurgus and Solon, and therefore could not have borrowed any ideas from them.

### SECTION XXXIII. He mutilated the New Testament, wherever it contained Quotations from the Old.

THEIR hatred of the Old Testament was indeed so great that, because of it, they mutilated many passages in the New Testament. Even in the books they did accept, they rejected (x) everything that related to the Law and the Prophets.

--- Page 294 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument that Marcion's "Antitheses"—his list of contradictions between the Old and New Testaments—actually demonstrate the wisdom of a single God who adapts His laws to the needs of different eras.</meta>

<margin>SECTION 34.</margin> Marcion will never prove that the Being who gave the Jewish law is not the same as the God of the Christians. For those rules and requirements of the ceremonial law presented by Marcion as being directly opposite to the Gospel were actually appropriate <note>original: "rightly calculated"</note> for the people they were given to. Even though they would be unsuitable for those living under the different circumstances of the Gospel, this temporary (*b*) difference and apparent opposition only demonstrate the wisdom of that God. He adapts Himself to different circumstances, which quite rightly require a change in approach.

---

[Tertullian writes:] To equip his heresy, Marcion devised a "dowry" for it: a work titled *Antitheses* <note>A Greek word meaning "Oppositions" or "Contradictions." Marcion's book argued that the God of the Old Testament was a different being from the God of the New Testament.</note>, named for its collection of conflicting points. This work was designed to force a separation between the Law and the Gospel. By doing so, Marcion divided God into two different beings, one for each "instrument"—or as it is more commonly called, each Testament. He did this so that he could use his *Antitheses* to support his own version of the Gospel. I could have struck these arguments down in a face-to-face clash, but it was more effective to refute them using the very Gospel Marcion tries to protect. Although it is easy to meet his claims with a formal challenge, I will actually accept them and treat them as valid, showing that they actually support our side. In this way, our own "antitheses" against Marcion will make him even more ashamed of his own blindness. Therefore, I admit that a different order was followed in the old arrangement under the Creator, and another in the new arrangement under 

<column-break/>

Christ. I do not deny that there is a difference in the records of speech, the requirements of virtue, and the disciplines of the law, provided that all this diversity is consistent with one and the same God. <note>original Latin: "instrueret, dotem quandam commentatus est illi, opus ex contrarietum oppositionibus Antitheseis cognominatum... Non nego distare documenta eloquii, præcepta virtutis, legis disciplinas, dum tamen tota diverſitas in unum et eundem Deum competat."</note> *Against Marcion, Book 4, chapter 1.*

(*b*) Remove Marcion’s title, his intentions, and the specific goal of his work, and it provides nothing other than a demonstration that the same God is both perfectly good and a judge—because these two attributes belong to God alone. Even his effort to oppose Christ to the Creator in those examples actually points toward unity. It was not surprising that there was a difference in timing: God was sterner in the past for an untamed people, but later He was milder for those who had been disciplined. Thus, through the *Antitheses*, the order of the Creator as reformed by Christ can be more easily shown. <note>original Latin: "Aufer titulum Marcionis... Quia nec mirum erat diverſitas temporalis ſi poſtea Deus mitior pro rebus edomitis, qui retro auſterior pro indomitis."</note> *Against Marcion, Book 2, chapter 29.*

### SECTION 35. *Marcion accepted only eleven books of the New Testament; of the Gospels, he accepted only that of Luke, and even that was mutilated.*

<margin>Section 35.</margin>
Marcion accepted only eleven books of the New Testament, and these were strangely shortened and altered. He divided them into two parts, calling one "The Gospel" (*i*) and the other "The Apostolicon" <note>A collection of apostolic writings, specifically Marcion’s edited versions of ten of Paul’s epistles.</note>. The former contained only one of the four gospels—namely, that of St. Luke (*k*)—and even this was mutilated, altered, and even corrupted with additions <note>original: "interpolated"</note> in a great variety (*l*) of places. He would not allow it to be called—

---

<columns>2</columns>

(*i*) MEGATHIUS: I will show that the Gospel is one. <note>original Greek: "Δειξω οτι εν εστι το Ευαγγελιον." From *Dialogues Against the Marcionites*, section 1, page 12.</note>

MEGATHIUS: I do not believe your false *Apostolicon*. ADAMANTIUS: Produce your *Apostolicon*. <note>original Greek: "τω σω Φαλσω ου πιστευω Αποστολικω. Προσευεγκε το αποστολικον σου." From *Dialogues Against the Marcionites*, page 8.</note>

MARCIONITE: I am persuaded by my *Apostolicon*. ADAMANTIUS: I have your *Apostolicon*. <note>original Greek: "τω εμω αποστολικω πειθομαι. Εχω το αποστολικον σου." From *Dialogues Against the Marcionites*, page 47.</note>

MARCIONITE: We receive nothing beyond the Gospel and the *Apostolicon*. <note>original Greek: "Ημεις πλειον του Ευαγγελιου, και του Αποστολικου ου δεχομεθα." From *Dialogues Against the Marcionites*, page 58.</note>

Taking into his hands those very books mentioned before which he possesses, namely what they call the Gospel and the so-called *Apostolicon*. <note>original Greek: "Αυτας δη τας τυ προειρημενου βιβλους ας κεκτηται μετα χειρας λαβων, το τε παρ αυτων λεγομενον Ευαγγελιον, και Αποστολικον καλουμενον." From Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 42, page 310.</note>

(*k*) He uses only this specific version, the Gospel according to Luke. <note>original Greek: "Μονω δε κεχρηται τουτω τω χαρακτηρι τω κατα Λουκαν Ευαγγελιω." From Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, page 309.</note>

Of the Gospels, he accepted only that according to Luke. <note>original Greek: "Ουτος εκ μερ των Ευαγγελιων το κατα Λουκαν εδεξατο μονον." From Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book 1, chapter 24.</note>

For among those commentators whom we possess, Marcion seems to have chosen Luke for the purpose of cutting it up <note>original Latin: "Nam ex iis commentatoribus quos habemus, Lucam videtur Marcion elegisse quæ cæderet." From Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book 4, chapter 2.</note>.

Therefore, Marcion is to be challenged on these points, because he omitted the other Gospels and insisted on Luke instead. <note>original Latin: "Itaque de his Marcion flagitandus quod omissis eis Lucæ potius institerit." From Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book 4, chapter 5.</note>

<column-break/>

And many other things which were said by Luke—which both Marcion and Valentinus use—for they are not permitted to accept some of the things said by Luke while rejecting others. <note>original Latin: "Et alia multa quæ—a Luca dicta... Non enim conceditur eis—quædam quidem recipere... quædam vero refutare." From Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book 3, chapter 14.</note>

*See also Dialogues Against the Marcionites, section 1, from pages 6–12.*

(*l*) And besides these things, he cut down the Gospel according to Luke, removing everything written regarding the genealogy <note>original Latin: "generatione," referring to the birth narrative and ancestry of Jesus.</note> of the Lord. <note>original Latin: "Et super hæc id quod est secundum Lucam Evangelium circumcidens et omnia quæ sunt de generatione Domini conscripta auferens." From Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book 1, chapter 27.</note>

I will now come to the things written by him—or rather, his forgeries. For he has only the Gospel according to Luke, and that is mutilated from the beginning because of the Savior's conception and his coming in the flesh. And not only did the one who ruined himself (rather than the Gospel) cut off the beginning, but he also cut off the end and many middle parts of the words of truth. Furthermore, he added other things contrary to what was written. <note>original Greek from Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 42, No. 9. This refers to Marcion removing the birth narrative of Jesus to support his belief that Jesus was not truly born of a woman but appeared suddenly as an adult.</note>

### SECTION 36. *He rejected the Genealogy and Baptism of our Saviour.*

<margin>Section 36.</margin>
According to Irenaeus (*p*), Epiphanius (*q*), and Theodoret (*r*), Marcion also rejected the genealogy and baptism of Christ. If we compare this with a passage from Tertullian—

---

(*m*) In *Against Marcion*, he certainly attributes no author to his own Gospel. <note>original Latin: "Contra Marcion, Evangelio scilicet suo, nullum adscribit auctorem." Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book 4, ch. 2.</note>

The "rope of contention" <note>An ancient idiom for a tug-of-war or intense dispute.</note> must be pulled regarding the Title as well—I say mine is the true one; Marcion says his is. <note>original Latin: "De Titulo quoque funis ducendus est contentionis—Ego meum dico verum Marcion suum." Ibid., ch. 4.</note>

(*n*) MEGATHIUS: I will show that the Gospel is one. ADAMANTIUS: Who is the one who wrote it? This Gospel which you say is the one? MEGATHIUS: Christ. ADAMANTIUS: Did the Lord himself write that he was crucified and rose on the third day? Let it be written. MEGATHIUS: The Apostle Paul added to it. ADAMANTIUS: For was Paul present at the crucifixion of Christ? MEGATHIUS: He wrote the Gospel simply. <note>original Greek: "Δειξω ευ ειναι Ευαγγελιον... αυτος εγραψεν το ευαγγελιον απλως." From *Dialogues Against the Marcionites*, section 1, page 12.</note>

For they are also accustomed to attributing Luke’s ordered account <note>original: "digestum"</note> to Paul. <note>original Latin: "Nam et Lucæ digestum Paulo ascribere solent." Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book 4, ch. 5.</note>

(*o*) In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, he proposes that God descended into the city of Galilee, Capernaum. <note>original Latin: "Anno quinto decimo principatus Tiberiani proponit Deum descendisse in civitatem Galileæ Capharnaum." Tertullian, Book 4, ch. 7.</note>

And he set this as the beginning of the Gospel: "In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar," and so forth. <note>original Greek: "Και αρχην τω Ευαγγελιω εταξε ταυτην, εν τω πεντεκαιδεκατω ετει Τιβεριω Καισαρος, και τα εξης." Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 42, No. 11.</note>

(*p*) And taking away everything that is written regarding the generation <note>meaning: the birth/ancestry</note> of the Lord. <note>original Latin: "Et omnia quæ sunt de generatione Domini conscripta auferens." Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book 1, ch. 27.</note>

(*q*) For the style indicates it is the Gospel according to Luke, but it has been mutilated so that it has neither beginning, middle, nor end; it resembles a garment eaten by many moths. For immediately at the beginning, he cut off all the things handled by Luke from the start—that is, the part where he says, "Since many have undertaken," and so forth; the things about Elizabeth, and the Angel announcing the good news to the Virgin Mary; John and Zechariah; the birth in Bethlehem; the genealogies; and the account of the Baptism. Having cut all these out, he jumped away <note>meaning: he skipped directly to the later narrative</note>. <note>original Greek: "Ο μεν γαρ χαρακτηρ το κατα Λυκαν σημαινει το Ευαγγελιον... ταυτα παντα περικοψας απεπηδησε." Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 42, No. 11.</note>

(*r*) And having cut out the genealogy and most other things. <note>original Greek: "Και την γενεαλογιαν περικοψας τα πλειςα." Theodoret, *Heresies*, Book 1, ch. 24.</note>

For this reason, we can more easily accept Tertullian’s assertion in the sense explained above.

## SECTION 37. He also rejected the History of the Temptation.

<margin>SECTION 37.</margin>
If Marcion removed the story of the temptation of Jesus, he might have done so for the same reason that some others rejected Christ's mourning over Jerusalem, the account of his agony in the garden, and the mention of the angel strengthening him. As we are informed by Epiphanius <margin>(z) <note>original Greek/Latin: "And he wept, it is written in the Gospel according to Luke in the uncorrected copies." See Father Simon's *Critical History of the New Testament*, part 1, chapter 12, p. 111. See also Mill's *New Testament* on this passage. "These things seem to have been erased by some who feared attributing such clear signs of human weakness to Christ." Jansen, *Concordance and Commentary on the Gospels*, chapter 137.</note></margin> and Hilary <margin>(a) <note>original Latin: "Nor indeed should we be ignorant that in very many Greek and Latin manuscripts, nothing is found written either about the approaching angel or about the bloody sweat." Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book 10.</note></margin>, these groups did this so they would not attribute too much human weakness <margin>(b) <note>original Greek: "But they also removed the saying, fearing it, and not understanding its purpose and its power." Epiphanius, ibid.</note></margin> to our Saviour. <note>Marcion and similar groups struggled with the idea of a divine being experiencing suffering, fear, or temptation, which are human traits.</note>

It seems very probable that the Marcionites did not admit the history of the temptation, based on a passage in Epiphanius <margin>(c) <note>original Greek: "For once when I was debating with one of his disciples, a Marcionite, and saying that it is written in the Gospel that the Spirit led him [Jesus] into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil, he naturally replied: how could Satan tempt one who is God, and greater than himself, and his Lord, as you say Jesus is?" Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 42, p. 342.</note></margin>. Epiphanius gives an account of a dispute he had with a certain follower of Marcion. When Epiphanius produced this passage of scripture to prove that Christ was a real man, the follower gave him the following answer: "that it was impossible for Satan to tempt Christ, who was truly God and—according to the opinion of Epiphanius—Satan's Lord and Sovereign."

It compares this to other groups who removed passages showing Jesus's human frailty, such as his agony in Gethsemane.</summary>

### SECTION 38. *An Account of many other Alterations made by him in St. Luke's Gospel.*

<margin>Section 38.</margin>
We will proceed with the account given to us by Epiphanius <note>An influential 4th-century bishop and historian who wrote extensively against various Christian sects he considered heretical.</note> regarding the alterations, omissions, or interpolations <term>interpolations: insertions of new material into a text</term> that Marcion and his followers made in St. Luke's Gospel. It appears from the passage quoted previously (d) that where we read, *for a testimony unto them* (Luke 5:14), Marcion read, *that this may be a testimony unto you*. In verse 24, he transposed (e) the words *upon the earth* <note>original Greek: "eis tēn gēn"</note>, making them follow *sins* <note>original Greek: "hamartias"</note> instead of *men* <note>original Greek: "anthrōpōn"</note>, as they do in our current copies. This is such a minor variation that it likely arose from him finding it in some particular manuscript rather than from any designed alteration. The next passage quoted by Epiphanius (f), chapter 6:5, is read both here and in the repetition of it prefixed (g) to his refutation of Marcion from this text, exactly as in our current copies. The reason for him introducing this text could not be to point out a variation in Marcion's gospel,

# MARCION

<margin>SECTION 38.</margin>

The fourth instance of an alteration is from Luke 6:17, where Marcion read "among them" <note>original Greek: *εν αυτοις*</note> instead of "with them" <note>original Greek: *μετ αυτων*</note>. (l) However, the sense here is the same with one particle as with the other: for "among" <note>original Greek: *εν*</note> may simply be a Hebraism <term>Hebraism: a Hebrew idiom or grammatical structure used in another language</term> and can signify "with" as well as the Greek word for "with" <note>original Greek: *μετ*</note>.

In chapter 8:19, Marcion removed (m) "his mother and his brothers" <note>original Greek: *η μητηρ αυτου, και οι αδελφοι αυτου*</note> from this verse. Tertullian speaks in a way that would lead one to think that Marcion had added to the Gospel of St. Luke by inserting from the Gospel of Matthew that answer of our Savior found in Matthew 12:48: "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" For he represents Marcion, (n) as well as all (o) the other heretics who deny the nativity <term>nativity: the birth of Jesus Christ</term>, as using these words as their most common and favorite argument. But Marcion might have used these words against those who accepted the authenticity of Matthew's Gospel without actually inserting them into his own gospel; or, Tertullian might have been quoting from memory and thought that to be in Luke which was only in Matthew, as he has done in at least three other instances. (p)

### SECTION XL. *The Catholic Christians asserted the Antiquity of the unmutilated Gospel.*

<margin>SECTION 40.</margin>
To demonstrate that these alterations, omissions, additions, and corruptions were not authentic, the Catholic Christians (*g*) <note>The term "Catholic" here refers to the universal, orthodox church of the time, as opposed to sectarian groups like the Marcionites.</note> asserted that their copies of Luke's Gospel were more ancient than Marcion's. They (*h*) maintained the genuineness and integrity of the complete Gospel in opposition to...

---

<margin>(g)</margin>
"For Marcion, having encountered Paul's Letter to the Galatians—in which Paul rebukes even the Apostles themselves for not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, and also accuses certain false apostles of perverting the Gospel of Christ—attempts to destroy the standing of those Gospels which are published as authentic and under the name of the Apostles, or even of apostolic men. He does this so that he may transfer to his own Gospel the credibility which he takes away from theirs." <note>original: "Sed enim Marcion nactus epistolam Pauli ad Galatas... ut scilicet fidem, quam illis adimit, suo conferat." Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book 4, Chapter 3.</note>

See this passage translated and explained at length in *Credibility of the Gospel History*, Part 2, Volume 2, Chapter 27, page 575, note C.

"I say my version is the true one; Marcion says his is. I claim Marcion's version is corrupted; Marcion claims mine is. Who shall decide between us, except the factor of time? Time grants authority to whatever is found to be older and presumes corruption in whatever is proven to be more recent. Otherwise, how absurd would it be if, after we proved our version is older and Marcion’s is more recent, ours was still seen as false before it even had the truth as its source? Or that Marcion’s version should be believed to have faced competition from ours before it was even published? Finally, that the truest version should be considered the one produced latest, after so many great works and documents of the Christian religion have already been published? These could not have been published without the truth of the Gospel—that is, before the truth of the Gospel existed. Regarding Luke's Gospel specifically: our version is so much older than Marcion that Marcion himself once believed it. Certainly, his *Antitheses* <note>A famous work by Marcion where he contrasted the Old Testament God with the New Testament God to show they were supposedly different beings.</note> not only admit to this but emphasize it. If the Gospel referred to as Luke's is the very one Marcion attacks through his *Antitheses*, he certainly could not have attacked it unless he had first found it. A 'correction' cannot come before the fault it corrects. Thus, by 'emending' the text, he confirms both points: that our version is earlier (because he is emending what he found) and that his is later (since he made his own new version by modifying ours)." <note>original: "Ego meum dico verum; Marcion suum... id posterius, quod de nostri emendatione constituens suum et novum fecit." Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book 4, Chapter 4.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>(h)</margin>
"In short, if it is established that what is earlier is truer, what is from the beginning is earlier, and what is from the Apostles is from the beginning, it will likewise be clear that what has been held as sacred in the churches of the Apostles was handed down by the Apostles themselves. Let us see: what milk did the Corinthians drink from Paul? By what rule were the Galatians corrected? What do the Philippians, Thessalonians, and Ephesians read? What do the Romans also [say] about..." <note>original: "In summa, si constat id verius quod prius... quid etiam Romani de..." Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book 4, Chapter 5. The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

### SECTION XLI. *Marcion rejected the Acts of the Apostles.*

<margin>SECTION 41.</margin>
Marcion did not include the *Acts of the Apostles* in his New Testament canon. This is clear from Epiphanius (i), who says that Marcion’s New Testament consisted of an *Evangelium* <note>original: Evangelium; the Gospel</note> and an *Apostolicon* <note>original: Apostolicon; a collection of apostolic letters</note>. The *Evangelium*, as previously noted (j), contained only the Gospel of Luke. The *Apostolicon* (l) consisted of ten of the (k) Epistles of Paul. These two books (m) were the only ones...

<column-break/>

...let them speak from nearby, those to whom the Gospel was left—sealed with the blood of both Peter and Paul. We also have churches nurtured by John. For even if Marcion rejects his Revelation <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, the order of Bishops, when traced back to its origin, will stand with John as its author. Likewise, the noble lineage of the other churches is recognized. I say, therefore, that among those apostolic churches—and not only them, but all that are joined with them in the fellowship of the sacrament—that Gospel of Luke has stood firm from the beginning of its publication, which we most strongly defend; whereas Marcion's version is unknown to most, and known to none except to be condemned. <note>original: "de proximo sonent, quibus Evangelium et Petrus et Paulus sanguine quoque suo signatum reliquerunt... Marcionis vero plerisque nec notum, nullis autem notum ut non eo damnatum." Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book 4, Chapter 5.</note>

The *Acts of the Apostles* is clearly excluded from his catalogue of authentic books, as given by Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius (c. 310–403 AD) was a bishop and counter-heresy writer</note>. The same thing appears from the more ancient authority of Tertullian, who begins his fifth book against Marcion (*n*) by showing the absurdity of Marcion’s conduct. Tertullian points out that Marcion rejects the history and *Acts of the Apostles*, yet receives St. Paul as the chief of the apostles—even though Paul's name is never mentioned in the Gospels alongside the other apostles. This is especially contradictory since the (*o*) account given by Paul himself in the first and second chapters of Galatians confirms the account which we have in *Acts*. But the reason why he rejected this book is, as Tertullian (*p*) says, very evident: from the *Acts*, we can plainly show that the God of the Christians and the Creator (the God of the Jews) were the same being, and that Christ was sent by Him and no other. <note>Marcion was a dualist who believed the harsh "Creator God" of the Old Testament was distinct from the "Merciful God" revealed by Jesus. He rejected any book that linked the two.</note>

The arguments against Marcion which follow in this fifth book are all drawn from only those ten epistles of St. Paul which are the same as those mentioned by Epiphanius. They are placed in exactly the same order, except that the Epistle to Philemon is placed last in (*q*) Tertullian, and that to the—

## SECTION XLIV. *In the First Epistle to the Corinthians.*

In the first epistle to the Corinthians, the 9th chapter, Section 44, 8th verse, where we read: "Or does the law not say <note>original OCR: "faith"; likely a misreading of "saith"</note> the same also?" He changed it into: "Or does not the law of *Moses* say the same?" By inserting the word *Moses*, he intended to make the apostle <note>original: "apostile"</note> insinuate that it was not the law of the God of the Christians.

In chapter 10, verse 9, Epiphanius <margin>(m)</margin> accuses *Marcion* of having changed *Lord* <note>original Greek: *κύριον* (kyrion)</note>—which according to Epiphanius was the true reading—into *Christ* <note>original Greek: *χριστόν* (christon)</note>, which is the reading found in our present copies. But whatever Epiphanius thought, it is probable that *Lord* was the true reading. For some person who thought the sense was harsh with *Christ* might change it into *Lord*. But no good reason can be assigned for the change happening the other way around. <note>The author is discussing a textual variant in 1 Corinthians 10:9 regarding whether the Israelites tempted "the Lord," "God," or "Christ" in the wilderness.</note>

In the 19th verse of this same chapter, *Marcion* <margin>(n)</margin> changed the phrase "that the idol is anything" <note>original Greek: *οτι ειδωλον τι εστιν* (hoti eidōlon ti estin)</note> into "that what is offered in the temple is anything" <note>original Greek: *οτι ιεροθυτον τι εστιν* (hoti ierothyton ti estin)</note>.

<column-break/>

(l) "He changed it, for it reads, 'No, and the law says these things' (in our copies it is 'Or does not the law also say all these things?'). He immediately says, 'If also the law of Moses says these things.'" <note>original: *Metallaxamenos...*</note> *Epiphanius, ibid. p. 320. B.* Here "if" <note>original: "EI"</note> is put for "or" <note>original: "η"</note>. And because it is written as "or" elsewhere and not placed where Epiphanius wants it as the conjunction "although," who would believe Marcion was so foolish as to say the law does not say those things, and yet immediately add that it is written in the Mosaic law? *Mill’s Testament on this passage.*

2. Does not Epiphanius understand "or" in the same sense as Dr. Mill? *See Epiphanius, Heresies 42. p. 355.*

(m) "But Marcion, instead of the Lord, substituted Christ." <note>original: *O de Markiōn anti tō kyriou, christon apōsato.*</note> *Epiphanius, ibid. p. 358. B.*

(n) "What then do I say? That an idol-sacrifice is anything, or that idolatry is anything? But Marcion added 'temple-sacrifice'." <note>original: *Ti oun phēmi...*</note> *Epiphanius, ibid. p. 358. D.* It is noted as an addition because Epiphanius read in his copy only: "What then do I say? Is an idol-sacrifice anything?"
