In the 14th chapter and 19th verse, Marcion read <margin>(o)</margin> "on account of the law" <note>original Greek: διὰ τὸν νόμον (dia ton nomon)</note> instead of "with my understanding" <note>original Greek: διὰ τοῦ νοὸς μοῦ (dia tou noos mou)</note>, as it is in our copies, or "with my mind" <note>original Greek: τῷ νοῒ μοῦ (tō noi mou)</note> as Epiphanius and some very ancient Greek manuscripts read.

In the 15th chapter and the 38th verse, Marcion <margin>(p)</margin> substituted "spirit" <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα (pneuma)</note> instead of "body" <note>original Greek: σῶμα (sōma)</note>. He also left out the latter clause of the 38th verse, and the whole of the 39th, 40th, and 41st verses, as well as the first clause of the 42nd verse, and introduced part of the 44th verse before the latter clause of the 42nd. For the Marcionite, in the dialogue ascribed to Origen <note>likely the *Dialogue on the True Faith in God*</note>, says it is read this way in their *Apostolicon* <note>Marcion's version of the New Testament</note>: "God gives it a spirit, as it has pleased him. It is sown a natural body <note>original: "animal body"</note>, it is raised a spiritual body. It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption," etc. In the 45th verse of this chapter, Marcion <margin>(q)</margin> substituted "Lord" <note>original Greek: κύριος (kyrios)</note> instead of "Adam" in the latter clause; and in the 47th verse he omitted <margin>(r)</margin> the word "man" in the latter clause.

<header>MARCION.</header>

## SECTION XLV.
### In the Second Epistle to the Corinthians.

<margin>Section 45.</margin>
In the second epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 4, verse 3, Marcion understood "the God of this world" <note>original Greek: Θεος του αιωνος τουτου (Theos tou aiōnos toutou)</note> to be the Creator. He considered him here as being opposed to the good God, or the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was the God of the Christians. 

In opposition to this, Irenaeus, <margin>(f)</margin> Tertullian, <margin>(t)</margin> and others <margin>(u)</margin> who wrote against the Marcionites, were in favor of placing a comma after "God" <note>original Greek: Θεος (Theos)</note>, and referring "of this world" <note>original Greek: αιωνος τουτου (aiōnos toutou)</note> to the unbelievers <note>The OCR reads "αρκων," likely a transcription error for "απιστων" (unbelievers), matching the Latin "infidelium" in the footnotes</note>. Their reading was: "In whom God has blinded the eyes of the unbelievers of this world." To us today, who are but little interested in the dispute with the Marcionites, this sense appears very harsh; it is one instance among many others of how far the heat of controversy will carry men. In the 13th verse of this same chapter, Marcion...

<column-break/>

<margin>(f)</margin> "Regarding what they say, that Paul openly stated in the 2nd to the Corinthians: *In whom the God of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers*; and they say that one is the God of this world, while the other is he who is above every principality, and beginning, and power: it is not our fault if those who say they know the mysteries above God do not even know how to read Paul. For if anyone reads according to Paul’s custom—as we have shown from many other places that he uses hyperbaton <note>a figure of speech where the natural word order is inverted</note>—and reads it thus: *In whom God*, then making a distinction and a small pause <note>original Latin: diastematis</note>, reads the rest together as one: *has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this world*, he will find the truth; so that it says, *God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this world*." — Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book 3, chapter 7, page 210. Oxford Edition, 1702.

<margin>(t)</margin> "Marcion seized upon this by reading it as, *in whom the God of this age*, showing the Creator to be the God of this age, suggesting another God of another age. We, on the contrary, say it should be punctuated thus: *In whom God*; then: *has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age*." — Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book 5, chapter 11, page 467. 36. 1597.

<margin>(u)</margin> Augustine, in *Against Faustus* (Book 21, chapters 2, 9), mentions this, but seems better pleased to understand "the God of this world" <note>original Greek: Θεος του αιωνος τουτου</note> as the Devil. "Therefore, in an evil work—that is, the blinding of unbelievers—if the Devil is also understood as persuading them through malice, so that it is punctuated as 'the God of this world,' it does not seem absurd to me: 'of this world,' that is, of wicked men who wish to flourish only in this world... whose God is their belly, etc." — Chapter 9.

<summary>This page analyzes the debate between Marcion and the early Church Fathers over 2 Corinthians 4:4. Marcion interpreted "the God of this world" as the inferior Creator deity, while writers like Irenaeus and Tertullian argued for a different punctuation of the verse to avoid that conclusion.</summary>
<keywords>Marcion, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Augustine, 2 Corinthians, God of this world, Creator, dualism, biblical interpretation, hyperbaton</keywords>

<margin>Section 45.</margin> Marcion (*x*) erased the words "according as it is written: I believed, and therefore have I spoken" <note>original Greek: *κατα το γεγραμμενον· επιστευσα, διο ελαλησα* (kata to gegrammenon; episteusa, dio elalēsa)</note>.

### SECTION XLVI.
### *In the Epistle to the Romans.*

<margin>Section 46.</margin> In the epistle to the Romans, which is placed fourth in the *Apostolicon* <term>Marcion's collection of processed Pauline epistles</term>, Tertullian (*y*) informs us that Marcion had made great erasures. However, Tertullian says he will not point out every particular passage mutilated by him; instead, he intends only to mention others which, according to Marcion’s own principles, he might have been expected to expunge because they argued against his views. Tertullian produces these as instances of Marcion’s "negligence and blindness."

Epiphanius has given us no specific examples of corruptions or mutilations made by Marcion in this epistle. The passages he produces from it are only intended to confute Marcion by using those texts which Marcion himself allowed to be genuine. Epiphanius finds fault (*z*) with Marcion for ranking Romans as the fourth book in his *Apostolicon*, remarking that he did so because he "would have nothing right." However, we are informed by Origen—or rather by Rufinus (*a*) in his edition of Origen's *Commentary on this Epistle*—that Marcion omitted the last two chapters as spurious, ending the epistle in his *Apostolicon* with the 23rd verse of the 14th chapter.

It is also notable that Tertullian (*b*) quotes no passage from the 15th or 16th chapters in his refutation of Marcion using the passages contained in this epistle.

---

(*x*) <note>original Greek: *Εχοντες δε το αυτο πνευμα της πιστεως και ημεις πιστευομεν, διο και λαλομεν. εξεκοψε δε το κατα το γεγραμμενον.* (Having the same spirit of faith, we also believe, and therefore speak. But he cut out the part "according as it is written.")</note> *Epiphanius, ibid, page 367. C.*

(*y*) <note>original Latin: *Quantas autem foveas in ista vel maxime epistola Marcion fecerit, auferendo quæ voluit, de nostri testamenti integritate parebit. Mihi sufficit quæ proinde eradenda non vidit, quasi negligentias et cæcitates ejus accipere.* (How many pits Marcion has dug, especially in this epistle, by taking away what he wished, will be evident from the integrity of our own testament. It is enough for me to accept those parts which he did not see fit to erase as instances of his negligence and blindness.)</note> *Against Marcion, Book 5, chapter 13, page 469. 38. 1597.*

(*z*) <note>original Greek: *Της προς Ρωμαιος τεταρτης επιστολης. ουτως γαρ εστι παρα τω Μαρκιωνι κειμενη, ινα μηδεν ορθον παρ αυτω ειη.* (The fourth epistle, to the Romans. For so it is arranged by Marcion, so that nothing of his might be correct.)</note> *Epiphanius, ibid, page 368. B.*

(*a*) *See Origen: or rather Rufinus: Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 14, 23.*

(*b*) *See Tertullian against Marcion, Book 5, chapter 14.*

## SECTION XLVII.
->*In the First Epistle to the Thessalonians.*<-

The fifth book in Marcion’s <term>Apostolicon</term> <note>Marcion's specific collection of the letters of the Apostle Paul</note> is the First Epistle to the <term>Thessalonians</term>. <term>Epiphanius</term> (c) says that this epistle was so entirely corrupted by Marcion that he had selected nothing from it on which to base any refutations of him or his doctrine. <term>Tertullian</term>, however, was of a different mind. From his writings, it appears that although Marcion may have made alterations, enough was left untouched to show the absurdity of his opinions. Tertullian says (d) that it will not be unprofitable to attend to the shorter epistles, for there is a "pleasantness" <note>original Latin: *favor*, suggesting a certain grace or benefit</note> in a few words. Accordingly, he draws arguments from the 2nd, 4th, and 5th chapters of this first epistle.

Tertullian notes (e) that the word "own" <note>original Greek: *ιδίους* (idious)</note> in the 15th verse of the 2nd chapter <note>1 Thessalonians 2:15: "Who both killed the Lord Jesus, and their **own** prophets..."</note> was an addition made by this <term>heretic</term>. This word is found in our present copies, but it is missing from some of the most ancient Greek manuscripts (f) and was omitted by <term>Origen</term>, as well as by Tertullian and several others.

***

(c) "The fifth [epistle], to the Thessalonians—for so it stands in Marcion—being so entirely corrupted by Marcion that we could find nothing in it to use against him." <note>original Greek: *Της προς Θεσσαλονικεις πεμπτης επιτολως, ετως γαρ κειται εν τω Μαρκιων–τα παντα τω Μαρκιωνος διεφαγμενος απ αυτης εχοντες, ιδειν εξ αυτης πολεμιθα.* (Note: the Greek contains several transcription errors in the OCR.)</note>

(d) "I shall not be reluctant to attend to the shorter epistles as well. There is a certain grace even in a few words." <note>original Latin: *Breuioribus quoque epiftolis non pigebit intendere. Est fauor et in paucis.*</note>

(e) "Even if the word 'own' is an addition by the heretic." <note>original Latin: *Licet fuos adjectio fit haeretici.*</note>

(f) See Mill’s Testament on this passage; also the *Dialogue against the Marcionites*, section 4, page 125; and the *Reply to Africanus*, page 234.

<summary>This page discusses Marcion's version of 1 Thessalonians, highlighting a disagreement between Epiphanius and Tertullian regarding whether the text was too corrupted to be used for refutation. It specifically notes a textual variant in 1 Thessalonians 2:15 regarding the word "own."</summary>

### SECTION XLVIII. *In the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians.*

<margin>SECTION 48.</margin>
<margin>(g)</margin>
<margin>(b)</margin>
<margin>(i)</margin>
Epiphanius (g) affirms the same concerning the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians—the sixth in Marcion’s <term>Apostolicon</term> <note>Marcion’s curated collection of the Apostle Paul’s letters</note>—as he had previously stated regarding the first: namely, that the reason he selected nothing from it was because it was entirely corrupted by Marcion. Tertullian (b), however, cites several passages from this second epistle to refute this <term>heretic</term> <note>Marcion, who taught that the God of the New Testament was different from the God of the Old Testament</note>, and he accuses him only (i) of erasing "in flaming fire" <note>original Greek: εν πυρι φλογος (*en pyri phlogos*)</note> from the 8th verse of the first chapter, lest he should attribute vengeance and the infliction of punishment to Christ, whom he regarded as the son of the "good God." <note>In Marcion's theology, the "Good God" was a deity of pure mercy, distinct from the judgmental Creator God of the Hebrew Bible.</note>

### SECTION XLIX. *In the Epistle to the Ephesians, which was called by him the Epistle to the Laodiceans.*

<margin>(k)</margin>
The Epistle to the Ephesians is the seventh, according to the order in which Marcion placed St. Paul’s writings. Tertullian (k) says Marcion had entitled this the

***

(g) <note>original Greek: Της προς Θεσσαλονικεις δευτερας, εκτης δε κειμενης παρα τω Μαρκιωνι — ομοιος διαγραφει– σις απ' αυτου την Μαρκιωνος, παλιν αλλην εξεδιδε– Σα.</note> "The second [epistle] to the Thessalonians, which is sixth in Marcion's order—similarly, he erased parts of it, and Marcion again published another [version]." # M A R C I O N.
<sig>N n 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: said,</meta>

<margin>SECTION 49.</margin>
...the Epistle to the Laodiceans, as if to show his great diligence in investigating this matter. According to Epiphanius, as previously quoted (l), he had some fragments in his *Apostolicon* <note>Marcion's curated collection of the Apostle Paul's letters</note> of what was called the Epistle to the Laodiceans. The passage he quotes from his *Apostolicon* under this title (m) is clearly taken from Ephesians 4:5–6, with only the addition of "one Christ" <note>original Greek: εις χριςος (*eis christos*)</note> inserted between the words "one baptism" and "one God."

Mr. Jones asserts (n) "that it does not appear Tertullian ever saw Marcion's *Apostolicon*." However, it seems highly probable to me that he had seen and compared it with his own copy, since he provides an account of several variations in this *Apostolicon* compared to his own version of the epistles. What Marcion included in his *Apostolicon* under the title of an "Epistle to the Laodiceans" is explicitly stated by Epiphanius to be only "parts" <note>original Greek: μερη (*merē*)</note> or fragments. It is possible that by the time of Epiphanius, certain passages from the Epistle to the Ephesians and other letters of St. Paul were inserted into the *Apostolicon* used by the Marcionites of that era. These may have been taken from an epistle that bore the title "Epistle to the Laodiceans," even though in the *Apostolicon* used during Tertullian's time, the Epistle to the Ephesians itself carried that title. What is certain is that Tertullian (o) quotes specifically from those ten epistles of St. Paul that Epiphanius says Marcion accepted—and from those only. Furthermore, they are arranged in the same order by both authors, except for the differences mentioned previously.

It was said (p) that Epiphanius places Philemon ninth and Philippians last, while Tertullian places Philippians ninth and Philemon last. Epiphanius, by saying (q) that Marcion received only ten epistles of St. Paul, further shows that what was added in the *Apostolicon* <note>Marcion’s collection of Paul's letters</note> of Marcion under the title of the "Epistle to the Laodiceans"—in those places, if any, where it differed from the other ten epistles—was not considered the genuine writing of St. Paul. <margin>Section 39</margin>In the 9th verse of the 3rd chapter, he erased the preposition *in*, in order to give a different turn to the whole sentence; which, to align with his notions, must be translated as follows: "And to make all men see by Jesus Christ, what is the fellowship of the mystery, which has for ages been hidden **from** God the creator of all things." <note>Marcion’s theology distinguished between a lower Creator God and a higher Supreme God; by changing "hid in God" to "hid from God," he suggested the Creator was ignorant of Christ's mystery.</note> This is a construction which the Greek language will by no means allow. If the word "in" <note>original Greek: ἐν</note> is left out, the following words for "God" and "creator" should be in a different grammatical case <note>original: it should be "of" (ου) and "creating" (κτιενοντος)</note>. 

In chapter 5, verse 31, Marcion erased some words. According to Epiphanius (z), he only removed the phrase "unto his wife"; but Tertullian (a) quotes the text as if Marcion had omitted the entire clause, "and shall be joined unto his wife," which Dr. Mill thinks (b) was indeed the case. However, in the manner in which Epiphanius represents it, the sense remains complete: "For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined (to the Lord mentioned in verse 29), and they two shall be one flesh, etc." 

In chapter 6, verse 2, he omitted the latter clause (c), "which is the first commandment with a promise," lest the Mosaic law should be seen as being established or validated by this statement.

## SECTION 50. *He probably did not much alter the Epistle to the Colossians.*

<margin>SECTION 50.</margin>

### SECTION 53. *An Argument from this in favor of the Authenticity of the New Testament.*

The evidence to be drawn from this overview in favor of the authenticity of the books of the New Testament is very strong. # LUCIAN OR LEUCIUS.

<margin>SECTION 1.</margin>

[Epi]phanius had completely omitted some names and included others; he expanded some accounts and shortened others. He reduced the sixty heresies that appeared after the time of Christ (which we find in the works of Epiphanius) to fifty-seven. He did this by treating very similar groups as a single heresy, whereas Epiphanius had listed them as two distinct ones. In the current case, since Epiphanius had himself stated that Lucian followed Marcion in all things, Augustine <note>original: "Austin"</note>—in the short account he was giving of heretics—might have thought it unnecessary to speak of him as distinct from Marcion, since he could find little or no difference between them.

I have placed at the bottom of the page the account of this person given by Philaster (q) and the author (r) of the *Additions to Tertullian*. However, they call him Lucan. Their sequence of names is Cerdon, Marcion, Lucan, and Apelles; this helps to show that they mean the same person whom Epiphanius calls Lucian. He is also mentioned by Tertullian himself (s) as one who does not allow for the resurrection of the body. Tertullian also calls him Lucan, as does Origen in his book *Against Celsus*. Origen says (t) he did not know of any Christians who had altered the text of the Gospel, except the followers of Valentinus and Marcion, and perhaps those of Lucan.

### SECTION III. *Of his Opinions.*

<margin>Sect. 3.</margin>
SECONDLY, we will discuss his opinions. His views were clearly explained in the section previously cited (d). That account is further confirmed by what we have just quoted and by what we will now proceed to mention.

# HISTORY OF HERETICS:

### SECTION IV.

<margin>Section 4.</margin>
The Marcionites <note>term: followers of Marcion of Sinope, a 2nd-century teacher who rejected the Old Testament and emphasized a dualistic view of God.</note> spoke of a resurrection that might be called a figurative resurrection, which (_n_) they applied only to souls. They considered souls to be dead while they were in the body; therefore, the death of the body was the life—or in their phraseology, the resurrection—of the soul. This is consistent with the Platonic doctrine, which represented the soul as being in a prison while confined in the body. Docetism <note>original: "Doctism." This is the belief that Christ's physical body and sufferings were only appearances, not reality.</note> seems to have derived its origin from this philosophy. For the followers of this opinion were principally among the higher classes of men and were chiefly those who had been converted from Heathenism <note>term: Greco-Roman pagan religions.</note> to Christianity. Lucian might therefore very probably be a believer in the resurrection of the souls of animals <note>original: "brutes."</note> in this sense, as well as in the resurrection of the souls of men. For it was a Marcionite tenet, to which he also undoubtedly gave his assent, that the souls of men and the souls of animals (_o_) are of the same kind. Thus far, Philaster <note>term: a 4th-century bishop and author of a catalog of heresies.</note> is undoubtedly right in saying that he believed the souls of men and beasts to be alike. This is one proof among many others that he was a follower of Marcion and not a Manichean <note>term: a follower of Mani, whose dualistic religion emerged in the 3rd century, later than the Marcionites.</note>, and therefore he is justly placed, as observed before, in the second century.

(_n_) "He says that the soul alone is the resurrection, and life, and salvation." <note>original: Ψυχη δε Ανατασις ειναι λεγει, και ζωη και σωτηρια μονη. *Epi. Ibid. p. 305. B.*</note>

(_o_) "I think this wretched man, along with those who think this way, [held] that the same soul exists in humans and in animals." <note>original: Νομιζω δε ο ελεηνος ετος αμα τοις ετω φρονεσι, οτι η αυτη ψυχη εν τοις ανθρωποις και ζωοις υπαρχει. *Epi. Ibid. p. 330. B.*</note>

<summary>This page explains that the Marcionites viewed "resurrection" as the release of the soul from the prison of the body, a view influenced by Platonic philosophy. It further argues that Lucian (Leucius) believed human and animal souls were identical in nature, identifying him as a 2nd-century Marcionite rather than a later Manichean.</summary>

### SECT. V. *A Belief in another Kind of Resurrection, ascribed to him by Tertullian.*

<margin>Section 5.</margin>
Tertullian indeed here ascribes to him the belief in a different kind of resurrection. He says (p) it was Lucian's opinion that a "third thing," which was neither soul nor body, was to be raised. Consequently, this resurrected being was not a man, but might even be a bear. Dr. Mill (q) understands this as pointing to Lucian's belief in the Pythagorean transmigration of souls <note>term: Reincarnation, or the movement of a soul into a new body after death, a concept associated with the Greek philosopher Pythagoras.</note> from one body to another, and even into the bodies of animals. According to this view, men were endowed with the souls of other men, and even animals <note>original: "brutes"</note> sometimes possessed souls that had previously resided in a human body. Epiphanius, in his refutation of Marcion regarding the rule against eating meat, says (r) that the transmission <note>original: "traduction"</note> and passage of souls from one body to another was a common opinion

---

<columns>2</columns>

(p) <note>original Latin: "Omnes enim fere hæretici eam (animæ salutem)..."</note> "For almost all heretics, in whatever way they desire it, still do not deny the salvation of the soul. Let one individual, Lucanus, see to it; he does not even respect this substance [the soul], which he dissolves according to Aristotle’s philosophy and substitutes something else in its place. He claims a 'third thing' will be resurrected, which is neither soul nor flesh—that is, not a man, but perhaps a bear, such as Lucanus himself." *Tertullian, On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 2, page 315.*

(q) <note>original Latin: "Tum vero quod prodigiosam nescio quam resurrectionem..."</note> "Then truly, because he devised some monstrous resurrection in which neither the human soul nor the body was to be raised, but a third something—specifically (based on the Pythagorean hypothesis concerning the transmigration of souls from bodies into the bodies of both men and beasts, which he approved) men were endowed with the souls of others, and therefore were not the same as they had been before, just as beasts were endowed with human souls. This is how I interpret Tertullian’s words based on Photius." *Mill’s Prolegomena, 334, page 37. Oxford edition.*

<column-break/>

(r) <note>original Greek: "Διδασκει γαρ ουτος εμψυχων μη μεταλαμβανειν..."</note> "For he teaches people not to consume living things, saying that those who eat meat are liable to judgment because they are, in effect, eating souls... for the meat is not the soul, but the soul is within the meat. And when we say there is a soul in animals, just as the human soul is precious... but this wretched man thinks like those who hold these views. This is idly supposed by many of the wandering heresies; for indeed Valentinus, Colobarsus—all of them—and the Manichaeans, say there are transfers of souls and re-embodiments of the soul." *Epiphanius, Against Heresies, 42, page 330, B. C.*

### SECTION VI. *A General Account of his Writings.*

<margin>Section 6.</margin> THIRDLY. I proceed to give some account of his writings.
Grabe <note>John Ernest Grabe (1666–1711), a theologian known for his work on early Christian manuscripts.</note>, who applied himself very particularly to these matters, has assured us (*t*) that he was the author of many forgeries under the names of the holy apostles; and (*u*) that he himself had found several fragments of his writings in manuscript which were never yet published, but which he intended to give to the world in their proper places. Had he lived to have completed his design, perhaps many pieces would have clearly appeared to have been the forgeries of this person, about which there are now some remaining doubts. However, he has been long, and justly, regarded as the grand framer of Apocryphal books <note>term: Religious texts that were not included in the official Bible, often because their origins or teachings were considered questionable by the early Church.</note>: in which, as Photius the Patriarch <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar.</note>

<header>SECTION 6.</header>

## LUCIUS OR LEUCIUS.

The Patriarch <note>original: "Arch"</note> of Constantinople says, (x) “His style is entirely inconsistent and varied. The construction and words which he makes use of, though they are sometimes far from being undignified, are nonetheless for the most part very common and unrefined. In his writings, there are no traces of a smooth and flowing phraseology, or of a natural grace similar to that which we find in the style of the Evangelists and Apostles.” Pope Gelasius (y) has condemned him and his works in the strongest terms, declaring that all those books which go under the name of the travels of Andrew and the other apostles were forged by Lentitius (as he is called there) or Leucius; he declared that all his writings are apocryphal <note>term: Religious texts not accepted as part of the official Bible.</note> and he himself is a disciple of the Devil. It is, however, necessary to observe that all the contradictions, silly stories, unrefined language, and inaccuracies which are now in these books are not to be blamed entirely on Leucius. It is evident from some of the pieces themselves that they have been interpolated <note>term: To have had new (and often unauthorized) material inserted into the original text.</note>, as Beausobre (z) has clearly shown, and that they have been altered by several different hands, some of whom were extremely ignorant.

I would also further remark that this heretic is called by many names, such as *Lucanus*, *Lucius*, *Leicius*, *Leucius*, *Lentitias*, *Leontius*, *Lentius*, *Seleucus*, *Leucius Charinus*, and even *Nexobarides* and *Leonides*. These all refer to one and the same person, as is fully shown by Mr. Jones (a) and Beausobre.

<margin>(x) <note>original Greek: "Ἡ δὲ φράσις, ως το παντελες, ανωμαλος τε και παρηλλαγμενη..."</note> "His style is completely inconsistent and altered. For in his constructions and words, he occasionally uses them not without care, but for the most part they are rustic and low. And there is not a trace of the even and concentrated phraseology, nor of the sufficient innate grace, by which the word of the Gospels and Apostles is formed." Photius, Code 114.</margin>

<margin>SECTION 7.</margin>
Eastern philosophy <note>The author refers here to Gnosticism and dualistic systems from the East that emphasized a struggle between light and darkness.</note> had spread among Christians long before Mani <note>original: "Manes," the 3rd-century founder of Manichaeism.</note> emerged; and this Leucius is very justly considered as a predecessor to him, and a source from which Mani and his followers derived some of their principal arguments. For, as I have previously observed, he believed in a principle of evil as well as a principle of good and a principle of justice. The Manichees <note>term: Followers of a dualistic religion that viewed the world as a conflict between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note> therefore readily accepted his writings, which contained sentiments so favorable to their own. Because of this, it is probable that the author of that letter included among Jerome’s works was led to call him a Manichee. Neither Augustine <note>original: "Austin"</note> nor Pope Gelasius apply this name to him in the passages referred to by Mr. Jones; they only say that the Manichees respected his writings. If he had been a member of this sect, the date assigned to him by Mr. Jones would have been correct. But as he was a contemporary of Marcion <note>term: A 2nd-century teacher who rejected the Old Testament and believed the God of the Jews was different from the God of the New Testament.</note> and was his student, that date is undoubtedly wrong. John Ernest Grabe, *(e)* a proper and accurate judge in these matters, declares that he was the successor of Marcion and a heretic of the second century.

## SECTION 9. *The Writer was not a Jew.*

<margin>SECTION 9.</margin>
There are Hebraisms <note>term: linguistic structures or idioms from the Hebrew language used in Greek or English text.</note> in the phrasing, which induced Mr. Jones to attribute this piece to some Jew or Hellenist <note>term: A person of Jewish descent who lived in a Greek-speaking culture and used the Greek language.</note>. However, he himself later admits (*o*) that it might have been composed by Leucius Charinus, or our Leucius, who borrowed from some earlier forgery, and that the version we have now is different from his. 

For in the fragment preserved by Augustine <note>original: "Austin"</note>, Mary is said to be from the tribe of Levi, whereas in our present copies, she is said (*p*) to be descended from the royal race and family of David. Although it must be acknowledged that there are some Hebraisms in this piece and some allusions to Jewish customs, it is also certain that there are other things which are contrary to facts well known among

### SECTION 11. A current Tradition that *Joseph* was a Widower, and had Children by his former Wife.

<margin>SECTION 10.</margin>
The opinion that *Joseph* was a widower and had children by a former wife when he was betrothed to *Mary* was common in the early ages of the church. *Origen* mentions it in his commentary on Matthew *13:55 (u)* and says many believed that the brothers of Christ mentioned there were the children of *Joseph* by a former wife. He says many believed that the "brothers" of Christ mentioned there were the children of Joseph by a former wife, and that they were led to this opinion by certain passages in the *Gospel of Peter* or the *Book of James* <note>Also known as the Protevangelion of James</note>. Eusebius (x) gives the same reason for why James was called the brother of Christ. Epiphanius (y) has frequently mentioned this same thing. He says that James was the son of Joseph by a former wife and was therefore called the brother of Jesus. He further states that Joseph was about eighty years old when he married Mary and that he had six children by a former wife.

He states that Joseph was the brother of Cleophas and the son of James, who was surnamed Panther. He notes that Joseph's first wife was of the tribe of Judah and that he had six children by her—four sons and two daughters. ### SECTION XV.
*He was the Forger of the Gospel of Nicodemus.*

The *Gospel of Nicodemus*, or the *Acts of Pilate*, as it is otherwise called, was also a forgery produced by our Leucius. There were probably some accounts <margin>(g) *Jones's Canon*, vol. 2, p. 404.</margin> transmitted by Pilate to Tiberius concerning the events related to Jesus Christ. This was because it was always the custom for Roman governors to send an annual report from their provinces to the Senate or the Emperor regarding the most significant events, especially if anything new or extraordinary occurred. Eusebius expressly tells <margin>(r) "An old custom existed that the governors of provinces should report any new developments to the person holding the imperial power, so that nothing would escape his notice. Accordingly, Pilate informed the Emperor Tiberius of the reports circulating throughout all of Palestine regarding the resurrection of our Savior Jesus Christ from the dead. He reported the other miracles he had heard of, and that because Jesus rose from the dead, many now believed him to be a god." <note>original Greek: "Παλαιοῦ κεκρατηκότος ἔθους τοῖς τῶν ἐθνῶν ἄρχουσιν... κ.τ.λ."</note> *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 2, chapter 2, p. 40. C. D.</margin> us that this was the case in this instance. Justin Martyr, the first and most ancient apologist <term>apologist</term> <note>A writer who offers a formal defense of a belief or cause, in this case, early Christianity.</note> for the truth of the Christian religion, appeals to these accounts <margin>(f) "And that these things occurred, you can learn from the Acts recorded under Pontius Pilate." <note>original Greek: "Καὶ ταῦτα ὅτι γέγονε δύνασθε μαθεῖν ἐκ τῶν ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου γενομένων ἄκτων."</note> *First Apology*, p. 76. D. "That he did these things, you can learn from the Acts recorded under Pontius Pilate." <note>original Greek: "Ὅτι τε ταῦτα ἐποίησε, ἐκ τῶν ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου γενομένων αὐτῷ μαθεῖν δύνασθε."</note> *Ibid.* p. 84. C. The former of these refers to his crucifixion, the latter to his working miracles.</margin> in his address to the Emperor Marcus Antoninus. <margin>(t) *Credibility*, Part 2, vol. 1, chapter 10, p. 259—first edition.</margin> But whether such accounts were really transmitted by Pilate or not, it is evident that a report of this kind was circulating early in the second century.

From this, the idea was taken, and the current forgery owes its origin to this tradition. A great part of this work <margin>(u) *See this gospel in Jones's Canon, vol. 2, p. 322, 401, but particularly from p. 370–396.*</margin> is taken...

SECTION 15. [This section is] devoted to providing an account of the things seen in the afterlife by Charinus and Lenthius, which they are said to have written down. Now, as Mr. Jones observes, <note>refers to (x) in margin</note> (x) this is none other than Leucius Charinus. Although they are said to be the names of the two sons of Simeon, everyone knows they are not Hebrew, but Greek or Roman names. Our Leucius, therefore, seems to have been the original creator of a book of this type. 

However, in the existing copies, there are certainly interpolations—later additions—to what he originally composed. These include details such as the characters making the sign of the cross before relating what they had seen; the descent of Jesus into hell to rescue the patriarchs <term>patriarchs</term> <note>In this context, the Old Testament ancestors of the Jewish people, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note>; his address to all his saints, commanding them to live by the "word of his cross"; his signing them with the sign of the cross before they were led into paradise; and many other similar details. All of these elements strongly suggest the superstitions of a later era. 

This explains why it is said that the vision was written down by Lenthius and Charinus. A forger living in later times likely took this section from a work by Leucius, adding whatever seemed necessary to fit his own perspective. Thus, a large part of the work may be rightly attributed to our Leucius.

From the phrasing at the beginning of the 27th chapter, Charinus and Lenthius appear to have been just one person, <note>refers to (y) in margin</note> (y) though they are later multiplied into two distinct people to give their vision an air of miraculous authority. Each of these two supposedly wrote an account of the vision on...

### SECTION 19. Some Account of the Contents of this Book.

This book of the *Acts* or *Journeyings of the Apostles* contained a number of foolish and ridiculous stories. Because Leucius belonged to the sect of the Encratites <term>Encratites: an early Christian sect that practiced strict asceticism, particularly forbidding marriage and the consumption of meat and wine</term>, he could never have approved of a Christian servant being prostituted to a pagan husband in place of his wife. However, it is consistent with his known principles—and therefore not improbable—that he might have included something regarding the moral scruples of Maximilla.

### S E C T. XX. *These Forgeries prove the Truth of the Canonical Scriptures.*

<margin>SECTION 20.</margin>
One obvious conclusion to be drawn from this long account of the forgeries of Leucius is that the scriptures of the New Testament—particularly the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles—were already received with great respect and regarded as writings of high authority. Otherwise, he would not have thought of publishing books under the names of the Evangelists and Apostles to gain a following.

Furthermore, these forged writings do not oppose, but rather confirm the general account given to us in the canonical <term>canonical: referring to the books officially accepted as genuine and authoritative scripture</term> scriptures. They all take for granted the dignity of our Lord's person and His power to perform miracles; they acknowledge the historical reality of people such as Matthew and the other Evangelists, as well as Peter and the other Apostles. They authenticate the general and leading facts contained in the New Testament. They presuppose that the Apostles received a commission from Christ to spread His religion and a supernatural power to enforce its authority. In this way, they indirectly establish the truth and divine origin of the Gospel.

<summary>This page argues that the apocryphal forgeries of Leucius actually serve to prove the early authority of the New Testament, as the forger relied on the established reputations of the Apostles to gain credibility. Despite their heretical leanings, these texts confirm the core historical claims and figures of the Christian Gospel.</summary>

### *Concerning APELLES*

### PART 1. *His History*

### SECTION 1. *Regarding his Time*

<margin>Section 1.</margin>
Apelles is not mentioned in the works of Irenaeus or Clement of Alexandria. Nevertheless, several ancient authors have spoken of him. He is often mentioned by Tertullian in his books against Marcion <term>Marcion: a prominent 2nd-century Christian leader whose teachings, known as Marcionism, were rejected by the early Church as heretical</term> and elsewhere. Tertullian even published a treatise specifically against his <margin>(a)</margin> followers, but it is no longer extant. Apelles is also mentioned several times by <margin>(b)</margin> Origen.

Apelles is discussed by Basnage <margin>(c)</margin> under the year 141 AD. Tillemont thinks he lived around <margin>(d)</margin> the year 180. Cave places him <margin>(e)</margin> at the year 188. Since Apelles was an acquaintance of Marcion and <margin>(f)</margin> was an old man in the time of Rhodon (who flourished <margin>(g)</margin> around the year 190), I think we may place his active period at about the year 160.

### SECTION 2.
<margin>(h) "Some believe Marcion. But the disciple is not above his master. This Apelles, the reformer of Marcion’s followers, should have remembered." <note>original: *Credunt aliqui Marcioni. Apelles was at first (h) a disciple of Marcion. However, he made several changes to Marcion’s system, as we are assured by various authors. Tertullian (i) and others claim this was due to instructions he received from Philumene, a young woman who claimed to have prophetic revelations. It is also sometimes said, particularly by Tertullian, that (k) Apelles was guilty of some act of sexual misconduct, which went against the strict rules of the Marcionite institution <term>The Marcionites practiced strict asceticism, often forbidding marriage and demanding celibacy from their followers</term>. But the nature of this act is not clearly (l) explained. If it had been common sexual immorality, it likely would have been stated plainly. We might therefore be led to think that Apelles had simply married. But even that is not certain. Indeed, there is some evidence to the contrary, as may appear later in this history.

## SECT. III. *No Foundation for the Story of his Incontinence.*

<margin>SECTION 3.</margin>
**B**EAUSOBRE says there <note>original: *m*</note> are good reasons to suspect that story to be false. One reason is the testimony given to Apelles by Rhodon, as recorded in Eusebius. Rhodon says that <note>original: *n*</note> Apelles was respected for his old age and his disciplined <term>original: "abstemious"—meaning self-denying, particularly regarding food, drink, and luxury</term> way of life. Rhodon, who had a conference with Apelles and argued against him, would not have spoken this way about a man who was burdened by the charge of shameful conduct. Secondly, in all probability, the woman mentioned is Philumene, that fanatical virgin who claimed to be a prophetess and who, it is said, persuaded Apelles that the *Old Testament* was not a divine revelation. Thirdly, St. Jerome contents himself with saying that <note>original: *p*</note> Apelles had Philumene as an associate in his beliefs, without adding anything else dishonorable to either of them. In short, Tertullian should not have criticized Apelles on this point. ### Sect. 3.

I would like to add that Rhodon and various other writers who give an account of Apelles—and who speak of Philumene as a visionary woman and his teacher—say nothing scandalous about either of them. Furthermore, according to Tertullian himself, (q) Apelles, despite differing from Marcion in some ways, still continued to condemn marriage. This leads me to believe that Apelles never married; and therefore, it is very likely he never did anything worse than marrying. <note>In the ascetic context of Marcionism, marriage was viewed as a spiritual failure; the author is suggesting that if Apelles avoided marriage, he likely avoided other sexual "sins" as well.</note>

Such behavior would have been loudly condemned by all church writers in general. It could not have been omitted by *any* of them. Tertullian’s hints refer to things supposedly done after Apelles had become a student of Marcion—not things done in his youth, but in his mature years. This makes it even less likely that other writers on heresies would have omitted the details if anything truly scandalous had been done by him.

Therefore, what is said regarding Marcion’s displeasure with Apelles should, in all likelihood, be understood as a difference of opinion. Apelles founded a new sect and drew several of Marcion’s disciples into his own movement with the help of the virgin Philumene, who is often described as a woman claiming divine inspiration. To the passages already referred to or quoted, others (r) might be added. However, I do not think it is proper to include the foolish story about her here, as it appears in some editions.

Apelles answered that the knowledge of God was a very difficult thing and that exactness in matters of an obscure nature was not of the utmost importance. This interpretation is not entirely inconsistent with the nature of Rhodon's account. Nevertheless, it is very probable that Rhodon believed there was a confusion of ideas in Apelles's mind.

### SECTION V. Of his Writings.

<margin>SECTION 5.</margin> Apelles was an author. His book, or books (if there were two), seem to have contained inquiries regarding difficult texts in the Old Testament. This can be argued from a quotation in Origen <margin>(a)</margin> concerning Noah's ark, and from another in Saint Ambrose <margin>(b)</margin> concerning the tree of life in Paradise.

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>(y) [Jerome says:] Apelles, another old heretic, was once met by him [Rhodon] and held up to ridicule because he said he did not know the God he worshipped. <note>original: *Apellem senem alium haereticum a se quondam conventum, et risui habitum, eo quod Deum quem coleret, ignorare se diceret.* From Jerome's *De Viris Illustribus* (On Illustrious Men), chapter 17.</note>

(z) [Philaster says:] Apelles was his [Marcion's] disciple, preaching things similar to Marcion in certain respects. When asked by some how he felt about the faith, he replied, "I do not need to learn from Marcion to propose two co-eternal principles. ### SECTION VI. His Country of Origin is Uncertain.

<margin>SECTION 6.</margin>
I believe it is not stated anywhere by Tertullian, Epiphanius, or any other ancient writer which country Apelles was from. He first met Philumene in Alexandria, but that does not seem to have been his birthplace or his usual place of residence. Rhodon, who held a conference with Apelles in his old age, was <note>original: (g)</note> from Asia <note>Apelles's critic Rhodon was likely from Roman Asia (modern-day Turkey).</note>. Therefore, I find it likely that Apelles was also from that same region.

This concludes our summary of Apelles's life. Let us now examine his specific beliefs.

### PART II. *Concerning his Specific Beliefs.*

### SECTION VII. *He believed in one primary Source, who created another inferior Deity.*

<margin>Section 7.</margin>It has already been mentioned that Apelles differed from Marcion in several ways. For, as the writer Rhodon says, he <note>original: (b)</note> believed in a single principle <note>original: *archē*—a Greek term for a first cause or fundamental source</note>. Furthermore, he <note>original: (i)</note> held to one principle, just as our own religion teaches.

Epiphanius explains this more thoroughly: Apelles <note>original: (k)</note> taught that there is one God, who is perfectly good, one primary source, and one inexpressible power that has no name. He taught that this holy and good God, who reigns over all, created one other God, who then created the heavens, the earth, and everything in this world. I have included in the margin <note>original: (l)</note> the portion of Philaster’s article on Apelles that relates to this point. Tertullian often speaks of that inferior deity of Apelles who made the world, who was only—

<column-break/>

(*b*) He confesses one principle. <note>original: Μιαν αρχην ομολογει. Ap. Eus. p. 177. B.</note>

(*i*) For he spoke of one principle, just as our own doctrine teaches. <note>original: Ελεγε γαρ μιαν αρχην, καθως και ημετερος λογος. Ib. D.</note>

(*k*) Apelles now says, and those who follow him, that there are not three principles, nor two, as Lucian and Marcion believed. Instead, he says there is one good God, and one principle, and one inexpressible power . . . this same holy and good God, the high and good God, made one other God. This second God, who was created, built all things: the heaven, the earth, and everything in the world. <note>original: Φασκει γυν Απελλης... Hær. 44. N. 1. p, 381. A.</note>

(*l*) For I declare that there is one principle, whom I recognize as God, which God made the angels. He also made another power, whom I know to be a second God, and who is the power of the God who made him. However, this God who made the world is not good, he says, like the one who made him. He is subject to that God by whom he was made, and he obeys his will, his orders, and his commands in all things. The Arians are now his companions and supporters, preaching and thinking in the same way. <note>original: Ego enim unum principium... Ph. H. 47. p. 48.</note>

### SECTION IX. *Apelles was not a Docetic in his opinion concerning the body of Christ.*

<margin>Section 9.</margin>Regarding his opinion concerning Christ, Epiphanius writes in this manner: He (s) also says that in the final times Christ was revealed, being the son of the good God and his Holy Spirit. He came for the salvation of those who would believe in him. Nor was he merely an appearance <note>The "Docetics" (from the Greek *dokein*, "to seem") believed Christ's body was a spiritual illusion; Apelles rejected this, asserting that Christ had a physical, though non-human, body.</note>, but he truly possessed flesh, though it was not from the Virgin Mary. For as he descended from the heavenly <note>original: "supercelestial"</note> places to this earth, he gathered a body for himself from the four elements. Having thus formed a body for himself, he truly appeared in this world and taught people the knowledge of heavenly things. And he says that Jesus was truly crucified, and afterward showed that same flesh to his disciples. As he ascended, he returned his body to the elements from which he had taken it and returned to heaven.

That account is very consistent <note>original: "agreeable"</note> with Tertullian, who says that (t) Apelles and various disciples of Marcion left him...

<margin>(s) "...being the son of the good God who is in the age, and his Holy Spirit... And coming not in appearance, but having taken true flesh... Christ allowed himself to suffer in that very body, and rose in truth, and showed that flesh to his disciples." <note>original Greek: υἱον οντα τῆ ἐν αιω αγαθω θευ, και το αγιον αυτη πνευμα. . . . Και ελθοντα υ δόκησει πεφοινικαι, αλλα εν αληθινω σαρκα ειληφεναι . . . εδικεναι ο χριτος εαυτον παθειν εν αυτω τω σωματι, και εζακυθειν εν αληθεια, και εδιξειν αυτη την σαρκα τοις εαυτυ μαθηταις. Epiphanius, *Heresies* (H.) 44. chapter 2. pages 381, 382.</note></margin>

<margin>(t) "But certain students of that man from Pontus [Marcion], forced to be wiser than their teacher, concede to Christ the reality of flesh, without however giving up their rejection of his birth. They say he had flesh, but was not born. We have come therefore... from Marcion to Apelles, who—after he fell from Marcion’s discipline because of a woman, and then was overturned in spirit by the virgin Philumene—began to preach that Christ had a solid body, but without being born... They confess that Christ truly had a body. From where did the matter come? From where the flesh, if not born? From the stars, they say, and from the substances of the higher world, he borrowed his flesh. And certainly they propose that a body without birth is not to be wondered at, since even among us [Christians] it is accepted that angels were permitted to take on flesh without the work of a womb." <note>original Latin: *Sed quidam discentes Pontici illius supra magistrum sapere compulsi, concedunt Christo carnis veritatem, sine præjudicio tamen renuendæ nativitatis. Habuerit, inquiunt carnem, modo non natam. Pervenimus igitur. . . a Marcione ad Apellem, qui postea quam a disciplina Marcionis in muliere carne lapsus, dehinc in virginem Philumenen, spiritu eversus est, solidum Christi corpus, sed sine nativitate, suscepit ab ea prædicare. . . Confidentur vere corpus habuisse Christum. Unde materia? Unde caro, si non nata? De sideribus, inquiunt, et de substantiis superioris mundi mutuatus est carnem. Et utique proponunt, non esse mirandum corpus sine nativitate, cum et apud nos angelis licuerit, nulla uteri opera, in carnem processisse.* Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ* (De Carne Christi), chapter 6, page 362. C. D. 301. 10.</note></margin>

<summary>This page explains that Apelles diverged from other Gnostic teachers by asserting that Christ possessed a real, physical body rather than a mere illusion. However, he still denied the incarnation through the Virgin Mary, claiming instead that Christ constructed a body from the stars and elements which he later discarded upon his ascension.</summary>

First of all, no one would ever have announced to him that his mother and brothers were standing outside if they were not certain both that he had a mother and brothers, and that those were the ones they were then announcing." <note>original Latin: Sed quoties de nativitate contenditur... I think it worthwhile to transcribe and place at the bottom of the page a long passage from Jerome <margin>(i) "Origen says in many places... that a double error exists in the Church: our own, and that of the heretics. . . We 'innocent and simple' ones say [the physical body rises]: while the heretics, including Marcion, Apelles, and Valentinus. . . completely deny the resurrection of the flesh and body, granting salvation only to the soul. They say we claim in vain that we will rise following the example of the Lord, since the Lord himself rose as a phantom; and not only was his resurrection a mere appearance, but his very birth was <term>to dokein</term> <note>original Greek: τω δοκειν</note>, that is, it was seen 'supposedly' rather than actually happening. [Jerome says] both opinions displease him: he flees from both the 'flesh' of our people and the 'phantoms' of the heretics." <note>original Latin: Dicit Origenes in pluribus locis... duplicem errorem verſari in Eccleſia; noſtrorum, et hæreticorum. . . Hæc nos innocentes et ruſticos dicere: hæreticos vero, in quorum parte ſunt Marcion, Apelles, Valentinus . . : penitus carnis et corporis reſurrectionem negare, et ſalutem tantum tribuere animæ... quum ipſe quoque dominus in phantaſmate reſurrexerit: et non ſolum reſurrectio ejus, ſed et ipſa nativitas putative viſa magis ait quam fuerit... *Ad Pamm. ### PART III. *Which Scriptures are received.*

## SECTION XI. *In other matters, he generally agreed with Marcion.*

Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403) was a church father known for his "Panarion," a massive work detailing and refuting various heresies.</note> says that in other matters, Apelles agreed with Marcion. It is therefore somewhat probable that he continued to condemn marriage, as previously argued from the writings of Tertullian. I do not recall any ancient writers noting that Apelles made any alterations to Marcion's system regarding this point.

We now at length come to his views about the scriptures.

## SECTION XII. *He did not pay much regard to the Old Testament.*

The extent to which Apelles rejected the Old Testament may be a matter of debate. Rhodon, as quoted by Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339) was a historian of the early Christian church.</note>, says that <margin>(k) "Being persuaded by the utterances of a demon-possessed virgin named Philumene, [which he regarded as] seeds of an opposing word..." <note>original Greek: Ταῖς δε προφητείας ἐξ ἀντικειμενων λογω σπερματος πειθομενος ἀποφθεγμασι παρθενῳ δαιμονωσῃ, ὀνομα Φιλυμενῃ. *Ap. Eus. p. 177. B.*</note></margin> Philumene, through her visions, persuaded Apelles to reject the Old Testament. Rhodon likewise tells us <margin>(l) "He said that the prophecies refute themselves because they have spoken absolutely nothing true; for they are contradictory, false, and inconsistent with one another." <note>original Greek: Έφη, τας μεν προφητειας εαυτας ἐλεγχειν, δια το μηδεν όλως ἀληθες ειρηκεναι, ἀποφασι γας ὑπαρχειν και ψευδεις, και εαυταις ἀντικειματ ται. *P. 178. A.*</note></margin> that Apelles claimed the Prophets were full of contradictions and inconsistencies, and therefore they refuted themselves. Origen mentions this in his books written against Celsus...

Celsus <note>Celsus (2nd century AD) was a Greek philosopher and a prominent opponent of early Christianity.</note> says (*m*) much the same. ### SECTION XIII. *His views regarding the New Testament were probably not very different from Marcion’s.*

### SECTION XIV. *It is likely that he rejected the beginning of St. Matthew's Gospel, as well as that of St. Luke.*

<margin>Section 14.</margin>

Origen (r), in a letter to his friends at Alexandria, joins Marcion and Apelles together in a censure for altering the Gospels and "the Apostle" <note>Early Christian writers often referred to the collection of Paul’s letters as "the Apostle."</note> (meaning both parts of the New Testament). However, perhaps Origen’s words do not necessarily imply that Apelles followed Marcion in every single alteration of scripture. Furthermore, as we only have a Latin version of that letter, we must not be too precise <note>original: "nice"</note> in our remarks.

# CHAPTER XIII.

## *On the* S E T H I A N S.

### SECTION I. *Some general observations concerning these heretics, and the Ophites and Cainites.*

<margin>Section 1.</margin>
The historian Tillemont discusses the Cainites (a) under the entry for the Nicolaitans. He groups together (b) the Ophites and the Sethians. He claims that the heretics known as the Ophites derive their doctrine from the Nicolaitans and Gnostics. It is believed they did not appear until after the Heracleonites and some other branches of the Valentinians. Therefore, we cannot date their origin before the year 150, nor much later, as they were known to Irenaeus. This is his view <note>original: "So he"</note>.

Irenaeus, at the conclusion of his first book, includes two chapters: the first is on the Ophites and Sethians, whom he links together; the other is on the Cainites. The first chapter is long, and there he seems to intend for us (c) <note>original: "Tales quidem secundum eos sententiae sunt: a quibus multiplex capitibus fere de Valentini schola generata est." Translation: "Such indeed, according to them, are their opinions; from which a many-headed [sect] was generated, mostly from the school of Valentinus." *Against Heresies*, Book 1, chapter 30 [also numbered as 34], section 15, p. 112. See also chapter 31 [also 35], section 3, p. 113.</note> to believe they all originated from the Valentinians. Yet in the following chapter, regarding the Cajans <note>A variation of the name "Cainites."</note>, he speaks as if the Valentinians had actually descended from them (d) <note>original: "A talibus matribus, et patribus, et proavis, eos, quia Valentino sint, sicut ipsae sententiae et regulae ostendunt eos." Translation: "From such mothers, fathers, and ancestors, they exist, because they are of Valentinus, just as the opinions and rules themselves show them to be." Chapter 31, section 3, p. 113.</note>. A large part of his long chapter on the Ophites and Sethians is very obscure. For this reason...

<margin>SECTION 1.</margin> I shall not attempt to translate or transcribe it. But shortly, I shall take several specific details from it.

The (*e*) Cainites, or Cainists, and Ophians <note>The Ophians, or Ophites, were a Gnostic sect who held the serpent—*ophis* in Greek—in high regard for supposedly bringing knowledge to humanity.</note> are mentioned by Clement of Alexandria. He gives no distinct account of them. But he says that some heretics are named based on their opinions, or the objects of their veneration, such as the Cainists and Ophians.

Philaster has three chapters on the Ophites, Cainites, and Sethians. They are placed by him among the heresies that existed before Christ, and they are the very first in his catalogue. Nor does he include anything that might lead us to think they were Christians, except that in the article on the Sethians he says they (*f*) not only said that Christ descended from Seth, but also that he was Seth himself.

In Epiphanius, and in Augustine, who follows him, the order of discussion is Ophites, Cainites, and Sethians. The author of the *Additions to Tertullian* observes the same order and provides a long article on each. Theodoret joins the Sethians and Ophites together and then provides a distinct article for the Cainites.

(*f*) <note>original: "De Seth autem ipso Christum Dominum genus deducere aiunt. ### SECT. II. *Epiphanius’s Account of the Sethians.*

<margin>Section 2.</margin>
Having given this general view of the most ancient catalogues of <term>heresies</term><note>A "heresy" in this context refers to a belief or sect that deviated from the established doctrines of the early Christian church.</note>, where these people are mentioned, I choose to begin with the Sethians. And Epiphanius’s account shall be our text.

He says: neither the Sethians, nor the former heresy of the Cainites, are to be found everywhere. He (*g*) thinks however, that he had seen some of them in Egypt: but he could not recollect in what part of it.

The (*h*) Sethians, he says, boast that they are descendants of Seth, the son of Adam, whom they mightily extol, saying that he was an example of righteousness and every virtue. They also call him **Christ** and say he is the same as **Jesus**. They say that the world was made by angels, and not by the supreme power. Let us go over these things.

## SECT. III. *They called themselves the Descendants of Seth*.

### SECTION 3.
They said they were descendants of Seth, the son of Adam. There is nothing remarkable in this, for all people living since the <term>Flood</term><note>The author refers to the biblical story of Noah's Flood, after which humanity was believed to have descended from Noah, a descendant of Seth.</note> are his descendants. However, they boasted that they were the "children of Seth," likely meaning they were the children or people of God, rather than the children of Cain, who belonged to the evil one (*i*), and were not the offspring of the evil one or "men of the world." 

In this, they were likely referring to various texts in the books of Genesis and Numbers (*k*). For the Sethians (*l*) were likely of Hebrew descent and Christians by profession; being well-acquainted with the Jewish scriptures, they were often led to speak of themselves in this way. <term>Rhenford</term><note>Jakob Rhenferd (1654–1712) was a German-born orientalist and scholar who wrote extensively on early Christian sects.</note> understood it this way, and his reasoning appears to be very probable (*m*).

<margin>(*i*) *1 John 3:12.*</margin>
<margin>(*k*) See *Genesis 3:15, 4:25 and 26. Numbers 24:17.*</margin>
<margin>(*l*) <note>original: "Nempe illud filii Sethi, in vaticinio Bileami Num. xxiv. 17. Ecclesiam vel fideles notat, quos Messias suo beneficio fit servaturus. Et ætuti gallina glocitando sub alas suas convocabir, fovebitque ac defendet Messias omnes filios Sethi. Ita enim hæc verba reddenda et explicanda esse, ex nexu et scopo totius orationis et significatu vocis... Altingius solide atque præclare evicit..."</note> "Indeed, that phrase 'sons of Seth' in the prophecy of Balaam in Numbers 24:17 denotes the Church or the faithful, whom the Messiah would save by his favor. And like a clucking hen, the Messiah will call together, cherish, and defend all the sons of Seth under his wings. Altingius has soundly and excellently proved that these words should be translated and explained in this way, based on the context and purpose of the whole speech and the meaning of the word [unclear] and the shortcomings of other versions." Rhenford's *Dissertation on the Sethians*, note 6, page 166. *Philological Works*, Utrecht, 1722.</margin>

### SECT. IV. *They spoke of Seth in a very honorable manner.*

<margin>Section 4.</margin>
They attributed all virtues to Seth. Nor can anyone say that they did so without reason. They also called him Christ and said he was the same as Jesus. In what they said of Seth, it is likely they were referencing Genesis 3:15 and 4:25 <note>Genesis 3:15 refers to the "seed of the woman" who will crush the serpent's head; Genesis 4:25 describes the birth of Seth as a replacement for Abel.</note>. However, there is probably some mistake or misrepresentation here; for, as we shall see shortly, they claimed that Christ was a descendant of Seth.

...one born of the barren Elizabeth, the other of Mary, a virgin. They say that the appearing of Jesus was foretold by John, who preached the baptism of repentance and baptized Jesus so that the Christ, when he descended, might find a pure vessel. They believe that Jesus, being born of a virgin by the operation of God, was wiser, more holy, and more excellent than all other men. They claim that Christ, the companion of Wisdom, came down upon him, and thus Jesus was made the Christ. 

This, they said, was not rightly understood by all Christians. They argued that the truth is that once Christ had come down upon Jesus, he immediately began to work miracles, heal diseases, and preach the true God, thus clearly showing himself to be the son of the First Man <note>In Gnostic theology, the "First Man" (Anthropos) refers to a high primordial divine being</note> (or the promised Messiah). At this, the rulers <term>powers</term> <note>The "powers" or "rulers" refers to the Archons, the spiritual beings who Gnostics believed governed the physical world and opposed the true God</note> became offended and conspired to put him to death. 

They say that the Christ, along with Wisdom, then forsook him, and so only the human Jesus was crucified. However, the Christ did not forget Jesus but raised him from the dead. Nevertheless, when he was risen, his disciples did not recognize him at first. They attempt to support their opinion that Christ came down upon Jesus and then departed from him—as just mentioned—by pointing out that the disciples do not record him performing any miracles either before his baptism or after his resurrection. He stayed with his disciples for eighteen months, and having sufficiently instructed them during that time—especially those few he deemed worthy—he was received up into heaven, and Christ sat down at the right hand of God.

### SECTION VII. *By Christ who descended upon Jesus, they probably meant the Holy Spirit.*

<margin>Section 7.</margin> Irenaeus <note>Saint Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD) was a Greek bishop known for his writings against Gnosticism</note> says they believed that the Christ descended upon Jesus at his baptism. It is very likely that by "the Christ," they meant the Holy Spirit. This may be considered confirmed by Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD) was an influential theologian and church historian</note> in his account of the Sethians and Ophites <note>The Ophites were a Gnostic sect who, like the Sethians, held complex views on the origins of the world; they were named after the Greek word for "serpent"</note>, whose words (*q*) I shall place below. They also said that when Jesus was led away to be crucified, the Christ (or "Wisdom") within him departed, and that Jesus alone was crucified. Their meaning, probably, was that the divine nature in Jesus did not suffer. They said that Jesus stayed with his disciples for eighteen months after his resurrection. In this, there is possibly some mistake or misrepresentation. I think that Irenaeus is the only person who mentions this; it is not found in Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), a bishop known for his "Panarion," a massive work cataloging and refuting heresies</note>, or Theodoret, or other ancient writers on heresies. On the whole, these Sethians appear to have been good Christians. They believed that Jesus was born of a virgin and was a most excellent man; that John, born of Elizabeth, prepared the way for him and baptized him; and that the Holy Spirit descended upon Jesus at his baptism. After this, he performed miracles of healing and taught true religion, and clearly showed himself to be the promised Messiah. They believed that Jesus was crucified, was afterwards raised from the dead, and was received up into heaven, where he sat at the right hand of God. And if these were Jewish

Since they were likely Jewish believers, it may be argued from their calling themselves by such a universal <note>original: "Catholic"</note> denomination as that of "Sethians" that they approved of the calling of the Gentiles. Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD) was a prominent theologian and bishop of the early church</note> also confirms the report that they believed Jesus was born of a virgin and that the Christ came down upon him from heaven. <note>original Greek (*r*): "They say that Jesus is different from the Christ; and that Jesus was born of the virgin, while the Christ descended upon him from heaven." ### SECTION VIII. *An Account of what Books they used.*

<margin>Section 8.</margin>
Let us now see what books they possessed and utilized. Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD) was a bishop known for his "Panarion," a work cataloging and refuting various heresies</note> says they had certain books written by themselves, attributed to the names of great men: seven books of Seth, and others; another attributed to Abraham, which they call his *Revelation*; and others with the name of Moses. <note>original Greek (*s*): "Writing certain books in the names of great men: saying there are seven books in the name of Seth; they call other books 'Allogeneis' (of another race); another in the name of Abraham, which they also claim is a revelation... others in the name of Moses, and still others in the names of others." (H. 39. n. 5. p. 286. C.)</note> Afterward, Epiphanius speaks of other books called the *Jubilees*, and another book called the *Little Genesis*, which contained the names of the wives of Cain and Seth. <note>original Greek (*t*): "As is found in the *Jubilees*, also called the *Little Genesis*, etc." (Ibid. n. 6. p. 287. B.)</note>

But it is possible that the books called the "seven books of Seth" were not attributed to him as the author, but only contained an account of his being the "seed" <term>seed: offspring or lineage</term> obtained after the death of Abel.

The book titled *Abraham's Revelation* was likely not attributed to him as the actual author, but instead probably contained an account of his faith (*x*), the covenant made with him, and the promises he received.

The books bearing the name of Moses might (*y*) have been his *Pentateuch* <term>the first five books of the Bible</term> in Hebrew. Gentile Christians, who typically preferred the Septuagint <term>the Greek translation of the Old Testament</term> version, would not have understood the Hebrew original.

Satis illis causa erat, cur libros illos Sethi et $\alpha\lambda\lambda o\gamma\epsilon\nu\hat{\omega}\nu$ nomine vocarent, quod in illis de Setho, ejusque doctrina, vita, et rebus gestis... vel si qua alia ratione ipsi libitum fuerit." What fault is there in having books titled with the name of Seth? You might say it is impudence and a lie to attribute books they wrote themselves to Seth. But where is the proof that they attributed the authorship to him? There was reason enough for them to call those books by the name of Seth and *Allogenon* [Foreigners], because they dealt with Seth, his doctrine, life, and deeds, and also with the "other seed," the sons of Seth and their city, laws, and benefits—even if they did not claim Seth himself was the writer. Indeed, it is easy to understand that a teacher who taught these doctrines about the sons of Seth in a school or church might also judge them worthy to be recorded in writing. ### SECTION 9. *Which Scriptures They Accepted.*

<margin>Section 9.</margin>
There can be no doubt that the Sethians respected the books of the Old Testament. Irenaeus <note>Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD) was a prominent Greek bishop and theologian known for his writings against Gnosticism.</note> takes particular notice of this (z). We can also see from the long passage quoted from him earlier that they accepted the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, especially the first chapters of both, which contain accounts of the birth of John the Baptist and Jesus, as well as John’s baptism and ministry. They likely accepted all the Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, and most other books of the New Testament. This is suggested by the clear knowledge they seem to have had of our Lord's miracles, death, resurrection, and

Vide et n. 10."</note> They categorize the Prophets in this way: Moses, Joshua (son of Nun), Amos, and Habakkuk belonged to Jaldabaoth; Samuel, Nathan, Jonah, and Micah <note>Note: Micah is listed twice in the original Latin distribution.</note> belonged to Jao; Elijah <note>original: "Hebiam."</note>, Joel, and Zechariah belonged to Sabaoth; Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and Daniel belonged to Adonai; Tobit and Haggai belonged to Eloi; Micah and Nahum belonged to Horei; and Ezra and Zephaniah belonged to Astaphaei. <note>These names—Jaldabaoth, Jao, Sabaoth, Adonai, Eloi, Horei, and Astaphaei—represent the seven "Archons" or planetary rulers in Gnostic cosmology. ### SECTION II. *Observations tending to show the incredibility of these accounts.*

<margin>SECTION 2.</margin>
These are the accounts left to us of these men. But can they be true? It seems not. For, first, the wickedness attributed to these men is unbelievable. It is not easy to imagine that any number of men calling themselves Christians would honor Cain, Korah <note>original: "Core"; Korah was a biblical figure who led a rebellion against Moses (Numbers 16).</note>, and Judas, and all those who are justly condemned in the scriptures of both the Old and the New Testament for the most notorious wickedness. (*k*)

Secondly, the account is inconsistent and therefore refutes itself. It is not possible that men could be extremely wicked in practice and in principle while simultaneously being concerned about the salvation that comes through the cross of Christ, and honoring Judas (*l*) for his love of truth and his anxious concern for the salvation of the world and the general good.

---

<columns>2</columns>

(*k*) "Indeed, that men of the kind Epiphanius describes here ever existed in any number, and established a group or sect, has so little appearance of truth that it seems to surpass all belief. For although in the early times of Christianity certain most wicked and shameful men crept into the Church, as Peter and Jude testify; yet it does not seem likely to us that they were of such great and monstrous impudence that—while they wished to be seen as Christians (even if they were not)—and while they knew the history of Cain and the rest of those criminals... they would want to publicly profess themselves as their associates, and boast of it, and derive the merit of their own race and origin from the most wicked and miserable of all two-legged creatures." <note>original: Latin from Jacques Rhenferd, *On the Sethians*, chapter 61, page 191. Rhenferd was a 17th-century Dutch scholar who questioned the accuracy of early reports on "heretics."</note>

<column-break/>

(*l*) "And also another heresy broke out, which is called that of the Cainites. And they indeed magnify Cain, as if he were conceived and procreated from a certain powerful virtue... Those who assert this also defend Judas the traitor, mentioning that he was admirable and great because of the benefits he is boasted to have conferred on the human race. For some of them [offer] a thanksgiving to Judas..." <note>original: Latin text likely quoting Epiphanius or Irenaeus describing the Cainite doctrine.</note>
