<margin>SECTION 1.</margin>
Thirdly, the origin of this denomination of Cainites may be accounted for in another way, without assuming they were a particular sect. It might have arisen from the Sethians <note>original: "m"</note>. Those who called themselves by that name and extolled their ancestor Seth <note>In Gnostic tradition, Seth (the third son of Adam) was often viewed as a pure, spiritual ancestor of the enlightened.</note> could hardly avoid speaking out against Cain. And they might sometimes say of those who lived a different course of life from themselves that they acted as if they were the "children of Cain," who belonged to the evil one; they might have said such people seemed to show themselves to be kin to Korah <note>original: "Core"; Korah was a biblical figure who led a rebellion against Moses.</note>, Dathan, and even Judas himself.

<margin>Tertullian, *Against All Heresies*, ch. 47, p. 251. B. C.</margin>
They think that Judas should be given credit for this reason: for they say that Judas, noticing that Christ wanted to subvert the truth, handed him over so that the truth could not be subverted. And others argue the opposite, saying: because the powers of this world did not want Christ to suffer—fearing that salvation would be prepared for the human race through his death—Judas, looking out for the salvation of the human race, handed Christ over. He did this so that salvation (which was being hindered by the spiritual powers opposing Christ’s suffering) could not be blocked at all; and therefore, the salvation of the human race could not be delayed through Christ’s passion <note>original: "Judæ propter hanc cauſam reddendam putant. Animadvertens enim, inquiunt, Judas, quod Chriſtus vellet veritatem ſubvertere, tradidit illum, ne ſubverti veritas poſſet. Et alii ſic contra diſputant et dicunt: quia poteſtates hujus mundi nolebant pati Chriſtum, ne humano generi per mortem ipſius ſalus pararetur, ſaluti conſulens generis humani, tradidit Chriſtum, ut ſalus, quæ impediebatur per virtutes, quæ obſiſtebant ne pateretur Chriſtus, impediri omnino non poſſet: et ideo per paſſionem Chriſti non poſſet ſalus humani generis retardari."</note>.

<margin>Augustine, *On Heresies*, 18.</margin>
At the same time, they consider Judas the traitor to be something divine, and they regard his crime as a benefit. They assert that he foreknew how much the passion of Christ would profit the human race, and for that reason, he delivered him to the Jews to be killed <note>original: "Simul et Judam traditorem divinum aliquid putant, et ſcelus ejus beneficium deputant: aſſerentes eum præſciſſe, quantum eſſet generi humano Chriſti paſſio profutura, et occidendum Judæis propterea tradidiſſe."</note>.

<note>original: "m"</note> For when the leaders of the Sethians held up Seth before their listeners as an example of Christian life and all piety and virtue, it could hardly have happened without

<column-break/>

their exposing, by way of contrast, the impiety of Cain and others, and the horrific punishments they suffered. Just as these same people called themselves and their followers "sons of Seth" because they followed in the footsteps of Seth's faith and piety, so too they could, by the same logic, call those whom the Apostle Jude says "entered the way of Cain" the "sons of Cain." Thus he would have done with those other examples, repeatedly emphasizing: those who live with such-and-such morals declare by their actions, and as if publicly professing it, that they are not sons of Seth, but are the sons, brothers, and kin of the Sodomites, Esau, Korah, Balaam, and finally Judas the traitor. From this, anyone can perceive and understand how easily their teaching could be taken by certain unskilled teachers—especially Gentiles—in such a way that they thought there was a particular sect of this kind, who actually professed themselves to be Cainites, Sodomites, or Esauites, or used any other infamous names condemned to eternal darkness found in the sacred scriptures <note>original: "Cum enim Sethianorum antiſtites Sethum . . . auditoribus ſuis vitæ Chriſtianæ, et pietatis virtutiſque omnis exemplar ab oculos ponerent: vix fieri potuiſſe, quin per Antitheſin Caini aliorumque impietatem, et horrendas quas paſſi ſint pœnas expoſuerint. Quemadmodum vero iidem ſe ſuoſque Sethi filios appellabant, quod veſtigia fidei et pietatis Sethi premerent, . . ita quoque eos, quos Judas *viam Caini* ingreſſos ait, eodem jure *filios Caini* dicere potuerunt. . . . Ita et in reliquis illis exemplis fecerit, atque identidem ingeminatit: qui his illis moribus ſunt, illos re ipſa declarare, et quaſi publice profiteri, ſe non Sethi, ſed Sodomæorum, Eſaui, Coræ, Bileami, Judæ denique proditoris, filios, fratres, affines eſſe. Unde quotuſquiſque non perſpiciat atque intelligat, quam facile illorum doctrina ab imperitis quibuſdam doctoribus, maxime Gentilibus, eo accipi potuerint, quo putarint eſſe peculiarem quandam ſectam ejuſmodi, . . qui profeſſi ſint, ſe Cainitas, Sodomitas, Eſavitas eſſe, et ſi quæ alia infamia et æternis tenebris damnata nomina in ſacris literis legantur." For a similar purpose, I will quote at length the author of the *Additions* (x) to Tertullian’s book *On Prescriptions* <note>original: *De Præscriptione Haereticorum*</note>, whom I transcribe below.

### SECTION IV. *There never was a sect of Christians who called themselves Cainites, or who professed the principles described above.*

<margin>Section 4.</margin>
Since this was a common way of speaking among men at that time, especially among the Sethians, I think it may be questioned whether there ever was a sect of Christians, or any group of people, who called themselves "Caians" and professed the principles mentioned earlier. It is more likely that certain wicked men were described as "children of the evil one," resembling Cain and other villains mentioned in the Scriptures. Consequently, some writers—who were eager to increase the number of known heresies, or who were simply led into error—took the opportunity to speak of a formal sect with that name.

<columns>2</columns>
(x) "But from that source also emerged the heresy called the Sethians. The doctrine of this perversity is as follows: that two men, Cain and Abel, were created by angels; because of them, great strife and discord arose among the angels. For this reason, that Power which is above all powers—whom they call the Mother—decided that Seth should be conceived and born in Abel's place after they said Abel was killed, so that those angels might be thwarted... For they say the mingling of angels and humans was wicked. For this reason, that Power (whom, as we said, they call the Mother) brought about a flood <note>original: *cataclysmum*</note> as a punishment, so that the offspring of that mingling would be destroyed, and only the pure, uncorrupted seed would be preserved. However, those who had established the first seed secretly and hiddenly—without the Mother Power’s knowledge—sent Ham into the ark along with those eight souls. They did this so that the seed of malice would not perish but be preserved with the others. Once restored to the earth after the flood, it grew like the others, spreading until it filled and occupied the whole world." <note>original: *De Præscriptione Haereticorum*, chapter 47, page 251. C. D.</note>

<column-break/>

### SECTION 3.

For knowing that Abel was killed, she <note>This refers to the "Mother from above," a Gnostic divine figure often identified as Sophia or Barbelo, who oversees the spiritual realm.</note> procured the birth of Seth and placed her power in him: that is, a divine principle and spark from above. Through this, he became the chosen seed and was inclined toward righteousness and all virtue. In this way, the lineage of Seth was separated from the other race <note>Cain's lineage</note> from the very beginning. 

But in process of time, they say, the lineages of Cain and Abel (or Seth) mingled together, and wickedness prevailed upon the earth. The Mother from above, looking down and seeing this, determined to secure a holy seed. Accordingly, she brought on the flood and destroyed all mankind in general, so that for the future, there might be only a pure, holy, and righteous race of men in the world within the family of Seth. 

Nevertheless, Ham, a child of the evil angels, clandestinely got into the ark. For eight souls were saved within it, seven of whom were of the good race. But because Ham was also preserved—who was one of the other race—error, ignorance, lack of consideration, and by degrees all manner of wickedness sprang from him. This continued until at length the world became as wicked and disorderly as it had been before the flood. 

But from Seth, through a continued succession—though not in the ordinary way, but in a wonderful manner—descended Jesus the Christ. He lived among men, sent from the Mother above; that is, being born of a virgin and anointed for his office by the Holy Spirit of God, whom the Sethians spoke of as the "Mother of all." So says Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403 AD) was a bishop and counter-heretical writer whose work *Panarion* is a primary source for Gnostic beliefs.</note>. And to the like effect...

### SECTION 4. *There was never a sect of Christians who called themselves Cainites, or who followed the principles described above.*

<margin>Section 4.</margin>
Since this was a common way of speaking among people, especially among the Sethians, I believe it is questionable whether there was ever a Christian sect, or any group of men, who called themselves "Caians" <note>original: "Caians" or Cainites</note> and followed the principles mentioned above. Instead, some wicked men were described as "children of the evil one" and said to resemble Cain and other bad figures mentioned in the Scriptures. Consequently, some writers—who were eager to list as many heresies as possible—took this opportunity, or were led by mistake, to speak of a sect with that name.

<columns>2</columns>
(x) But a heresy also proceeded from that source, which is called the Sethian. The doctrine of this perversity is this: that two men were created by angels, Cain and Abel. Because of them, great contentions and discords arose among the angels. For this reason, that Power <note>original: "virtutem," often meaning a divine emanation or "Aeon" in Gnostic thought</note> who is above all powers, whom they call "the Mother," when Abel was killed, willed that this Seth should be conceived and born in the place of Abel, so that those angels might be rendered powerless. . . For they say the minglings of angels and humans were wicked; for which reason that Power, whom (as we have said) they pro-

-nounce to be "the Mother," brought on a cataclysm <note>the Great Flood</note> for vengeance, so that the seed of that mixture might be removed, and this seed alone, which was pure, might be preserved whole. But those who had established the previous seed secretly and hiddenly, without that Mother-Power knowing, sent Ham into the ark along with those eight souls, so that the seed of malice might not perish. Instead, being preserved with the others and returned to the lands after the flood, it grew like the rest, spread abroad, and both filled and occupied the whole world. *From The Prescription of Heretics, chapter 47, page 251, parts C and D.* <note>original: "De Praes. c. 47. p. 251. ### CHAPTER XV.
*Of the Ophianis, or Ophites.*

## SECTION I. The Ophianis are said by Irenaeus and Theodoret to be the same as the Sethians.

<margin>Section 14.</margin> We come next to the Ophianis <note>original: "Ophianis," an archaic spelling of Ophites, a Gnostic sect whose name is derived from the Greek word 'ophis' (serpent)</note>, who are joined with the Sethians by Irenaeus and Theodoret in the same chapter, as was observed formerly. The opinions of each group are represented together by Irenaeus and Theodoret as common to both. Consequently, the Ophites—according to this view of the matter—were Hebrew believers, or Jewish Christians, as well as the Sethians, and were one and the same people or sect under different titles and denominations. They were called Sethians because they frequently spoke of themselves as descendants of Seth and the children of God, and Ophianis from some other particular...

In response to some points raised by Celsus <note>Celsus was a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity.</note>, Origen says that (*l*) those who are called Ophians are so far from being Christians that they are as ready to slander <note>original: "calumniate"</note> Jesus as Celsus himself. Nevertheless, it is possible Origen might be mistaken here. I choose not to place much weight upon a passage in Origen's Latin commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew where (*o*) the Ophians are mentioned alongside various Christian heretics. This mention may have been added to the original by the translator or by someone else since then.

### HISTORY OF HERETICS

<margin>Section 3.</margin> They are generally supposed to have been Christians. It was not uncommon for Catholic writers to say of heretics that they did not agree with them in anything but name. This passage might therefore lead us to believe they were Christians by profession, or at least a Christian sect. Origen speaks of them in a similar way in another place, saying that (*q*) <note>original: "L. 6. p. 656. C. D."</note> they are far removed from the true Christian doctrine held by sound Christians. 

Again, Celsus directs (*r*) <note>original: "Εξης δε τοις εξετασθεισιν ο κελσος ως προς παντας χρισιανους αποτεινει λογον... Οφιανοι γαρ..." Origen writes: "Next, Celsus addresses his discourse to all Christians in general, even though what he says can only be applied to those who are altogether estranged from the doctrine of Jesus, such as the Ophians, who (as we said before) entirely deny him."</note> his discourse to all Christians in general; yet what he says can only be applied to those who are completely estranged from the doctrine of Jesus—such as the Ophians (who, as we said before, disregard him) and some others. This same criticism could also be leveled at a Christian sect that was believed to be deeply in error. 

Furthermore, Origen speaks of the Ophians as attributing the knowledge that humans possess to the serpent. This is the same thing said of them by other writers, who categorized them as a Christian sect. Additionally, Celsus referred to a "Diagram" <note>The "Ophite Diagram" was a ritualistic map or illustration used by the sect to depict the journey of the soul through the celestial spheres.</note> which Origen managed to obtain. Origen says he supposes (*s*) <note>original: "L. 6. p. 648. C. D. 653. D."</note> it belongs to the Ophians. However, that Diagram contains expressions that probably belong to Christians. For they speak (*t*) <note>original: "Ενθεν ειλικρινης πεμπομαι, Φωτος ηδη μερος υιου και πατρος..." The Greek text translates to: "From there I am sent pure, already a portion of the light of the Son and the Father; may grace be with me, yes, Father, may it be with me... a perfect work for the Son and the Father; may grace be with me, yes, Father, may it be with me... by the Living Word."</note> of the **Father** and the **Son**, and the **Living Word**. They pray repeatedly that the **Grace of the Father may be with them**, not to mention other similar expressions. 

Later, Origen also represents them as invoking seven angels, or God under seven different names. Most of these names are certainly Hebrew and, as (*u*) <note>original: "Ibid. p. 657. A."</note> Origen admits, were taken from the Jewish scriptures.

# OPHIANS OR OPHITES

<margin>Section 3.</margin> ...out of the scriptures: several of which are also found in Irenæus’s chapter on the Sethians and Ophites, such as Jaldabaoth, Jao, Sabaoth, Æloæus, Adonæus, Astaphæus, and Horæus <note>These are names of the "Archons," or planetary rulers, in Gnostic cosmology, many of which are derived from Hebrew names for God.</note>. This leads me to believe they were Christians, but still very much attached to Judaism. When Origen says that they would not admit anyone into their society without cursing Jesus, it seems to me that he mistook them for unbelieving Jews. In reality, they were Jews by birth (or Hebrews), but Christians by religion and profession. In several of his passages quoted earlier, Origen seems to speak of them as a Christian sect, though one so erroneous and absurd in its opinions that he felt they did not deserve the name of "Christians." However, I suspect that Origen had a very imperfect knowledge of the actual views of these men.

As for the claim made by some that they believed the serpent was Christ: this must be a mistake. The truth is, they considered the bronze <note>original: "brasen"</note> serpent in the wilderness to be a "type" or symbolic figure of Christ <note>A reference to Numbers 21:9 and John 3:14, where the serpent raised by Moses is seen as a prophecy of Jesus on the cross.</note>. As for the stories of them worshipping a serpent, keeping a living serpent in a chest, and bringing it out to partake in or consecrate the Eucharist <note>The Christian rite of Holy Communion.</note>—these are mere slanders <note>original: "calumnies"</note>. 

The story of them keeping a living or real serpent in a chest is mentioned by no one except Epiphanius and his followers, Augustine and John of Damascus <note>original: "Damascen"</note>. That story is not found in Irenæus, nor Philaster, nor Theodoret, nor in the additions to Tertullian’s *Prescription Against Heretics* <note>original: "Additions to Tertullian's book of Prescriptions."</note>.

# OPHIANS OR OPHITES.

<margin>Section 3.</margin> They drew these names from the scriptures, several of which are also found in Irenaeus’s chapter on the Sethians and Ophites: such as Jaldabaoth, Jao, Sabaoth, Eloaeus, Adonaeus, Astaphaeus, and Horaeus <note>These are names of the 'Archons' or planetary rulers in Gnostic cosmology, often derived from Hebrew names for God like Yahweh (Jao), Sabaoth (Lord of Hosts), and Adonai (Lord).</note>. This leads me to think they were Christians who remained very much attached to Judaism. When Origen says that they would not admit anyone into their society without first cursing Jesus, it seems to me that he mistook them for unbelieving Jews. In reality, they were Jews by birth—Hebrews—but Christians by religion and profession. In several of his previously quoted passages, he seems to speak of them as a Christian sect, albeit a highly erroneous one, whose opinions were so absurd they did not deserve the name of Christians. However, I suspect that Origen had a very imperfect knowledge of the actual views of these men.

As for the claim made by some that they believed the serpent was Christ, this must be a mistake. The truth is, they considered the bronze serpent in the wilderness <note>original: "brasen serpent"; a reference to the story in Numbers 21 and its typological link to Jesus in John 3:14.</note> to be a "type" or symbolic figure of Christ. Regarding the stories of them worshipping a serpent, keeping a living snake in a chest, or bringing it out to participate in or consecrate the Eucharist <term>the Christian ceremony of Holy Communion</term>, these are mere calumnies <note>original: "calumnies"; false and malicious accusations.</note>. The story of them keeping a living or real serpent in a chest is mentioned by no one except Epiphanius, and his followers Augustine and John of Damascus. That story is not found in the works of Irenaeus, Philaster, Theodoret, nor the additions to Tertullian’s *Prescription Against Heretics*.

->NOTE BY THE EDITOR.<-

These Ophians <note>original: "Ophians"; now more commonly known as the Ophites, a Gnostic sect that gave special significance to the serpent.</note> can scarcely be considered Christian heretics. This seemed to be the case to me when I was completing the history of the Basilidians. I had accordingly mentioned it as my opinion at the end of Book II, chapter 2, section 27, page 117. However, by the advice of a learned friend, I omitted it there, lest it should be deemed premature, because it represented them in a different manner from how Dr. Lardner himself afterwards considered them.

If they were a Christian sect, which I still doubt, they were certainly very erroneous in their opinions. The Simonians <note>Followers of Simon Magus, often called the "father of all heresies" by early church writers.</note>, who are regarded by many as Christian heretics, appear to me in the same light as the Ophians. The following quotations from Origen are the grounds of my opinion regarding both these sects. Dr. Lardner, however, did not consider them in the same light as they strike me. Perhaps he may be right. With the utmost deference, therefore, to his superior judgment, I will simply give the substance of what I had inserted in the place referred to before, and leave it to the reader to decide which of the two opinions appears to be better founded.

The Simonians, Origen (a) tells us, would never confess Jesus to be the Son of God. Simon was probably an impostor who wanted to overturn the entire Christian doctrine.

### S E C T. I. *Of his Opinions.*

<margin>(a)</margin>SECTION I. ARTEMON <margin>(a) "And a certain Artemon, whom some call Artemas, held opinions similar to us regarding the God of the universe, saying that He is the creator of all; but he said that the Lord Jesus Christ was a mere man, born of a virgin, and superior in virtue to the prophets. He also said that the Apostles had preached these things—distorting the meaning of the divine scriptures—and that those who followed after them taught that Christ was God, which he was not." <note>original Greek: Και Αρτεμων δε τις, ω τινες Αρτεμας ονομαζουσιν... H. F. [Haereticarum Fabularum Compendium], Book 2, Chapter 4, p. 220. B. C.</note></margin> (also called Artemas, according to Theodoret) agrees with us in acknowledging the supreme Deity and recognizing Him to be the Creator of the universe. However, he claimed that our Lord Jesus Christ was a mere man <note>original: "mere man"; in theology, this view is called Psilanthropism, the belief that Jesus was purely human and not divine.</note>, born of a virgin, and superior in virtue to the Prophets. He asserted that this was the original doctrine of the Apostles, though in doing so he perverted the intended meaning of the Holy Scriptures. He further claimed that it was only after the time of the Apostles that some began to teach the divinity of Christ without any basis in reason.

### SECTION II. *He based his teachings on Scripture and respected its authority.*

<margin>SECTION 2.</margin>
Here we see at once what Artemon's doctrine was: that he based it upon the Scriptures and acknowledged the authority of the Apostles.

I previously <margin>(b) Volume 3, chapter 32, pages 36–50.</margin> gave a detailed account of a work by an anonymous author written against the followers of Artemon, which is believed to have been written around the year 212. Theodoret strongly agrees with him. The purpose <margin>(c) Ibid, page 40.</margin> of the first passage quoted from that work, found in the writings of Eusebius, was to show the novelty of that <margin>(d) "To refute the mentioned heresy, which asserts that the Savior was a mere man, as if it were not a recent innovation..." <note>original Greek: Την γαρ τοι δεδηλωμενην αιρεσιν, ψιλον ανθρωπον γενεσθαι τον σωτηρα φασκουσαν, ου προ πολλου ο νεωτερισθεισαν διευθυνων. κ. λ. C.</note></margin> opinion—the idea that our Savior was a mere man <note>original: "mere man"; the theological view that Jesus was purely human and not divine.</note>. They further asserted that the truth of the Gospel had been preserved until the time of Victor <note>Victor I (died 199 AD), the thirteenth Bishop of Rome.</note>, the thirteenth Bishop of Rome; but they claimed that by the time of his successor, Zephyrinus <note>Zephyrinus (died 217 AD) succeeded Victor as Bishop of Rome.</note>, the truth had been corrupted.

->ARTEMON.<-

### SECTION IV. *Regarding the time when he lived.*

Tillemont <note>Sébastien le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698) was an influential French ecclesiastical historian.</note> believes that <gloss>(1)</gloss> Theodotus the Tanner (also called a currier <term>a specialist who finishes tanned leather</term>) lived before Artemon, and this may indeed be the case. However, since they both must have lived around the same time, and since Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–c. 458 AD) was a prominent theologian and bishop in Syria.</note> mentions Artemon first and then Theodotus—and because the previously mentioned book by the anonymous author was titled *An Argument Against the Heresy of Artemon*, even though it mentions several others—I have chosen this order without intending to definitively determine who came first.

Nevertheless, it must be acknowledged that the author identifies Theodotus the Tanner as the originator of that opinion. It is possible that the reason he titled his work against the heresy of Artemon was that Artemon was still alive at the time and had promoted the doctrines of his predecessors with notable success. Tillemont supposes that Artemon's influence began around the year 200 AD.

### CHAPTER XVII.

### Regarding THEODOTUS.

#### SECTION I. *Regarding his Time and Opinions.*

<margin>SECTION I.</margin>Theodotus of Byzantium, called the Tanner <term>a person who treats animal skins to produce leather</term>, lived—according to William Cave <note>William Cave (1637–1713) was a prominent English church historian known for his works on early Christianity.</note>—around the year 192 AD. Samuel Basnage <note>Samuel Basnage (1638–1721) was a French Protestant historian who wrote extensively on church history.</note> speaks of him around the year 187 AD. I have *(a)* already given a distinct account of the work by an anonymous writer against Artemon, which is supposed to have been published around the year 212, where this Theodotus is mentioned. That author, along with Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD) was the "Father of Church History."</note> who transcribes his work, assumes that Theodotus held the same opinion as Artemon, who said that *(b)* Jesus Christ was a mere man <note>original Greek: Ψιλον ανθρωπον γενεσθαι</note>. Moreover, that author *(c)* asserts that Theodotus was the "founder of this heresy" <note>original Greek: Τον της αιρεσεως ταυτης ευρετην</note> and says that *(d)* he was excommunicated by Victor <note>original Greek: Βικτωρ απεβαλλε Θεοδοτον τον της αιρεσεως—Victor I was the Bishop of Rome from approximately 189 to 199 AD.</note>.

## SECTION II. *Passages from ancient authors concerning him.*

<margin>SECTION 2.</margin>
The summary by Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403 AD) was a bishop and a fierce opponent of heresy.</note> is to this effect: The (*e*) Theodotians are so called from Theodotus, a tanner of Byzantium. He was highly educated in Greek literature and philosophy. Having been arrested with several others during the persecution of that time, he was the only one who <term>fell</term> <note>original: "fell" — In the early church, to "fall" meant to commit apostasy or renounce one's faith under the threat of death or torture.</note> while the others suffered martyrdom. Being frequently reproached for this, he conceived the idea of saying that Christ was only a man, so that he might no longer be accused of having denied God.

What Epiphanius says here regarding Theodotus's learning is very consistent with what the aforementioned author (*f*) says about this group of men in general.

Later, I will have occasion to make long extracts from the larger article by Epiphanius, which I would like to present together. Therefore, I will proceed immediately to transcribe some other authors.

Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD) was an influential theologian and church historian from Syria.</note> says only (*g*) that Theodotus the Tanner of Byzantium held the same opinion as Artemas <note>Artemas is a variation of the name Artemon.</note> but nevertheless was the leader of a different faction. He was excommunicated...

(*e*) <note>original: "Θεοδοτιανοι, οι απο του Θεοδοτου σκυτεως..." — Theodotians, those from Theodotus the tanner from Byzantium, who was highly skilled in Greek education. Along with several others during the persecution of that time, he alone fell away while they suffered martyrdom. Because he was reproached, he conceived the idea of saying Christ was a mere man, so that he might not be accused of denying God; thus he taught. (Epiphanius, *Anacephalaeosis*, p. 397, No. 8, B. C.)</note>

(*f*) <note>original: "Γεωμετριαν επιτηδευουσιν . . . Ευκλειδης γουν..." — They apply themselves to geometry... among some of them, Euclid is diligently studied. (*g*) <note>original: "Και Θεοδοτος δε ο Βυζαντιος ο σκυτευς..." — And Theodotus the Byzantine, the tanner, thinking these same things as this man [Artemas], led another faction. <header>THEODOTUS.</header>

### SECTION III. He is accused of denying Christ in a Time of Persecution.

<margin>(o) "And if the heresy were not still being preached there." <note>original Greek: Και ει μη υπηρχεν η Διεαισις εις αυτη κηρυττομενη.</note> *Against Heresies* 54. n. 1. p. 453. A.
(p) "A tanner by trade, but very learned in speech." <note>original Greek: Σκυτης την τεχνη, πολυμαθης δε τω λογω.</note> Ibid.
(q) "I do not know in what kind of persecution." <note>original Greek: Ουκ οιδα εν τινι εν οποιω διωγμω.</note> Ibid. 13.</margin>

In his longer article, Epiphanius says he does (o) not know whether any followers of that heresy still existed in his day. However, he intends to relate what he has found in various writings concerning them. He then states that Theodotus was from Byzantium (the city later called Constantinople) and was a **tanner** by trade, though he was very learned. 

Following this, he adds that (q) during some persecution—Epiphanius does not specify which one—Theodotus and many others were arrested by the Governor of the city. All the others, when interrogated, gave a noble testimony for Christ and obtained a <term>heavenly crown</term> <note>In early Christian literature, a "heavenly crown" refers to the reward of martyrdom—dying for one's faith.</note>. 

Theodotus, however, denied Christ. Unable to endure the scorn and insults directed at him in his own country because of this failure, he traveled to Rome. There, he met some of his acquaintances who reminded him of his <term>fall</term> <note>original: "fall" — A term for apostasy, or the act of renouncing one's faith under pressure or torture.</note>. They remarked that it was strange for a man of such great knowledge to deny the truth. In response, he offered a poor excuse for himself, claiming that he had "only denied a man." After this, he consistently promoted the doctrine that Jesus was a mere man, born of a human father.

### SECTION IV. Two Observations on what Epiphanius says of him.

<margin>SECTION 4.</margin>
There are two things worth noting here: first, the <term>fall</term> <note>original: "fall" — In this context, the act of renouncing one's Christian faith under the pressure of persecution.</note> of Theodotus, which was mentioned by Epiphanius earlier and by some other writers. However, Epiphanius did not know exactly when it occurred or the full details of the event. No other writers have specified these details either. This failure does not appear to have been mentioned by the anonymous author who wrote against Artemon, whom I quoted extensively (r) earlier. If that story had been included in that author's work, Eusebius would almost certainly have noticed it. It is also not mentioned by Theodoret.

Second, Epiphanius accuses Theodotus of teaching that Jesus was born in the ordinary human way, just as all other men are. This claim is not made by other historians and contradicts the author of the *Additions to Tertullian’s Prescriptions*, who states that Theodotus's doctrine held that Jesus was born of a virgin. Furthermore, Theodoret says that Theodotus's opinion was the same as that of Artemon, who also held that Jesus was born of a virgin.

### SECTION V. The Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments were accepted by him.

<margin>SECTION 5.</margin>
Epiphanius then moves on to examine some of the arguments that Theodotus and his followers used to support their teachings. In this regard, Epiphanius's account is very useful to us, as he reveals which biblical texts they emphasized and which scriptures they relied upon.

<margin>Section 5.</margin>The first text that he mentions is (*f*) John 8:40: "But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth, which I have heard from God." Theodotus likewise argued, as Epiphanius relates, (*t*) from Matthew 12:31–32. He also argued, says our author, (*u*) from what the law says of Christ in this manner, in Deuteronomy 18:15: "The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like me." Therefore, says he, the Christ raised up by God was not God, but a man. For he was to be one of them, and a man, just as Moses was. From this, we see that Theodotus accepted the Old Testament. Again, he argued that Christ was a man from (*x*) Isaiah 53:3: "A man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief."

If Epiphanius can be relied upon, he also argued from (*y*) Luke 1:35. This seems to show that Theodotus did not think Christ was born in the same way as other men. <note>This refers to the Virgin Birth; despite some claims that Theodotus believed Jesus was the biological son of Joseph, this citation suggests he accepted the miraculous conception.</note> He also emphasized (*z*) Acts 2:22: "*A man approved among you by signs and wonders*" and (*a*) 1 Timothy 2:5. <note>1 Timothy 2:5 states there is one mediator between God and men, "the man Christ Jesus."</note>

From all of this, it is manifest that this Theodotus and his followers accepted the scriptures of the Old and the New Testament just as other Christians did.

### SECTION VI. There were several of the same Name in the second Century.

<margin>Section 6.</margin> There were several others with this name in the second century.

First, a Valentinian <note>A follower of Valentinus, whose Gnostic school believed Christ was a divine being who only appeared to be human.</note>. William Cave, in his account of Theodotus the Tanner, attributes to him all the opinions which he has

<columns>2</columns>

<column-break/>

The argument used by Theodotus is based on a mistaken translation in the Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament, often cited as LXX.</note>, who read <term>אנש</term> <note>Hebrew: *anash*</note> as if it were a noun signifying "man." In reality, it is a participle and signifies "being in an incurable, desperate state." <note>This refers to Jeremiah 17:9. In modern Bibles, it usually reads "The heart is... desperately wicked" or "beyond cure," but Theodotus’s Greek Bible read "He is a man, and who shall know him?" which he used to argue Jesus was merely human.</note> But even if it were a correct translation, no argument for his purpose could be drawn from it.

<header>THEODOTUS. SECTION 7.</header>

[William Cave] has (*b*) collected from the oriental doctrine appended to the works of Clement of Alexandria. But that is confusing things as different and opposite as can possibly be. Theodotus the Tanner is counted among those who did not believe Jesus existed before his birth to Mary. This is very different from the views represented by Cave from the work mentioned above. And yet Fabricius (*i*) seems to have shared Cave's opinion. Tillemont realized that (*k*) the Theodotus mentioned in these extracts was a Valentinian <note>A follower of Valentinus, a mid-2nd-century Gnostic teacher who believed in a complex system of divine emanations.</note>. Beausobre had no doubt of it, and says that he (*l*) flourished around AD 130.

Second, there is Theodotus the Montanist <note>A follower of Montanus, a 2nd-century movement characterized by claims of new prophetic revelations and strict asceticism.</note>, mentioned by Eusebius (*m*) in his *Ecclesiastical History*.

Third, there is Theodotus the Banker, mentioned by the anonymous author we quoted extensively long ago. In that text, he is explicitly said (*n*) to be a disciple of Theodotus the Tanner.

# THEODOTUS. SECTION 7.

The account (t) regarding the Melchisedechians is short. He <note>Likely referring to Augustine, the author cited in the margin.</note> knew nothing of the author of this sect, as Epiphanius had not mentioned him in his summary. Nor indeed has Epiphanius anywhere mentioned Theodotus the Banker. For, as observed above, he supposed the Melchisedechians to be a branch of the followers of Theodotus the Tanner, or that they separated from them into a new sect called Melchisedechians. Nor does Philaster make any mention of Theodotus the Banker, though he has two (u) chapters of opinions concerning Melchizedek, and one of them is longer than usual.

Epiphanius says—in a manner quite consistent with Theodoret or the author of the *Additions to Tertullian*—that (x) the Melchisedechians believed Melchizedek to be a great power (y) in the heavenly realms, and even greater than Christ. They held this view because Christ is said to have been made a priest "after the order of Melchizedek" (Psalm 110:4). They also endeavored to support their opinion from what is said by Paul of Melchizedek in the Epistle to the Hebrews 7:3: *Without father, without mother.*

Epiphanius later mentions various opinions among Christians concerning Melchizedek. Perhaps he could have just as easily classified each of these opinions as a distinct heresy, as he did with this one.

<margin>(t) The Melchisedechians believe that Melchizedek, the priest of the most high God, was not a man, but was a power of God. <note>original Latin: *Melchisedeciani Melchisedec sacerdotem Dei excelsi, non hominem fuisse, sed virtutem Dei esse arbitrantur.* Augustine, *Heresies* 34.</note>
(u) See *Heresies* 52, p. 106; *Heresies* 144, p. 312, 318. <note>original Latin: *Vide H. 52. p. 106. H. 144. p. 312. 318.*</note>
(x) *Heresies* 55, section 1. <note>original: *H. 55. n. 1.*</note>
(y) That he exists on high in unnamable places. <note>original Greek: *Ειναι δι αυτον ανω εν ακατονοματοις τοι ποις.* Ibid. 468. B.</note></margin>

<margin>Section I.</margin>
William Cave <note>author of *Historia Literaria*</note> speaks of Hermogenes as living around the year 170. Samuel Basnage places him at 168, as does Jean Le Clerc. Tillemont says he must have appeared before the end of the reign of Marcus Aurelius <note>original: "Marc Antonine"</note>, who died in 180, and I also choose to place him around that time. ### SECTION III. An Account of Hermogenes, and those who wrote against him.

<margin>Section 3.</margin>
However, as a summary may be useful, I shall provide here the account from Theodoret, which is to this effect: Hermogenes (t) <note>original: "Ὁ δὲ . . . ἐξ ὑποκειμένης ὕλης καὶ συν- ἀγεννήτῳ τὸν θεὸν ἔφη δημιουργῆσαι τὰ πάντα· ἀδύνατον γὰρ ὑπέλαβεν ὁ ἐμβρόντητος καὶ τῷ θεῷ τῶν ὅλων, ἐκ μὴ ὄντων δημιουργεῖν. Οὗτος τῷ κυρίῳ τὸ σῶμα ἐν τῷ ἡλίῳ εἶπεν ἀποτιθῆναι· τὸν δὲ διάβολον καὶ τὰς δαίμονας εἰς τὴν ὕλην ἀναχυθήσεσθαι." — "He said that God created all things out of underlying matter, which was also unbegotten; for the foolish man thought it impossible even for the God of the universe to create out of nothing. This man said that the Lord's body was deposited in the sun, and that the devil and the demons would be dissolved back into matter."</note> taught that God made the world out of matter which was co-eternal with Him. For this foolish man thought it was not possible for God to make all things out of nothing <term>creation ex nihilo</term>. He also taught that our Lord's body was deposited in the sun, and that the Devil and demons would eventually be resolved back into raw matter. Theophilus, Bishop of Antioch, and Origen both wrote against him.

We still possess a treatise by Tertullian written against the heresy of Hermogenes. He also refers to another work against him (u) concerning the origin of the soul, which is no longer extant.

### SECTION IV. *He was skilled in painting, and was originally a Christian.*

<margin>SECTION 4.</margin>
We learn from Tertullian that Hermogenes (*x*) was skilled in painting. Whether he practiced it as a trade, or only for his own amusement, is not entirely certain from Tertullian's phrasing. However, it seems somewhat likely that he was a painter by profession. It also appears that Hermogenes was originally a Christian. Tertullian does not say that he brought his principles with him from paganism <note>original: "Heathenism"</note>, but rather that from (*y*) being a Christian, he became a philosopher and a Stoic. We may conclude that (*z*) Hermogenes was not only learned and talented, but also virtuous, for Tertullian seems unable to charge him with any actual vice. He only hints that Hermogenes held more favorable views on marriage than some others did <note>Tertullian, later in life, joined the Montanists and held extremely strict views against remarriage, which explains his hostility here</note>. He also seems to dislike Hermogenes' painting, though the exact nature of the fault is not clearly stated.

<margin>SECTION 2.</margin> Augustine calls them (*q*) Galatians <note>These "Galatians" were a small sect following Hermogenes and Seleucus, distinct from the inhabitants of Galatia mentioned in the New Testament</note>. In Augustine's writings, these are placed late in the list of heretics, appearing after all those mentioned by Epiphanius; his information is taken entirely from Philaster. In my own account of Hermogenes, therefore, I shall make little or no use of those specific points. Hermogenes is mentioned by Eusebius and Jerome in their accounts of the works of Theophilus of Antioch, which I mentioned (*s*) formerly. However, our main information concerning Hermogenes must be gathered from Tertullian.

### SECTION III. *Some Account of him, and those who wrote against him.*

<margin>SECTION 3.</margin> However, as a summary may be useful, I shall include the account given by Theodoret, which is to this effect: Hermogenes (*t*) taught that God made the world out of matter which was co-eternal <note>Existing eternally alongside God</note> with him. For this foolish man thought it was not possible for God to make all things out of nothing. He also taught that our Lord's body was deposited in the sun, and that the Devil and demons would eventually be resolved back into matter. Against him wrote Theophilus, Bishop of Antioch, and Origen.

We still possess a treatise by Tertullian written against the heresy of Hermogenes. He also refers to another work against him (*u*) concerning the origin of the soul, which is no longer extant.

## SECTION V. Some Account of his Opinions concerning the Eternity of Matter.

<margin>SECTION 5.</margin>
Theodoret informed us that Hermogenes asserted the eternity of matter, out of which God made the world, rather than out of nothing <note>The theological concept of creation *ex nihilo*.</note>. The primary purpose of Tertullian’s book is to refute that notion, which was also the opinion of the Stoics—a group Tertullian (*a*) mentions very frequently in relation to this. He calls Hermogenes and others who hold that opinion (*b*) Materialists <note>original: "materiarios"</note>. He also speaks of this (*c*) in another work. Furthermore, he represents at length the reasonings of Hermogenes to show why he believed God made the world out of pre-existent matter. “For,” says he, “God (*d*) must have made

---

(*a*) "...not wishing that He should have made all things out of nothing... From there he took from the Stoics the idea of placing matter alongside the Lord, which itself had always been, neither born nor made, having neither beginning nor end, out of which the Lord afterward made all things." <note>original: "nolens illum ex nihilo universa fecisse... Inde sumpsit a Stoicis materiam cum Domino ponere, quæ ipsa semper fuerit, neque nata, neque facta, nec initium habens nec finem, ex qua Dominus omnia postea fecerit." *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 1, page 265. D. 335.</note> "Since he denies that matter was born or made." <note>original: "Cum enim neget, materiam natam aut factam." *Ibid.* chapter 3, page 267. B. 336.</note> See also chapters 4, 5, and 6.

(*b*) "For I hear that, according to Hermogenes and other materialist heretics, that [original] earth was indeed formless, invisible, and raw; but that our [current] earth consequently obtained form, appearance, and cultivation from God." <note>original: "Audio enim, apud Hermogenem, ceterosque materiarios hæreticos, terram quidem illam informem et invisibilem et rudem fuisse: hanc vero nostram proinde et formam, et conspectum et cultum a Deo consecutum." *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 25, page 278. B. 13. 346.</note>

(*c*) "This will be the matter which has set us at odds with Hermogenes and others, who presume that God worked all things out of matter, and not out of nothing." <note>original: "Hæc erit materia, quæ nos commisit cum Hermogene, ceterisque, qui Deum ex materia, non ex nihilo operatum cuncta præsumunt." *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 16, page 297. B. 10. 394.</note>

(*d*) "Establishing first that either the Lord made all things from Himself, or from nothing, or from something else... Therefore, he did not make them from Himself. Furthermore, he [Hermogenes] contends that He could not have made them from nothing. Defining the Lord as Good and Best, who wishes to make things as good and best as He is; indeed, that He wishes and does nothing that is not good and best. Therefore, all things ought to have been made good and best by Him according to His own nature. However, evil is found to have been made by Him—certainly not by His choice or will... That which He did not do by His own choice, must be understood to have been made from the defect of some thing, and is undoubtedly from matter. He adds another point: God was always God and also Lord, never *not* God. However, He could in no way always have been considered Lord, just as He was always God, if there had not been something always existing in the past, over which He was always considered Lord. Therefore, matter always existed alongside God the Lord." <note>original: "Præstruens, aut Dominum de semet ipso fecisse cuncta, aut de nihilo, aut de aliquo... Igitur non de semetipso fecisse. Proinde ex nihilo non potuisse eum facere, sic contendit. Bonum et Optimum definiens Dominum, qui bona atque optima tam velit facere quam sit: immo nihil non bonum atque optimum et velle eum et facere. Igitur omnia ab eo bona et optima oportuisse fieri secundum conditionem ipsius. Inveniri autem et mala ab eo facta, utique non ex arbitrio, nec ex voluntate. . . . Quod ergo non ex arbitrio suo fecerit, intelligi oportere ex vitio alicujus rei factum, ex materia esse sine dubio. Adjicit et aliud: Deum semper Deum etiam Dominum fuisse, nunquam non Deum. Nullo porro modo potuisse illum semper Dominum haberi, sicut et semper Deum, si non fuisset aliquid retro semper, cujus Dominus semper haberetur. Fuisse itaque materiam semper Deo Domino." *Against Hermogenes*, chapters 2, 3, page 296. A. B, C.</note>

made the world out of himself, or out of nothing, or out of something. That God should make the world out of himself is too obvious an absurdity to need a long refutation. And regarding the idea that God did not make it out of nothing, he argues in this manner: He establishes as a certain truth that God is good—even most good and excellent. He, therefore, cannot choose or desire evil. And yet, there is evil in the world. Consequently, this was necessary, and can be attributed to nothing but matter. Furthermore, he was always "Lord." But he could not have been always Lord as well as God if there had not always been something subject to him <note>Hermogenes argued that for God to be "Lord," there must have been an eternal "servant" or subject, which he identified as matter.</note>. It follows, therefore, that (*e*) God made the world out of something—even matter.”

<margin>(f) "And yet, how does Hermogenes persuade us that matter is evil?" Chapter 11, page 270. D. 340. "Come now, let us believe that matter is evil and most wicked." Chapter 12, page 271. I do not need to expand any further. However, I do not see that Hermogenes argued so much from the impossibility of God’s making the world out of nothing as from the unsuitability <note>original: "unfitness"</note> of it. If the world had been made out of nothing, he feared that the evil within it must be attributed to the will of God, which would have been a reflection on His goodness. But matter, out of which the world was made, being inherently (*f*) evil, he supposed that he thereby defended <note>original: "vindicated"</note> the Divine Being.

### SECTION VI. *He believed one supreme God, unchangeably good.*

<margin>(g) "Thus Hermogenes introduces two gods... an unbegotten God. But is not matter also unbegotten? Both would be without beginning and without end... Or how, he asks, can God’s authority and substance be preserved while matter exists in this way? How can he be seen as the sole and first author and confessed as the Lord of all? ... He says it is consistent with God's nature that he alone is the first, the author and Lord of all, and comparable to no one." Chapters 4, 5, 6, pages 267, 268, 337. <note>original: "Ita Hermogenes duos deos infert . . . . Innatus Deus. An non et innata materia? Ambo fine initio fine fine. . . . Dicit falvum Deo effe, ut et folus fit, et primus, et omnium auctor, et omnium Dominus, et nemini comparandus."</note>

"Just as we believe God is good and the best... furthermore, a certain nature... which remains incorruptible and unchangeable in the good presence of God." Chapter 12, page 271. B. <note>original: "Sicut Deum bonum et optimum credimus . . . porro naturam certam, . . quam in bono apud Deum incorruptibilem et indimutabilem."</note></margin>

<margin>(h) "He adds other reasons that are not entirely bad, if they were placed in a better light: that is, expressed in clearer language and arranged in a more convenient order." Le Clerc, *Church History*, 168, note 14. <note>original: "Addit et alias rationes non omnino malas, fi in meliore luce collocarentur: hoc est, clariore dictione exprimerentur, et commodiore ordine disponerentar."</note></margin>

<margin>(i) "Therefore, he asks, would God make things out of nothing so that evils might also be blamed on his will? The blindness of heretics in this type of argument is truly great. They either want another creator who is good and excellent, or they propose matter alongside the Creator, so that they can derive evil from matter rather than from the Creator. Yet no concept of God is freed from this question; he would still seem the author of evil—whoever he is—because even if he did not create it himself, he permitted it to be made by someone else and from somewhere else." Chapter 10, page 270. B. <note>original: "Ergo, inquit, ex nihilo faceret, ut mala quoque arbitrio ejus imputarentur? Magna, bona fide, cxcitas hæreticorum pro hujufmodi argumentatione. "For you labor in vain to prevent God from being seen as the author of evils; for even if he made things out of matter, they will still be blamed on him who made them, just as far as he made them." Chapter 14, page 272. SECTION 6. **T**ERTULLIAN says that (g) if matter were eternal, there would have to be two Gods. But Hermogenes did not accept that conclusion. He asserted there is only one God, supreme over all, the maker of the world, and unchangeably good, with whom no other being could be compared. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that (h) Tertullian has effectively refuted the opinion of Hermogenes. He also correctly observes that (i) the theories of Hermogenes and others for explaining the origin of evil are not satisfactory. <note>Tertullian argues that blaming "matter" for evil does not absolve God, because if God used that matter to create the world, he is still responsible for the final product.</note>

# HERMOGENES

## SECTION VII. *He ascribed to Matter an irregular Motion, but introduced no Aeons.*

<margin>(k) "However, you make it common between them that they are moved by themselves, and are always moved. What less do you ascribe to matter than to God? This would be the entire fellowship of Divinity: freedom and eternity of motion. But God moves in an orderly way; matter moves in a disordered way. For, according to the analogy of a boiling pot, the motion of matter, you say, was like that—turbulent, restless, and incomprehensible due to the excess of the struggle—before it was arranged." Chapters 42, 43, 45; pages 234, 287, 288. <note>original: "Commune autem inter illos facis, quod a femet ipfis moventur, et femper moventur. Quid minus materiæ quam Deo adfcribis? Totum confortium Divinitatis hoc erit, libertas et æternitas motus. Sed Deus compofite, materia incondite movetur. Nam, fecundum ollæ fimilitudinem fic erat, iniquis, materiæ motus, antequam difponeretur, concretus, inquietus, inadprehenfibilis, præ nimiætate certaminis."</note></margin>
Hermogenes originally ascribed an irregular and turbulent motion to matter (k).

<margin>(l) "For I hear, according to Hermogenes and the other heretics who believe in the eternity of matter, that that earth was indeed formless, invisible, and crude in itself; but this earth of ours has consequently obtained form, appearance, and order from God." Chapter 25, page 278.
Afterwards he adds: "But when it received arrangement from God and was adorned, it ceased from its [original] nature." Chapter 43, page 287. <note>original: "Audio enim, apud Hermogenem, cæterofque materiarios hæreticos, terram quidem illam informem et invifibilem et rudem fuiſſe: hanc vero noſtram proinde et formam, et conſpectum et cultum, a Deo conſecutam... Poſtea inferſ: at ubi accepit compoſitionem a Deo, et ornata eſt, ceſſavit a natura."</note></margin>
We now perceive the scheme of Hermogenes. He did not introduce any Aeons <note>Aeons were divine emanations or lesser deities common in Gnostic systems; Hermogenes rejected these in favor of a more direct creation.</note>, nor any Creator different from the one God the Father. But he said that matter was eternal, and God made the world out of it. To this matter he ascribed all the evil and all the defects which exist in any creatures. Matter had always possessed a confused, irregular, and turbulent motion. God brought order, beauty, and proportion out of that confused and unrefined <note>original: "indigested"</note> matter (l).

<summary>Hermogenes argued that while God is the sole creator, He formed the world from eternal, pre-existing matter that possessed an inherent, chaotic motion. He used this theory to explain the origin of evil and imperfection without resorting to the Gnostic concept of Aeons.</summary>

### SECTION IX.
*Some other opinions of his about the origin of the soul, human liberty, the devil, demons, and a future judgment.*

Tertullian asserted the existence of human liberty <note>The author uses "liberty" here to mean free will or the capacity for choice.</note>. I believe he (q) does not deny that Marcion and Hermogenes also held this view.

<margin>(q) "That we naturally possess free will <note>original: αυτεξυσιον (*autexousion*)</note>, we have already shown both to Marcion and to Hermogenes." *On the Soul*, chapter 21, p. 324. C. 658.</margin>

Theodoret, as quoted earlier, stated that Hermogenes taught that the Devil and demons would eventually be resolved back into matter. This is not surprising, since they were originally formed from it. Furthermore, he possibly considered the gathering of matter—or some part of it—to be the abyss and the place of torment assigned to (r) the Devil and his angels at their final condemnation.

<margin>(r) "But if the end of evil will occur then, when its leader, the devil, goes into the fire which God prepared for him and his [angels], he is first banished into the pit of the abyss." *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 11. p. 271. A. B. 6. 340.</margin>

From this, we are led to observe that (s) this man believed in a future judgment and probably all the other major tenets <note>original: "articles"</note> of religion. That he believed in a future judgment is evident from the passage just transcribed and from another mentioned a short while (t) ago.

<margin>(s) "...and so we labor in vain to remove evil from ourselves; then God also commands and prescribes this in vain; indeed, God also established judgment in vain, since he would be punishing injustice [without cause]." *Ibid.* p. 271. A. 340.</margin>

<margin>(t) See note (p), the third passage on the previous page.</margin>

### SECTION 11. *He never established a separate communion.*

<margin>Section 10.</margin>
So, we have noted all the specific opinions attributed to Hermogenes by the ancient writers. However, it is possible that none of these accounts are reliable except for those found in Tertullian. It seems somewhat likely to me that Hermogenes never formed a distinct sect or established a separate religious community <note>original: "communion"</note>. For Tertullian says nothing about him holding separate meetings. I suspect, therefore, that Hermogenes was willing to take communion with Catholic Christians <note>In this 2nd-century context, "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or mainstream church, rather than the modern Roman Catholic denomination.</note> if they would allow him, even though he indulged in speculations that led him toward views that were somewhat unusual.

### SECTION 11. *His testimony to the Scriptures.*

<margin>Section 11.</margin>
It only remains for us to consider his testimony regarding the Holy Scriptures.
Le Clerc notes that (u) Tertullian debates with him as someone who accepted the authority of the Scriptures. Indeed, in his arguments against Hermogenes, Tertullian quotes every part of the Bible as if Hermogenes accepted them, especially the books of Moses, (x) and

---

(u) "And therefore he deals with him as with a man who would admit Holy Scripture." *Ecclesiastical History, p. 722, note 13.* <note>original: "Ideoque cum eo agit, quasi cum homine, qui S. scripturam admitteret."</note>

(x) "But I will also appeal to the original record of Moses, from which the opposing side tries to support its suspicions ungratefully, so that it might not seem to be instructed from elsewhere than where it should be. Therefore, he took the opportunity of certain words, as it is generally the custom of heretics to twist even simple things. For even 'the beginning' itself, in which God made the heaven and the earth, they want [to be] something..." <note>original: "Sed et ad originale instrumentum Moysi provocabo... Nam et ipsum principium... aliquid volunt..." This passage from Tertullian's *Against Hermogenes* argues that Hermogenes misinterpreted the opening of Genesis to support his theory of pre-existent matter.</note>

He argued that (y) the Scriptures do not explicitly state that God made the world out of nothing <note>The doctrine of *creation ex nihilo* (creation out of nothing) was a central point of debate between early Christian theologians and those influenced by Greek philosophy.</note>. He speaks as if Hermogenes should have feared such behavior and the consequences that follow from it.

## SECT. XII. He received both the Old and New Testament.

<margin>SECTION 12.</margin>Tertullian refers to (a) the Book of Proverbs. He quotes (b) David in Psalm 102, and several of the Prophets by name.
It is apparent that Hermogenes and others (c) respected Christ, the Prophets, and the Apostles. Tertullian quotes both the Old and New Testament to him, particularly (d) the Gospels of St. Matthew and (e) St. John, and (f) the Epistles of Paul.
Taking everything into account, I believe it is clear that Hermogenes accepted and respected the scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, just as other Christians of his time did.

## SECT. XIII.
### No Account of any Writings of his.

There is no record of any surviving writings by Hermogenes, though it is highly probable that he was an author. This might be inferred from many passages in Tertullian (g) and from the general nature of his arguments. <term>Cave</term><note>William Cave (1637–1713), an English church historian.</note>, however, at the conclusion of his entry on this subject, triumphs in the loss of Hermogenes's works, if indeed any existed (h). I am sorry to see this, as such an attitude seems to me beneath a man of letters. The notions and reasonings of Hermogenes could have done no harm to anyone today who is capable of critical examination. On the contrary, we might have made good use of his works, just as we have with the fragments of Heracleon and other early writers.

***

(g) "And indeed, I will turn his own inventions <note>original: *epinoemata* — a Greek term for ideas or mental constructions</note> back against him." <note>original: "Et quidem epinoemata illius retorquebo adversus illum." *Chapter 3, page 267. B.*</note> "For Hermogenes also attacks the arguments of certain people who say that evils were necessary for the illumination of good things." <note>original: "Nam et Hermogenes expugnat quorundam argumentationes, dicentium, mala necessaria fuisse, ad inluminationem bonorum." *Chapter 15, page 273. B.*</note> "Then you add... Above... Forgetful of these things, you later infer." <note>original: "Dehinc subjicis . . Supra . . Horum immemor, postea infers." *Chapter 43, page 287. B.*</note>

(h) "Truly, the zeal of the godly and their own impiety have deservedly condemned those writings, blasphemous against God, to eternal darkness." <note>original: "Verum scripta ista in Deum blasphema piorum zelus et propria impietas aeternis tenebris merito damnavit." *H. # M O N T A N I S T S.

<margin>Section 2.</margin>Regarding the martyrs of Lyons, who are supposed to have suffered in the year 177—or at the earliest, in 167—Eusebius says that *(l)* the followers of Montanus were only then beginning to be known in the world. He expresses himself again to *(m)* a similar purpose in his account of the books of Apollinaris written against them; Apollinaris flourished around the year of Christ 176.

Nevertheless, *(n)* Pearson and *(o)* Beausobre are of the opinion that Montanism appeared in the year 156 or 157, soon after the middle of the second century; and Baratiere *(p)* places it in 126. But it seems to me that Eusebius could not be much mistaken, as he was generally very well acquainted with ecclesiastical antiquity and had before him the works of many ancient writers involved in this controversy. However, if any should be disposed to place the beginning of this affair ten or fifteen years earlier, the difference would not be very great.

Epiphanius, who is not always exact in his chronology, says that *(q)* Montanus set up his pretensions in the nineteenth year of Antonine the Pious, or about the year of Christ 156. His reasons for that calculation are assigned by Petavius in his critical observations <note>original: "animadversions"</note> upon him. Tillemont should also be *(r)* consulted.

### SECTION III. *The Origin of Their Name, and the Extent and Duration of Their Opinions.*

<margin>Section 3.</margin> They are called <margin>(*s*) *See Theodoret, Compendium of Heretical Fables, Book 3, chapter 2.*</margin> Montanists from their founder, Montanus; Phrygians and Cata-Phrygians from the region of Phrygia where they first emerged; and Pepuzians from a village in Phrygia called Pepuza, which they revered as another Jerusalem <note>The Montanists believed that the "New Jerusalem" described in the Book of Revelation would descend from heaven and be established at Pepuza.</note>.

Irenaeus has not explicitly mentioned the Montanists anywhere in his writings. However, he is supposed to refer to them, or intend to describe them, in <margin>(*t*) *Book 3, chapter 11, page 192. Book 4, chapter 33. [also 53.] number 6. page 271. Massuet edition.*</margin> two places of his work *Against Heresies*. They are mentioned clearly twice by <margin>(*u*) "But even the Phrygians; for they now call those who do not adhere to the new prophecy 'soulish' <note>original: *psychikoi*. This was a derogatory term used by Montanists to describe mainstream Christians whom they considered lacking in the Spirit.</note>." *Clement of Alexandria, Stromata Book 4, page 511. A. See also Stromata Book 7, page 765. C.*</margin> Clement of Alexandria. For a time, they were even supported <margin>(*x*) "For that same man [Praxeas] then compelled the Bishop of Rome—who already recognized the prophecies of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla, and by that recognition was bringing peace to the churches of Asia and Phrygia—by asserting false things about the prophets themselves and their churches, and by defending the authorities of his predecessors, both to revoke the letters of peace already sent out and to cease from his purpose of accepting the spiritual gifts." *Tertullian, Against Praxeas, chapter 1, page 634. C.*</margin> by a Bishop of Rome. However, learned men are not in agreement as to whether this was Bishop Victor or someone else.

This group survived for a long time. The Cata-Phrygians are expressly mentioned in the Edicts of Constantine <margin>(*y*) *See before, Vol. 7. 397. 421.*</margin> against heretics. Epiphanius states that <margin>(*z*) *Heresies 48, number 14, page 416.*</margin> they were still present in his day in Cappadocia, Galatia, and Phrygia, and were numerous in Cilicia and at Constantinople.

HISTORY OF HERETICS:

<margin>Section 4.</margin> ...him <note>original: "abscisum et semivirum"</note> "cut off" and "a half-man" in a note (*h*) regarding the passage. Cyril of Jerusalem says that (*i*) Montanus was a man covered all over with filthiness and impurity, not fit to be mentioned. And Isidore of Pelusium affirms that (*k*) he was guilty of adultery. But I believe that these testimonies were written too late to be reliable. Neither Eusebius, nor the authors he quotes—some of whom were contemporaries with Montanus and others who lived shortly after him—charge him with any such thing.

We previously mentioned a report that (*l*) Montanus and Maximilla committed suicide. However, the author who mentions that story did not believe it himself. We are therefore under no obligation to give it any credit. The conduct of the sect will be considered shortly.

### SECTION V. *Of his Companions and Assistants, and their Prophecies.*

<margin>Section 5.</margin> Eusebius speaks of (*m*) Alcibiades and Theodotus as having joined with Montanus from the beginning. But the people most frequently mentioned as his assistants and prophetesses are two women named Prisca (or Priscilla) and Maximilla. They are said to (*n*) have been married women who abandoned their husbands. It is possible they did not attend to their household duties as much as they should have.

---

<margin>(*h*) He calls him "cut off" and "half-man" <note>original: "Abscisum vocat et semivirum"</note> because Montanus was from Phrygia, where the priests of the goddess Cybele were traditionally castrated.</margin>
<margin>(*i*) "The most wretched man, filled with every kind of uncleanness and licentiousness," <note>original: "Ο αθλιωτατος, και πασης ακαθαρσιας και ασελγειας πεπληρωμενος..."</note> etc. *Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 16, number 8, page 247. B.*</margin>
<margin>(*k*) "...plainly caught as an adulterer." <note>original: "...μοιχο δε φανερως εαλωκοτος."</note> *Isidore of Pelusium, Book 1, letter 243.*</margin>

<margin>Section 5.</margin>
And once they believed they were inspired and that God had qualified them for significant service to his church, they might have considered themselves reasonably excused from low and private concerns—though still without violating the respect expected of them by their husbands. Jerome says that they were *(o)* rich and noble women, and that they used their wealth to greatly promote the interests of the sect. However, I cannot say for certain whether his account is reliable. William Cave calls them *(p)* "two profligate women," but surely such harsh language could have been spared. Hardly any of the ancient writers expressed themselves so severely when speaking of these deluded women. Even if they had, we do not need to follow their example unless they appear to be speaking with good reason.

Although Priscilla and Maximilla were the most notable supporters of Montanus, there were other women whom the group believed possessed the gift of prophecy. Tertullian *(q)* speaks in strong terms of a "sister" who conversed with God and angels.

Some of the prophecies of these individuals were published in writing. Epiphanius quotes a book called *(r)* *The Prophecy of Montanus*, and he cites Montanus's own words several times *(s)*.

# MONTANISTS

<margin>Section 6.</margin>the Father. Augustine, who in the first part of his article says that the <term>Cataphrygians</term> <note>original: "Cataphrygians"; another name for the Montanists, referring to their origins in Phrygia.</note> honored Montanus as the <term>Paraclete</term> <note>original: "Paracletus"; a term from the Gospel of John meaning the "Comforter" or "Advocate," usually identifying the Holy Spirit.</note>, and Priscilla and Maximilla as prophetesses, later adds: they claimed that the Lord’s promise concerning the Holy Spirit was fulfilled in them rather than in the Apostles. Philaster wrote to a similar effect. St. Jerome sometimes says they believed the Holy Spirit was present in Montanus.

The truth seems to be that they believed God had provided additional revelations through Montanus for the perfection of believers. They did not deny that the Holy Spirit had descended upon the Apostles on the famous day of Pentecost; however, they believed that some things were left to be revealed later, at a time and to a person of God’s choosing. Even so, they could not have thought that this inspiration of Montanus was equal to that of the Apostles, since it did not involve the core articles of faith, but mainly addressed matters of outward order and discipline. <note>See note (g) below.</note>

Tertullian heartily embraced this "new prophecy." However, he states: "We preach no other God, and no other Christ."

Section 6. Nor do we have any other rule of faith, though we are more in favor of fasting and less in favor of marrying than other people. In another place (*i*) and in another work, Tertullian speaks to a similar purpose. He says again that it (*k*) was impossible for any new revelation to contradict the doctrine of Christ. I have placed some other passages of his in the <margin>notes</margin> <note>original: "margin"</note> showing his respect for this manifestation and his persuasion that spiritual gifts were bestowed upon Montanus and his friends in an uncommon degree. The manner in which they delivered their claimed prophecies was considered disagreeable. They seemed to be deprived of the exercise of reason for a time: (*n*) this induced several Catholic writers, in their arguments against them, to show that neither the prophets of the Old nor the New Testament prophesied in a state of <term>ecstasy</term> <note>original: "extasy"; a trance-like state where the speaker was believed to lose conscious control of their mind.</note>. ### SECTION VII. *Of the Opinions of the Montanists.*

<margin>SECTION 7.</margin>
As for the resurrection of the body and other major articles of the Christian religion, all writers who cataloged heresies testify to the Montanists' (*s*) belief in them. And, as Tertullian observes, these doctrines (*t*) are not weakened, but are instead established, confirmed, and illustrated by these "overflowings of the spirit."

They are, however, charged by some with not holding the correct doctrine concerning the Trinity. Epiphanius says that (*u*) concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they agree—

<header>HISTORY OF HERETICS:</header>

<margin>Section 7.</margin> —agree with the Catholic church. Theodoret's account is that (*x*) Montanus made no innovation in the doctrine of the Trinity or the creation of the world. However, he adds that afterwards (*y*) some of his followers denied the hypostases <term>hypostases: the distinct persons of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) as individual realities</term> and agreed with the views of Sabellius and Noetus <note>Sabellius and Noetus taught that God was a single person who simply appeared in different forms or "modes."</note>. The author of the *Additions* to Tertullian's book *Prescriptions against Heretics* says there (*z*) were two parties among them who held different sentiments about the Trinity. It must be considered probable that some of them followed the Sabellian or Unitarian <note>In this historical context, "Unitarian" refers to those who believe God exists as only one person.</note> scheme. For this is affirmed by many writers of antiquity: by (*a*) Jerome and (*b*) Isidore of Pelusium, as well as the others just mentioned.

B.*</note>

(*y*) "But some of them, in a manner similar to Sabellius, denied the three persons [hypostases] of the Godhead, saying that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same person, similar to the view of Noetus of Asia." <note>original Greek: Τινες δε αυτων τας τρεις υποστασεις της θεοτητος σαβελλιω παραπλησιως ηρησαντο, τον αυτον ειναι λεγοντες και πατερα και υιον και αγιον πνευμα παραπλησιως τω ασιανω νοητω. *Ibid. p. 227. ### SECTION VIII. *Of the Peculiarities in their Manners, Discipline, and Doctrine.*

<margin>Section 8.</margin>
We now proceed to observe their peculiarities. But after all, I suppose they esteemed themselves good Catholic Christians. For though Tertullian scornfully calls the Catholics sometimes "soulish" <note>original: "animal" or *psychici*, a term used by Montanists to describe those they believed lacked the higher spiritual inspiration of the "New Prophecy"</note> and the like, he does not reckon them heretics <note>original Latin: "Heretics take away marriage. The soulish force it. The former [heretics] not even once; the latter [Catholics] marry more than once." *De Monog. cap. 1. p. 673.*</note>, but distinguishes them from such people.

In general, we may say they made a profession of great strictness <note>original Latin: "Montanus and those who follow the schism of Novatus took the name of purity for themselves, believing that second marriages should be prohibited from the communion of the church." *Hieron. ad Tit. T. 4. P. 1. p. 414. F.*</note>. And therefore they are frequently mentioned together with the Novatians <note>The Novatians were another early Christian group known for their rigorous discipline and refusal to readmit those who had fallen away during persecution.</note> and called Puritans <note>original Latin: *Cathari*, meaning "the pure ones."</note>.

One thing in which they innovated was condemning second marriages for everyone <note>original Latin: "However, they are rigid, not because they themselves do not commit even worse sins, etc." *Ad. Marcell. T. 4. p. 65. near the end.*</note>. Whoever married a second time, even if his first wife was dead, was excommunicated by

Id. Adv. Jovin. L. 2. T. 4. p. 195. M.*</note>

<margin>Section 8.</margin> by them. All ancient writers agree on this account of them. It also appears in Tertullian’s (*f*) writings to be a part of the discipline which they constantly taught <note>original: "inculcated"</note>.

They also had many rules about fasting and abstinence.

Apollonius, as quoted in Eusebius (*g*), blames Montanus for imposing laws regarding fasting. Theodoret says that (*h*) Montanus established new fasts in addition to those that were customary in the church. A passage from Tertullian (*i*), provided in the notes below, confirms this account.

The Catholics <note>referring to the "universal" or mainstream church of that era</note> argued that such things should not be *imposed* on people. If anyone thought it right to practice self-denial <note>original: "mortify themselves"</note>, they were at liberty to do so. However, practices not commanded by Christ and his Apostles were not to be required as necessary. This was the argument some made, as appears from (*k*) Tertullian.

---

(*f*) "But even if a limit is now placed on marrying—which spiritual reason among us, on the authority of the Paraclete <note>The Holy Spirit; the Montanists believed the Paraclete spoke directly through their prophets</note>, defends—it prescribes only one marriage in the faith." <note>original Latin: *Sed et si nubendi jam modus ponitur, quem quidem apud nos spiritualis ratio, Paracleto auctore, defendit, unum in fide matrimonium præscribens.*</note> *Against Marcion, Book 1, chapter 30, p. 452. B.*

"We know only one marriage, just as we know only one God." <note>original Latin: *Unum matrimonium novimus, sicut unum Deum.*</note> *On Monogamy, chapter 1, p. 673. B. See the same throughout.*

(*g*) "He who laid down laws for fasting." <note>original Greek: Ὁ νηστείας νομοθετήσας.</note> *Book 5, chapter 18, p. 184. C.*

(*h*) "And he introduced new fasts contrary to the custom of the church." <note>original Greek: Καὶ νηστείας καινὰς παρὰ τὸ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἐπεισήγαγεν ἔθος.</note> *Ibid, p. 227. B.*

(*i*) "They accuse us of keeping our own fasts, of often extending our prayer watches <note>original: *stationes*, periods of fasting and prayer</note> into the evening, and of also observing 'dry-fasts' <term>xerophagias</term> <note>A strict diet of dry foods, excluding meat, juices, and wine</note>, keeping our food free from all meat, all juices, and

<column-break/>

any particularly succulent fruits, so that we neither eat nor drink anything with the quality of wine; and also of abstaining from the bath, which is consistent with a dry diet." <note>original Latin: *Arguunt nos, quod jejunia propria custodiamus, quod stationes plerumque in vesperam producamus, quod etiam xerophagias observemus, siccantes cibum ab omni carne, et omni jurulentia, et vividioribus quibusque pomis, ne quid vinositatis vel edamus, vel potemus, lavacri quoque abstinentiam, congruente arido victui.*</note> *On Fasting, chapter 1, p. 701. Itaque de cetero differenter jejunandum ex arbitrio, non ex imperio novæ disciplinæ, pro temporibus et causis uniuscujusque. Sic et Apostolos observasse, nullum aliud imponente jugum certorum et in commune omnibus obeundorum jejuniorum, &c.*</note> *On Fasting, chapter 2, p. 702. B.*
