-># MONTANISTS.<-

<margin>Section 8.</margin>
Jerome says they (*l*) kept three Lents in the year. Perhaps this was the practice of some in the sect in later times. Since it is not mentioned by Tertullian, it can be assumed it was not commanded by Montanus himself. In another place, Jerome shows how the Montanists and some others (*m*) likewise argued from our Lord's words in Matthew 9:15 <note>“But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast.”</note>.

They did not allow the church the power to forgive major sins committed after baptism; nor did they believe (*n*) those who fell into such sins should ever again be admitted to full communion, (*o*) even if they repented. Indeed, Tertullian seems to say that (*p*) there is no salvation or forgiveness for such people, and that Christ (*q*) does not intercede for them.

They were also against fleeing from persecution (*r*) and against paying money to ransom themselves from the mistreatment of persecutors.

***

<columns>
2
<column>

(*l*) "We fast for one Lent according to the tradition of the Apostles, in agreement with the whole world. They observe three Lents in a year, as if three Saviors had suffered." <note>original: *Nos unam quadragesimam secundum traditionem Apostolorum, toto nobis orbe congruo, jejunamus. Illi tres in anno faciunt quadragesimas, quasi tres passi sint salvatores.*</note> *To Marcella, Volume 4, p. 65.*

(*m*) "Some believe that fasts should be held during the forty days after the Passion; although the days of Pentecost and the coming of the Holy Spirit immediately following indicate a time of celebration for us. On the occasion of this testimony, Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla also observe a Lent after Pentecost: because when the bridegroom is taken away, the children of the bridegroom ought to fast, etc." <note>original: *Nonnulli putant idcirco post dies quadraginta passionis, jejunia debere committi... Et ex hujus occasione testimonii Montanus, Prisca et Maximilla, etiam post Pentecosten faciunt quadragesimam: quod ablato sponso filii sponsi debeant jejunare, &c.*</note> *Commentary on Matthew, chapter 9, volume 4, p. 31. M.*

(*n*) "They shut the doors of the Church against almost every sin." <note>original: *Illi ad omne pene delictum Ecclesiæ obserant fores.*</note> *Jerome to Marcella, p. 65.*

(*o*) "He who learned this from the Apostles, and taught it with the Apostles, never knew of a second repentance promised by the Apostles for the adulterer and the fornicator." <note>original: *Hoc qui ab Apostolis didicit, et cum Apostolis docuit, numquam mœcho et fornicatori secundam pœnitentiam promissam ab Apostolis norat.*</note> *On Modesty, chapter 20, p. 741. (*p*) "I even hear that an edict has been put forward, and a peremptory one at that: the 'Sovereign Pontiff'—that is, the 'bishop of bishops'—decrees: 'I remit the sins of adultery and fornication to those who have performed penance.' Far be it, far be it from the bride of Christ to have such a proclamation!" <note>original: *Audio etiam edictum esse propositum, quidem peremtorium: Pontifex scilicet Maximus, quod est episcopus episcoporum, edicit: Ego et mœchiæ et fornicationis delicta, pœnitentia functis dimitto. For these, there will be pardon through Christ, the intercessor with the Father. But there are also sins contrary to these, which are more serious and deadly, which do not receive pardon: murder, idolatry, fraud, apostasy <note>original: *negatio*, or denial of the faith</note>, blasphemy, and certainly also adultery and fornication, and any other violation of the temple of God. A.*

C.*

HISTORY OF HERETICS:

<margin>Section 8.</margin> They refused to pay bribes to their persecutors or to seek any relief from the suffering they caused. Furthermore, they met together openly and in large numbers, in a way that many other Christians considered unwise or indiscreet. Tertullian wrote a book on this subject which can be consulted. This leads us to observe that these people had their own separate assemblies in which every part of Christian worship was performed. However, according to Jerome, the structure of their church hierarchy was somewhat different from that of most others.

When Asterius Urbanus wrote around the year 232, they boasted of having many martyrs. This must be understood as referring to martyrs for the Christian faith in general, rather than for the specific doctrines of Montanism.

They were also Millenarians <term>Millenarians: Those who believe that Christ will return to rule on earth for a literal 1,000-year period.</term>, as is evident from the writings of Tertullian.

D.*

(*t*) "There is a sister among us today who has been granted the gifts of revelations, which she experiences in the spirit through ecstasy in the church during the Lord's services... ### SECTION IX. *Of their Secret Rites, and the Slanders cast upon them on this Account.*

<margin>Section 9.</margin> After all the things that have already been mentioned, we must not overlook the accounts of their secret rites <note>original: *mysteries*</note>. Several writers from the fourth and fifth centuries inform us that it was reported that they (z) took a child about a year old and pricked him all over with needles. They mixed the blood they extracted with wheat flour, and from this, they made their (a) sacramental bread. If the child survived, he was considered a high priest; if he died, he was regarded as a martyr. I have placed passages from many authors relating to this matter at the bottom of the page: (b) St. Cyril of Jerusalem, (c) Isidore of Pelusium, (d) Epiphanius, (e) Philaster, (f) Augustine, (g) Theodoret, etc., and (h) Jerome.

***

<columns>2</columns>

(z) See Mr. Robert Turner, *Of the Calumnies cast upon the Primitive Christians*, pages 52–53.

(a) *Augustine, Volume 6, Heresies 26, page 5, chapter 3.* See the passage in note (f) on this page.

(b) "For it is enough to speak of this through these shameful words for the sake of the dignity of the women present... they most miserably slaughter little children and chop them up for an unlawful meal, under the pretext of what they call their mysteries." <note>original Greek: Αυταρκες γαρ τουτο δια δυσφημων ειπειν, των παρουσων γυναικων σεμνοτητος ενεκα... Και αθλιωτατα παιδια γυναικων μικρα σφαττων, και κατακοπτων εις αθεμιτον βρωσιν, προφασει των καλουμένων παρ αυτοις μυστηριων.</note> *Catechesis 16, number 8, page 247.*

(c) "For he is associated with sorceries and child-killings, as well as adulteries and idolatries, etc." <note>original Greek: Μαγγανειαις γαρ και παιδοκτονιαις, μοιχειαις τε και ειδωλολατρειαις συντιθεται. κ. λ.</note> *Isidore, Book 1, Epistle 242.*

(d) "They say a terrible and unlawful deed is done. For during a certain festival, they prick a very young child all over his body with bronze needles, and they collect his blood for their own use, supposedly for a sacrifice." <note>original Greek: Δεινον τε και αθεμιτον εργον φασι γινεσθαι. Παιδα γαρ κομιδη νηπιον κατα εορτην τινα δι ολου του σωματος κατακεντωντες ραφισι χαλκαις, το αιμα αυτου προσποριζονται εαυτοις, εις επιτηδευσιν δηθεν θυσιας.</note> *Heresy 48, number 14, page 416 C. See also number 15, page 417 C.*

<column-break/>

(e) "Where both the mystery of the Cynics (or actors) and the cursed wickedness regarding the infant are celebrated. For they say they mix the infant's blood into their sacrifice at Easter <term>Pascha: The feast of Easter or Passover</term>." <note>original Latin: Ubi et mysterium Cynicorum, (Scenicorum) et infantis execranda celebratur impietas. Dicunt enim eos de infantis sanguine in Pascha miscere in suum sacrificium.</note> *Heresy 49, pages 103–104.*

(f) "They are reported to have deadly sacraments. For they are said to make their Eucharist from the blood of a year-old infant, which they squeeze out of its whole body through tiny puncture wounds, mixing it with flour and making bread from it. If the boy dies, he is held by them as a martyr; if he lives, he is held as a great priest." <note>original Latin: Sacramenta perhibentur habere funesta. Nam de infantis anniculi sanguine, quem de toto ejus corpore minutis punctionum vulneribus extorquent, quasi Eucharistiam suam conficere perhibentur, miscentes eum farinæ; panemque inde facientes. Qui puer si mortuus fuerit, habetur apud eos pro martyre: si autem vixerit, pro magno sacerdote.</note> *Heresy 26. See also Heresy 27.*

(g) "Concerning their mysteries, some spread certain rumors; but they themselves do not admit to them, calling the accusation a slander." <note>original Greek: Περι δε των μυστηριων τινες μεν θρυλλουσι τινα. εκεινοι δε ου συνομολογουσιν, αλλα συκοφαντιαν την κατηγοριαν καλουσι.</note> *Volume 4, page 227 C.*

(h) "I pass over the wicked mysteries which are spoken of regarding the nursing boy and the martyr-to-be, made into bread <term>confarrata: A Roman term for a traditional marriage cake, here used to describe the ritual bread</term>. I prefer, I say, not to believe it. Let everything involving blood be false." <note>original Latin: Prætermitto scelerata mysteria, quæ dicuntur de lactente puero, et de victuro martyre confarrata. Malo, inquam, non credere. Sit falsum omne quod sanguinis est.</note> *To Marcella, page 65.*

### SECT. IX. *Of their Mysteries, and the Slanders Cast upon them for this Reason.*

<margin>Sect. 9.</margin>
After everything previously discussed, we must not overlook the accounts of their secret rituals <term>mysteries: private religious rites often hidden from the uninitiated</term>. Several writers from the fourth and fifth centuries report that the Montanists took a child about a year old and pricked him all over with needles. They supposedly mixed the extracted blood with wheat flour to make their sacramental bread <term>sacramental bread: bread used in the Eucharist or Holy Communion</term>. If the child survived, he was regarded as a high priest; if he died, he was honored as a martyr. I have provided passages from various authors regarding this matter at the bottom of the page: St. Cyril of Jerusalem, Isidore of Pelusium, Epiphanius, Philaster, Augustine, Theodoret, and Jerome.

---

<columns>2</columns>

(*z*) See Mr. Robert Turner, *Of the Calumnies cast upon the Primitive Christians*, pages 52–53.

(*a*) *Augustine, Volume 6, Heresy 26, page 5, column 3.* See the passage in note (*f*) on this page.

(*b*) "For it is enough to describe this through disgraceful hints, out of respect for the modesty of the women present... They slaughter the wretched little children of women and cut them up for an unlawful meal, under the pretext of what they call their mysteries." <note>original: Καὶ ἀθλιώτατα παιδία γυναικῶν μικρὰ σφάττων, καὶ κατακόπτων εἰς ἀθέμιτον βρῶσιν, προφάσει τῶν καλουμένων παρ' αὐτοῖς μυστηρίων.</note> *Catechesis 16, number 8, page 247.*

(*c*) "For he is associated with sorceries, infanticides, adulteries, and idolatries." <note>original: Μαγγανείαις γὰρ καὶ παιδοκτονίαις, μοιχείαις τε καὶ εἰδωλολατρείαις συντίθεται.</note> *Isidore, Book 1, Epistle 242.*

(*d*) "They say a terrible and unlawful deed takes place. For they claim that at a certain festival, they take a very young infant and prick his whole body with bronze needles to obtain his blood, supposedly for the performance of a sacrifice." <note>original: Παιδα γαρ κομιδη νηπιον κατα εορτην τινα δι ολου του σωματος κατακεντωντες ραφισι χαλκαις, το αιμα αυτου προσποριζονται εαυτοις...</note> *Heresy 48, number 14, page 416 C. See also number 15, page 417 C.*

<column-break/>

(*e*) "Where both the mystery of the Cynics (or theatrical performers) and the cursed wickedness regarding an infant is celebrated. For they say that they mix the blood of an infant into their sacrifice at Passover." <note>original: Dicunt enim eos de infantis sanguine in Pascha miscere in suum sacrificium.</note> *Heresy 49, pages 103–104.*

(*f*) "They are said to have deadly sacraments. For they are reported to make their Eucharist by pricking a year-old infant all over its body with tiny wounds to extract blood, mixing it with flour, and making bread from it. If the boy dies, he is held as a martyr among them; if he lives, he is held as a high priest." <note>original: ...de infantis anniculi sanguine, quem de toto ejus corpore minutis punctionum vulneribus extorquent, quasi Eucharistiam suam conficere perhibentur...</note> *Heresy 26. See also Heresy 27.*

(*g*) "Concerning their mysteries, some people spread certain rumors. But they [the Montanists] do not admit to them; instead, they call the accusation a slander." <note>original: ...ἐκεῖνοι δὲ οὐ συνομολογοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ συκοφαντίαν τὴν κατηγορίαν καλοῦσι.</note> *Volume 4, page 227 C.*

(*h*) "I pass over the wicked mysteries which are spoken of concerning a nursing child, and of a future martyr made with flour. I prefer, I say, not to believe it. Let everything involving blood be false." <note>original: Prætermitto scelerata mysteria... Malo, inquam, non credere. Sit falsum omne quod sanguinis est.</note> *To Marcella, page 65.*

# HISTORY OF HERETICS:

<margin>SECT. 9.</margin> Based on the passages from these authors, it is easy to make several observations. Augustine and some others seem to have assumed that this was a standard part of their secret rituals <term>mysteries: private religious rites often hidden from the uninitiated</term>, or the Eucharist. However, Epiphanius and Philaster speak as if it belonged only to an annual festival held around Easter. Cyril attributes both immorality <term>lewdness: here, sexual misconduct</term> and cruelty to their rituals. He also suggests that they not only killed but also ate infants—unless this last part refers only to their blood being mixed with flour. Isidore of Pelusium charges them with magic, infanticide, immorality, and idolatry. He and Cyril of Jerusalem are the only writers who speak with absolute certainty. Epiphanius, Philaster, and Augustine express doubt, describing the matter as nothing more than a rumor. Theodoret notes that there are stories about their rituals, but the Montanists themselves do not admit they are true. They claim the stories are false and nothing but slander <term>calumnies: false and malicious statements designed to damage a reputation</term>. Jerome is not inclined to believe the common story and states that he is willing to omit any mention of it.

Undoubtedly, this was a mere slander and a work of fiction. If such things had been practiced by them, they would not have been omitted by the historian Eusebius and all the authors he cited. Nor would Tertullian <note>Tertullian: a prominent early Christian author known for his strict moral standards who eventually joined the Montanist movement</note> ever have associated with them. The common nature and the clear falsehood of this story should teach us not to be so quick to accept accusations against anyone labeled as a heretic.

### SECT. X. *Of their Testimony to the Scriptures.*

<margin>SECT. 10.</margin>
It remains for us to observe their testimony concerning the Scriptures.

Philaster expressly says they (*i*) receive the Law and the Prophets. Epiphanius, in his larger work, states that (*k*) they receive all the Scriptures, both the Old and the New Testament. In his arguments with them, he appeals to the Scriptures as being (*l*) of undisputed authority to them. His summary is to this effect: they (*m*) receive the Old and New Testament. However, alongside the ancient prophets, they introduce others, boasting of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla. Theodoret says that (*n*) Montanus had two women who were prophetesses and called their writings "prophecies." Later, he says that the (*o*) prophecies of those two women were held in higher esteem by the Montanists than the divine Gospel. This, surely, must be an exaggeration <note>original: "aggravation"; in this context, an overstatement intended to make the group's errors appear more severe</note>. Caius, however, as we may remember, complained early on of (*p*) their composing new writings, or scriptures, and granting them too much authority. Athanasius (*q*) speaks of their respect for Montanus and Maximilla as being extravagant.

---

<margin>(*i*) They accept the Prophets and the Law. <note>original Latin: *Isti Prophetas et Legem accipiunt.*</note> *H. 49.*</margin>
<margin>(*k*) They also receive all scripture, the Old and New Testament. <note>original Greek: *Δέχονται και αυτοι πασαν γραφην, παλαιαν και νεαν διαθηκην.*</note> *H. 48. n. 2. p. 402. C.*</margin>
<margin>(*l*) For by comparing the things said by them with both the Old and the New Testament, let us truly test them. <note>original Greek: *Συγκρινοντες γαρ τα παρ αυτων ειρημενα, και κατα την παλαιαν διαθηκην και καινην εν αληθεια—δοκιμασωμεν.*</note> *Ibid. n. 3. p. 404. D.*</margin>
<margin>(*m*) They who receive the Old and New Testament; but they introduce other prophets after the [ancient] prophets, boasting of a certain Montanus, and Priscilla, and Maximilla. <note>original Greek: *Οιτινες παλαιαν και νεαν διαθηκην δεχονται· ετερους δε προφητας παρεισφερουσι μετα τους προφητας, μοντανον τινα αυχουντες και πρισκιλλαν και μαξιμιλλαν.*</note> *P. 396.*</margin>

# HISTORY OF HERETICS:

<margin>Section 10.</margin>
Nevertheless, there can be no good reason to doubt that they received all the scriptures of the Old and New Testament just as other Christians did, and with similar respect. Tertullian—several of whose remaining works were written after he became a Montanist—bears witness to this. Our collections from his work, made previously <note>original: "formerly"</note> (*r*), and some passages of his transcribed in this article, are sufficient to satisfy any inquisitive person. From the same writer, it appears that they received, in particular, the Acts of the Apostles and the book of Revelation. Passages from later authors show that the sect had not changed its mind but continued to receive the (*s*) book of Acts, St. (*t*) John’s Gospel, and (*u*) Revelation.

# HISTORY OF HERETICS:

### C H A P. XX.

->*Of P R A X E A S.*<-

#### S E C T. I. *Of the Time in which he lived.*

<margin>**Section 1.**</margin>
Samuel Basnage discusses Praxeas (*a*) under the year 194. Caesar Baronius places him under the year (*b*) 196, as does Henri Spondanus (*c*) in his summary <note>original: "abridgement"</note>. Tillemont says that he (*d*) did not appear until after the two Theodoti <note>original: "Theodots"</note>. The earliest of these was Theodotus of Byzantium, who first published his heresy during the reign of Pope Victor, or shortly before. The other Theodotus was his disciple. Therefore, Praxeas may also have appeared under Victor. He must be placed during Victor's reign or that of his successor, Zephyrinus. For he had already appeared before Tertullian became a Montanist, which happened no later than AD 207.

---

(*a*) *Political and Ecclesiastical Annals* <note>original Latin: "Annales Pol. Ecc."</note>, Year 194, page 206.
(*b*) Under the year 196.
(*c*) Under the year 196, number 7, page 169.
(*d*) *Ecclesiastical Memoirs* <note>original French: "Mem. Ec."</note>, Volume 3, Praxeas, introduction.

# HISTORY OF HERETICS:

### SECTION II. *What ancient writers say of him, and by whom he is omitted.*

<margin>Section 2.</margin>There is no mention made of Praxeas by Irenaeus or Clement of Alexandria. He is not mentioned by Cyril of Jerusalem, nor by Epiphanius or Theodore. Nor has Eusebius mentioned him. Philaster and Augustine have no distinct articles for Praxeas, but speak of him in their chapters on Sabellius <note>Sabellius was a 3rd-century teacher whose name became synonymous with the "Monarchian" view that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are simply different modes of one God.</note>. He is mentioned several times among other heretics by (*e*) Optatus of Milevi. He is likewise spoken of by (*f*) Jerome and (*g*) Pacian. Tertullian calls him a recent (*h*) heretic. He certainly did not appear until after the Montanists. Agreeable to this, the author (*i*) of the *Additions to Tertullian's Prescriptions* places him last of all, after the Montanists and after the two Theodoti. But it is Tertullian himself who will afford us the best assistance for tracing the history and opinions of Praxeas, as he wrote a treatise against him which is still in existence.

In the case of Praxeas the Patripassian <term>Patripassian: a term for those who believed that God the Father himself suffered on the cross, as they did not distinguish the Father from the Son as separate persons.</term>, who entirely denies the Son and contends that the Father suffered. <note>original Latin: "Apud Praxeam Patripassianum qui ex toto filium negat et patrem passum esse contendit."</note> *Ibid. ### SECTION III. *Concerning his Country.*

<margin>Section 3.</margin>
Philaster <note>k</note> and Augustine <note>l</note> say that Praxeas lived in Africa. It appears from Tertullian that he was there for some time, although he also says that Praxeas came from Asia to Rome. Beausobre, therefore, concludes that he was a presbyter <term>presbyter: an elder or minister in the early church.</term> of Asia. <note>m</note> However, I do not think these expressions can determine with certainty that he was from that country. The little notice taken of him by Greek writers, and the frequent mention of him by Latin authors, may lead us to think he was a Latin, rather than a Greek or an Asiatic.

The sequence of Tertullian's narrative suggests that <note>n</note> Praxeas, having been in Asia where he saw the pretended prophecies of Montanus and his women followers, informed the Bishop of Rome about them when he arrived in that city. And

### SECTION IV. *He suffered for the Cause of Christ.*

<margin>Section 4.</margin> Praxeas had suffered imprisonment, and perhaps other hardships, during the height of a persecution for the sake of the Christian religion. Following this, upon his arrival in Rome, he openly declared his opinions concerning Christ, which were not accepted by everyone. He promoted these views particularly in Africa, where he gained many converts.

### SECTION V. *He was once proven wrong and signed a Recantation, but later returned to his former principles.*

<margin>Section 5.</margin> A certain person had a dispute with him there on that subject and gained such an advantage over him that Praxeas admitted he was refuted. He signed a recantation <term>recantation: a formal statement withdrawing or disavowing a previously held belief.</term>, which was still in the possession of the Catholics <note>In this context, "Catholics" refers to the mainstream, "universal" church as opposed to the sectarian or "heretical" groups like the Montanists.</note> when Tertullian wrote against him. The debater who gained that advantage was very likely Tertullian himself, though out of modesty, he does not say so explicitly. Since that recantation was kept by the Catholics, it is reasonably concluded that Tertullian was a member of the mainstream church at that time. Indeed, he explicitly states that he was, and that it was his later decision to take

### SECTION VII. *A Vigorous Defender of the Unity of God.*

<margin>Section 7.</margin> He asserted the unity of God and (q) denied a real Trinity, as Tertullian states at the beginning of his treatise against him. Furthermore, he (r) held a view similar to the Jewish doctrine, denying the distinct personality of the Son and the Spirit. He argued (s) that by the "Word" one should understand the wisdom, the will, the power, or the voice and command of God—not a distinct personal substance, which he believed would be introducing two Gods.

Praxeas moreover said that (t) the man Jesus was the Son of God and born of the Virgin, and that (u) the Father dwelt

### S E C T. VIII. *He would not allow that the Father suffered.*

<margin>Section 8.</margin>
With regard to Praxeas and his followers, we know from Tertullian himself that he did not actually say the Father suffered. They only allowed for (*z*) "compassion" <term>Compassion: here used in its literal Latin sense of *compati*, meaning "to suffer with" another, rather than just feeling pity.</term> with the suffering Son. ## SECT. IX. *He received the Old Testament and the New, both Gospels and Epistles.*

Tertullian argues against them using every part of Scripture, assuming that they accepted (g) its authority and were required to agree with its true sense and interpretation.

Having quoted the Psalms and Isaiah, he says (h) that it is unnecessary to provide more passages, even though many others could be added. After arguing extensively from the Old Testament, (i) he proceeds to the New Testament and cites both Gospels and Epistles, specifically quoting the Gospel of St. John and St. Paul’s First Epistle to Timothy. He presents a long argument, or a series of quotations, from St. John’s (k) Gospel, spanning eight or nine chapters and nearly as many pages. And in this work by Tertullian, the (l) beginning of that Gospel is quoted—

<margin>(g) "Rest assured; when we say the Father died by the same reasoning that you say the Son died, we do not blaspheme the Lord God; for we do not say he died in his divine substance, but in his human substance." <note>original: "quies [quiesce], et nos eadem ratione Patrem mortuum dicentes qua vos Filium, non blasphemamus in Dominum Deum: non enim ex divina, sed ex humana substantia, mortuum dicimus."</note> Chapter 29.</margin>

<margin>(h) "But you will have to prove as clearly from the scriptures as we prove that he made a son for himself, etc." <note>original: "Probare autem tam aperte debebis ex scripturis quam nos probamus illum sibi filium fecisse, &c."</note> Ibid. chapter 11.</margin>

<margin>(i) "These are a few out of many. For we do not strive to examine all the scriptures." <note>original: "Hæc pauca de multis. Nec enim affectamus universas scripturas evolvere."</note> Chapter 11.</margin>

<margin>(k) "If I do not settle this question with the Old Testament scriptures, I will take confirmation of our interpretation from the New Testament. ... For behold, in both the Gospels and the Apostles, I find a visible and an invisible God. ... John exclaims, in a sense (chapter 1:18): 'No man has seen God at any time.' And the Apostle also confirms regarding God (1 Timothy 6:16): 'Whom no man has seen, nor can see.'" <note>original: "Si hunc articulum quæstionibus scripturæ veteris non expediam, de Novo Teſtamento sumam confirmationem noſtræ interpretationis. . . . Ecce enim et in Evangeliis et in Apoſtolis viſibilem et inviſibilem Deum deprehendo. . . . Exclamat quodammodo Ioannes: Deum nemo vidit unquam. Utique nec retro confirmat et Apoſtolus de Deo: Quem nemo vidit hominum, ſed nec videre poteſt."</note> Chapter 15.</margin>

<margin>(l) From chapter 21 to chapter 27. And first of all, the very preface of John the Evangelist demonstrates that formerly... <note>original: "A. cap. 21. ad. cap. 27. Et in primis, ipſa ſtatim præfatio Joannis Evangelizatoris demonſtrat, quod retro"</note></margin>

### SECTION 10. *He founded his arguments upon a great variety of passages from both the Old and the New Testament.*

<margin>SECTION 10.</margin>
Not only did Tertullian endeavor to refute the followers of Praxeas using Scripture, but they themselves argued from it. Fortunately, he has informed us of some of the texts upon which they insisted.

They were very moved, he says, (p) by any passages of the Old or New Testament that speak of there being only one God: particularly where it is said in Isaiah 45:5, *I am the Lord, and there is no one else; there is no God besides me.* And chapter 44:24, *I am the Lord who makes all things; who stretches forth the heavens ALONE; who spreads abroad the earth by myself.*

In the New Testament, (q) they relied heavily upon the answer which our Lord made to Philip in John 14:9–10.

->They<-

D. p. 504. 16.*
"Therefore there is one God the Father, and there is no other beside Him. Look at what follows passages of this kind and you will find that they generally relate to the promoters and worshippers of idols, so that the unity of the divinity may expel the multitude of false gods." <note>original Latin: "Igitur unus Deus Pater, et alius absque eo non est. A.*

### CHAPTER XXI.

### *Of JULIUS CASSIANUS.*

#### SECTION I. *On the Time in Which He Lived.*

<margin>Sect. 1.</margin> Julius Cassianus, or Cassian, is supposed by <note>original: "(a) Cave"</note> William Cave to have flourished about the year 174. According to <note>original: "(b) Tillemont"</note> Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont, he lived around the year 200. Perhaps he might be just as well placed between both these dates, at about 190. There is little notice taken of him by any ancient writer, except for Clement of Alexandria. I shall quote all the passages in which Clement mentions him, in the order in which they appear, and make a few short remarks.

#### SECTION II. *In His Writings, He Argued from the Old as well as the New Testament.*

HISTORY *of* HERETICS:

<margin>SECTION 2.</margin> Beausobre <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738) was a French Protestant theologian known for his comprehensive history of Manicheism.</note> has some interesting observations, which (i) can be found in his history of Manicheism. I should also mention that Theodoret (l), in his section on Secundus (whom he calls a successor of Valentinus), mentions several other leaders of groups that diverged slightly from the original Valentinian system. ## SECTION III.
->Of his Opinions, Country, and<-
->Philosophical Speculations.<-

<margin>SECTION 3.</margin> From all this, we perceive that Julius Cassian, who seems to have been a contemporary of Clement of Alexandria, was a Christian, a Docetic <note>original: "Docete"; one who believed Jesus' physical body was an illusion.</note>, and an Encratite <note>A member of an ascetic sect that practiced strict self-denial, especially regarding marriage and food.</note>. It appears highly probable that he accepted the scriptures of the Old and New Testaments just as other Christians generally did. While he quoted the *Gospel according to the Egyptians*, it is not certain whether he held it in the same high regard as he did the other Gospels. However, because of that reference and the specific attention given to him by Clement of Alexandria—whereas other writers, as far as we know, have omitted any mention of him—

### CHAPTER XII.

->*Of the Helcesaites, or Ossens.*<-

#### SECTION I. *The time is uncertain when they arose.*

<margin>Sect. 1.</margin>We have already spoken of this sect (a), the time of whose rise is uncertain. Epiphanius (b) <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer who compiled a famous catalog of heresies called the Panarion.</note> places Elxai—from whom they derived their name—under the Emperor Trajan <note>Roman Emperor from 98 to 117 AD.</note>. Eusebius <note>A 4th-century historian known as the "Father of Church History."</note> places the appearance of the sect much later. For having mentioned some persons in Arabia against whom Origen <note>A prominent 3rd-century Christian scholar and theologian.</note> disputed, he adds (c), "At that time also there sprang up another perverse opinion, called the heresy of the *Helcesaites*, but it became extinct almost as soon as it appeared."

<margin>Sect. 2.</margin>Origen makes mention of it in a discourse to the people regarding the eighty-second Psalm, in these words: "There has very lately come among us a person highly conceited of himself, supposing he should be able to defend an atheistical and wicked opinion, newly (d) arisen to infest our churches, called the heresy of the Elcesaites <note>A variant spelling of Helcesaites.</note>. I will lay before you the evils contained in that opinion, so that you..."

## SECTION IV. *Of the Ossenes <note>original: "Offens"</note>, who were the same as the Elcesaites, also called Sampsaeans: Their Period and Opinions.*

<margin>SECTION 4.</margin>

As the sect of the Ossenes was closely connected with the Elcesaites and regarded Elxai <note>A legendary figure among Jewish-Christian baptizers in the 2nd century</note> with veneration, it is proper to speak of them in this place. They are reckoned by Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer famous for his "Panarion," a catalog of heresies</note> to be a Jewish sect; but it will appear that they were Christians, and the same as the Sampsaeans or Elcesaites.

"The Ossenes," says Epiphanius, "agree with the aforementioned (namely, the Nazarenes). They are Jews, as well as those previously mentioned; they are said to have had their origin in the country of Nabataea <note>original: "Nabatis"</note>, Iturea, Moab, and Areil, which lie beyond the Valley of Salt <note>A region likely near the Dead Sea</note>. To these joined Elxai in the time of the Emperor Trajan, after the coming of our Savior. He was a false prophet. He (†) composed a book formatted as a prophecy, as if it were a work containing divine wisdom. They likewise say he had a brother named Jexe or Jexeus. He was an impostor of the Jewish nation and pretended to have a zeal for Jewish rites, yet did not live according to the Law himself. He taught men to swear by salt, water, the earth, bread, heaven, the air, and the wind. Sometimes he speaks of seven other witnesses; namely, heaven, water, and..."

(f) *Against Heresies <note>original: "Ad Hær."</note> 19. No. 1. p. 39, 40. A.*

As the sect of the Ossenes was closely connected with the Elcesaites and regarded Elxai with veneration, it will be proper to speak of them in this place. They are reckoned by Epiphanius <note>a 4th-century bishop and historian known for his "Panarion," a treatise against heresies</note> to be a Jewish sect; but it will appear that they were Christians, and the same as the Sampseans or Elcesaites. The (/) Ossenes, says Epiphanius, agree with the aforementioned (namely, the Nazarenes). They are Jews, as well as the previous ones; they are said to have had their origins in the country of Nabataea, and Iturea, and Moab, and Areil, which lie beyond the Valley of Salt. To these, Elxai joined himself in the time of the Emperor Trajan, after the coming of our Savior. He was a false prophet. He (t) composed a book in the style of a prophecy, as if it had been a work containing divine wisdom. They likewise say he had a brother named Jexe or Jexeus. He was an impostor of the Jewish nation and pretended to have a zeal for Jewish rites, but yet he did not live according to the Law himself. He taught men to swear by salt, water, the earth, bread, heaven, the air, and the wind. Sometimes he speaks of seven other witnesses; namely, heaven, water, and

### HELCESAITES OR OSSENES. <note>original: "Ossens"</note>

Elxai forbade men to worship toward the east and enjoined them to worship toward Jerusalem everywhere. This was truly enough of a foundation on which to base such a malicious insinuation, which in the end only amounts to this: that the object of superstitious regard toward which this holy father <note>referring to Epiphanius</note> and his heretical opponent were to turn their faces during divine worship might happen to be at opposite points of the compass.

Augustine <note>original: "Austin"</note> is only notable for the time in which he places this sect, it being the 32nd (g) in his catalogue of ninety heresies; whereas in Epiphanius, it is the 53rd, though he reckons no more than eighty in total. What Augustine says of them (h) is copied from Epiphanius's summary. He also mentions them under the entry for Ebionites (i), referring again to Epiphanius.

Theodoret (k) speaks of them in the following manner: 
The Elcesaans <note>original: "Elceſæans"</note>, who are named after a certain Elcesai who started this heresy, borrowed various fictions from several other heresies and thus formed their own unique error:

In other matters, they hold beliefs similar to the Ebionites." <note>original Latin: "Elceſæos et Samſæos hic tanquam ordine ſuo commemorat Epiphanius quos dicit a quodam pſeudopropheta eſſe deceptos qui vocabatur Elci, ex cujus genere duas mulieres tanquam Deas ab eis perhibet adoratas. <meta>This page continues the examination of the Helcesaites (or Elcesaans) based on the writings of Theodoret, exploring their Christology, their use of magic and astrology, and their rejection of traditional apostolic authority in favor of a revealed "heavenly book."</meta>

Section 4.

In their opinions concerning the beginning of all things, they agree with us, for they say there is one unbegotten Being, and they call him the master of all things. But they do not teach that there is only one Christ; instead, they believe in one above and another below. They represent him as having dwelt in many people in the past, and finally having descended to earth. Sometimes they acknowledge that Jesus is from God; at other times, they say he is a spirit. Sometimes they say he had a virgin for his mother, but in other of their writings, they do not even admit this much. They believe he migrates <note>original: "tranſmigrate"</note> into other bodies and appears differently every time.

They use songs, invocations of demons, and ritual washings in the consecration of their religious elements. They profess to follow astrology, magic, and the mathematical error <note>original: "mathematical error"—in this context, "mathematics" referred to the superstitious practice of astrology or numerology used to predict the future</note>, and they call themselves prognosticators. They have rejected the Apostle <note>Early Christian writers often referred to St. Paul simply as "the Apostle." Many Jewish-Christian sects rejected Paul because he opened Christianity to Gentiles without requiring the Jewish Law</note> altogether and have composed a certain book which they claim fell down from heaven. He who follows this book will receive a remission <note>forgiveness</note> of his sins—but a remission different from that which Christ bestowed. Against this heresy, Origen has written well. However, Alcibiades of Apamea, in Syria, has commended it.

<margin>(1) See <note>original: "Vide"</note> page 430, note (b)</margin>

So far Theodoret's account goes. Regarding this, it may be observed that Epiphanius does not mention anything about them teaching two Christs (one above and another below), unless a passage concerning Elxai previously referred to <margin>(1)</margin>—which was introduced by him under the article on the Ebionites—might be thought to convey such a meaning. He had been representing Ebion as holding the opinion that Christ was born of the seed of Joseph by natural conception <note>original: "ordinary generation"</note>, and his followers as differing in their sentiments.

The author continues by describing their sentiments concerning Christ, noting that all of them entertain some absurd and perplexed notions about Him. He proceeds: (m)

> “However, since the time that Elxai the false prophet joined himself to them—who was followed by those known as the Sampsæans, Ossens, and Elcesaites—they have adopted various imaginative notions from him concerning Christ and the Holy Spirit. For some of them claim that Christ was Adam, meaning the first man formed by God and animated by His breath. But others among them say that He is from above; that He was created before all things and is a spirit; that He is superior to angels and is the Lord of all. They believe He is called Christ and has obtained an eternal inheritance in the heavens, but that He comes here to earth whenever He pleases, just as He came in the form of Adam and appeared to the Patriarchs <note>The "Patriarchs" refers to the biblical ancestors of the Israelites, primarily Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note> while clothed in a body. They claim that the same being who came to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob was the same one who appeared in these last days; that He assumed the very same body that Adam had; and that He was seen by men, was crucified, was raised from the dead, and ascended into heaven. Yet, whenever they choose, they contradict all of this and say that the Spirit who was the Christ came into and clothed itself within the man called Jesus. Thus, there is much obscurity and confusion among them on this point, since they sometimes offer one opinion and sometimes another regarding this matter.”

<margin>Section 4.</margin>
This passage also illustrates what Theodoret mentions as part of their belief: namely, that Christ transmigrates <note>Moves from one body to another; a form of reincarnation or successive manifestation.</note> into other bodies and appears differently each time. Perhaps this was only a consequence of their opinion as Unitarians <note>In this context, "Unitarians" refers to those who believed God is a single person rather than a Trinity, often leading to the view that Jesus was a human manifestation of God's power.</note>—that God, or the divine power, appeared differently in various manifestations of Himself.

### SECTION V. *On the name of the founder of this sect, and several authors who mention him.*

<margin>SECTION 5.</margin>
Theodoret calls this person Elcesai, whereas in the *Synopsis* of Epiphanius (n), he is called Elxa, and in his larger work, Elxai or Elxaios. He admits that this heresy was composed of the opinions of several others and speaks of it in the past tense. From this, one may conclude that the heresy no longer existed but had become extinct long before—consistent with what Eusebius said. Epiphanius does not charge them with magic, although Theodoret does. However, to lessen the weight of this accusation, it should be observed that the ancient fathers—as has been frequently mentioned—were very likely to charge people with this crime if there was anything in their doctrines or rites that the fathers did not fully understand. If this charge were true, it is unlikely that Epiphanius would have omitted it, as he was not hesitant to attribute magic to the heretics he mentioned and lived much closer to their time than Theodoret did.

SECTION 6. Baronius discusses these people under the year 249 AD, in section seven.
Pagi discusses them under the year 247, section twelve.
Basnage <note>original: "Bafnage"</note> places them under the year 104, sections three through eight.

<margin>(x) Volume 2, Part 2, p. 85.

(z) "Elxai, the author of the Elcesaites, appeared under Trajan" <note>original French: "Elxai auteur des Elcesaites paroit sous Trajan"</note>. Ibid., p. 198.</margin>
Tillemont discusses them (x) under the specific article dedicated to the heresy of the Elcesaites. In his index <note>original: "table of matters"</note>, there are references to other sections concerning these people besides the main article. For instance, he says (y) that when the Ebionites joined them, they became entirely corrupt in their conduct. Furthermore, he states (z) that Elxai, the founder of the Elcesaites, emerged during the reign of the Emperor Trajan <note>Trajan reigned from 98 to 117 AD</note>.

<margin>(a) Vol. 1, Book 3, No. 2, p. 165.

In the section previously cited (a), Fleury describes Elxai as joining himself to the Ossens <note>original: "Offens"</note> during the reign of the Emperor Trajan. There, he provides a fairly detailed and full account of Elxai's unique beliefs <note>original: "tenets"</note>, based on what Epiphanius wrote in his articles on the Ebionites and Ossens. However, Fleury discusses the Elcesaites under the year 247, near the end of the Emperor Philip’s reign (b). He notes that this was more of a revival of an old error than a completely new one, as it shared a close similarity <note>original: "affinity"</note> to the teachings of Elxai from the time of Trajan.

### HELCESAITES OR OSSENS.

The timing and duration of this heresy <note>original: "hereofy," likely an OCR error for "heresy"</note> is debated quite extensively and with good reason. According to Eusebius, it faded away shortly after it emerged, and its origins were not long before Origen preached his sermons <note>original: "Homilies"</note> against the followers of this sect. For Origen's words, as previously quoted from Eusebius (c), <margin>(c) *History of the Church* [Historia Ecclesiastica], Book 6, chapter 38, p. 233.</margin> state that it had "newly emerged against the churches" <note>original Greek: νεωςι ἐπανακυψαντης ταις εκκλησιας</note> (d). <margin>(d) "having newly emerged against the churches."</margin>

Now, this could not have been long before the year 244 AD (e), <margin>(e) Ibid., chapter 36, p. 232. *Credibility of the Gospel History*, Part 2, vol. 3, p. 202.</margin> because it was not until that year that Origen permitted his sermons to be recorded in writing. But Epiphanius, on the other hand (f), <margin>(f) *Against Heresies* [Adversus Haereses] 53, No. 1, p. 461. B. Petau Edition.</margin> explicitly says that they were called Elcesaians after a man named Elxaios or Elxai (g); <margin>(g) Either spelling is acceptable, as both Elxai [Ηλξαι] and Elxaios [Ηλξαιος] appear on the same page. His followers are indeed called "Elcesaites" [Ελκεσιταις] by Eusebius and Origen; but Theodoret calls them "Elcesaians" [Ελκεσαιους], as does Epiphanius. From what Theodoret says, it is evident he considered the "Elcesaites" of Origen and Eusebius to be the same sect as the "Elcesaians" of Epiphanius, even though he called their founder Elcissai [Ελκισσαι] and not Elxa [Ηλξα] or Elxaios [Ηλξαιος]. This small difference in the reading provides no room for a supposition that the founders or the people were different, since the same person is called by Epiphanius Elxa [Ηλξα], Elxai [Ηλξαι], and Elxaios [Ηλξαιος].</margin> and he assures us that Elxai flourished (h) <margin>(h) Ibid., 19, No. 1. A. p. 40.</margin> and joined himself to the Ossens during the time of the Emperor Trajan, which must have been sometime around or before the year 117 AD, for in that year Trajan died.

The following theory may possibly reconcile this difference. Those who held such tenets were not distinguished by the name of Elcesaites or Elcesians until shortly before the time when Origen preached against them; instead, they went by the name Ossens or Ebionites. Elxai had some connection with the followers of both those sects, or at—

<margin>SECTION 6.</margin> This shows that the opinion and practice of Elxai, their founder, was directly opposite. For he introduces him instructing his disciples in this way: (q) “My children, do not draw near to the appearance of fire, because this is a deception and will cause you to go astray; for when you think it is near, it is actually far off. ### SECTION VII. On the Longevity of this Sect.

<margin>SECTION 7.</margin>
Regarding the longevity of this group, according to <term>Epiphanius</term> <note>original: "Epiphanius" (c. 310–403), a Bishop of Salamis who cataloged various Christian heresies.</note>, (t) some of the <term>Sampseans</term> <note>original: "Sampſeans"; a sect closely related to or identical with the Elcesaites, possibly named from the Hebrew word for "Sun."</note> were still in existence at the time he wrote. They lived in <term>Nabathis</term> and <term>Peraea</term> and regarded two women from the family of <term>Elxai</term>—<term>Marthus</term> and <term>Marthana</term>—as divine figures. Marthana was still alive when Epiphanius was writing, or at the very least, had died only a short time before.

This report might seem to contradict what has been quoted from <term>Eusebius</term> <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), often called the "Father of Church History."</note>; however, perhaps his words should not be taken in their most literal sense. He may have only intended to inform us that, as a result of the opposition it faced from <term>Origen</term> <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253), an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note>, this sect never spread very far. It was mainly confined to those places near <term>Palestine</term> where it first began, and its followers were few in number and mostly lived in great obscurity.

Indeed, it appears from one of the passages last mentioned that their numbers were quite small; for he says (u) that those still in existence were merely some of the remnants of the <term>Offsens</term> <note>original: "Offſens"; likely a variation of Ossens or Essenes.</note> who were now called <term>Sampseans</term>.

<margin>(t) *Against Heresies* [Adv. Hær.] 19. No. 2. D. p. 40. Ibid. 53. No. 1. p. 461.</margin>

<margin>(u) "They are some remnants and still exist... which is the race called Sampseans." <note>original Greek: Ἡ επι λειψανα και διαχυ υπῆρχη · · · οπες γινος των Σαμφαιων (Σαμφειων) καληται. Ibid. p. 40.</note></margin>

## SECTION VIII.
### *What Parts of Scripture they received.*

<margin>(x) *Page 425, note (e).*</margin>
<margin>(y) *See page 427, notes (n) and (o).*</margin>
<margin>(z) *Ibid. note (q).*</margin>
<margin>(*) At first glance, there seems to be a slight discrepancy between the accounts given by Eusebius and Epiphanius regarding the parts of the Old Testament rejected by these heretics. However, it should be noted that the expression in Eusebius is general, while in Epiphanius it is specific, a point which <term>Theodoret</term><note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457) was an influential theologian and bishop who wrote about early Christian heresies.</note> confirms. The words "uses all the books of the Old Testament" <note>original Greek: "κέχρηται ἐν τοῖς παλαιαῖς ἀπὸ πάσης παλαιαῖς"</note> can therefore be understood as consistent with their rejection of the Prophets.</margin>It appears from the passage quoted from <term>Eusebius</term><note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), a historian who provided much of our knowledge of the early Church.</note> at the beginning of this article that they accepted the Old Testament as well as the Gospels in the New Testament. However, they rejected specific passages in several parts of these, and they rejected the <term>Apostle</term><note>The term "the Apostle" in this context almost always refers specifically to St. Paul, whose letters were often rejected by Jewish-Christian sects like the Elcesaites.</note> entirely. <term>Epiphanius</term><note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a bishop known for his "Panarion," a massive work cataloging and refuting various heresies.</note> says (y) they used the same book as the <term>Ebionites</term> and <term>Nazarenes</term><note>These were early Jewish-Christian groups who maintained Jewish customs and law while following Jesus.</note>, as he had frequently mentioned before. This undoubtedly refers to a copy of the Gospels that differed somewhat from the version in common use among other Christians. He also notes that they respected another book, which they claimed was written by the brother of <term>Elxai</term>. He adds (z) that they accepted neither the writings of the (*) Prophets nor the Apostles. 

<note>For Eusebius himself explains the next word in a similar way. "Evangelical scripture" <note>original Greek: "Ευαγγελικῇ"</note> is used by him to distinguish the New Testament, just as "Old" <note>original Greek: "παλαιαις"</note> is used for the Old Testament. Although he had said that they quoted passages from every part of the New Testament—"from every part of the Gospel scripture" <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ πάσης γραφῆς εὐαγγελικῇ"</note>—he immediately adds that he "rejects the Apostle" <note>original Greek: "ἀθετεῖ τὸν ἀπόστολον"</note>. This is the same as Epiphanius's statement that "they do not receive the Apostles" <note>original Greek: "οὔτε ἀποστόλους δέχονται"</note>. For this reason, the first part of Eusebius's account can be understood as being in perfect agreement with the author's statement that "they do not receive the prophets" <note>original Greek: "οὔτε προφήτας δέχονται"</note>.</note>

## HELCESAITES OR OSSENS.

The reader will no doubt be pleased to find the whole of this in Section 9, specifically in note (d).

(d) <term>Scaliger</term><note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609) was a leading French religious scholar and philologist.</note> also attempted to explain the meaning of this very difficult passage. He said, "I can conclude that there is no *outpouring* <note>original Latin/Greek: *nullam ἕκχυσιν* (ekchysin)</note> here." But as soon as I looked at them, I saw three phrases that this great man did not recognize, which he presents as simple sentences in chapter 27 of his *Refutation* <note>original: *Elenchi*</note>. However, it is nearly reckless to deny that it is a prayer, since Epiphanius affirms it is indeed a prayer. ("A greater outpouring of slaughtered victims, except only what is then said in the boast." <note>original Greek: *μείζων ἔκχυσις των σφαγώ- νιων, αλλ̓ η μόνον εν τη αύχη τότε λεγεται.*</note>) Epiphanius could not have been mistaken here, taking for an Ossen prayer what is clearly just a simple sentence. The Ossen sect still flourished in the time of that holy Father [Epiphanius], from whom he could very easily have learned whether they used such a prayer during their worship. If it is indeed a prayer, Scaliger missed the mark entirely, as there is nothing prayer-like in the sentence: *“He who tramples on poverty, tramples on fraud, etc.”*

In our judgment, the most learned Johannes Croius has most excellently handled the arrangement of the words; we most willingly give our support to his explanation. "Affliction has passed from my fathers: tribulations crush me; tribulations from my fathers crush me. ## CHAP. XXIII.
### Of the *A L O G I A N S*.
### SECTION I. *The Account of them by Epiphanius and Philaster, as rejecting John's Gospel and the Book of Revelation.*

SECTION I. The Alogians—as we call them, says (a) Epiphanius in his summary—reject God the Word <note>original: *Logos*</note> coming from the Father, and do not accept either the Gospel according to John or his Book of Revelation.
Augustine (b) <note>original Latin: *Alogi propterea sic vocantur...* "The Alogi are so called because they are, as it were, 'without the Word' (for *logos* is the Greek word for 'word'), because they refused to receive God the Word. In his larger work, Epiphanius speaks of this heresy as arising (c) after the Cataphrygians <note>The Cataphrygians were more commonly known as Montanists, a prophetic Christian movement.</note>, Quartodecimans <note>A group that celebrated Easter on the 14th day of the Hebrew month of Nisan, regardless of the day of the week.</note>, and others. He also says (d) that he gave them the name of "Alogians" <note>This name was a pun: *a-logos* means both "against the Word" and "without reason/irrational."</note>. He says they (e) <note>original Greek: *...αποβάλλεσθαι ιωανν τας βιβλεις...* "...they reject the books of John... they do not accept the Gospel according to John, nor his Revelation. And if they had accepted the Gospel but rejected the Revelation, we might say [an apology could be made]... but since they do not accept these books proclaimed by the same John... for they say they are not John's, but Cerinthus's, and they say they are not worthy to be in the church."</note> reject the writings of John. They receive neither his Gospel nor his Revelation. John speaks in his General <note>original: "Catholic"</note> Epistles and mentions those he calls "Antichrists." They <note>The Alogians.</note> say these letters were not written by John and instead ascribe them to Cerinthus <note>Cerinthus was an early Gnostic teacher whom tradition often cast as the arch-enemy of the Apostle John.</note>, claiming they are not worthy to be received by the church. Afterwards, Epiphanius says: they argue in this manner so that (f) they may not seem to reject the Gospel and the Revelation of John—and perhaps his Epistles as well—without a reason. For these works are all of a piece and agree with one another. Once more, he says: they (g) claim that John’s Gospel should not be included in the New Testament because it is not consistent <note>original: "of a piece"</note> with the other parts.

Thus writes Epiphanius. However, one does not know exactly what he wants us to think of these men: whether they rejected all the writings commonly attributed to St. John, or only his Gospel and the Revelation. Mill, however, flatly says (h) that they rejected all of St. John’s writings. Damascen, agreeing with Epiphanius’s summary, says (i) they rejected the Gospel of John and his Revelation.

Before we proceed any further, it should be observed that Philaster also mentions a (k) heresy that rejected John’s Gospel and Revelation, ascribing both to Cerinthus. He does not give this group a specific name.

## SECT. II. *There never was any such Heresy.*

<margin>Section 2.</margin>Having cited all these passages, it is time to deliver my own opinion: which is, that this is a fictitious heresy. There were never any Christians who rejected St. John's Gospel and first Epistle while still receiving the other Gospels and the other books of the New Testament. There is no mention of them in Irenaeus, Eusebius, or any other ancient writer before Philaster and Epiphanius. Nor has Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrrhus (c. 393–458 AD) was an influential theologian and church historian.</note> thought it fit to borrow anything from Epiphanius here; he has no account of this heresy.

## SECT. III. *Some Account of Epiphanius's Article of the Alogians.*

<margin>Section 3.</margin>Epiphanius's article on the Alogians is long and contains several good remarks regarding the Evangelists and for reconciling their various accounts. At the same time, it contains some confusion. For in one place (1), he mentions Porphyry and Celsus <note>Porphyry and Celsus were famous pagan philosophers who wrote influential critiques of Christianity.</note> as if he intended to consider their objections against the history recorded in the Gospels. Nevertheless, the article seems to concern Christians who, as he says, did not receive the Logos <note>original: "Logos" (Greek: Word). A title for Jesus Christ used in the opening of John's Gospel.</note> and who rejected John's Gospel and the Revelation, refusing to allow them to be in the New Testament or considered canonical <note>Accepted as official, authoritative scripture.</note>. Heathens rejected all the books of the New Testament. And some Christians...

## SECTION V.
*A Groundless Opinion Among the Moderns Concerning the Unitarians of the Second Century.*

<margin>Section 5.</margin>
There has been a notion among learned modern scholars that the Unitarians <note>Early Christians who believed in the single personhood of God, often called Monarchians by historians</note> of the second century, who appeared soon after the Apostles, rejected St. John's Gospel. Fabricius, in a note upon the previously cited chapter of Philaster, speaks to the same (m) purpose. But how groundless that supposition is must clearly appear from our accounts of Theodotus, Praxeas, and others who held that same principle.

->Written by Dr. LARDNER, and *sold by* J. JOHNSON, No. 72,<-
->*St. Paul's Churchyard,* LONDON.<-

I. THE CASE of the DEMONIACS <note>original: "demoniacs"; referring to individuals believed to be possessed by demons</note>, mentioned in the New Testament; four discourses upon Matthew 5:19. With an appendix for further illustrating the subject. Price 2s. 6d. Being a supplement to *The Credibility of the Gospel History*.

II. ANCIENT JEWISH AND HEATHEN TESTIMONIES TO THE TRUTH of the CHRISTIAN RELIGION, in 4 volumes, quarto <note>a book size where each printed sheet is folded twice to create four leaves</note>. Price £2 2s. *sewed* <note>meaning the pages were stitched but the book was not yet given a hard leather binding</note>.

III. A LETTER written in the year 1730, concerning the question: Whether the *Logos* <note>original Greek: *Logos*, meaning "the Word" or "Divine Reason"</note> supplied the place of the human soul in the person of Jesus Christ? To which are now added two postscripts: The first, containing an explanation of those words, *the Spirit, the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of God*, as used in the Scriptures. The second, containing remarks upon the third part of the late Bishop of Clogher’s *Vindication of the Histories of the Old and New Testament*. Price 3s.

IV. A DISSERTATION upon the TWO EPISTLES ascribed to CLEMENT of ROME, lately published by Mr. Wetstein, with large extracts from them, and an argument showing them not to be genuine. Price 1s.

V. REMARKS upon the late Dr. WARD’S DISSERTATIONS on several passages of the SACRED SCRIPTURES, wherein it is shown, besides other things: That St. John computed the hours of the day after the Jewish manner; who the Greeks were in John 12; who the Grecians <note>Hellenistic or Greek-speaking Jews</note> were in Acts 6; the purpose of the Apostolic Decree in Acts 15; that there was but one sort of Jewish proselytes <note>converts to Judaism</note>; and wherein the fault of St. Peter lay, and how St. Paul may be vindicated. Price 2s. 6d.

VI. SERMONS upon VARIOUS SUBJECTS, Volume II. Our Savior’s thirst on the cross. The greatness of Jesus in his last sufferings. Divine testimonials given to Jesus during his last sufferings. The Roman soldiers and the Jewish rulers. Jesus the Son of Man. Jesus the Son of God. Christ’s poverty our riches. Christ’s farewell wish of peace to his disciples. The apostolical benediction. On praying in the name of Christ. The woman who anointed Jesus with precious ointment. The kingdom of heaven taken by force. Virtue recommended under the similitude of white raiment. The great mystery of godliness. Price 5s. *bound* <note>meaning the book includes a permanent hardcover binding</note>.

->Written by Dr. LARDNER, and sold by J. JOHNSON, No. 72,<-
->St. Paul’s Churchyard, LONDON.<-

I. **The Case of the Demoniacs**, mentioned in the New Testament; four discourses on Matthew 5:19. With an appendix for further illustrating the subject. Price 2s. 6d. This serves as a supplement to *The Credibility of the Gospel History*.

II. **Ancient Jewish and Heathen Testimonies** to the truth of the Christian religion, in 4 volumes quarto <note>original: "4to"; a book size where each sheet is folded twice to create four leaves</note>. Price £2 2s. *stitched*.

III. **A Letter** written in the year 1730, concerning the question: Did the Logos <note>original: "LOGOS"; a Greek term for "Word," referring to the divine nature of Christ</note> take the place of the human soul in the person of Jesus Christ? To which are now added two postscripts: The first containing an explanation of those phrases, *the Spirit, the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of God*, as used in the Scriptures. The second containing remarks upon the third part of the late Bishop of Clogher’s vindication of the histories of the Old and New Testament. Price 3s.

IV. **A Dissertation** on the **Two Epistles** attributed to Clement of Rome, recently published by Mr. Wetstein <note>Johann Jakob Wettstein (1693–1754), a Swiss theologian and pioneer in New Testament textual criticism</note>, with large extracts from them and an argument showing that they are not genuine. Price 1s.

V. **Remarks** on the late Dr. Ward’s **Dissertations** on several passages of the Holy Scriptures. This work shows, among other things: that Saint John calculated the hours of the day according to the Jewish custom; who the "Greeks" were in John 12 and the "Grecians" in Acts 6; the purpose of the Apostolic Decree in Acts 15; that there was only one type of Jewish proselyte <note>proselyte: a person who has converted from one opinion, religion, or party to another</note>; and discusses where Saint Peter’s fault lay and how Saint Paul may be justified. Price 2s. 6d.

VI. **Sermons on Various Subjects**, Vol. II. Topics include: Our Savior’s thirst on the cross; the greatness of Jesus in his last sufferings; divine testimonies given to Jesus during his last sufferings; the Roman soldiers and the Jewish rulers; Jesus the Son of Man; Jesus the Son of God; Christ’s poverty as our riches; Christ’s farewell wish of peace to his disciples; the apostolic benediction; on praying in the name of Christ; the woman who anointed Jesus with precious ointment; the kingdom of heaven taken by force; virtue recommended under the metaphor of white clothing; and the great mystery of godliness. Price 5s. *bound*.

->Also lately published,<-

I. **Memoirs of the Life and Writings** of the late Reverend Dr. Nathaniel Lardner. This volume includes several letters from Dr. Waddington (the late Bishop of Chichester), the late Archbishop of Canterbury, Dr. Chandler, Mr. T. Morgan, etc., along with other original papers. To which are added eight sermons on various subjects. Price 5s. *bound*.

II. **Observations on Various Passages of Scripture**. This work places many passages in an entirely new light; determines the meaning of several that cannot be understood by common scholarly methods; proposes probable theories on others that differ from those previously recommended; and illustrates the rest more fully than has been done before by using details mentioned in travel journals and voyages to the East.
->By the Reverend T. HARMER.<-
->*Second Edition in Two Volumes, Octavo <note>original: "Octavo"; a book size where each sheet is folded three times to create eight leaves</note>, with large additions, chiefly from the manuscripts of the late*<-
->*SIR JOHN CHARDIN, price 13s. bound.*<-

**N. B.** This is the work so frequently quoted with approval by Bishop Lowth <note>Robert Lowth (1710–1787), a renowned Hebrew scholar and Bishop of London</note> in his notes on Isaiah, and Dr. Priestley <note>Joseph Priestley (1733–1804), the famous scientist and dissenting theologian</note> in his *English Harmony of the Evangelists*.
